#424. Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement

Burnham says migration to the UK is "different" now compared to pre-Brexit

The prime minister says he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and European Union.

Speaking to the Sunday Times, Andy Burnham said he wants pursue a new type of relationship with Brussels, potentially including full EU membership or joining the single market, which would require free movement.

"I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this," he told the newspaper.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said there could be "no return" to free movement after the 2016 EU referendum, while Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the prime minister's comments were a betrayal of voters who supported Brexit.

Burnham has previously committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

He has said that any fundamental changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.

Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the "leave" campaign raising issues about rules allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.

But the prime minister suggested the type of migration experienced during the years of EU membership was "different" from the challenges faced now.

"It was generally younger people, not always, but spending a few years, then going back," he said in his told the Sunday Times., external

"And obviously the ease of that worked for British people as well."

He acknowledged that freedom of movement "had very significant challenges associated with it".

"Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different," he said.

"The balance of migration has changed, hasn't it, since then? I think we've just got to have an honest discussion about those things."

Burnham's willingness to re-open some of the most sensitive debates in British politics has been a feature of his first months in power.

In an interview with the BBC in September, Burnham said Britain could go "all the way" towards rejoining the European Union.

However, in his latest remarks, the prime minister stressed: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."

The Schengen Agreement allows passport-free travel across EU countries. While the UK did not previously abandon the pound while it was an EU member, the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the single currency.

The remarks were made ahead of his meeting with EU chiefs at a summit on 20 November in Brussels, where he is expected to pitch options for a reset of relations with the bloc.

The shadow home secretary said EU free movement would amount to "handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe".

Philp said: "The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it."

Burnham won the Greater Manchester seat of Makerfield at a by-election in June, ahead of him becoming prime minister the following month. The constituency voted to leave the European Union in 2016.

As a candidate in the by-election, Burnham had promised not to "re-run" Brexit arguments and said he was "not proposing that the UK considers rejoining the EU".

In response to the Sunday Times interview, Farage said: "This is a total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch".

"He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty," the Reform UK leader added.

#425. Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus

Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda

Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.

The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.

The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.

The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no ​Ebola cases and that, if ​it did, it would make that information ​public.

The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.

Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video ‌link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.

Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, ​but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.

Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same ​space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”

The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.

Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.

“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.

Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.

The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

#426. "C'est le moment !" : le mouvement étudiant, principal rival du pouvoir en place pour les législatives en Serbie dimanche

Recevez l'essentiel de l'actualité et restez à jour avec nos newsletters

Activez les notifications franceinfo et ne manquez rien de l’actualité

Vous pouvez changer d’avis à tout moment dans les réglages de votre navigateur.

Né du drame de l'effondrement d'une structure de la gare de Novi Sad, en 2024, le mouvement de contestation étudiant bouscule l'échiquier politique serbe. En déposant sa propre liste pour les élections législatives anticipées qui ont lieu dimanche, la coalition citoyenne s'impose comme la principale rivale de l'homme fort du pays, Aleksandar Vučić.

Pour sauvegarder cet article, connectez-vous ou créez un compte franceinfo

L'accident de Novi Sad, il y a deux ans, avait fait 16 morts et provoqué un mouvement de contestation sans précédent, emmené par des étudiants. Pendant des mois, le mécontentement s'est fait entendre à travers tout le pays : blocus des campus, occupation de l'espace public dans les rues des villes de Novi Sad, Nis et Belgrade. Des manifestations qui ont parfois réuni jusqu'à 100 000 personnes, dans un pays qui compte moins de sept millions d'habitants, malgré la violence policière et la censure des médias.

L'opposition a accusé les pouvoirs locaux, mais aussi les autorités nationales, de fraudes lors de la rénovation de la verrière en béton de Novi Sad. Un symbole, pour eux, de la corruption qui gangrène tout le pays. Pendant des mois, ils ont réclamé une enquête transparente, et ont fini par obtenir la tenue d'élections législatives anticipées. Aujourd'hui, leurs revendications sont portées par une liste qui se trouve en position de concurrencer le pouvoir en place.

Cette liste, baptisée Les étudiants gagnent, regroupe des étudiants bien sûr, mais aussi des professeurs d'université, des enseignants, des experts, et même d'anciens sportifs. En tout, 250 universitaires et personnalités publiques, sélectionnés lors d'assemblées plénières étudiantes. La tête de liste est Ilija Srdanovic, 54 ans, cardiologue, professeur à l'université de médecine de Novi Sad. A ses côtés, la star du basket serbe, Dejan Bodiroga, 53 ans, actuel président de l'Euroleague de basket, Dejan Soskic, ancien gouverneur de la banque centrale serbe, le philosophe Aleksandar Baucal, des acteurs... Des figures issues de l'élite intellectuelle du pays. Le parti se veut réformiste, démocratique et anti-corruption.

Son programme (le Plan étudiants), est un programme de rupture avec le pouvoir en place. Il est axé sur la lutte contre la corruption et le crime organisé, ainsi que sur l'éducation, le logement et la santé. Les étudiants ont demandé aux partis d'opposition de les soutenir et de ne pas présenter de candidats face à leur liste. En septembre, lors du dévoilement des 30 premiers noms sur la liste, une professeure de français exultait : "C'est le moment de l'unité, affirmait-elle, de l'association et de la solidarité entre les citoyens !" Selon des sondages cités par la télévision régionale N1, cette liste pourrait recueillir de 37% à 45% des intentions de vote, contre 47% à 48% pour celle du pouvoir en place. Jeudi 22 octobre, des milliers de personnes ont accueilli les étudiants venus de toute la Serbie pour leur dernière grande mobilisation avant le scrutin de dimanche.

Fin septembre, le président Aleksandr Vučić a annoncé sa démission. Une manœuvre politique stratégique, avec la ferme intention de briguer le poste-clé de Premier ministre, pour conserver la réalité du pouvoir après les législatives anticipées. Elu président pour la première fois en 2017 et réélu en mai 2022, Aleksander Vučić ne semble avoir aucune intention de lâcher le pouvoir. Son parti Serbie unie a mobilisé toutes les ressources de l'Etat et des médias à son profit. Quelques heures avant sa démission, il avait utilisé ses pouvoirs constitutionnels pour gracier des dizaines de personnes, notamment des étudiants et des fidèles de son parti, soupçonnées d'infractions commises lors des manifestations.

Le président serbe donne raison aux manifestants antigouvernementaux en évoquant la tenue de législatives anticipées en octobre

Il y a quelques semaines, Zoran Kesic, présentateur vedette d'une émission satirique populaire, supprimée depuis, avait ouvert son programme avec cet avertissement : "Ces élections détermineront si nos enfants resteront ici". Pour l'organisation Reporters sans frontières, le pays entre "dans la dernière phase de la mainmise sur les médias". Ce scrutin du 25 octobre s'annonce comme un véritable référendum sur l'avenir démocratique de la Serbie.

#427. Ukraine says Starlink connection 'now stable' after network limits

Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations

Ukraine now has a "stable connection" to Starlink, its defence minister has said, after its military suffered days of restricted connectivity on the satellite internet network.

Kyiv relies on the Starlink and its military-grade counterpart Starshield for piloting drones and operations within Ukraine, but last week accused US President Donald Trump of telling owner Elon Musk to place limits on it.

This meant drones would lose connection when travelling at 161km/h (100mph) or more, it said. Trump denied doing so before saying Musk had "put it back".

Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said that speeds of more than 400km/h were now possible on the network, indicating that full capability had been restored.

"This result is above all important for our front, for our soldiers, for the operation of drones, for logistics and for communications," he said in a statement on Saturday.

Ukraine's military uses the network of 10,000 low Earth orbit satellites extensively for military operations, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield.

Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, which Musk said was controlled by the US military when he suggested the Pentagon could be behind the recent issues.

Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.

The debacle over Starlink began last week, and emerged during a broader diplomatic row between Trump and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

Faced with midterm elections next month, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the US market - a move criticised by Ukraine and its European allies.

Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.

While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.

Zelensky said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.

Meanwhile, fighting on the ground continues.

Russia's ministry of defence wrote on Telegram on Saturday that their air defences shot down 616 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones, striking a number of regions across the country, including Russian-annexed Crimea.

Sergey Aksyonov, the region's Moscow-backed governor, said restrictions on electricity and water had been put in place because of power cuts caused by the drone strike.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian authorities said they struck a missile component manufacturer, a chemical plant and an aircraft at a military airfield inside Russia in the past 24 hours.

They also said that Russia carried out 88 air strikes using 309 glide bombs and 10,270 kamikaze drones on Friday.

#428. Marktbericht: Nasdaq kommt unter die Räder

Der KI-Boom beherrscht weiter die Wall Street. Die erste Euphorie ist aber vorbei - die Anleger wollen vielmehr endlich Ergebnisse der horrenden KI-Investitionen sehen. Meta ist ein warnendes Beispiel.

Mal nimmt die Börse, mal gibt sie - die altbekannte Börsenweisheit fand in der Nacht in New York einmal mehr Bestätigung. Waren es zuvor die verlockenden Aussichten auf die scheinbar unendlichen Möglichkeiten der Künstlichen Intelligenz (KI), die den Aktienkursen und Indizes immer neue Rekordhöhen bescherten, wird ein Themenwechsel beim Thema KI immer lauter.

Zuletzt schon gab es kaum einen Quartalsbericht, in dessen Vorfeld es keine Bedenken gegeben hätte, dass die hohen Bewertungen der KI-Tech-Riesen womöglich zu hoch seien. Anders gesprochen, die Firmen mussten liefern, sonst droht Ungemach - denn die Fallhöhe ist hoch.

"Es gibt derzeit definitiv eine gesunde Skepsis gegenüber KI", sagte Brendon Dashiell, Portfoliomanager bei Bogart Wealth. Die bereits hohen Bewertungen machten die Branchentitel anfällig. "Jeder kleine Rückschlag am Markt kann daher bei diesen Aktien zu einem starken Kursverlust führen."

Genau das ist in der Nacht der Meta-Aktie passiert, die um rund sieben Prozent nachgab, im Tagestief lag der Verlust sogar noch höher. Pläne des Internetriesen zur Aufstockung der Investitionen schürten abermals Befürchtungen, dass die Technologiegiganten in einem bereits gesättigten Markt mehr Anleihen für den Ausbau der KI-Infrastruktur auflegen werden.

Allein Meta steckt in diesem Jahr mindestens 135 Milliarden Dollar in den Ausbau seiner KI-Infrastruktur. Das Geld dafür liefert weiter das boomende Werbegeschäft. Konzernchef Zuckerberg baut Rechenzentren für Künstliche Intelligenz im Wettbewerb mit Vorreitern wie dem ChatGPT-Entwickler OpenAI aggressiv aus.

"Die Botschaft scheint immer deutlicher zu werden: Der Markt ist nach wie vor bereit, hohe Investitionen in KI zu belohnen, stellt jedoch immer höhere Anforderungen an die Renditen", sagte Santiago Mateo, Leiter des Aktienbereichs der CaixaBank AM. "Die Anleger wollen Nachweise dafür, dass sich die Investitionen in ein stärkeres Wachstum, eine bessere Monetarisierung und letztendlich in Gewinnen niederschlagen."

Während die Investitionen von Meta Marktteilnehmer zweifeln lassen, kamen die Quartalszahlen selbst gut an. Analyst Doug Anmuth von der Bank JPMorgan sprach in einer ersten Reaktion von guten Zahlen. Im vergangenen Quartal hatte Meta den Konzernumsatz im Jahresvergleich um 26 Prozent auf fast 65 Milliarden Dollar gesteigert. Unter dem Strich gab es einen Gewinn von fast zehn Milliarden Dollar nach 2,7 Milliarden vor einem Jahr.

Auch Halbleiteraktien, der Kern des KI-Booms, gaben auf breiter Front nach. Papiere des Platzhirsch Nvidia fielen um über vier Prozent, Micron um über sechs- und Broadcom ebenfalls rund vier Prozent. Die Börse fragt sich schon lange, wie lange der Boom noch weitergeht. denn noch immer übersteigt die Nachfrage das Angebot - was bedeutet, dass auch die Preise steigen. Aber kann das ewig so weitergehen und vor allem, zu welchem Preis?

Der DAX kann die schwachen Vorgaben der Nasdaq nicht ignorieren und fällt am frühen Nachmittag ebenfalls um rund 0,7 Prozent. Der Index liegt damit um die Marke von 25.200 Punkten. Damit deutet sich ein Wochenverlust von rund 1,6 Prozent an. Neben den schwachen Vorgaben der Nasdaq belasten weiter die hohen Ölpreise und die Sorgen um die französischen Staatsfinanzen das Geschehen.

Im Technologiesektor gehe es längst nicht mehr um die grundsätzlichen Wachstumsperspektiven Künstlicher Intelligenz (KI), sondern um die Frage, ob sich die Investitionen jemals in entsprechend hohe Gewinne verwandeln ließen, erläuterte CMC-Markets-Experte Andreas Lipkow.

#430. Ärzte suchen nach Ursache: Kollabierter Kompany fehlt dem FC Bayern wochenlang

Vincent Kompany befindet sich nach seinem Zusammenbruch in einem stabilen Zustand und wird noch "einige Tage" im Krankenhaus bleiben. Das berichtete Bayern Münchens Sportvorstand Max Eberl am Tag nach dem medizinischen Notfall. "Wir haben gestern Abend auch gesprochen. Auch mit seiner Frau. Das war für uns alle natürlich kein schöner Moment", sagte Eberl vor dem Auswärtsspiel beim SC Freiburg an diesem Sonntag (17.30 Uhr bei DAZN und im Liveticker bei ntv.de).

"Das zeigt mal wieder, dass der Fußball nicht das Wichtigste im Leben ist. Das Wichtigste ist die Gesundheit", sagte Eberl weiter. Über die Ursache des Zusammenbruchs wolle er nicht spekulieren. "Ich bin jetzt hier kein Mediziner und werde keine Zusammenhänge herstellen. Natürlich machen die Ärzte seit gestern Abend nichts anderes, um herauszufinden, was es ist. Die Untersuchungen haben auch ein Stück weit Ergebnisse gebracht. Aber das bedarf noch weiterer Untersuchungen."

Oberste Priorität habe, dass der 40 Jahre alte Belgier "gesund wird, dass er sich in Ruhe erholen kann. Und auch dann erst wieder zurückkommen soll, wenn er sich fit fühlt. Und das wird die größte Aufgabe von uns werden, ihn zu schützen, auch ein Stück weit vor sich selber."

Bis auf Weiteres übernimmt das Trainerteam um Assistent Aaron Danks die Aufgaben des Chefcoaches. "Wir fangen nicht an, irgendwelche Zeitkorridore aufzubauen", sagte Eberl. Aber man rede "nicht von Tagen, sondern von Wochen. Im Moment muss er sicherlich auf seinen Körper hören und sich die Zeit nehmen, die er braucht." Der Engländer sprang schon einmal für Kompany ein, als dieser im Champions-League-Halbfinalspiel in der vergangenen Saison gegen Paris Saint-Germain wegen einer Sperre von der Tribüne aus zuschauen musste.

Kompany war am Freitag auf dem Trainingsgelände des FC Bayern zusammengebrochen, als er eine Einheit der Amateurmannschaft verfolgt hatte. Der Belgier wurde daraufhin mit einem Notarztwagen in eine Klinik gebracht. Das für heute geplante Regionalliga-Spiel der Bayern-Amateure wurde kurzfristig abgesagt.

Zuletzt hatte der Bayern-Coach mit einer Virusinfektion und Hüftproblemen zu kämpfen. Den 6:1-Sieg gegen RB Leipzig verfolgte er überwiegend im Sitzen, anschließend verpasste er mehrere Trainingseinheiten und eine Pressekonferenz. Beim Champions-League-Spiel gegen den FC Arsenal am Mittwoch stand er wieder an der Seitenlinie.

#431. UEFA gegen Infantino: Lager belauern sich bei FIFA-Council - Europa sucht nach Gegenkandidat

FIFA-Präsident Gianni Infantino bittet beim ersten Aufeinandertreffen mit seinen Kritikern aus Europa um Entschuldigung - doch befriedigende Antworten blieben aus. Die UEFA bleibt auf Konfrontationskurs.

"Das ist das Ziel, dass wir an der Spitze der FIFA eine andere Person sehen möchten", sagte Bernd Neuendorf, der Präsident des Deutschen Fußballbundes (DFB), nach dem Treffen des FIFA-Councils in Zürich. Er blieb damit bei seinem Standpunkt im Bezug auf den umstrittenen FIFA-Präsidenten Gianni Infantino.

Der gesamte europäische Fußballverband UEFA ist sich einig, dass Infantino seinen Posten aufgeben sollte. Bei einem Treffen der UEFA vor einer Woche in Berlin, hatten sich alle Mitgliedsverbände mit Ausnahme von Aserbaidschan für eine Ablösung Infantinos ausgesprochen.

Allerdings bräuchte es dazu einen geeigneten Gegenkandidaten, der bei der Wahl des nächsten FIFA-Präsidenten im März 2027 in Marokkos Hauptstadt Rabat, gegen den Schweizer antritt.

Infantino möchte sich wiederwählen lassen und hat bereits Unterstützung vieler Verbände signalisiert bekommen. Afrikas Fußballverbände stehen geschlossen hinter ihm, die Verbände Südamerikas und weite Teile Ozeaniens ebenfalls. Asiens Verbandsvertreter sind dagegen gespalten.

Die Nominierungsfrist endet am 18. November. UEFA-Präsident Aleksander Ceferin hatte eine Kandidatur ausgeschlossen, auch Nasser Al-Khelaifi steht nicht zur Verfügung. Der Katarer ist Präsident von Champions-League-Sieger Paris Saint-Germain und Vorsitzender der europäischen Klubvereinigung (EFC).

Laut Medienberichten soll auch der Kanadier Victor Montagliani, Chef des Verbandes für Nord- und Mittelamerika und die Karibik (CONCACAF), kein Interesse an einer Kandidatur haben.

In britischen Medien wieder der Name Arsène Wenger genannt. Der ehemalige Erfolgstrainer des FC Arsenal arbeitet seit 2019 als FIFA-Direktor eng mit Infantino zusammen. Dennoch soll er Wunschkandidat mehrerer Fußballbosse aus Europa sein.

Auch Michele Kang, milliardenschwere Investorin im Frauenfußball, wird gehandelt. Bestätigt oder dementiert ist beides nicht. Die UEFA will vor dem 17. November erneut zusammenkommen, auch um in der Kandidatenfrage weiter zu beraten.

"Wir brauchen eine integre Persönlichkeit, von der wir annehmen dürfen, dass sie dem Verband eine Reputation zurückgibt, die er definitiv verloren hat", sagte Neuendorf nach der Sitzung des FIFA-Councils, bei der die europäischen Kritiker erstmals seit dem Ausbruch des Machtkampfes auf Infantino getroffen waren. "Wenn sich so eine Person findet, dann wird die Debatte, denke ich, auch nochmal einen ganz anderen Drive kriegen. Wir gehen auch davon aus, dass das passiert."

FIFA-Chef Gianni Infantino bat indes auf der Council-Sitzung des Fußball-Weltverbandes um Entschuldigung, ließ aber wichtige Fragen offen. "Wir haben sehr viele kritische Fragen gestellt, befriedigende Antworten hat es aus meiner Sicht nicht gegeben", sagte Neuendorf nach dem rund dreistündigen Treffen.

Das Vertrauen in Infantino sei nach den Ereignissen rund um die WM im Sommer "vollständig verloren gegangen", führte der DFB-Präsident aus. Die Council-Mitglieder der Europäischen Fußball-Union (UEFA) hatten mehrere Punkte auf die Agenda gehoben: darunter Infantinos Vorhaben, Anteile an FIFA-Turnieren an Personen aus dem Umfeld von US-Präsident Donald Trump zu verkaufen, die Verleihung des FIFA-Friedenspreises an Trump oder der "Fall Balogun" bei der WM, bei dem der US-Angreifer nach einer telefonischen Intervention Trumps bei Infantino trotz Roter Karte im nächsten Spiel wieder auflaufen durfte.

Die englische Verbandschefin Debbie Hewitt teilte mit: Infantino habe "durchaus reumütig" geklungen, an ihrer Haltung habe sich aber nichts geändert. "Ich habe keine neuen Informationen erhalten, die mich meine Haltung anders beurteilen lassen als vor der Sitzung", sagte die 63-Jährige.

Beschlossen wurde die Einrichtung einer Arbeitsgruppe, die sich mit möglichen Reformen im Weltverband beschäftigen soll. Sie werde "den Governance-Rahmen der FIFA eingehend prüfen", teilte der Weltverband mit, es gebe dafür aber noch keinen Zeitplan.

Außerdem bestätigte die FIFA, dass ein sogenannter Entwicklungsfonds für die 211 Mitgliedsverbände in Höhe von 6,35 Milliarden US-Dollar aus ihren Rücklagen eingerichtet und bei der Sitzung im Dezember finalisiert werden soll.

Im nächsten Vierjahreszyklus würde damit jeder Mitgliedsverband rund 25 Millionen US-Dollar (etwa 22 Millionen Euro) erhalten, bisher waren es zehn Millionen US-Dollar. Eine großzügigere Verteilung der Einnahmen des Weltverband hatte zuvor unter anderem die UEFA gefordert.

#432. Lewis Hamilton aims to extend career till early 2030s so he can race in African Grand Prix

41-year-old set on ‘dream to be able to race in Africa’

Rwanda to host despite criticism of human rights record

Lewis Hamilton has said he hopes to remain racing in Formula One until he can take part in the African Grand Prix which is set to take place in Rwanda in the 2030s. The seven-time world champion believes it is right that F1 is to hold a race there despite criticism of the country’s human rights record.

Last week F1 confirmed Rwanda was to host the African Grand Prix having concluded a 10-year agreement for the meeting on a purpose-built circuit, with the first race set for the early 2030s. It is lined up to be held on a circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital, Kigali, which has yet to be constructed and marks a return to the African continent for the first time since it last held a race at Kyalami, South Africa in 1993.

Hamilton has been championing a race in Africa for some time. The 41-year-old is understood to be currently contracted with Ferrari until the end of the 2027 season, and speaking before this weekend’s US Grand Prix he said he would like to continue racing for at least another four years in order to make it to the meeting in Rwanda.

“I’m now forced to have to stay a lot longer because we have a race in Africa and that’s been my dream to be able to race in Africa,” he said. “So, I have to keep fighting to try and stay fit if I can. If I can still punch out good results over the next year, we’ll keep it going.”

Hamilton would be at least in his mid-40s if he was to continue until 2030. F1’s current oldest driver is 45-year-old Fernando Alonso.

F1’s deal with Rwanda is for a 10-year period but because of the country’s human rights record the award of the race has been criticised as an act of sportswashing.

Britain’s 18-year-old Freddie Slater will make his Formula 1 free practice debut for ⁠Audi at next week’s Mexico City Grand Prix.

Audi entered Formula 1 this year ⁠after taking over ⁠the ​Sauber team, and Slater was the first driver signed to the team’s new driver academy.

Slater ⁠finished second in the Formula 3 standings to Ugo Ugochukwu in his debut season while ⁠racing for Trident Motorsport. He is slated to move ​to Formula 2 with Invicta ‌next year.

"Getting behind the wheel of an F1 car at a grand prix weekend is a big moment for me and something I’ve been dreaming of since I was a kid," Slater said. “I’ve learned a ‌lot this year, and these Free practice outings with Audi F1 Team will be another opportunity ​to keep gaining on-track experience."

Slater is also slated to drive in the first practice session at next month’s Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

"We have seen Freddie making great progress ⁠throughout recent years, both on and off the track; ​it is ​the right time for ​Freddie to step up," Audi racing director and ​academy director ‌Allan McNish, a former F1 driver himself, said.

"These ​appearances ​in Mexico and Brazil will give him valuable experience of a Formula 1 race weekend, and another chance to continue his development." Reuters

“A 10-year grand prix ‘presented by Visit Rwanda’ is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities,” said Felix Jakens, Amnesty UK’s head of campaigns. “Rwanda is buying into the world’s biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from ⁠its appalling human rights record. Formula One says sport can be ‘a positive force for good’. That rings hollow if F1 shrugs off who it is partnering with. Rwanda’s authorities are prolific in arbitrary detention, torture and the repression of free speech.”

Hamilton nonetheless felt the meeting would serve as a force for good in Africa and that there also should be more education about the continent.

“I’m really, really hopeful for that grand prix,” he said. “Of course, I don’t get to choose where we go, and naturally there’s problems all over the world today, so I’ve seen many of the stories but I think we really have to approach it with humility.

“There’s a lot that we don’t know. I mean, growing up in England, they never ever taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum. A lot of the problems they have there are still results of colonialism, and the West intervening.

The best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s action

“I really hope, and I still have hopes, that Africa unites. I know there’s many people that don’t want that to happen, because they would be so powerful if they did, but I’m still hopeful that at some stage they will.”

The new race is being backed by the government of Rwanda and the Rwanda Development Board, who intend to develop the venue as a destination not only for motorsport but for promoting economic growth. The country has recently invested heavily in hosting sporting events, including cycling’s road world championships, cricket’s Women’s Challenge Trophy, the 2023 Fifa congress and the Basketball Africa League.

Hamilton felt that at least the race would present an opportunity for people to take a greater interest in Africa.

“Going doesn’t mean that you neglect the things that are happening there,” he said. “Hopefully many people start to educate themselves a little bit more of what is happening there, what has happened there for hundreds of years and I hope that does spark the conversation. Then I guess I’ll finish it off with, I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping that at some stage we get to.”

Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli goes into this weekend’s US Grand Prix in a position to clinch his first F1 title. The 20-year-old holds a 102-point lead over his teammate George Russell and will become Formula One’s youngest world champion if he wins, Russell finishes ninth or lower and Hamilton is fifth or lower.

#433. Ukraine depends on Starlink - can Europe plug the gap?

A man offers residents in Kherson, Ukraine, the use of his Starlink internet after a Russian strike

Ukraine is in desperate need of a new satellite internet service, but a fast and reliable alternative to Elon Musk's Starlink network simply doesn't exist - yet.

Last week's sudden slowdown of the service in Ukraine, which affected Kyiv's ability to defend itself from Russian attacks, has shown how vulnerable the country can be, and sharply increased Europe's urgency to have its own military-grade satellite network.

There are a few alternatives, but they are all lagging behind Starlink, which is the world's largest satellite constellation.

France's Eutelsat, with its OneWeb internet service, is the main alternative - but it only has about 600 active satellites, compared to Starlink's 10,000-plus.

The EU is working on a new network to rival Starlink, IrisÂ², however it won't be up and running until 2029.

For Ukraine's troops on the ground, several of whom spoke anonymously to the BBC, reliable connectivity is the difference between life and death.

"God forbid they shut it off completely, it would be an absolute catastrophe," said one. "I don't give a damn how much an alternative costs when our lives are on the line."

For now, Ukraine's best bet is to join Govsatcom, the EU's satellite sharing network - but it cannot be used for military warfare like controlling drones.

Watch: Who controls Ukraine's access to Starlink?

Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?

Who actually controls Ukraine's access to Starlink?

Starlink and its military-grade service, Starshield, are both owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX company and have dominated the global satellite market for years.

Ukraine relies on Starlink for communications on the battlefield and Starshield for military purposes like drone warfare. The network is able to provide fast, real-time connectivity, which is crucial for defence and intercepting Russian attacks.

"You can't employ drone warfare without this kind of high-speed internet connection," said Vincent Tourret, a researcher at the French Institute of International Relations.

Last week's slowdown, which has only just been restored, highlighted the risks of relying on a US provider at a time when tensions between Kyiv and Washington continue to deteriorate.

"Ukraine's defence cannot depend on Trump's or Musk's whims," French MEP, Christophe Grudler, tweeted.

Who authorised the Starlink restrictions is still not clear, with a confusing blame-game ongoing between the Pentagon, Donald Trump and Elon Musk.

While Starlink has been one of Ukraine's greatest assets in this conflict, the "flipside of that dependence" has been exposed, explained Kari Bingen, director of the Aerospace Security Project at CSIS.

"This is a critical military capability that Ukraine relies on, but doesn't control."

Ukrainian soldiers set up a Starlink terminal on the battlefield

Starlink is not the only satellite network Ukraine can access, so if it goes down there are other options - but experts say they aren't as fast, and troops the BBC spoke to, agree.

Starlink "gives us the upper hand when it comes to passing commands - even one or two seconds are critical when we can transfer data and orders faster, and you can really feel that advantage on the battlefield," a soldier said.

The terminals used to connect to the satellites are also an important factor. Starlink's are relatively small and lightweight, so they can be fixed to any kind of vehicle or drone.

Eutelsat's terminals "are slightly larger, so they can be fitted on the roof of a car, or on tanks, but they can't necessarily sit on small drones," said Eva Berneke, former CEO of the French satellite company.

They are also about five times more expensive, she added.

Rhetoric from the White House - like Donald Trump's scathing criticism of Nato and his threats against Greenland - have given the EU "some pretty brutal alarm bells", Berneke told the BBC.

She had only been at Eutelsat for a month when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and said she noticed a marked change in urgency from European authorities, as they looked to her company to help plug holes left by Starlink if it could not be relied upon.

Comments from Elon Musk have further heightened the need for an alternative: "Be quiet, small man... there is no substitute for Starlink," he tweeted, external at Poland's foreign minister last year, when the politician said he would "look for other suppliers" if SpaceX was unreliable.

Europe has realised its security depends on space, and it must "strengthen its satellite capacities, urgently," a spokesperson for the European Commission told the BBC.

Right now, it has Govsatcom, a network that was set up in January to share existing satellites between EU member states. Ukraine is not a full-fledged member (although it is trying to become one), but the Commission is in talks with Kyiv to join Govsatcom.

But even if Ukraine could connect tomorrow, the network could not be used for warfare operations like piloting drones, which Starshield is used for.

That could change by the start of next year, however, when the European Commission hopes commercial companies, like Eutelsat's OneWeb, will join the programme. This will give Ukraine some - but not all - of its military network needs.

French President Emmanuel Macron, with a Eutelsat terminal, at the International Paris Air Show last year

Eva Berneke told the BBC she is confident the company will be able to "support quite a lot of Ukraine's key military needs". But meeting its communications needs is another thing, because as is the case with most countries, they are varied and massive.

Eutelsat could not comment on Govsatcom, but told the BBC that "as the only European operator of a fully operational [Low Earth Orbit] constellation, we are committed to providing resilient connectivity to the businesses, governments and communities we serve".

No timeline has been given for when Ukraine will be able to join the Govsatcom network. When it does it will likely be as a reliable back-up to Starlink and Starshield.

But that's better than nothing, Vincent Tourret said. "If Starlink is shut down, it's good to have another way to stay connected, but it won't be enough for strikes or interceptions, at this stage."

Govsatcom is seen as a short-term safety net, until the stronger and more secure network, IrisÂ², external is up and running in 2029.

The ambitious project (pronounced Iris squared) is Europe's answer to Starlink and Starshield. It will be a defence-first programme, the European Commission says, with a focus on governments, military and emergency services. Ukraine has been guaranteed access to it from day one.

Part of the EU's space programme, the European satellite companies Eutelsat, SES and Hispasat are leading the project in a consortium called SpaceRISE.

It will still have far fewer satellites than Starlink, with 348 across low and medium earth orbit - but that shouldn't be seen as a negative, said Kari Bingen.

"Think about a flash light beaming down - those satellites will be able to cover a greater amount of the Earth, so you need fewer of them," she explained. "They're all trade offs - I would not take it as a negative, that IrisÂ² is planning for less satellites."

Tourret was more sceptical: "It's no gamechanger and no great saviour, I'm afraid".

A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, carrying 56 Starlink satellites, takes off from Cape Canaveral in March

A highly-produced video on the EU Space Policy's website declares: "With IrisÂ², Europe will no longer depend on others for satellite connectivity."

So does that mean Ukraine could switch off Starlink? No - that wouldn't be a good idea.

"Users need to think about communications resilience," Bingen said. "So if something happens to one system, you have other ways to maintain connectivity."

It's similar to how mobile phones work, explained Eva Berneke: "If you don't have 5G, you go back to 4G. And if you don't have 4G, you might use 3G, so you have multiple networks for resilience. It's the same idea in warfare."

But while a phone might not load pictures as quickly on 3G, for a drone operator, it can be deadly: "That is not a nice situation to have to be in when you're fighting a war."

IrisÂ² is not the only option. This week, Finnish companies Nokia and ICEYE, external announced they would look at developing satellite communications for Ukraine's military defences.

And a joint venture between European satellite makers Airbus, Leonardo and Thales, called Project Bromo, is hoped to be another competitor against SpaceX, but it is still in the very early phases.

Space projects take a long time, Berneke said, and need "a lot of money".

Designing the programme, making the satellites, launching them and then having enough of them in orbit for full coverage takes many years.

"Even if you gave me â¬8bn right now, I don't think I could have anything up there before 2032-2033," she explained.

Military work in Space is nothing new, and has been happening since the dawn of the space age in the 1950s. But the conflict in Ukraine has shown how integral it is to modern warfare.

"Communication is so important, and terrestrial communication platforms, whether it's 5G or fibre, can be attacked on the ground," Berneke said. "It is a lot harder to shoot down an entire satellite network. That's not something any military can do right now."

While we look to the skies, however, most of the world's communications are travelling via undersea cables - about 99% in fact. But these are vulnerable to attack - this week the UK government outlined new measures to protect its cables, after an increase in suspicious activity by Russian vessels.

"In a crisis or conflict, there are serious concerns that undersea cables will be cut... so if that happens it's good to have satellite communication as a backup," Kari Bingen said.

#434. Incendie de la mairie de Limoges : le parquet annonce la mise en examen et le placement en détention provisoire des deux suspects interpellés

Article rédigé par Clément Périé

l'essentiel Le parquet a annoncé ce 24 octobre la mise en examen et le placement en détention provisoire des suspects à l'origine de l'incendie de la mairie de Limoges. Les deux mis en cause sont âgés respectivement de 34 et 66 ans. Pour rappel, l'hôtel de ville de la préfecture de la Haute-Vienne a été ravagé par les flammes le 17 octobre dernier en marge d'une manifestation réunissant environ 5 000 personnes.

Les deux suspects à l'origine de l'incendie de la mairie de Limoges (Haute-Vienne) ont été mis en examen et placés en détention provisoire, a annoncé ce samedi 24 octobre le parquet auprès de l'AFP. Le parquet avait ouvert la veille une information judiciaire à l'issue de leur garde à vue, rappelle BFMTV.

Plusieurs chefs étaient retenus contre les deux hommes, notamment "tentative d'homicide sur personne dépositaire de l'autorité publique", "destruction en bande organisée du bien d'autrui par moyen dangereux pour les personnes", "association de malfaiteurs en vue de la préparation d'un crime", "menaces de mort à l'encontre d'une personne dépositaire de l'autorité publique" et "destruction d'un bien par moyen dangereux commis en raison de la qualité de dépositaire de l'utilité publique de son propriétaire".

À lire aussi : Violences du 17 octobre : la mairie de Limoges détruite par les flammes, comment des membres de l'"ultragauche" ont incendié ce bâtiment classé au patrimoine ?

Pour rappel, le 17 octobre dernier, en marge de la manifestation réunissant environ 5 000 personnes, des débordements particulièrement graves ont conduit à l'incendie de l'hôtel de ville de la préfecture de la Haute-Vienne. Les suspects se seraient notamment introduits dans l'édifice en brisant des vitres avant de déclencher un incendie, qui se serait propagé aux combles puis à l'ensemble du bâtiment.

Âgés respectivement de 34 ans et 66 ans, les deux suspects ont été interpellés mardi et jeudi, quelques jours après l'incendie ayant ravagé l'hôtel de ville de la commune. Le plus jeune, Hodei C.D., est notamment connu de la justice en raison d'une fiche S, le décrivant comme "un activiste d'ultragauche susceptible de commettre des actions violentes". L'homme originaire de la Creuse avait par le passé déjà participé aux actions du collectif écologiste et radical des "Soulèvements de la Terre". L'identité du deuxième suspect n'est pas connue à l'heure actuelle.

À lire aussi : Mairie de Limoges incendiée : "Activiste violent", fiché S pour son appartenance à l'ultragauche... Qui est Hodei C.D., 34 ans, le principal suspect interpellé ce mardi matin ?

En parallèle de l'enquête, le Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu s'est rendu sur place ce vendredi 23 octobre pour rencontrer le maire de Limoges, Guillaume Guérin (LR). Le chef du gouvernement a assuré que "l'État sera là" pour reconstruire l'hôtel de ville, datant de 1883.

#435. Why US investors are snapping up Germany's famed Mittelstand

Increasing amounts of US capital are flowing into Germany's traditional industrial firms and family-owned businesses. As many business owners struggle to find successors, more companies are becoming acquisition targets.

What do the long-established German companies Birkenstock, Viessmann, Linde and ebm-papst have in common? All have fallen into American hands.

Traditional German family-owned businesses and small-to-medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) have become increasingly attractive to US companies and investors.

Last year, US investors were involved in 76 acquisitions and investments in German industrial and manufacturing companies, according to an analysis by financial data provider PitchBook. The transactions were valued at about $29.5 billion (€26.3 billion) in 2025, nearly double the 2022 total. As of August 19, 2026, the figure stood at $23.9 billion.

"From what we are seeing in the market, the interest from US investors in German companies is definitely still there," said Samar-Ahmad Albrecht-Mahmood of Veracity Capital Investments, which advises companies looking to invest in Germany.

German companies, particularly those in the industrial and manufacturing sector, remain attractive, "because many of them are highly specialized, have strong customer relationships and very good technical know-how," he told DW. "In many cases, these are businesses that have built up a strong position in their niche over decades."

At the same time, many German business owners are reaching an age where they are thinking about selling their business, Albrecht-Mahmood underscored, pointing out that "there is often no successor within the family."

"This brings companies onto the market that might not have been available for sale a few years ago," he said.

Notable takeovers this year include ebm-papst, the Mulfingen-based manufacturer of electric motors and fans, which was bought by US company Madison Air for $5.4 billion in August.

In June, the long-established Augsburg-based company Everllence, formerly MAN Energy Solutions, was sold to Bain Capital, with the US investment firm acquiring a 51% stake in the company.

According to Die Deutsche Wirtschaft (DDW), a German business information network focused on the Mittelstand (medium-sized and family-owned companies), no country owns more German firms than the United States. Of the total 7,861 companies identified in the database "German Companies Under Foreign Ownership," 1,750 are currently held by US investors.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), one of the world's leading auditing and consultancy organizations, also underscored the growing US investor interest in acquiring German companies. In a report, titled Destination Germany, PwC said that while the number of acquisitions and equity investments has not increased, the financial volume of the deals has jumped.

The report highlighted, in particular, the acquisition of BASF Coatings by the US investment firm Carlyle, in partnership with the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), for around €7.7 billion.

The deal was struck on October 26, 2025, and closed on June 30 of this year.

According to a recent survey by the American Chamber of Commerce in Germany, about 62% of the US companies active in the country are expecting business conditions to improve over the next three to four years.

Meanwhile, some 52% of them are planning to expand their operations in Germany, up from 49% in 2024.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At first glance, however, the increase in US acquisitions and equity investments does not seem to align with the decline in US investment flows to Germany last year.

According to the Bundesbank, significantly less investment capital flowed from the US to Germany in 2025 than in the previous year.

While foreign direct investment in Germany has risen overall — from €57.4 billion in 2024 to a total of €86.1 billion last year — investment from the US amounted to only €11.8 billion, nearly 44% less than in 2024.

In contrast, investment from the United Kingdom rose to around €26 billion.

"I would say the trend is continuing, although perhaps not simply in terms of higher deal numbers every year," Albrecht-Mahmood said. "The general interest in good German industrial companies, especially strong Mittelstand businesses, remains high."

Relatively low valuations also play a role, the expert argued. "Compared to the US, we still see situations where German companies are valued more moderately, particularly in the SME segment. This can make acquisitions quite attractive for international buyers."

This article was originally written in German.

L'Ukraine dispose à nouveau d'une "connexion stable" au système Starlink de SpaceX. Alors que Kiev se plaignait depuis plusieurs jours d'une limitation de la vitesse de ces terminaux de communication, cruciaux pour l'armée, le ministre de la Défense a annoncé, samedi 24 octobre, disposer à nouveau d'"une vitesse supérieure à 400 km/h". "[Nos] systèmes de surveillance enregistrent une reprise de la vitesse de Starlink/Starshield", a déclaré Ievguén Khmara dans un communiqué.

La limitation de la vitesse de la connexion au réseau développé par Elon Musk, constatée sur fond de tensions entre Kiev et Washington, entravait notamment les capacités de l'armée ukrainienne à utiliser certains drones employés contre la Russie. Son rétablissement "est avant tout important pour notre front, pour nos militaires, pour le fonctionnement des drones, pour la logistique et pour les communications", a continué le ministre. Il s'est enfin félicité de "la position ferme du président ukrainien au plus haut niveau", estimant qu'elle "porte ses fruits".

Le président ukrainien, Volodymyr Zelensky, avait accusé Washington d'être à l'origine de ces limitations, et de ne pas avoir averti Kiev à plusieurs reprises de l'arrivée de missiles russes avant qu'ils ne frappent. La Maison-Blanche et Elon Musk avaient démenti chacun être à l'origine du bridage de ce système satellitaire. Vendredi, Donald Trump avait annoncé que le milliardaire avait "relancé" le réseau pour l'Ukraine.

#437. Palestinian families displaced as Israeli forces demolish Hebron homes

More than 200 families have been displaced, Palestinian officials say

The Israeli military has launched a sweeping crackdown in the occupied West Bank, demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron and displacing hundreds of families, according to local officials.

Footage shared online showed destruction caused by Israeli bulldozers, with at least one whole street appearing to have been flattened. The military has also cordoned off the city, heavily restricting the movement of its 200,000 residents.

The operation was announced by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday, in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen in an attack on a checkpoint. Three other Israeli soldiers were injured, and the gunmen were also killed.

Netanyahu said on Friday that buildings around the site of the attack and the neighbourhoods that the two gunmen were from would be "destroyed".

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said about 2,000 residents had been displaced by the operation, which centred on the Ein Deir Baha and Farsh al-Hawa neighbourhoods, and targeted homes, businesses, industrial sites and infrastructure.

He said dozens of families had been forced to spend the night outside, with some told to leave without taking their vehicles, while homes were marked for demolition with spray paint.

He added that he believed the military planned to displace a total of 2,500 people from about 0.35 sq km of urban land. The city's governor and deputy mayor meanwhile said at least 200 families had been displaced.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) did not respond immediately to the BBC's request for comment. It said in a statement on social media that it had dozens of targets across the West Bank and that its operations would last for several days.

Wreckage was seen around the site of Friday's shooting following demolitions by Israeli forces

Bulldozers began demolitions on Friday afternoon

Photos of one of the suspected gunmen in Friday's attack were shared by AFP news agency

It is common practice for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis in the West Bank - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment.

Netanyahu likened the operation to previous operations in Palestinian refugee camps in the north of the territory, when the Israeli military demolished hundreds of homes and displaced tens of thousands in 2025.

Friday's shooting came during a tense time for the region, with Israel's general election taking place in four days' time.

Netanyahu - who has built his campaign on the promise of security - cancelled his party's campaign events for Friday morning and headed to Hebron, wearing protective armour and posting a video on social media from the scene.

"We will evacuate the residents, go house to house, remove the weapons we find there, and deal with and destroy all terrorist infrastructure," he said.

He also announced he had reviewed plans for the largest military operation in the West Bank since 1967 - though did not say when it could be carried out. It is not clear whether the ongoing Hebron operation forms part of that.

In an interview with Israel's i24 television channel released on Saturday, he threatened "a very big surprise" for the Palestinian Authority (PA), which governs parts of the territory.

In a statement, the PA called for "urgent international action that went beyond condemnation" to prevent further forced displacement.

Meanwhile, his far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for Israel to launch a campaign in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza or Lebanon," while far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir called for Israel to dismantle the PA.

Speaking to journalists, Hebron Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari said the operation was "driven by the elections," and that Netanyahu and his ministers were attempting to secure the votes of the far-right and the settlers.

#439. Erneut mutmaßlicher Drohnenangriff auf Schiff vor Rumäniens Küste

Ein weiteres Handelsschiff soll nahe der rumänischen Küste Medienberichten zufolge von einer Drohne angegriffen worden sein. Es gebe mindestens ein Todesopfer. Rumäniens Präsident sieht die Verantwortung erneut bei Russland.

Im Schwarzen Meer ist wenige Kilometer von der rumänischen Küste entfernt erneut ein Handelsschiff Ziel eines mutmaßlichen Drohnenangriffs geworden. Das berichteten mehrere rumänische Medien übereinstimmend unter Berufung auf die für Rettungsaktionen zuständige Schifffahrtsbehörde in der Hafenstadt Constanta.

Der mutmaßliche Angriff ereignete sich laut den Berichten rund 13 Seemeilen von der Hafenstadt entfernt und damit knapp außerhalb von Rumäniens Hoheitsgewässern. Ein Mitglied der Besatzung sei ums Leben gekommen, weitere neun Besatzungsmitglieder hätten gerettet werden können. Nach drei weiteren vermissten Seeleuten werde noch gesucht. Auch das rumänische Innenministerium äußerte sich zu dem Vorfall: Das Schiff droht demnach zu sinken.

Es ist nicht die erste mutmaßliche Drohnenattacke auf Schiffe vor der Küste des Landes. Allein seit Monatsbeginn waren ähnliche Angriffe auf drei weitere gemeldet worden. Auch in bulgarischen Gewässern waren in den vergangenen Tagen mehrere Schiffe betroffen.

Wie bereits bei den vergangenen mutmaßlichen Angriffen sieht Rumäniens Staatspräsident Nicusor Dan die Verantwortung bei Russland. Zwar bestätigte er im Gespräch mit der Nachrichtenagentur Mediafax nicht, dass es sich um eine russische Drohne gehandelt habe. Dan sprach jedoch von einem weiteren "Eskalationsversuch Russlands" in Zusammenhang mit dem Krieg gegen die Ukraine.

Ähnlich äußerte sich EU-Kommissionschefin Ursula von der Leyen beim Kurznachrichtendienst X. Auch sie sprach von einer "weiteren Eskalation seitens Russlands im Schwarzen Meer" und warf Moskau einen "offenen Verstoß gegen das Völkerrecht" vor.

Wieder wurden Schiffe vor Bulgariens Küste von Drohnen attackiert. mehr

#440. Controversial US-backed vaccine trial in African newborns halted

Hepatitis B study in Guinea-Bissau that was to be funded by CDC and that drew global backlash ‘will not move forward’

The US-backed hepatitis B vaccine trial in African newborns that drew global backlash was halted, the lead researcher said on Wednesday.

It was “now clear” that the study “will not move forward in Guinea-Bissau”, Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer, a Danish researcher, wrote on LinkedIn, adding, “we were not given the necessary governmental approval.”

The minister of health in Guinea-Bissau, Quinhin Nantote, previously denied that the project would move forward. “This is not even remotely true,” Nantote told the Guardian in Portuguese last week.

The study was to be funded with $1.6m from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), along with another $1.6m from private partners like the Bill Ackman-backed Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.

“The solution is clear here: take the money and vaccinate as many kids as you can,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, who sharply criticized the proposed study as unethical.

The government of Guinea-Bissau now has control over the researchers’ vaccines, which they apprehended when they searched the offices of the Bandim Health Project on Monday.

It was vital to support Guinea-Bissau in rolling the immunizations out to all newborns as soon as possible, Offit said. Guinea-Bissau currently plans to offer the universal birth dose in 2028.

The Danish researchers, led by Schaltz-Buchholzer, Christine Stabell Benn and Peter Aaby, hypothesized giving live vaccines, like the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG), may have an overall mortality benefit beyond simply preventing illnesses like tuberculosis – but giving another vaccine like hepatitis B alongside it could dampen that effect.

Such a hypothesis was “fanciful” because the hepatitis B vaccine is a single protein among billions encountered by the immune system each day, Offit said.

“There’s no evidence for that, and it doesn’t make biological sense,” he continued. He also added that there was a very clear benefit to giving the vaccine to babies as soon as possible, because of high rates of hepatitis B in the country and the possibility of lifelong illness and death from infection.

The Danish researchers did not respond by press time to questions about the study or to this criticism. The CDC did not respond by press time to questions about whether the funding, which was appropriated through its global health work, would now be used to roll out the vaccine to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO).

“WHO recommends that all infants receive a first dose of the hepatitis B vaccine as soon as possible after birth – preferably within 24 hours – followed by at least two additional doses,” said Tarik Jašarević, a WHO spokesperson. “WHO remains committed to working with national authorities, researchers, and partners to ensure that all newborns – in Guinea‑Bissau and worldwide – receive timely, evidence‑based protection against hepatitis B.”

Those who declined participation in the study would not have received the vaccines – making true informed consent impossible, experts say.

“Imagine you’re a mother. You want to do the best for your child,” said Henrik Støvring, a Danish researcher who has co-published research raising questions about previous research from the Bandim project.

“If they decide to participate in the trial, they have a 50% chance of getting the vaccine for their children. But if they stay out, they have a 0% chance of getting the vaccine. So how can you say that’s a non-coercive informed consent?” Støvring asked.

The proposed trial led to distrust among Bissau-Guineans, who wondered if the vaccine – which has a decades-long record of being safe and effective – was being tested on Africans because it was dangerous, Schaltz-Buchholzer said in his post.

It “should be clear” that both birth vaccination schedules – with or without hepatitis B – are not “dangerous to anyone”, he wrote. There is a clear benefit to giving hepatitis B vaccines at birth, and not doing so can lead to lifelong danger, experts say.

Conducting a study like this “makes the case that there’s something that’s worthy of study, for which they have no evidence”, Offit said.

“We have millions and millions, arguably hundreds of millions, of children in this world who have gotten that vaccine as a birth dose or haven’t. If there was any evidence that this was problematic, you would know this by now,” Offit added. “We eliminated hepatitis B in the United States in children virtually within years of starting that program, so the benefits are clear.”

Schaltz-Buchholzer also cast doubt on the effectiveness and safety of the hepatitis B vaccine at birth, noting that he believes the study was canceled because it challenges “prevailing medical assumptions, such as that HBV0 does not have non-specific effects”. The study, in addition to looking at mortality, would have also examined side-effects such as skin conditions and neurodevelopmental conditions. Dozens of studies have shown no link between vaccination and autism.

“All newborns should be given a birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine,” Offit said. “Guinea-Bissau is a country that suffers a high incidence of chronic hepatitis B. That country, more than any other country, arguably, needs to launch this program.”

#441. Fußballwelt in Sorge um Kompany: Wie es beim FC Bayern nach dem Schock weitergeht

Der Zusammenbruch von Vincent Kompany hat auch in der internationalen Fußball-Szene Sorgen und eine große Anteilnahme ausgelöst. "Jeder bei Manchester City wünscht unserem ehemaligen Kapitän und der Klub-Legende Vincent Kompany schnelle Erholung", schrieb der ehemalige Klub des jetzigen Bayern-Trainers.

Ob in Kompanys einstiger sportlichen Wahlheimat England, in Belgien, wo er herkommt, oder in anderen Ländern des Kontinents: Die Nachricht aus München verbreitete sich schnell und löste entsprechende Reaktionen aus. "Jeder des portugiesischen Verbandes wünscht Dir schnelle Genesung, Vincent", kommentierte der Verband des Europameisters von 2004 den Bayern-Beitrag bei Instagram.

Bundesligisten und Zweitliga-Klubs reagierten ebenfalls, dazu auch der FC Burnley. Den englischen Verein hatte Kompany vor seinem Wechsel zum FC Bayern zwei Jahre lang trainiert. Landsmann Thibaut Courtois, Torwart des spanischen Topklubs Real Madrid, schrieb: "Werde bald wieder gesund, Freund."

Kompany war am Freitag zusammengebrochen, als er den Amateuren des deutschen Fußball-Rekordmeisters beim Training zugeschaut hatte. Der 40-Jährige war daraufhin mit einem Notarztwagen in eine Klinik gebracht worden.

"Ganz großer Schock, als die Nachricht gerade reingeplatzt ist", sagte Bundesforschungsministerin und FC-Bayern-Mitglied Dorothee Bär (CSU) dem Nachrichtensender WELT TV am Rande des CSU-Parteitags: "Der ist wirklich eine ganz herausragende menschliche Persönlichkeit. Und deswegen wünsche ich ihm alles Gute, Gottes reichen Segen - und hoffe, dass er ganz schnell wieder auf den Beinen ist."

Der FC Bayern werde alles tun, "damit er sich schnell erholt. Vinnie erhält alle notwendige medizinische Betreuung und Unterstützung und alle Zeit, die er benötigt", versicherte Sportvorstand Max Eberl in einer Mitteilung. Das Trainerteam übernehme Kompanys Aufgaben.

Zu den Co-Trainern des Belgiers gehört an erster Stelle Aaron Danks. Der Engländer sprang schon mal für Kompany ein, als dieser im Champions-League-Halbfinalspiel in der vergangenen Saison auswärts gegen Paris Saint-Germain wegen einer Sperre von der Tribüne aus zuschauen musste.

Der 43-Jährige ist für die tägliche Trainingsplanung verantwortlich. "Vincent hat seine Ausstrahlung und alles, was dazugehört. Aber die ganze Kleinarbeit kommt ja im Hintergrund auch von den ganzen Kollegen, die da im Trainerstab sind. Dementsprechend weiß jeder um die Idee, um die Dinge, die wir umsetzen wollen, defensiv wie offensiv", sagte Eberl damals, als Danks in Paris einspringen musste. Das Trainerteam sei "gut abgestimmt aufeinander", hatte Sportdirektor Christoph Freund betont.

Das müssen die Co-Trainer von Kompany nun am Sonntag wieder beweisen, wenn es zum Spitzenspiel zum SC Freiburg geht. Nur drei Tage später empfangen die Münchner den Zweitligisten 1. FC Magdeburg in der zweiten Runde des DFB-Pokals, ehe es zum Klassiker daheim gegen Borussia Dortmund (31. Oktober) und dem schweren Auswärtsspiel in der Champions League gegen Atlético Madrid (3. November) kommt.

Wie lange Kompany ausfallen wird, ist unklar. Er hatte zuletzt an einer Virusinfektion und Hüftproblemen gelitten. Am Dienstag hatte er zur Schonung bei der letzten Einheit vor dem Champions-League-Spiel gegen den FC Arsenal (2:2) pausiert und bei der obligatorischen Pressekonferenz gefehlt. Dort hatte ihn Danks schon vertreten.

Beim Spiel am Mittwochabend hatte Kompany seine Mannschaft aber an der Seitenlinie angetrieben. Nach dem Remis gegen den englischen Meister hatte er von gesundheitlichen Problemen berichtet. "Ich habe einen ziemlich saftigen Virus bekommen letzte Woche, habe dann natürlich nicht auf meinen Körper gehört und dann hat der Körper irgendwann gesagt: Jetzt hör mal auf!", sagte Kompany.

#442. Israel to close West Bank crossings on election day as crackdown escalates

An Israeli army vehicle passes near the closed entrance of Hebron, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank

All West Bank land crossings will be closed during Tuesday's election in Israel, the country's military says, and Palestinian workers will be barred from entering all settlements.

The restrictions come amid a crackdown in the occupied West Bank after Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers in the territory.

The Israel Defense Forces announced a "ban on the entry and exit of Palestinian workers throughout Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley, including industrial zones, as well as the closure of all land crossings" on Tuesday.

It said most workers would also be barred from settlements from Sunday, with the exception of industrial zones and a limited number of other areas.

Before the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, more than 100,000 Palestinian workers were permitted to enter Israel. Since then only a small fraction have had their permits restored.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a major operation on Friday in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen in an attack on a checkpoint. Three other Israeli soldiers were injured, and the gunmen were also killed.

The Israeli military have been demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron, with hundreds of families having been displaced.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said about 2,000 residents had been displaced by the operation, which has led to at least one whole street appearing to have been flattened, according to footage shared online.

Even before the entry and exit bans on workers were announced by the IDF on Sunday, the military had cordoned off the city, heavily restricting the movement of its 200,000 residents.

It is common for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis in the West Bank - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment.

Friday's shooting came during a tense time for the region, just days ahead of Israel's election taking place on Tuesday.

In an interview with Israel's i24 television channel released on Saturday, Netanyahu threatened a "very big surprise" for the Palestinian Authority (PA), which governs parts of the territory.

Hebron Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari said the operation was being "driven by the elections" and that Netanyahu and his ministers were attempting to secure the votes of the far right and the settlers.

On Saturday, thousands gathered in Tel Aviv for a large anti-government demonstration.

The protest was organised by the October Council, a group founded by the families of victims and hostages taken by militants on 7 October 2023, to demand accountability for the failure to prevent the Hamas-led attack.

"Three days before the election, we will hold the culminating event marking three years of struggle to uncover the truth, demand accountability, and establish a state commission of inquiry," the October Council wrote on X ahead of the rally.

The gathering saw the participation of the leaders of the four main opposition parties, including Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief of staff who is neck and neck with Netanyahu.

#443. "Une femme à la tête d'un garage, ça peut surprendre" : elle a repris le garage automobile de ce petit village du Lot et compte bien le développer

l'essentiel Nathalie Delpech dirige depuis janvier 2026 le garage NS Automobile à Mayrinhac-Lentour, dans le Lot, aux côtés de son mari Sébastien. Ancienne comptable et agricultrice, elle réalise son rêve entrepreneurial en développant l'achat et la vente de véhicules d'occasion. Lauréate du concours "101 femmes entrepreneures 2026", elle incarne une réussite féminine dans un secteur traditionnellement masculin.

Un garage automobile se dessine à la sortie de Mayrinhac-Lentour. C'est un des derniers commerces de ce petit village du Lot. Dans ce secteur d'activité pourtant majoritairement masculin, c'est bien une femme que l'on retrouve à la tête de l'entreprise. Depuis janvier 2026, Nathalie Delpech dirige NS automobile aux côtés de son mari, Sébastien.

Derrière les initiales "NS" se cache la volonté de créer une entreprise familiale. Le "N" de Nathalie Delpech et le "S" de Sébastien. Après sa journée de travail, au Syded, ce dernier rejoint son épouse au garage, le soir. Mais il devrait, "rapidement", s'engager à 100 % dans le projet.

Derrière son ordinateur, Nathalie Delpech multiplie les appels téléphoniques, accueille les clients, réalise les factures... "C'est mon lieu de vie ici", sourit celle qui multiplie les journées à rallonge. Mais, après de premiers mois intenses, la cheffe d'entreprise a fini par trouver son "rythme de croisière". Elle profite pleinement de ce nouveau quotidien. "C'est top. Et tellement enrichissant car j'apprends tous les jours", détaille la mère de famille.

Elle réalise surtout un rêve. "J'ai toujours eu envie d'être entrepreneuse. J'avais vu passer différentes offres, mais ce n'était pas forcément le bon moment", explique la gérante. C'est finalement début 2025 que les planètes s'alignent. Le couple apprend la vente du garage du village qu'ils habitent depuis quinze ans. "Là, c'était le bon moment. Nos enfants étaient assez grands", rembobine Nathalie Delpech. La reprise est effective en janvier 2026 et l'entrepreneuse a une idée bien précise de ce qu'elle veut faire de ce garage : conserver l'atelier mécanique et développer davantage l'achat et la vente de véhicules d'occasion en parallèle.

La Lotoise aux multiples vies, un temps agricultrice dans la ferme familiale, 12 ans comme comptable, puis employée d'un garage, avait le commerce dans la peau. "J'ai toujours baigné dedans depuis enfant. Je faisais les marchés quand j'étais petite", se souvient-elle. Alors, recevoir les clients et les conseiller est tout à fait naturel pour elle. Il a cependant fallu se perfectionner dans la connaissance de la mécanique. "Une femme à la tête d'un garage, ça peut surprendre. Donc c'est hyper important de montrer que l'on maîtrise le domaine", indique l'entrepreneuse, pour qui "les femmes peuvent exercer tous les métiers".

Dans l'atelier du garage, les quatre employés partagent la même opinion. "Ça ne change rien qu'elle soit une femme", souligne Gaëtan, mécanicien qui n'avait connu jusqu'alors que des chefs masculins. Tous reconnaissent également les qualités professionnelles de la patronne. "Elle est courageuse parce que gérer une boîte comme ça, c'est beaucoup de boulot", reconnaît Jean-François Thomas, l'ancien propriétaire du garage, désormais employé à l'atelier.

Et cette expertise est déjà reconnue par ses pairs. Nathalie Delpech a été lauréate du concours "101 femmes entrepreneures 2026", qui vient révéler le potentiel entrepreneurial. En septembre, ce sont les Trophées de la reconversion 2026 qui sont venus la consacrer dans la catégorie "Nouveaux métiers". "C'est une fierté d'être sélectionnée. Mais la mise en lumière, ce n'est pas forcément pour moi", s'amuse la gérante, qui n'aime pas se mettre en avant. La cheffe d'entreprise préfère se recentrer sur son activité à laquelle se joindra totalement son mari. Une entreprise qui semble prendre la bonne direction sous les ordres du couple.

#444. Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat

Watch as fire engulfs Hitler's mountaintop retreat

Police in the southern German state of Bavaria have detained a 33-year-old German man during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.

Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 local time (19:15 GMT) on Friday and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.

Some 200 emergency personnel were deployed to the scene where the blaze was still burning early on Saturday, as police said difficult terrain hindered efforts to bring the fire under control.

Police said they apprehended the man riding a motorcycle near the scene, German media reported. A criminal investigation has been launched.

There is currently nothing to suggest the involvement of further suspects, police official Gerhart Holzinger told a press conference on Saturday afternoon.

Public prosecutor Rainer Vietze said a psychiatric report had concluded the 33-year-old man showed signs of possible mental illness and diminished responsibility might therefore be assumed.

Vietze said a possible political motive was also being considered, but stressed the investigation was in its early stages.

The residence, above the town of Berchtesgaden, was one of several buildings in the area used by the Nazi dictator and his entourage during World War Two.

Hitler and top Nazi officials used his nearby Berghof residence to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941 and the whole complex was considered one of his headquarters.

He also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.

Local media reported that site had been "largely destroyed" and the public was urged to avoid the area.

Bavaria's Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann told reporters that the site would "under no circumstances remain a ruin", broadcaster BR24 reported. "It is important that we continue our work of remembrance," he added.

The retreat was seen smouldering on Saturday morning

Completed by the Nazis in 1938, the Eagle's Nest, which sits at an elevation of around 1,800m (5,900ft), escaped destruction after their defeat in 1945.

Since then, it has become a popular tourist destination and houses a mountain inn.

It serves as "a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship", according to its official website, external.

During WW2, Hitler and his followers were responsible for the deaths of tens of millions of people, including the mass murder of European Jews. Homosexuals, gypsies, the disabled and ethnic minorities were sent to concentration camps and put to death.

There has been a wider debate in Germany and Vienna over whether to preserve, repurpose or demolish buildings connected to Hitler.

While some say these buildings should be preserved for historical reasons, others have raised concerns that they could be used as monuments or places of pilgrimage for neo-Nazis and far-right extremists.

In June, Berlin authorities announced they would tear down one of Hitler's bunkers - described at the time as "the power centre of Nazi Germany" - to build flats and offices on the site.

Those critical of the plans said the bunker had "significant historical value" and that it should have been turned into a museum and memorial site with an exhibit about the end of the war.

And in July, after years of controversy, Austrian authorities refurbished the house in the town of Braunau am Inn in which Hitler was born and turned it into a police station.
