#466. Germany news: Emergency at Leipzig airport sparked by novice driver

Two men breached a fence at the Leipzig/Halle airport while practicing for a driving test. Meanwhile, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced an industrial AI partnership with Nvidia. DW has more.

This blog is now closed. Below is a roundup of the stories from and about Germany on Monday, October 19, 2026.

Berlin's Left Party, the Greens and the Social Democrats are set to move ahead on talks to form the next coalition government in the capital city.

The SPD's state leadership approved the motion with a wide majority in an online session, and the Greens voted overwhelmingly in favor of talks at a small party convention.

The Left Party has not scheduled a conference until October 31 because members of the party may be away because of school holidays.

The Left Party is hoping to have Elif Eralp lead the state government.

The coalition talks are set to open after weeks of tense negotiations and a dispute over alleged antisemitism within the ranks of the Left Party.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang unveiled a new artificial intelligence (AI) cooperation at a glitzy investment summit in Berlin on Monday evening.

"Germany is open for business," said Merz at the Invest in Germany event, adding that the combination of German engineering and cutting-edge AI technology would help strengthen the country's economy in the long term.

"Germany is open for investment and Germany is ready to grow at a faster pace," the chancellor continued, before joking: "If I were Jensen Huang, I would put on my leather jacket, take a flight to Berlin, meet the German Chancellor, and tell him, 'I'm ready to invest.'"

The partnership with Nvidia is intended to speed up the digital transformation of German industry and secure the country's technological sovereignty.

According to the company, Nvidia invested nearly $1 billion in Germany last year and holds stakes in numerous start-ups and established companies.

But Europe's largest economy has nevertheless struggled to attract foreign investment after years of weak growth, with high energy prices and labor costs continuing to deter businesses.

German officials were hoping that Monday's summit, which was attended by more than 200 domestic and international investment executives, would showcase Germany as an attractive investment destination, highlighting its sound public finances, status as the only G7 country with a triple-A credit rating, its universities, skilled workforce and tariff-free trade within the EU single market.

Further behind-closed-door talks are set to take place on Tuesday.

Do you remember those arrests in Germany last week, connected to an arson attempt at a Starlink control center in Poland?

The government in Warsaw called it a hybrid attack and accused Russia of recruiting organized crime elements for the alleged crime.

It's much too early to say for sure, but Bulgaria has now issued a pair of European arrest warrants against German citizens in a case that seems rather reminiscent in several regards.

The two 19-year-olds are accused of driving in from Serbia claiming to be tourists, setting fire to a series of antennae south of Sofia, and leaving the country again within a matter of hours.

Hermann Höllenreiner, a Sinti German raised in Bavaria who survived the Nazis' Auschwitz concentration camp as a child, has died aged 92.

Munich's Hanser Verlag publisher and the International Auschwitz Committee said that he had passed away last Friday, October 16, in Mettenheim in Bavaria, surrounded by his family.

Höllenreiner, known as "Mano" to his large Bavarian Sinti family, spent time at the Auschwitz-Birkenau, Ravensbrück and Sachsenhausen camps as a child.

"Only later in his life did he start to tell his story and became a major witness of the era, who hauntingly reported on the horrors of Auschwitz, the perpetrators and the victims, and above all of the still-persistnent discrimination of Sinti and Roma in Europe," Christioph Heubner, executive vice president of the International Auschwitz Committee, said.

"Mano Höllenreiner's biography and tales of suffering were enough for more than one life. What he saw with his own eyes as a child in Auschwitz and what was done to him — for many decades he didn't know how to speak out about it," Heubner said, thanking Höllenreiner for his "courage and humanity" in ultimately telling his story.

Höllenriener managed to flee one of the so-called "death marches" fleeing extermination camps in as Allied armies approached.

Author Anja Tuckermann told his story in a book whose title roughly translates as: "Mano. The boy who didn't know where he was."

He was initially found on a roadside and rescued by liberated French prisoners, who took him home with them. In 1946, he was reunited with surviving relatives in Germany.

Two men have admitted to breaking through a fence at Leipzig/Halle airport while one of them was practicing for a driving test, an incident that triggered a major security operation, police said on Monday.

The two, aged 20 and 32, handed themselves in to the police on Sunday evening, following the incident. The broken fence was first discovered by airport staff late on Saturday.

Police said the 20-year-old had been at the wheel despite not having a valid license.

An investigation was opened into the learner driver for fleeing the scene after breaking through the fence.

The mass-circulation Bild newspaper reported that the car involved, of which fragments were found at the site, was an Audi.

The airport was the site of a security scare in August, when an explosives-laden drone was found there near Ukrainian cargo planes.

German officials accused Russia of having planned an attack, something Moscow denied.

Germany's Rheinmetall defense group on Monday announced that it had acquired Romania's Mangalia shipyard at auction in partnership with Swiss shipping giant MSC.

Rheinmetall said it had paid approximately €138 million ($154 million) for the facility.   Acquisition is expected to be finalized within a few weeks.   Rheinmetall and MSC plan to develop the Black Sea shipyard near Constanța into a dual-use site for civilian and military shipbuilding for both domestic and international markets.

Rheinmetall says its Naval Systems division will use the facility to build four vessels commissioned by the Romanian government, including two 96-meter (305 foot) offshore patrol vessels and two 43-meter diving support vessels.   The company also intends to modernize the shipyard's infrastructure and expand its capacity.

"In doing so," said the company, ​"Rheinmetall ⁠is creating a scalable foundation for future ⁠projects in ​southeastern Europe and strengthens its position in a strategically important market."

The Foreign Ministry has summoned Iran's ambassador after two men were convicted of preparing attacks on Jewish figures and pro-Israel targets in Germany at the behest of Tehran.

"We vehemently condemn Iran's activities. We will not allow Iran to threaten our liberal society," the ministry wrote on X.

"We do not tolerate attacks on Jewish life and those who defend it anywhere, and particularly not in Germany," it wrote.

A Hamburg court on Thursday sentenced a 54-year-old man and a 43-year old man respectively to 8 1/2 and 4 1/2 years in prison for having spied on the president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, Josef Schuster, and Volker Beck, the president of the German-Israeli Society (DIG).

In the court's opinion, their actions were carried out in preparation for terrorist attacks, including the planned murders of  Schuster and Beck.

The court said the 54-year-old, who was said to have also done the groundwork for an arson attack on a kosher food store in Berlin, received his orders directly from officers in the Quds Force.

The Quds Force is the branch of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that is in charge of extraterritorial operations.

German industrial businesses employed some 496,000 fewer people at the end of 2025 compared to the start of 2019, according to a survey conducted by the Ifo Institute economic think tank.

Worst-hit has been the automotive industry, a key sector of the German economy, where 123,500 jobs were cut both at carmakers and suppliers, a decline of 13%.

But the metals sector also saw a marked decline in the number of jobs available, dropping 115,600 workers in the period, while the machinery sector bled 64,500 positions.

At the same time, more than 2.2 million additional jobs were created in the service sector, according to Ifo.

It said 391,000 new jobs had been established in the health sector and another 357,000 in social services, including care homes.

Joachim Ragnitz, managing director at Ifo Dresden, said the figures showed an "accelerated structural shift" in Germany.

"Ironically, the very sectors that have sustained our prosperity up to now are shrinking," he said.

"The new jobs are for the most part not being created where Germany is especially productive and innovative. That may slow down our growth potential in the future."

A German woman has died in a climbing accident in the Italian Alps, mountain rescuers said on Monday.

The 32-year-old woman, who was an experienced mountaineer, fell more than 50 meters (164 feet) to her death while on the Cengia dei Camosci, a difficult route on the 2,323-meter Grande Nabois mountain near the Slovenian border.

The rescue service said the accident was caused when a climbing hold gave way under the woman, who was accompanied by an Austrian fellow climber at the time.

Investigations are underway to clarify the exact circumstances of her death.

Carmaker Volkswagen intends to freeze the salaries of some 660,000 employees worldwide until 2030 as the company, along with the entire car industry, faces a range of challenges that have impacted its profits.

Trade union IG Metall confirmed earlier media reports of the plans, citing information given to employees by the works council.

The works council described the plans as unrealistic and said there would be considerable resistance to them.

If the company does implement them, employees could lose an estimated 10% of their purchasing power by the end of the decade.

The news comes after VW decided in September to cut 50,000 jobs worldwide in the coming years in addition to the reduction of 50,000 positions that had already been agreed.

Four plants in Germany are also at risk of being closed between 2031 and 2034.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Less than a third of leadership positions in Germany are held by women, a lower level than the EU average, statistics released on Monday showed.

According to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis), citing figures from the EU statistics authority Eurostat, women held just 30.3% of leadership positions in Germany, compared with 35.9% in the whole of the EU.

Only Cyprus, Italy and the Netherlands have lower rates than Germany in the bloc, while Sweden has the highest, at 44.4%, followed by Latvia, Estonia and Poland.

"The low proportion of women in leadership positions in Germany is particularly striking, as almost as many women as men are employed here," Destatis said, comparing the situation with Italy, which has almost the same level of female leadership but a much lower rate of female employment overall.

Destatis defines leadership positions as those involving the management of small companies, the management of large companies or departments within them and high administrative posts.

A two-day conference entitled "Invest in Germany Summit" is to begin on Monday evening in Berlin as the government seeks to shore up public-sector spending with private money.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will deliver the opening speech at the conference, which will be attended by an expected 200 representatives from large German and international companies.

The CEO of the US chip manufacturer Nvidia, Jensen Huang, is to be one of the key guests at the conference.

The German government is looking to cooperate strongly with the company, whose products are central to the boom in artificial intelligence, in a bid to help Germany catch up in the sector.

The German Economic Institute (IW) has, however, warned against any too high expectations from the summit, saying that high costs for labor, energy and bureaucracy in Germany were a deterrent to investment in the country.

"It would be naive to believe that the summit will change that in the short term. Companies don't choose Germany because of a promotional event. What matters is whether they can make money here," IW director Michael Hüther told the DPA news agency.

He said it would be more effective if the government were to swiftly implement its reform agenda.

A study by Allianz Research has shown that investment in Germany fell by 6.4% between 2019 and 2025, while it grew by 6.7% in the rest of the eurozone and a whole 20.2% in the US.

The DW newsroom in Bonn bids guten Tag to all its faithful readers at the start of a new week!

Today, we will be looking at a conference in Berlin that will seek to attract private investment in Germany to help make the country fit for the future, with the field of artificial intelligence a key focus.

New statistics are also to be released on Monday on women in leadership and government positions in Germany and the EU in 2025.

And the Leipzig/Halle airport has resumed normal operations after a security incident involving a breached fence triggered a large-scale police operation.

This occurred just weeks after an explosives-laden drone that German officials believe was intended to carry out an attack on behalf of Russia was found at the airport.

#467. Arbeitszeitreform: Wackelt der Acht-Stunden-Tag?

Zwölf Stunden am Stück in Deutschland arbeiten? Union und SPD streiten erbittert über die Reform des Arbeitszeitgesetzes. Es geht um Flexibilität, Tarifverträge und den Schutz von Beschäftigten.

Leuna, im ostdeutschen Bundesland Sachsen-Anhalt, ist einer der größten Standorte der Chemieindustrie in Deutschland. Mehr als 100 Unternehmen haben sich hier inzwischen angesiedelt. Noch recht neu ist eine Bio-Raffinerie für holzbasierte Chemikalien, die der finnische Biotechnologiekonzern UPM in Leuna gebaut hat. Dafür sucht das Werk Mitarbeiter.

Auf einem großen Jobportal wird unter anderem ein Chemikant für die Inbetriebnahme neuer Anlagen gesucht. Vorausgesetzt wird die Bereitschaft, in Schichten mit einer Dauer von zwölf Stunden zu arbeiten. Wie kann das sein? Das deutsche Arbeitszeitgesetz erlaubt als Standard maximal acht Stunden Arbeit pro Werktag. Möglich ist eine Verlängerung auf maximal zehn Stunden, wenn die Mehrarbeit wieder ausgeglichen wird. Und: Zwischen zwei Schichten müssen mindestens elf Stunden Ruhezeit liegen.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Wirtschaftsverbände und die konservativen Parteien CDU/CSU fordern schon lange eine Flexibilisierung der Arbeitszeit. Arbeitgeberpräsident Rainer Dulger verweist auf die europäische Arbeitszeitrichtlinie, die eine wöchentliche Höchstarbeitszeit von 48 Stunden erlaubt. "Die Spielräume werden fast überall genutzt, nur bei uns nicht", sagte Dulger im August der Deutschen Presse-Agentur.

Besonders in Branchen mit saisonalen Schwankungen, wie im Tourismus, bei Projektarbeit oder unregelmäßigen Arbeitsspitzen wie in der Gastronomie finden Unternehmen die bestehenden Regeln oft zu unflexibel. Sie würden Personal gerne effizienter einsetzen. "Das Arbeitszeitgesetz stammt aus der Ära von Telefax und Wählscheibe. Es kennt weder Notebooks noch Kita-Öffnungszeiten", so Dulger.

Union und Sozialdemokraten haben 2025 in ihrem Koalitionsvertrag vereinbart, des Arbeitszeitgesetz zu reformieren. Wörtlich heißt es: "Deshalb wollen wir im Einklang mit der europäischen Arbeitszeitrichtlinie die Möglichkeit einer wöchentlichen anstatt einer täglichen Höchstarbeitszeit schaffen - auch und gerade im Sinne einer besseren Vereinbarkeit von Familie und Beruf."

Allerdings hätte SPD das Gesetz am liebsten unangetastet gelassen, musste den Wunsch der Union aber akzeptieren. Die Sozialdemokraten verweisen darauf, dass längere Arbeitszeiten in Ausnahmen bereits möglich sind. Für Rettungsdienste beispielsweise, das Gesundheitswesen und Sicherheitsdienste. Auch in Kraftwerken, Raffinerien und eben auch in der Chemieindustrie darf bis zu zwölf Stunden am Stück gearbeitet werden.

Selbst dem Bundeskanzler scheint diese Ausnahme-Regelung bis vor Kurzem nicht geläufig gewesen zu sein. Anfang September 2026 besuchte Friedrich Merz die UPM-Raffinerie in Leuna. Er sei "völlig überrascht" gewesen, dass die Anlagen im kontinuierlichen Zwölf-Stunden-Schichtbetrieb laufen, erzählte er auf dem Deutschen Arbeitgebertag im Oktober in Berlin. Mit Zustimmung des Betriebsrats und ordnungsgemäß vereinbart.

Der Schichtleiter habe von einem "super guten" Arbeitszeitmodell gesprochen, das drei Arbeitstage pro Woche umfasse. "Er hat gesagt, wir haben viel Zeit für die Familien, das ist eine super Einteilung so." Das zeige, dass es gut wäre, das Arbeitszeitgesetz generell zu lockern, schlussfolgerte Merz. "Über acht Stunden zu arbeiten, ist keine Ausbeutung, sondern das kann für die Betriebe, auch für die Menschen in den Betrieben, eine gute Chance sein, ihre Arbeitszeiten flexibler einzusetzen", sagte der Kanzler und CDU-Vorsitzende auf dem Arbeitgebertag und fügte hinzu: "Wir sollten es machen."

Widerstand kommt allerdings aus der SPD und von den Gewerkschaften. Letztere lehnen eine Änderung des Arbeitszeitgesetzes ab. Die Gewerkschaft ver.di argumentiert, deutlich längere Arbeitstage hätten negative Folgen für die Gesundheit der Beschäftigten sowie Nachteile für Menschen mit Familien- und Pflegeaufgaben. Arbeitnehmer könnten in einzelnen Branchen zudem unter Druck geraten, längere Schichten gegen ihren Willen zu akzeptieren.

Entsprechend dem Koalitionsvertrag arbeitete im Juni 2026 das damals noch von Bärbel Bas geführte Bundesministerium für Arbeit und Soziales einen ersten Entwurf für die Reform aus. Allerdings versehen mit zusätzlichen Bedingungen: Ein Wechsel auf eine wöchentliche Arbeitszeit sollte nur dort möglich sein, wo Arbeitgeber und Gewerkschaften die Arbeitsbedingungen in einem sogenannten Tarifvertrag festlegen. Und das auch nur, wenn gleichzeitig Regelungen zum Gesundheitsschutz aufgestellt werden und wenn es eine elektronische Erfassung der Arbeitszeiten gibt.

Welche Idee dahintersteckt, erläuterte die arbeits- und sozialpolitische Sprecherin der SPD-Bundestagsfraktion Annika Klose. Flexibilisierung sei "keine Einbahnstraße". Im Koalitionsvertrag sei ausdrücklich auf die Vereinbarkeit von Familie und Beruf abgezielt worden. "Dass es also auch mal möglich ist, das Kind am Nachmittag zum Fußballtraining zu bringen und danach weiterzuarbeiten - aber eben nicht, dass mein Chef mir gegen meinen Willen sagt: Du hast morgen die Schicht von 9 bis 22 Uhr."

Die Union wies den Entwurf umgehend als indiskutabel zurück. Auch die Arbeitgeber schäumten. "Dieser Entwurf muss zurückgezogen und völlig überarbeitet werden", forderte Arbeitgeber-Präsident Rainer Dulger in einer Stellungnahme. Er strotze "vor Misstrauen". Der Zentralverband des Handwerks sprach von einem "Bruch mit den im Koalitionsvertrag vereinbarten Zusagen". Seitdem liegt die Reform auf Eis.

Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz stellte auf dem Arbeitgebertag nun Bewegung in Aussicht. "Das ist in der Tat überfällig. Ich glaube, dass wir das auch relativ schnell machen können, dass wir die Flexibilität des Arbeitsmarktes herstellen können."

Ob der neue SPD-Bundesarbeitsminister Alexander Schweitzer das genauso sieht, bleibt allerdings abzuwarten. Aus seiner Partei kam Anfang Oktober ein Papier zur Arbeitszeitreform, das einer Kampfansage gleichkommt. "Selbstbestimmt statt dereguliert" steht über den sieben Seiten, die von der SPD-Arbeitsgemeinschaft für Arbeit, der Jugendorganisation Jusos, der Arbeitsgemeinschaft "60plus" und den Frauen in der SPD unterzeichnet wurde.

In dem Papier beharren die Sozialdemokraten nicht nur auf den Punkten, die schon im Juni in dem Entwurf von Bärbel Bas auftauchten. Sie fordern darüber hinaus, Arbeitgeber und Beschäftigte sollten zukünftig "gemeinsam und einvernehmlich" über Arbeitszeiten entscheiden. Es sei nicht "im Sinne einer zeitgemäßen Reform des Arbeitszeitrechts", wenn nur die Chefs bestimmen könnten, wann die Beschäftigten Feierabend machen.

Politisch gesehen ist die Auseinandersetzung über die Arbeitszeitreform längst mehr als eine Debatte über Paragrafen. Sie ist ein Grundsatzstreit darüber, wie viel Flexibilität die Arbeitswelt künftig verträgt und wie stark der Staat die Beschäftigten dabei schützen soll. Sie ist aber auch ein weiterer Stolperstein für die ohnehin angeschlagene Regierung in Berlin.

#468. More than one million Lula supporters rally on eve of Brazilian election runoff

Nearly 159 million people to head to polls on Sunday in battle between leftwing incumbent and Flávio Bolsonaro

More than one million supporters of Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, have streamed on to Rio’s most famous beach for a giant protest they hope will propel him towards a historic election fightback against his far-right rival, Flávio Bolsonaro.

Nearly 159m Brazilians will vote in the election’s runoff on Sunday, with the pair tied in the polls after Bolsonaro won the first round on 4 October by 47% to 45%.

On Saturday, under a fierce sun, red-clad crowds packed the 2.5-mile Copacabana beach in an attempt to help Lula clinch a dramatic and unprecedented comeback. Never since the return of democracy to Brazil in the 1980s has the first-round loser managed to bounce back.

Josias Silva, a 61-year-old truck driver, voiced confidence that his 80-year-old president, who was first elected in 2002, would win a fourth non-consecutive term. He carried a homemade sign to the carnival-like procession reading: “Lula re-elected. Tomorrow will be a new day.”

“The people have woken up,” Silva said of the large pro-Lula street protests that have swept Brazil since the leftist’s first-round defeat, many led by students.

“Young people know we need this victory because otherwise we will have dictatorship again – and we don’t want dictatorship. We don’t want hatred. We don’t want guns. We want a country of love,” added Silva, celebrating the large number of people who came to witness one of the final presidential campaign rallies in Lula’s storied 50-year political career.

“There’s never been a demonstration like this one. This is the biggest protest in the history of Brazil. And we are going to win tomorrow with more than 60% of the votes,” Silva claimed.

Polls suggest a far tighter margin and most analysts see Bolsonaro, whose father, Jair Bolsonaro, was president from 2019 to 2022, as the slight favourite, having sold himself to voters as someone who will tackle chronic levels of violent crime with an iron fist.

However, in recent days Lula has appeared to regain the initiative and climb in the polls, amid a succession of scandals involving his rightwing foe. Last week the Brazilian magazine Piauí claimed that at the height of Brazil’s 2020 coronavirus outbreak, Flávio Bolsonaro attended a boat party attended by sex workers and vaccine lobbyists hoping to strike a deal with the government of his father.

Some experts speculate a Lula comeback may be possible. At the Copacabana rally – which Rio’s City Hall said attracted about 1.1 million people – activists unfurled an enormous yellow and green banner declaring: “WE ARE GOING TO TURN THIS AROUND!”

On Saturday afternoon, Lula attended an even larger rally on Paulista Avenue, in the heart of Brazil’s biggest city, São Paulo.

“I’m super excited. Lula’s going to win,” said Marta Moraes, a 59-year-old restaurateur, as she joined Saturday’s demo in Rio.

Moraes said the election was not about left versus right. “We’ve nothing against the right … what we’re against is Bolsonarismo,” she said, tears filling her eyes as she recalled how Flávio Bolsonaro’s father botched the response to Covid during his chaotic 2019-2022 administration.

“I lost four members of my family because of Bolsonaro’s neglect,” Moraes said.

Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula. Many Brazilian democrats fear he will be released – and could even return to government – if his son wins. Reports in the Brazilian press suggest several of Bolsonaro’s fellow plotters – who are now in prison or hiding in exile – may be given top military and police jobs in a Bolsonaro administration.

Cammy Marinho, a 49-year-old DJ and activist, said: “I’m here to prevent democracy becoming extinct – which is what the Bolsonaro family wants”.

Marinho said she had spent the past fortnight fighting to persuade people who voted for Bolsonaro, or did not vote in the first round, to back Lula.

“It’s non-stop work: in the bakery, in the supermarket, on the underground – whenever you feel there is an opening to talk to someone and show to them the reality, everything that Lula has done and is doing for the people and everything that this [Bolsonaro] family has done against the people,” she said.

Many marchers were part of the so-called “Lula’s Army” – a 10 million-member WhatsApp group that was created after the first round in the hope of turning the election around.

“Being a soldier in Lula’s army … means fighting for Brazilian democracy. This isn’t a normal election,” said Isabella Gaze, 64, a retired teacher and one of the group’s members.

“They constantly claim Lula is corrupt. But the truth is that they represent the most rotten and worst part of Brazilian politics. This is what we are fighting against now,” Gaze said of the Bolsonaros.

Many of the faces on Copacabana beach were teenagers, including 14-year-old Heitor Lopes da Silva. Silva had come from the city of Duque de Caxias in his wheelchair, with a placard that said: “Lula, I’m a person with a disability and I’m here to support you.”

“My whole life I’ve believed Lula was a good president. [Bolsonaro] represents the destruction of Brazil …. he represents sadness and death,” he said of the Bolsonaro-era Covid catastrophe.

Large crowds of Bolsonaro supporters also hit the streets, including in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais state, which has Brazil’s second-largest electorate after São Paulo, and is a key bellwether. No presidential candidate has ever won the presidency without securing Minas Gerais, where Bolsonaro led by just under 5% in the first round.

Thousands of Bolsonaristas gathered to see their candidate in a palm-lined plaza called Praça da Liberdade. To the booming sound of AI-generated funk carioca tracks praising Bolsonaro, a sea of supporters dressed in Brazil’s yellow football jersey waved Brazilian flags – and many of the United States too.

“The US is a great nation. Who wouldn’t want to be aligned with them?” said 56-year-old cosmetics entrepreneur Marcos Antonio, holding a flag that merged the emblems of both countries.

“I don’t want an alliance with Cuba or Venezuela. I want to move forward,” Antonio added. When reminded that Venezuela was currently aligned with the US after Donald Trump’s January invasion, he said: “True. But for now, a fully right-wing government hasn’t been installed yet. It’s in transition.”

Antonio Carlos Costa Jr, the 59-year-old owner of a shooting club, complained: “Lula did nothing for the country.”

Jair Bolsonaro relaxed gun ownership and buying laws – which security experts agree ended up diverting many firearms to criminal gangs – whereas Lula tightened regulations once again. “Jair Bolsonaro simply gave citizens the right to defend themselves, and his son will do the same,” said Costa Jr.

Lula supporters scoff at the idea that Bolsonaro, who has a history of well-documented ties with members of Rio’s paramilitary “militia” groups, could rid Brazil of criminality.

“If we vote the militias into power, we will be living in a dictatorship,” said Erika Cavalcante, 43, an architect who came to the march with a sign reading: “Don’t let the mobsters win.”

#469. Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm

When we landed by helicopter at Rosebank, this oil field was at the centre of a political storm - and set to be in the path of a real one.

We arrived on Wednesday morning, just a few hours after the UK government had granted consent for the production of gas from the Jackdaw field in the North Sea.

But already attention was shifting to this wild and windy patch of the North Atlantic â the next big decision for Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

Rosebank is bigger than Jackdaw, it would generate higher greenhouse gas emissions, and it could be far more lucrative for its owners, Adura and Ithaca.

Nicola Boyd loves her job on the Petrojarl Rosebank vessel

This summer, along with a camera crew, I travelled to Jackdaw, 150 miles east of Aberdeen.

Now we were the first journalists to visit Rosebank.

We came here - days before Storm Boelo arrived with strong winds and heavy rain - to scrutinise a controversial project which is at the heart of a national debate about climate change, energy policy and the economy.

But we also hoped for a rare glimpse into life offshore.

"It's good fun, it's interesting, every day can change," said Nicola Boyd, who runs the helideck, and greeted us as we struggled out of our lifejackets and survival suits.

Boyd has worked offshore for nearly a decade, including a year on Rosebank - where she spends two weeks at a time followed by three weeks' leave.

The Petrojarl Rosebank is moored in the North Atlantic waiting to see if production gets the go-ahead from the UK government

It's also a job that calls for steady legs and a strong stomach.

Unlike the fixed Jackdaw platform, this installation â 80 miles north west of ShetlandÂ âÂ is a large ship, a floating production, storage and offloading vessel (FPSO) named the Petrojarl Rosebank.

It's been chartered by the field's owners from Aberdeen-based Altera and, during my 48 hours on board, it was constantly but gently rolling on the North Atlantic swell.

With the understatement typical of an Orkney islander, lead mechanical technician Ewan Leonard told me the winter weather could be "a bit of a challenge."

"Last week we had a 30m heave coming through," he said, referring to the swell, "so we'll probably suffer more of that as the winter goes on."

Altera CEO Chris Brett told me that in the industry the environment west of Shetland is considered "as harsh as you get anywhere in the world."

Whatever your view on that industry, the sheer scale of what humans have achieved in such conditions is impressive.

Ewan Leonard says the winter weather can be "a bit of a challenge"

The deep reserves of skill, ingenuity and engineering prowess among the 122 people on board are obvious.

The jobs are well-paid and, according to Ewan Leonard, the facilities are excellent.

"We have single-man cabins, there's good gym facilities, there's a lot of rec rooms here."

Douglas Hogge, a production supervisor in charge of a team responsible for the safe extraction of oil and gas, agrees.

"There's the gym, the sauna," he said, adding "you can obviously go and get some fresh air. There's plenty of fresh air out there."

Food on board the ship was described as "fantastic"

"As you've seen yourself, the food is fantastic on board, so no complaints." added Leonard.

Everyone we spoke to agreed with that, praising the talented chefs who sent out all sorts of delicious dishes, from braised ox cheek to mackerel to pork loin, day and night.

As dusk gathers and the nightshift get ready for work with a strange breakfast of fillet steak and chocolate brownie pudding, the vessel begins to glow in the gloom.

It is a strange sight, the decks criss-crossed by a bewilderingly complex array of pipes, valves and bright yellow steelwork.

The ship is an array of pipes, valves and bright yellow steelwork

The ship doesn't move far, rotating around a fixed central point called the turret to face into the weather, making life a little easier for those on board.

If production is approved, oil and gas will be pumped up through the turret from wells in the field below, which contains an estimated 300m to 500m barrels, enough for perhaps 25 years.

"For myself and a lot of the guys, that would see us out to retirement," said Douglas Hogge.

"We need to see this approved," he added.

Environmental campaigners strongly disagree. They've been trying to stop Rosebank for years, with some success.

"The future of the energy sector in the UK is renewable energy," said Tessa Khan, executive director of the campaigning group Uplift.

Consent for production at Rosebank was first granted under the Conservative government in 2023.

But in 2025, after a challenge by Greenpeace and Uplift, the Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled the approvals of the UK's largest known untapped oil field and Jackdaw were unlawful because they had failed to take into account the climate impact of actually burning the fossil fuels in cars, homes and factories.

The judge, Lord Ericht, said the fields' developers could carry on with work short of producing oil and gas while they provided more detailed environmental assessments for the government and regulators to consider.

"We think Rosebank would be a disastrous decision and a terrible deal for ordinary people across this country," said Khan, urging prime minister Andy Burnham to prioritise renewables in his quest to re-industrialise the nation.

"If the government's interested in building investor confidence, giving the green light to a major new oil field is going to do the opposite," she argued.

Whatever happens with Rosebank and Jackdaw, the long-term trend for the industry is clear and it is one of decline.

It's a quarter of a century since oil production peaked and in recent years jobs in oil and gas have been disappearing much faster than they're being created in renewable energy such as wind and solar power.

The oil from Rosebank would be loaded onto tankers via a gigantic hose and nozzle, which looks like the super-sized pump of an enormous floating filling station.

From there it would be sold on the international market and, most likely, taken to continental Europe for refining.

Opponents say that proves the project is of little benefit to the UK and should be rejected.

Supporters argue that's not the case because UK and European energy markets are co-dependent, adding that Rosebank will generate millions in tax for the Treasury.

Neil McCulloch, chief executive of Adura â which owns 80% of Rosebank and is a joint venture between Shell and the Norwegian state energy firm, Equinor â is optimistic.

He points out that Rosebank contains not just oil but gas which would be piped to Shetland and on to the St Fergus terminal in Aberdeenshire, with the potential to heat 500,000 British homes at peak production.

Approval of this project, argues McCulloch, could pave the way for four more Jackdaw-sized gas developments in the waters west of Shetland â Tornado, Tornado East, Tobermory and Suilven.

"We would like to proceed with them," he said.

A surge in fossil fuel production if Rosebank is approved is exactly what campaigners fear.

It would, argues Tessa Khan, exacerbate the deadly and damaging impact of climate change for British teachers, nurses, firefighters and families worried about their children while making "huge profits for companies that are already incredibly profitable".

The oil from Rosebank would be loaded onto tankers via a gigantic hose and nozzle

When it comes to the impending UK government decision â which sources have told BBC News should come before Christmas â there is a strange mood at Rosebank.

The decision in favour of Jackdaw has clearly encouraged many on board but it has also highlighted the jeopardy they are facing.

For now, most workers we spoke to said they were just focusing on the job, with its strange rhythms and unusual restrictions â no ability to pop to the shops, no alcohol, a lot of special occasions missed.

And for some on board, very particular cravings.

For steward Liam Davidson, it is a desire to see his French bulldog, Bailey, at the end of his fortnight on board.

"My wee dog's at the heliport when I arrive," he said, "I do miss her."

It is hoped the decision on Rosebank will be made in the next few weeks

For Nicola Boyd, it's her double bed and a pizza delivery.

"I love seeing the family, but for me, it's the pizza," she told me.

But this time there might be a delay in delivering Boyd herself.

She is coming to the end of her fortnight but, as she helped us into our survival suits, the Met Office issued an amber weather warning for much of Scotland.

For Rosebank, it seems, there are stormy seas ahead, one way or the another.

#470. La résidence de villégiature d'Adolf Hitler, "le nid d'aigle", incendiée en Bavière, un suspect arrêté

Recevez l'essentiel de l'actualité et restez à jour avec nos newsletters

Activez les notifications franceinfo et ne manquez rien de l’actualité

Construit entre 1937 et 1938 près de Berchtesgaden, le Kehlsteinhaus devait servir de bâtiment de représentation au dictateur nazi, qui s'y est très peu rendu.

Pour sauvegarder cet article, connectez-vous ou créez un compte franceinfo

Perchée sur un éperon rocheux au-dessus de Berchtesgaden, en Bavière, la résidence de Kehlsteinhaus est plus connue sous le nom du "nid d'aigle". Le bâtiment, qui a servi de lieu de villégiature à Adolf Hitler, a été incendié, samedi 24 octobre, a annoncé la police allemande. "Une personne suspecte a été placée en garde à vue", a-t-elle fait savoir, précisant que personne n'avait été blessé.

Aucune information n'a encore pu être donnée quant à la cause de l'incendie. "L'enquête de la police judiciaire est en cours", a déclaré la porte-parole de la police, Lisa Maier. Elle "vise actuellement à déterminer si cette personne est impliquée dans l'incendie". Une conférence de presse de la police est prévue dans la journée.

Selon les forces de l'ordre, un détecteur de fumée du bâtiment a déclenché l'alarme incendie vendredi vers 21h50. Au petit matin, le feu continuait de ravager le bâtiment, selon une caméra météo. Près de 200 pompiers sont mobilisés pour éteindre l'incendie de cette bâtisse, très difficile d'accès.

Construit entre 1937 et 1938 près de Berchtesgaden, le Kehlsteinhaus faisait partie de la "zone interdite du Führer" d'Obersalzberg et devait servir de bâtiment de représentation à Adolf Hitler, qui s'y est très peu rendu. Popularisé dans de nombreux films américains d'après-guerre, le bâtiment offre une vue exceptionnelle sur un pittoresque paysage de montagnes qui tranche avec l'horreur du IIIe Reich, dont les politiques antisémites, racistes et expansionnistes ont provoqué la mort de millions de personnes et conduit à la Shoah. Depuis 1952, le bâtiment est utilisé comme restaurant et une exposition retrace l'histoire de la maison.

#471. Vanessa Trump says she is cancer-free six months after revealing diagnosis

Vanessa Trump and her 19-year-old daughter Kai

Vanessa Trump, the former wife of Donald Trump Jr, has announced that she is cancer-free following her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year.

Trump, 48, who has five children with President Donald Trump's eldest son, shared in a short video on her 19-year-old daughter Kai's Instagram account that her recent tests results "came back clear, so I'm finally cancer-free".

Following the Instagram post on Friday, Vanessa and Kai Trump released a longer video on Saturday, in which they discussed breast cancer awareness, early detection and prevention.

Vanessa Trump separated from Trump Jr in 2018 and announced last year that she had begun dating US pro golfer Tiger Woods.

"October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, a time to raise awareness about early detection, education, and support for those affected by breast cancer," Kai Trump wrote on Instagram.

"I sat down with my mom and Dr. Nicole Saphier to talk about my mom's journey with breast cancer and learn more about prevention and early detection," she continued.

Kai's post received over 20,000 likes and hundreds of comments from people offering support and well wishes, including from American singer and media personality Mary Millben.

Vanessa Trump explained in the YouTube video that she experienced arm pain for several months before discovering a pea-sized lump in her breast, which testing confirmed was a cancerous tumour.

"It's a process you have to deal with," she said of the days spent waiting for her test results.

"You have to be mentally strong for yourself because you're going to need the strength to fight whatever challenge it is that's coming towards you."

Trump said she was first diagnosed with breast cancer in April. She publicly announced the diagnosis in May, saying in a social media post that she had undergone surgery and was working on a treatment plan with her medical team.

She eventually had a lumpectomy and radiation treatments, she said.

According to the American Cancer Society, the average risk of a woman in the US developing breast cancer is about 1 in 8, or 13%. The disease also accounts for 30% of all new female cancers every year, according to the group.

Surgery cures most breast cancers, but if some disease remains, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and endocrine therapy can reduce the long-term risk.

Treatments have been advancing, including more targeted therapies for early breast cancer, new types of hormonal therapies, and more precise and effective radiotherapy.

#473. A women's commune sounds like a great retirement option. But I have my doubts | Polly Hudson

Think back to those terrible flatshares in your 20s. Cohabiting with friends can seem like a dream, but the reality is sometimes less Golden Girls – more Young Ones

In most female friendships between women with male partners, the following occurs, sometimes regularly. It usually happens after one of them has delivered a passionate rant – or if not technically a rant, then certainly rant-adjacent. The women’s eyes lock, the instinctive understanding between the two of them undeniable, and then the one who has been complaining about her partner will say: “I wish I could just live with you instead.” If there are more than two women present, the conversation may move on to communes. There are inevitably wistful sighs.

That fantasy could become a reality. “Positive news” platform Upworthy has explored the phenomenon of gen X and boomer women playing the long game and pulling a Golden Girls: rather than living alone, post widowhood or divorce, they are moving in together.

This follows an article published by AARP (a US not-for-profit organisation that advocates and provides resources for people aged 50 and older) chronicling a retreat in New Mexico called … Golden Girls Weekend. Here, groups of women in their 50s to early 70s discussed the pros and cons of communal living. There have been four of these workshops so far, with another planned for next month. They are run by the Modern Elder Academy, a “midlife wisdom school”, and it has opened next month’s event to men. The academy’s founder, Chip Conley, explained that the focus was on women because he had found that they were more likely to have seriously discussed the idea. “You don’t see guys talking with their friends: ‘What if someday we can live together?’ You just don’t.” Funny, that.

In a reader opinion poll on preferred living arrangements that Upworthy ran alongside its story, the largest group (33.7%) chose the option “Next Door? Perfect. Same House? No”, with only 16.2% going for: “Absolutely, let’s start picking roommates.” The important clarification “Yes, but I need my own bathroom” was selected by 29.4%, but a not-inconsequential 20.7% opted out with: “I prefer my own space, thank you.”

As blissful as the idea of shacking up with my female friends – or anybody who occasionally closes a cupboard door and understands that items left on the stairs aren’t an interior design choice – sounds, I’m worried it would be a mistake in practice. Not all dreams are meant to come true.

Memories of twentysomething flatshares loom large, but at least at that point we were all trying to coexist as peacefully as possible. Famously, the best part of ageing is the reduction in caring what anyone thinks of you that occurs exponentially with each advancing year. This does not sound like a recipe for harmonious living – more like The Young Ones, but old.

I once had a flatmate who regularly enjoyed daytime intimacy with her boyfriend, always leaving her door wide open. Her room was next to the kitchen, so you couldn’t make toast without feeling you were involved in a menage a trois. They had a mostly physical relationship, and I have never been thinner. None of us ever said anything, because nobody wanted to be a spoilsport. We were in our 20s, finally away from our parents and free to act in a mortifying manner and never have to be aware of it.

Imagine that scenario in your 70s or 80s – there’s a Blanche in every friend group, after all. It’s unlikely that your cohabitants would keep stumm, out of jealousy if nothing else.

It is easy to be mates when you all have separate quarters to return to, but what if you are constantly together and there are crumbs on the counter, toothpaste in the sink, an empty milk bottle in the fridge? What if – horror of horrors, irony of ironies – they don’t close cupboard doors either? Living with blokes might be (ha, might be!) challenging, but, in truth, it’s never going to be a picnic making the compromises necessary for sharing a home with any human being. Even a woman.

Let’s not forget that pulling a Golden Girls didn’t work for the Golden Girls much of the time – that’s what put the “com” in the “sit”. It seems the best way to thank someone for being a friend is to retain separate addresses.

#474. The homeless man living in front of a London mega-mansion

Anders Fernstedt lives in London without any money. The Swedish native has built a most unusual home under the porch of a house worth over €200 million. How did that happen?

There's a lot of stopping and staring in Knightsbridge. This part of central London is within a stone's throw of Buckingham Palace, Hyde Park and Harrods, bringing inquisitive tourists in droves.

While it may not divert quite as many eyeballs as the seat of the British monarchy, a curious collection of plants, garden umbrellas, shopping bags and children's toys filling a building's entrance causes many a curious glance.

The peculiar arrangement on a grand portico is what Anders Fernstedt, a man from Sweden who fell on hard times, has been calling home for more than three years already.

That building hosting his makeshift setup was, just a few years ago, London's most expensive house.

The mega-mansion at 2-8A Rutland Gate sold in 2020 for a then-record £210 million (€244 million, $278 million) to Hui Ka Yan, the founder of China's Evergrande group, who was sentenced to life in prison last month.

Hui never moved in and the house was registered under his wife's name. The freezing of her assets means it can't be seized by liquidators and the house is in a state of limbo.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

So too was Fernstedt when he first stumbled across it. "I just thought, it would be a shelter for the night. I'm an avid camper, like an amateur botanist. I'm not afraid of nature," he told DW.

Fernstedt has never been inside the property, which appears to be in a state of disrepair. Instead, he gradually built his home in the portico, where grand columns guard the 45 rooms, indoor swimming pool and 116 windows. Year round he sleeps under the portico roof and a large umbrella which provides a hidden nook in which he's placed mattresses and bedding.

"I haven't had a bad night's sleep for as long as I can remember. And that goes for four seasons. It's not cold in the winter, and because I don't have walls, I get the breeze in the heat," he said.

"My conceit when I started was that sort of fake dream. Oh, I'm just a boy, my parents are in the house, everything's normal, I just asked them for permission to camp on the balcony."

Fernstedt was raised by his mother in Sweden before embarking on a range of careers at home and in the US, building a name for himself in the tech world.

In 2016, he moved to England where he worked as a journalist and fact checker at publications including The Economist, before work dried up around the time of the COVID pandemic.

A share in a tech company from his days in the US gave Anders a nest egg he relied on. But it couldn't last forever and he found himself living in a tent and then temporary accommodation, where he experienced violence and brushed up against people with severe addictions.

"Perhaps in this contemporary world, the biggest curiosity about my lifestyle is I'm completely off money," he said.

Fernstedt has built relationships with bakeries, cafes and florists in which he gets unused food, flowers for his home and use of power. He also makes use of a homeless charity in nearby Victoria for showers, clothing donations and socializing. But he's also made himself a broadly accepted part of one of London's most affluent neighborhoods.

"This is a very sophisticated neighborhood. I'd stayed for a few weeks and I knew everybody knew that I was here. And I thought, how can I sort of convey my presence without being present? And I thought, my constituency has to be the neighbors' children and grandchildren. Because if they plead my case at the kitchen table, my prospects improve," he said, by way of explaining the toys that line his abode.

"It is, in a way, a squirrel's nut collection," he added, when asked if he's worried about leaving his possessions out in the open. "I have so many nuts that I won't notice when something disappears."

There are some neighbors who do object to his presence, but Anders does his best to keep his home neat and his life quiet. Indeed, many others feel his presence prevents the house being a target for thieves or vandals. Overall though, he's found the community welcoming.

"Sometimes they introduce themselves asking what might I want or need. And my stock answer being: 'well, what you just gave me, a little bit of normal time, right? And neighborly banter'," he said. "Sometimes I'll be given food and very elegant Italian dinner jackets and clothes have arrived on a few occasions."

Not all homeless people in London have found such a stable lifestyle. Homeless charity Crisis estimates that there are over 200,000 people classified as homeless in England's capital, where "4,392 people were recorded sleeping rough in London between April and June, up from 4% on the same time last year. This is up 58% compared to 10 years ago."

According to government figures, there were 105,138 empty homes in London in 2025, or 1 in every 37 homes. Andy Burnham, who became British Prime Minister in July, has since vowed to offer "every rough sleeper in England a route off the streets by Christmas."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With such an enormous price tag, even after six years of being abandoned, Fernstedt knows that the house he lives at could potentially become untenable at virtually any moment.

But over the last few years, it's given him something he craved when pitching up his tent or being moved from one scary temporary residence to the next.

"I'm no longer really worried that I'll cycle around the corner and everything will be gone. Because I've been here so long, I'm free of worrying now, and if we worry too much, we won't be happy."

#475. Stade Toulousain : "On espère que ça va s'arrêter un jour" Dorian Aldegheri rejoint à son tour la longue liste de blessés

l'essentiel Dorian Aldegheri, pilier droit du Stade Toulousain, a quitté le terrain sur protocole commotion après dix minutes de jeu contre l'USAP. Victime d'une commotion cérébrale, il devrait être absent au moins dix jours, manquant le match contre la Section Paloise. Un nouveau joueur indisponible qui rejoint la liste impressionnante des blessés du club "rouge et noir".

Le pilier droit a dû quitter ses partenaires après à peine dix minutes de jeu. Dorian Aldegheri est sorti du terrain sur protocole commotion après un plaquage sur un joueur de l'USAP. Après être resté au sol pendant de longues secondes, le joueur a rejoint les vestiaires, s'appuyant sur deux membres du staff stadiste.

Remplacé par le jeune Tomas Rapetti, le joueur toulousain ne sera pas autorisé à reprendre sa place. Comme l'a expliqué l'entraîneur Laurent Thuery après la rencontre, le joueur de 33 ans a subi une commotion cérébrale. "Le protocole n'a pas été positif, mais je n'en sais pas plus pour l'instant", a-t-il expliqué. "On va avoir des nouvelles de Dorian en début de semaine, si ce n'est pas positif, bien sûr il sera forfait..."

À lire aussi : REPLAY. Stade Toulousain-Perpignan : Toulouse laisse filer la fin de match et le bonus offensif mais s'impose face à l'USAP ! Revivez le match de Top 14

Aldegheri va devoir observer une période de repos de 10 jours (minimum) et ne pourra pas prendre part au déplacement de dimanche prochain sur la pelouse de la Section Paloise. Il rejoint une impressionnante liste de joueurs indisponibles : Meafou, Menoncello, Flament, Ramos, Willis, Vergé, Mallia, Merkler, Marchand, Chocobares, Roumat, Ainu'u, Barassi et autres Delpy, Epée, ou Hawkes.

À lire aussi : Stade Toulousain : nouvelle alerte en deuxième ligne ! Joel Merkler à son tour touché et contraint au forfait face à Perpignan

Et en cette semaine où les internationaux vont rejoindre leurs sélections respectives, Tomas Rapetti a été convoqué par les Pumas. Le poste de pilier droit va, à l'image de la deuxième ligne, se trouver aussi à flux tendu. Après la rencontre, Matthis Lebel a eu la formule qui résume la pensée qui anime le Stade Toulousain en cet automne : "On espère que ça va s'arrêter un jour."

#476. Orkanböen möglich: Erster Herbststurm fegt über Deutschland - Verletzte und Bahnchaos

Bäume stürzen um, ein ICE wird abgeschleppt, mehrere Menschen werden verletzt: In Teilen Deutschlands richtet Sturmtief "Luise" Schäden an. Im Laufe des Tages lässt der Wind zwar nach. Doch am Abend zieht Sturmtief "Manja" heran. Eine Region dürfte besonders betroffen sein.

Nach dem ersten kräftigen Herbststurm des Jahres steht Deutschland ein weiterer stürmischer Tag bevor. Sturmtief "Luise", international "Austen" genannt, hat am Freitag vor allem im Westen und Südwesten Menschen verletzt und den Bahnverkehr stark behindert. Mit dem Orkantief "Manja" folgt der nächste Sturm. Besonders betroffen sein dürften die Nordseeküste und die Inseln.

Schwere Folgen hatte der Sturm in Nastätten im Rhein-Lahn-Kreis in Rheinland-Pfalz. Dort warf eine Böe am Freitagnachmittag ein Gestell um, während in der Nähe ein Oktobermarkt stattfand. Nach Angaben der Polizei wurden zwei Menschen schwer verletzt. Einer von ihnen schwebte in Lebensgefahr und wurde mit einem Hubschrauber in eine Klinik gebracht. In Seligenstadt im Kreis Offenbach traf ein abgerissener Ast einen Radfahrer, den die Feuerwehr befreien musste. Im saarländischen Lebach wurde ein Fußgänger von einem Werbeschild leicht verletzt.

Auf der Schiene kam es zu zahlreichen Störungen. Am Karlsruher Hauptbahnhof flog ein Gegenstand in die Oberleitung. Reisende berichteten von "massivem Funkenschlag". Bei Pforzheim prallte eine Regionalbahn mit Hunderten Fahrgästen an Bord gegen einen Ast und musste auf der Strecke stehen bleiben.

Bei Aachen blieb ein ICE mit 280 Fahrgästen nach einem Oberleitungsschaden liegen und wurde von einer Diesellok zum Bahnhof Stolberg geschleppt. Auch bei Neuss und in Stuttgart blockierten umgestürzte Bäume die Gleise. Allein im Saarland rückte die Polizei bis zum Abend zu 59 sturmbedingten Einsätzen aus. Der Europa-Park in Rust schloss vorübergehend seine großen Achterbahnen im Freien.

In Duisburg haben Sturmböen im gesamten Stadtgebiet Bäume zum Sturz gebracht. Einer stürzte auf einen Kiosk, an weiteren Stellen fielen Bäume in Stromleitungen, wie die Feuerwehr mitteilte. Bäume und Äste mussten demnach von Straßen entfernt werden. Eine Autofahrerin fuhr den Angaben zufolge in einen umgestürzten Baum. Verletzte gab es bisherigen Erkenntnissen zufolge nicht. Die Feuerwehr zählte rund 40 Sturmschäden-Einsätze, wie es hieß. Auch in Remscheid musste die Feuerwehr eigenen Angaben zufolge abgebrochene Äste und umgestürzte Bäume beseitigen. An der A1 stürzte ein größerer Baum gegen eine Lärmschutzwand. Die Autobahn wurde ihn Fahrtrichtung Köln zeitweise gesperrt.

Nach Angaben des Deutschen Wetterdienstes (DWD) zieht "Luise" im Laufe des Samstags Richtung Ostsee und Dänemark ab. Tagsüber lässt der Wind vorübergehend nach, an der Küste sind aber weiter Sturmböen möglich. Ab dem Abend zieht von Westen "Manja" heran. In der Nacht zum Sonntag drohen kräftiger Regen und stark auffrischender Südwestwind. Bis Sonntagvormittag kann laut DWD regional Regen in "unwetterartigen Mengen" fallen.

Der Sonntag wird nach DWD-Angaben außer im Südosten ein windiger bis stürmischer Tag. An der Nordsee sind Böen bis 100 Kilometer pro Stunde und einzelne Orkanböen möglich, ebenso am Feldberg im Schwarzwald. Das Bundesamt für Seeschifffahrt und Hydrographie erwartet von Sonntag bis Montag deutlich erhöhte Wasserstände. In Hamburg könnte eine Sturmflut auflaufen, dann würde der tiefer gelegene Teil des Fischmarkts überflutet. Wyk auf der Insel Föhr hat den Deichdurchlass am Hafen geschlossen.

Probleme gibt es auch für Urlauber zum Ende der Herbstferien in Niedersachsen. Die Schnellfähren nach Helgoland fahren am Wochenende nicht, die Halligen werden am Sonntag und Montag nicht angesteuert. Köln und Aachen raten, Wälder, Parks, Friedhöfe und Alleen zu meiden. In Erfurt bleiben die Friedhöfe das ganze Wochenende geschlossen. Am Montag soll sich das Wetter dann beruhigen.

#477. British woman dies trying to save sons on Bahamas snorkelling trip

Mother, 36, died after current off North Bimini reportedly swept away two boys, who were later rescued, police say

A British woman has died in the Bahamas while trying to rescue her two sons after a current swept them away as they were snorkelling.

The Royal Bahamas police force said it had launched an investigation after the death of a 36-year-old woman on Tuesday.

The force said they believed she was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island of North Bimini when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.

The police said that in an attempt to rescue her boys, “the woman was also swept away”. The children were later rescued from the water.

The Foreign Office said it was in contact with the woman’s family and was providing support.

Bimini is a small island group between the largest landmass in the Bahamas, Andros, and Miami in the US. It is the closest point in the Bahamas to the US mainland.

The islands are best known for once being home to Ernest Hemingway and are also home to a world-leading shark research centre.

In a statementposted on social media, the Royal Bahamas police force said: “According to the preliminary report, shortly after 10am, officers at the Alice Town police station received information that a female was unresponsive at the North Bimini ferry dock.

“Officers responded and, upon arrival, learned that the woman had been transported to the local clinic for medical attention, where she was subsequently pronounced dead by a local doctor despite efforts to save her life.

“Preliminary information indicates that the deceased was snorkelling with her husband and two sons near the southern point of the island when a strong current reportedly swept both children away.

“In an attempt to rescue her sons, the woman was also swept away.

“She was later rescued and transported to the ferry dock, where CPR was reportedly administered. Foul play is not suspected at this time.”

An autopsy would be carried out to help determine the exact cause of death, the statement said.

A Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office spokesperson said: “Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.

“We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family.”

#478. Doris Dörrie und "Frau Winkler": Sterbehilfe per Roboter?

Während die Welt über die Gefahren Künstlicher Intelligenz diskutiert, lotet die Filmemacherin Doris Dörrie aus, wie humanoide Roboter unseren Umgang mit Alter, Pflege und selbstbestimmtem Sterben verändern könnten.

Hamburg in naher Zukunft: Statt Paketboten bringen Roboter die Pakete, im Café fährt ein sprechender Servierwagen zwischen den Tischen umher, auf den Straßen begegnet man humanoiden Robotern, die Hunde ausführen; oder auch umgekehrt: Menschen, die einen Roboterhund spazieren führen. Ansonsten wirkt diese Welt erstaunlich normal.

In dieser Szenerie beginnt Doris Dörries neuer Film "Frau Winkler verlässt das Haus". Im Mittelpunkt steht eine ältere Dame, die nach einem Sturz nicht mehr alleine zurecht kommt. Doch ihre einzige Tochter kann die Pflege nicht dauerhaft übernehmen. Die Lösung scheint schnell gefunden: ein Pflegeroboter mit eingebautem EOL-Programm. EOL steht für "End of Life Mode", sprich: Der Roboter begleitet nicht nur durch den Alltag, sondern leistet unter bestimmten Voraussetzungen auch Sterbehilfe, nämlich wenn der Mensch dies selbst wünscht und medizinische Kriterien erfüllt sind.

Doris Dörrie greift in ihrem Film mit großer Leichtigkeit gleiche mehrere gesellschaftliche Schwergewichte auf: Es geht unter anderem um die Herausforderungen, vor denen alternde Gesellschaften wie beispielsweise Deutschland, Japan oder auch China stehen, es geht um das Thema selbstbestimmtes Sterben und eine Mutter-Tochter-Beziehung, die die Schuldfrage zwischen den Generationen stellt. Es sind Themen von universeller Relevanz, auch wenn die Handlung in Deutschland verankert ist.

"Ich schreibe das, was mich selbst bewegt und interessiert", sagt Doris Dörrie im Interview mit der DW. Dörrie zählt zu den bekanntesten deutschen Filmregisseurinnen der Gegenwart. Der Durchbruch gelang ihr 1985 mit der Komödie "Männer"; später machte sie unter anderem mit Filmen wie "Kirschblüten – Hanami" auch international auf sich aufmerksam.

Sterbehilfe gehört zu den komplexesten ethischen und gesellschaftlichen Fragen unserer Zeit. Entsprechend unterschiedlich fallen die Regelungen weltweit aus: Während einige Länder aktive Sterbehilfe unter bestimmten Voraussetzungen erlauben, ist in anderen jede Form der Beihilfe zum Sterben verboten und strafbar.

Doris Dörrie stellt mit ihrem Film die Frage: Was passiert, wenn eine KI beginnt auszurechnen, wie kostenintensiv die Pflege eines alten Menschen ist und ob sich diese Belastung für eine Gesellschaft noch "lohnt"? Der Grundgedanke an sich ist nicht neu, sagt Dörrie, und verweist auf die japanische Legende von Narayama, die auch im Film Erwähnung findet: Der Überlieferung zufolge war es die Aufgabe der ältesten Kinder, ihre betagten Eltern auf einen Berg zu bringen, um sie dort sterben zu lassen, weil die Nahrung nicht für alle ausreichte. "Und in der Diskussion befinden wir uns ja auch schon zum Teil: Können wir uns das überhaupt noch leisten, dass die Alten immer älter werden?"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Dörries Film darf der alte Mensch zwar ab einem bestimmten Gesundheitszustand selbst entscheiden, die Entscheidung aber dann auch nicht mehr zurücknehmen. Doch was genau heißt hier selbst entscheiden? "Das ist schon vertrackt", sagt Dörrie, denn die Frage sei ja, inwieweit man zu dieser Entscheidung auch gedrängt werde, "weil es dann nicht nur ökonomisch sinnvoller ist, sondern weil man auch für die Nächsten, also hier die Tochter, keine Belastung mehr ist?"

Der Film wirft diese Fragen teilweise indirekt und mit viel schwarzem Humor auf, etwa wenn die Pflegeberaterin von Frau Winkler das EOL-Feature als attraktive und vor allem unkomplizierte Zusatzoption anpreist, so dass man selbst gar nicht weiter tun müsse.

Doris Dörrie geht es nicht darum, die KI zu verteufeln. Ganz im Gegenteil. Im Film schafft es der Pflegeroboter, dem Frau Winkler den Namen "Pawlowitsch" gibt, dass die alte Dame wieder ein Stück Lebenslust gewinnt und tatsächlich das Haus verlässt - daher auch der Titel des Films.

"Wenn man durch Deutschland fährt, sieht man überall diese kleinen Einfamilienhäuschen, und in jedem zweiten Häuschen, wenn man sich die Statistik anschaut, lebt ein alter Mensch allein." Wenn KI hier helfen könne, warum nicht, sagt die Filmemacherin. Sie wolle genau diese Ambivalenz der Dinge untersuchen. "Die Dinge in Schwarz-Weiß einzuteilen, wäre sowieso nicht interessant und auch nicht richtig, glaube ich."

Sie selbst und das Filmteam hätten zudem beim Dreh erstaunt festgestellt, wie schnell man als Mensch eine Beziehung zu einem Roboter aufbauen könne. Sie erklärt sich das mit dem menschlichen Gehirn. "Wir halten alles, was sich bewegt und spricht, für ein Lebewesen. Wir können nicht anders." Und genau da müsse man hinschauen, so Dörrie, wenn man mit einer KI kommuniziere. "Wie sehr sind wir uns jedes Mal bewusst, dass wir mit einer Maschine reden und nicht mit einem Lebewesen? Das sind alles Dinge, die müssen wir jetzt erst lernen."

Schaut man sich die Entwicklung von KI an, zeigt sich, dass die Grenzen zwischen Mensch und Maschine immer mehr zu verschwimmen scheinen. Und genau deshalb ist es wichtig, darüber zu reden, so Doris Dörrie. Problematisch werde es ihrer Ansicht nach dort, "wo wir uns nicht mehr distanzieren und wo wir keine eigenen Gedanken mehr fassen". Als Menschen müssen wir uns die Frage stellen, so Dörrie, wer wir sind und was uns wirklich ausmacht. "Ich glaube, dass es einen großen Unterschied zwischen dem Roboter und uns gibt, und das ist das Spielen." Der Roboter könne ein Spiel vielleicht initiieren, "aber das Spielen an sich ist doch etwas zutiefst Menschliches, weil es erst mal sinn- und zweckfrei ist".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Neben diesen philosophischen Fragen, was das Menschsein ausmache, stellt die Filmemacherin im DW-Gespräch aber auch ganz konkret die Forderung nach KI-Regulierung in den Raum. "Wir haben auch über Atomwaffen irgendwann international geredet. Wir haben über alle möglichen Dinge in der Vergangenheit nicht nur geredet, sondern es auch geschafft, Lösungen zu finden." Und das müsse nun dringend angegangen werden. "Und ich glaube, dass wir uns da auch sehr beeilen müssen."

#479. Why the King's Caribbean tour could be 'biggest risk of his reign'

The planning is meticulous and dates back months, sometimes years, but there is always jeopardy.

King Charles III's visit to the Caribbean, which starts on Tuesday, takes him to three countries in nine days: the Bahamas, Guyana and finally Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (Chogm).

It also throws him directly into the heat of the debate over the payment of reparations - compensation from countries that took part in the slave trade - alongside questions of whether the King should be apologising for the UK's role in what he has previously described as an "appalling atrocity" that leaves an "indelible stain" on history.

"This is the biggest risk of his reign so far with so much just outside of his control," said author and historian Sir Anthony Seldon. "Questions about slavery, reparations and apologies mean the moral integrity of the monarchy is being questioned."

The King will make three significant speeches during the Caribbean trip and will follow government advice not to issue an official apology for Britain's role in the transatlantic slave trade.

A senior royal aide said that the King would "not shy away from the darkest days of our past" but stressed that decisions over apologies and reparations were matters for government.

The current Burnham administration, like those before it, will not pay reparations.

Buckingham Palace says that acknowledging the wrongs of the past will be built into the King's programme in all three countries.

But apologies, reparations, and republicanism are rich pickings for campaigners and protests are likely.

This is the reality for the King and Buckingham Palace, and they are accepting of it.

Those who've worked on the planning of the trip view protests as part of the open debate in the region and security preparations include their possibility.

Lurking in the back of Royal Household minds will also be memories of the last tour by senior royals to the Caribbean in the early part of 2022.

Then, as the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge, William and Catherine found themselves facing criticism over the optics of the trip - images of the royal couple reaching out to touch the outstretched hands of Jamaican children through a wire fence looked clumsy. Engagements designed as tributes to past royal visits appeared outdated. And protests also caused the cancellation of a small part of the schedule.

Everything will have been done to avoid those kinds of missteps on the 2026 Caribbean tour.

The Duke and Duchess of Cambridge shook hands with children through a wire fence during a visit to Trench Town on their 2022 tour

A woman holds a sign in protest as she waits for the arrival of William and Catherine on their tour

The leadership in the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda will celebrate the King and his work in protecting rainforests, creating cultural ties and reinforcing relationships around trade, energy, and agriculture.

But they do so against a backdrop of change.

The leaders of all three countries have voiced their support for reparatory justice.

In Antigua and Barbuda and the Bahamas, where the King is head of state, the conversation about becoming a republic has significant support.

Elected officials in the former no longer have to pledge allegiance to the King ending a 40-year tradition of swearing loyalty to the monarch.

"He pulled off an extraordinary triumph with President Trump in his US visit earlier this year and stood up to him and put him in his place in a way that no leader has done - while not incurring his wrath," said Sir Anthony. "If he can deal with the delicate nature of this trip for him personally, for the British monarchy, and the future of the Commonwealth, it could be an enormous success."

This Caribbean tour has to cut through a sea of royal distractions.

The King has spent much of the past three months in Scotland, where he is based over the summer.

It should have been a quieter time in the royal calendar, but it has been quite the opposite.

The surprise return of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex to the UK has been noisy. The level of coverage Harry and Meghan get is unsettling and, at times, irritating for the Royal Family.

The King's youngest son has not yet seen his father in person, but they are said to have talked.

Then enter Earl Spencer, the King's former brother-in-law, with his memoir, Swan Song, criticising the King's response to the death of Diana, Princess of Wales. It triggered a strong pushback from the Palace.

And in recent days, the serious claims made about Meghan's father, Thomas Markle, have drawn his daughter into a complex tale involving global police forces, sexual abuse allegations and further family trauma.

An impactful and successful Caribbean tour is a chance to switch focus.

But if royal stories back home are running hot, it can be hard to focus minds on the King's engagements over four thousand miles (6,437km) away.

Harry and Meghan's return to the UK has received a lot of coverage

Former Foreign Secretary David Lammy, who has strong family ties to the Caribbean, has accompanied the King on a number of trips outside the UK.

"He is our head of state. He is amongst some of the most recognisable figures in the world. For a small country like Guyana, the validation of a state visit is huge," said the Tottenham MP whose father came to the UK from what was then British Guiana and who also has relatives in Antigua and Barbuda. "My mother would forever recall the Queen's visit in 1996."

But there was also a recognition of that royal trip jeopardy.

"Knowing Guyana, Antigua and Barbuda as well as I do, he will be overwhelmingly received positively," Lammy said. "But these are lively democracies in which of course there will be some dissent."

A transatlantic flight, three countries over nine days and about 36 separate engagements when you're closing in on your 78th birthday is an intense schedule. It is also a reminder that the King is still dealing with a cancer diagnosis and having regular treatment. Buckingham Palace has reiterated its position that he is on a "positive trajectory".

Queen Camilla will only accompany the King on the Antigua and Barbuda leg of the visit for Chogm and a number of other engagements, including some around her own areas of interest â literacy and supporting efforts to end violence against women and girls.

The Queen, who will be 80 next July, is known to find the pace and hot conditions of some royal tours gruelling.

This is a trip that comes with potential pitfalls but also the possibility of great reward for the King.

"The King can be an extraordinarily empathetic and in tune figure," Sir Anthony said.

Pour sauvegarder cet article, connectez-vous ou créez un compte franceinfo

Le RN joue la continuité. Le congrès du Rassemblement national s'est ouvert à Orléans, samedi 24 octobre en début d'après-midi, avec la réélection sans surprise de Jordan Bardella à la tête du parti d'extrême droite. Seul candidat à sa succession, il a obtenu près de 98,98% des voix, avec un taux de participation proche de 68%.

Le sortant a recueilli 75 497 suffrages, contre à peine 779 bulletins blancs, selon les résultats annoncés par le député Yoann Gillet, chargé de l'organisation du congrès. Jordan Bardella va ainsi tenter de tourner la page de ces dernières semaines marquées notamment par des accusations d'écrits antisémites.

Avant la proclamation de son élection, Jordan Bardella avait remercié ses militants. "Une fois de plus, je vais avoir besoin de vous (...) pour conduire Marine Le Pen à l'Elysée", avait-il déclaré. En marge du congrès, une longue matinée de contre-manifestation a réuni dans le calme entre 13 000 personnes et 26 000 personnes.

#481. Three released without charge after fatal arson attack in Ireland

Flowers have been left at the home where four people died after an arson attack in Waterford

Three people, who were arrested in connection with a suspected arson attack which killed four family members in the Republic of Ireland, have been released, gardaÃ­ (Irish police) have said.

Philip and Kim English and two of their children - nine-year-old Jayden and 12-year-old Callum - died after their home in Birch Avenue, on the outskirts of Waterford was set on fire earlier this month.

A man aged in his 20s and a woman in her 30s were previously charged in connection with the attack.

On Saturday, gardaÃ­ said three people - two women in their 30s and a man in his 50s - who were arrested on Tuesday have been released without charge.

A fourth person, a man in his 20s who was arrested on Thursday, remains in custody.
