#483. The moment I knew: I admitted I had a crush on her. She replied, ‘Well, that’s good. Isn’t it?’

Actors Peter Houghton and Anne Browning played lovers onstage, but a shared sense of humour and a magazine horoscope flipped the script on their real-life relationship

Find more stories from the moment I knew series

Anne and I met in Melbourne in 1997 when we were cast in a production of Hamlet. We were both single and playing onstage lovers. The first time I saw her in the Melbourne Theatre Company cafeteria, she had a sleepy, grumpy face. I still recall those intense, slightly scary green eyes looking at me. I thought to myself: she is very attractive, but also quite formidable.

At first it was a little awkward, but humour was the key. We’d sit on the dusty rehearsal room floor in our tracksuits while the director was working with another actor. Instead of practising our lines, we’d flip through the faded 70s magazines left in the corner and make jokes about what the models in flares or with chopped beards might be saying as they shot the images.

One day by chance I flipped to the horoscopes. I asked Anne what the stars could have in store for us in 1972. She told me her sign was Scorpio – the same as mine. My aim was just to laugh at the bullshit of horoscopes but when I read it out, it stopped me cold: “You have met someone now through work who will be one of the most important people in your life, perhaps a partner and soulmate.”

It was weird and uncanny but we just laughed it off. I felt embarrassed because it sounded like some kind of calculated romantic ploy. I quickly flicked to the next page but somewhere in my brain I knew it was the truth.

Later, when the show was well under way, we were walking along St Kilda Road after a performance. We stopped at the lights and I summoned the courage to say: “I think I’ve got one of those crushes on you.” She looked at me and said: “Well, that’s good. Isn’t it?”

I took her cryptic and understated response as confirmation she felt the same way. It is very much her style – and I liked that it had a question mark on the end of it.

After the show closed our connection grew and we officially became a couple, filling our days and nights with dinner and theatre dates. She was living with her sister and I was living in this big groovy warehouse in Richmond with other actors. I liked that when she’d come to my place, the bohemian setting made me look a bit more impressive and artistic than I was.

Early on, we went on a hiking trip to Wilsons Prom. We were massively overpacked and it quickly emerged that neither of us was good at camping. As soon as we got back to the car we made a beeline to KFC and gorged ourselves on fried chicken after days of miserable camping stodge, secretly thankful we weren’t in nature any more.

Anne was violently ill all the way back – all that rich food after rehydrated dust! We both exposed ourselves as kind of daggy on that trip, and that was OK.

Anne and I share a clown-like heart that over the decades has helped us through hard times. Big life events like losing a parent have been somewhat easier because there’s a levity and lightness Anne brings – never letting me go into the dark places or stay there for too long.

Since meeting in that rehearsal room we’ve spent almost 30 years together, had two children and performed all over the world. Romantic love has its seasons, but really loving someone also has to do with trust. I trust her implicitly, she trusts me, and we don’t let each other down. We always show up for each other when it matters. We help each other realise our own dreams. That’s the thing about having a teammate you can rely on – it’s priceless.

We met working with each other as theatre artists, which we’re still doing now after all these years. A magazine from the 70s with an out-of-date horoscope written by a charlatan brought us together. I don’t believe in horoscopes … but I do believe in that one.

Peter Houghton, Anne Browning and Tom Gutteridge perform in the world premiere of Crapbox, showing from 27 October to 7 November at the Explosives Factory in St Kilda, Melbourne.

#484. The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future

The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future

Furious protesters are denouncing Israeli security forces as "Nazis" - but this is not a scene from a pro-Palestinian rally on the streets of London or Paris. This clash is in the heart of Israel, in which hundreds of ultra-Orthodox men in white shirts, black fedoras and long black frock coats face off against the military police.

The flashpoint is a building in the city of Modi'in, midway between Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, where a young ultra-Orthodox Jewish (or Haredi) man lives. The police have come to arrest him after he failed to report for military service.

The clash in early October, seen by the BBC in a video, is one of many in recent months in which one of the deepest schisms in Israeli society has become ever more exposed.

This widening fault line is playing out against the backdrop of the wars Israel is currently fighting, including the unresolved conflict against Hamas in Gaza - as well as increasing violence by extremist settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

Once a tiny minority, the ultra-Orthodox remain a group apart even as their numbers expand year by year. Currently, they are estimated to make up about 14% of the population, and the birth rate within the community remains far higher than among other Israelis. If their numbers continue to grow at a similar rate, they could make up one-third of the Jewish Israeli population by 2050.

As the ultra-Orthodox community becomes bigger, so has the debate around the expense of supporting them with stipends so they can devote themselves to full-time religious study. Subsidies to the group are estimated to cost the government 35bn shekels (Â£8.4bn) per year and, until recently, they were exempted from military service.

Now they're no longer an insignificant minority, they're facing pressure to engage more with wider Israeli society.

Ultra-Orthodox Jews have staged many protests against being drafted into the military

National security and the economy are two of the key issues this election. That means the division between the ultra-Orthodox and the majority of Israelis who believe they are not contributing their fair share to either is starker than ever.

With no outright majority likely for any current political alliance, and the future of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in doubt, the role of smaller parties - including Haredi parties - will once again be crucial in deciding who will govern Israel.

To have any chance of staying in power, Netanyahu needs to keep the ultra-Orthodox parties on side, however much pressure there is within Israel for their special status to be diminished.

From the ultra-Orthodox perspective, their social contract with the Israeli state is increasingly coming under pressure. Their all but exclusive focus on the study of Judaism's religious texts - such as the Torah, the Jewish Bible - means their education system is separate and many Haredim are not part of Israel's workforce.

For the ultra-Orthodox, the biggest issue of all is holding on to the exemption from serving in the IDF for students at traditional religious - or yeshiva - institutions. This dates back to the earliest days of the Israeli state when the Haredim were a miniscule community of survivors struggling to rebuild from the near extinction of the Holocaust.

But as Israel has become more embattled after the attacks of October 7, fighting wars on several fronts, their near complete absence from the country's conscription army has become more controversial.

Religious students and their rabbis believe that if young ultra-Orthodox men enter the military, they will be exposed to influences and behaviours that may decisively turn them away from their community. Beyond that, they believe that their staying true to the traditions of their community is vital for the very survival not only of Israel but the Jewish people.

When asked not long after October 7 why the ultra-Orthodox didn't contribute more to the military in such an emergency, one of the community's most senior leaders, Rabbi Dov Landau, said that not only should religious students not serve in the army, but they shouldn't even visit the wounded or attend the funerals of soldiers.

The Haredi birth rate is higher than in the rest of Israeli society

The rabbi said that in a time of such danger, only Torah students could protect Israel spiritually. "Salvation only comes through Torah learning, orderly Torah learning. And any neglect of or disruption to Torah learning, woe and alas for what will happenâ¦ The more Torah learners multiply, the more Torah learners increase their learning, the better. They protect us."

It would be a considerable understatement to say that this view is not shared by wider Israeli society. Polls have shown public support for conscripting the ultra-Orthodox surge throughout the war in Gaza. Many see it as a dereliction of responsibility by the Haredi community, made all the more galling by the fact that such a stance comes at the expense of taxpayers. The IDF has bemoaned a deficit in manpower, while many Israelis have had to serve hundreds of days in the past three years.

Dahlia Scheindlin is a leading political consultant and pollster in Israel. She says this issue is critical for Netanyahu and is key to understanding this moment in Israeli society against the backdrop of the war in Gaza, particularly among the political right. "Really the most burning, more immediate issue is the right-wing communities who are furious at the government for protecting the blanket exemption from the IDF at a time when, especially among the right, but really everybody in the Jewish community in Israel, is serving and many dying in these wars."

Two years ago, the Supreme Court ruled that the exemption for ultra-Orthodox men from serving in the military was effectively null and void. That could have meant that those dedicated to full-time religious study would now be drafted.

The reaction from the Haredi community was one of fury. Hundreds of thousands of Haredim held protests, blocking the main highways. And as with the incident in Modi'in, they tried to prevent the arrest of religious students for evading conscription. Protests have continued off and on, and densely-populated Haredi areas are often the backdrops for confrontation with the security forces.

This is a row that is playing out in the election.

There are two parties that have traditionally represented the Haredi community. One is United Torah Judaism â or UTJ â and represents Ashkenazi Jews, or Jews of European origin. The other is Shas, which was formed later and represents the Sephardi and Mizrahi â Jews from North Africa and the Middle East. They share a core agenda, which puts religious study above all else, including any questions around relations with the Palestinians.

Both UTJ and Shas have been part of Netanyahu's coalition - and they used their political clout to find ways to try to block enforcement of the Supreme Court ruling. On several occasions, they threatened to pull out of the alliance and bring the government down. UTJ acted on this but continued to support the government from outside, while Shas remained within the coalition.

Centre-right politician Gadi Eisenkot, who's shaped up as Netanyahu's main rival in this month's election, does not support their stance. He has made clear his belief that the idea of the ultra-Orthodox constituting a separate state within Israel with its own rules has become increasingly toxic. "A country that sends its best sons and daughters to fight and sacrifice their lives cannot tolerate a reality in which a state within a state exists," he said.

All this has meant that the issue of conscription exemption for ultra-Orthodox men is the number one priority on the electoral agenda of both Shas and UTJ.

A recent remark by a UTJ parliamentary candidate, Eliakim Stark, has raised the temperature further. He compared the plight of ultra-Orthodox men evading the military draft to the persecution of Jews during the Holocaust. It triggered furious rebukes from opposition leaders from across the political spectrum.

Daniel Goldman, an activist who specialises in Haredi issues, says that the two main Haredi parties feel increasingly embattled and less open to compromise.

He says the ultra-Orthodox don't believe that the state really needs their boys to bolster numbers. "It's at least partly down to the fact that the Haredi parties see the state as wanting to take their boys out of the community and change them from ultra-Orthodox to either regular religious or secular, God forbid, as they perceive it," he says. "And so in that environment of tension, they've actually hardened their positions."

Yitzhak Goldknopf from the UTJ, a former minister, has gone so far as to issue an ultimatum: "The Haredim will not change their way of life because there is an army and a war... If there is no choice and they must leave the country, they will leave."

But this is having a clear impact on the electoral fortunes of the Netanyahu coalition - of which Shas in particular has long been a key part. Without them, Netanyahu's alliance would fall short of the more than 60 seats needed for a majority in the Knesset.

Dahlia Scheindlin, the Israeli pollster, says that the refusal to give up the draft exemption by Shas and UTJ is damaging Netanyahu's coalition. "It is one of the main reasons why the coalition is unable to win back the kind of support that they had in 2022 when they won 64 seats," she says. "They're currently polling at about 50 to 52 seats."

All Netanyahu's challengers advocate for ending the ultra-Orthodox exemption and cutting funds to institutions or individuals who refuse the draft. On the left, Yair Golan has called for an immediate mobilisation of those who are eligible.

Benjamin Netanyahu is relying on Haredi support which may not materialise

So, despite statements from Shas and UTJ that they would switch allegiance from Netanyahu if he were to dilute his support, there seems for now nowhere else for them to go.

Anshel Pfeffer has been a leading commentator on the Israeli political scene for years - now mainly as the Economist's correspondent in Israel. He says Netanyahu's position looks shaky. "There are two things that are bringing together the current opposition bloc," he says. "One is obviously they want to replace Netanyahu and the other is they are capitalising on this really hostile environment nowadays towards the ultra-Orthodox, mainly over the issue of the draft to the army.

"Netanyahu has been willing for many years, to basically give the ultra-Orthodox whatever they want. They're not going to get that from the opposition."

Into this arena of resentment and intransigence, a new Haredi party has emerged this year, presenting itself as a break with the traditional mindset of Shas and UTJ.

Essentially, the Haredi Public Party is offering a compromise in which the ultra-Orthodox would contribute more to Israel as a whole while maintaining the core of their identity.

For the first time in the ultra-Orthodox community, it is also fielding two female candidates.

One of them, Ziva Ginz, explained to the BBC her party's position on the military draft. Key to it is men serving being allowed to remain culturally Haredi. "Anyone whose life is genuinely devoted to full-time Torah study should be able to continue learning. Everyone who isn't sitting and studying for a full day should serve alongside the rest of Israeli youth, in frameworks where a young man can enter as a Haredi and finish as a Haredi," she says.

But it may be too soon for such efforts at compromise to make an impact this election.

Anshel Pfeffer says that it's difficult to sway the base vote in the ultra-Orthodox community, where most still essentially follow what their rabbi says they should do.

"And once people are voting for other parties, they won't necessarily do so for another Haredi party," Pfeffer explains. "That's why we're seeing people like [far-right leader and National Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir making inroads in the Haredi community, because he's the only non-Haredi party leader who actually talks to young Haredi. Basically, every other party in Israel doesn't even try."

Ben-Gvir is making inroads with Haredi voters

This is reflected in the polls, which show his Jewish Power party is making gains.

If Ben Gvir's actions are increasingly seen as tainting Israel's international image with his support for policies such as annexing the occupied West Bank, his hard-right message is attracting a bigger core of support within the country. His ultra-nationalist ethos is not one that traditionally overlaps with policies of the Haredi parties, but they share a position on the right of Israeli politics.

So for some ultra-Orthodox voters looking for a new political home, Ben Gvir represents the nearest alternative. His self-portrayal as a strong man unafraid to take an extreme position against those he perceives as Israel's enemies in the face of international condemnation may attract some already leaning to the far right in the Haredi community.

Gadi Eisenkot has been firm in his support for Haredi Jews serving in the military

No alliance appears close to achieving a majority, however, so there is bound to be a lot of horse trading to secure a workable coalition after the vote.

Netanyahu will naturally apply his exceptional political skills to trying to find one way or another to stay in power.

As ever, that leaves the smaller parties with the ability to play the role of kingmaker. That's a role that the ultra-Orthodox parties have been known for in the past. But this time they may not be the decisive factor.

"The truth is, any small party can become a kingmaker," Dahlia Scheindlin says. "I don't think it would take too much to lure the Haredi parties away from Netanyahu... The thing is, though, I don't think the opposition parties will want to lure them in unless they have some promise that they're really prepared to make serious concessions on the draft. The opposition parties are absolutely staking their platforms and their promise to the voters on that issue."

This time, rather than being the kingmakers, it may turn out that the ultra-Orthodox parties help bring down the king.

#485. Rubio tells Cubans ‘now is the time’ to act to see political change

US secretary of state makes comments after Trump tells US rally warships could intervene on return from Iran

Marco Rubio urged Cubans seeking political change in their country to act, saying “now is the time” moments after Donald Trump told a Friday rally for candidates in south Florida that US warships could intervene in Cuba on their way back from the Iran war.

The US secretary of state, in his social media post addressed “to those who seek to create positive change”, urged Cubans to capitalize on Trump’s plans. “The disappointment of failed promises, corruption, and the privileged lives of only a few; seize this opportunity to create the change you desire through a discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA,” Rubio said.

The top US diplomat, whose parents left Cuba for the United States before the socialist revolution there, seemed to mistakenly use the word “discrete”, meaning separate, rather than “discreet”, meaning private or secret.

Trump first floated this idea earlier this year, but has not mentioned it in recent months. But he revived it in response to a shouted question from the crowd about the island nation. He was campaigning just days before midterm elections in which voters have expressed concern about the impact the US war on Iran has had on prices of goods from gas to groceries.

“We’ll do a little stopover,” Trump said. “Actually, what we’re going to do with Cuba is, we’re going to come back from Iran. Those beautiful ships will pass Cuba. We’ll have one of them stop about 50 yards off the coast. They’ll raise up their hands. And then we’re going to send Marco Rubio in to finish up the deal.”

Havana on Friday mocked the “desperation” of the US following the comments made by Rubio and Trump.

“Now the United States is resorting to public recruitment for the CIA,” Cuban deputy foreign minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio wrote on X.

“There must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste.”

Rubio and Trump have been bullish on action in Cuba, with Trump previously suggesting the country would “be next” in terms of intervention abroad, following the winding down of the Iran war he has long forecast but which has not yet happened.

In May, he and Rubio raised the specter of US military intervention in Cuba, a renewed threat that took on greater weight after the administration announced criminal charges against the island’s former leader, Raúl Castro. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that previous US presidents had considered intervening in Cuba for decades but that “it looks like I’ll be the one that does it”.

Rubio told reporters separately that Cuba had been a national security threat for years because of its ties to US adversaries and that Trump was intent on addressing it. While saying the Trump administration wanted to resolve differences with Cuba peacefully, Rubio voiced doubts that the US could reach a diplomatic resolution with the island’s current government.

Rubio has not addressed Cuba in depth in public for several weeks, with his last comments coming in a 29 September interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity.

“The truth is Cuba has already fallen. It doesn’t have a functional economy and it’s governed by people who continue to preach about some revolution that has been dead for 20 years that’s never worked,” Rubio said, without alluding to any CIA operation.

“We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path. We are hopeful … that there will be some people in there that open their eyes to the reality of what they’re facing. We’re never going to allow Cuba to become a base of operation against American interests or pose a threat to our national security. On that we are abundantly clear.”

Rubio and other top Trump aides have met with Cuban officials in recent months to explore possible improvements in relations. But the US side has come away unimpressed from those talks, leading to even more sanctions imposed on the Cuban government.

During his address to the United Nations general assembly last month, Trump said Rubio – son of Cuban immigrants, who has long taken a hard line against Cuba’s socialist leadership – was “deep into negotiations with Cuba”, saying he would “not allow a haven for foreign adversaries to threaten America on our own doorstep”.

Days later, Trump told reporters that he anticipated that the two countries “will make a deal”, adding: “I don’t think we’ll need the military. Cuba is failing very badly.”

Earlier this week, the two countries clashed at the United Nations as the Trump administration sought once again to build opposition for an upcoming annual vote condemning Washington’s decades-long economic embargo against Havana.

Cuba has struggled since 2020 with an economic and energy crisis. Its gross domestic product has shrunk , and its 10 million residents have endured blackouts, food shortages and inflation. There have been waves of protests, and hundreds of thousands of Cubans have immigrated, many to the United States.

#486. What Earth's sixth mass extinction event means for humans

Human activity is driving plants and animals to extinction at an unprecedented rate. As countries meet in Armenia to discuss ways to reverse nature loss, DW reveals how declining biodiversity is already harming people.

From the tiniest microbes in the human gut to giant whales in the ocean, biodiversity is the sum of all life on the planet. It's another word for nature. And because nature is like a team, every player has a job.

When various species from trees to animals work together, they regulate weather, maintain soil health, purify water and support food production. These benefits are known as ecosystem services and they underpin human well-being.

"It is really an abstract concept, but we experience it absolutely every day," said Rebecca Shaw, chief scientist at conservation group WWF. "And we almost never think about it when nature is functioning."

But as biodiversity declines, Shaw and other scientists are calling on the world to really think about it. Because biodiversity is struggling as humans push ecosystems to the brink through intensive farming, burning fossil fuels and pollution from sources like plastic and chemicals.

Over the past 52 years, monitored vertebrate populations have collapsed by an average of 73%, while freshwater ecosystems are faring worse with a drop of 85%, according to WWF's recent Living Planet report.

It tallies with other studies that show a million animal and plant species face extinction unless humanity reduces its pressure on nature.

"It is a really steep decline," said Shaw. "What it's telling us is that nature is in trouble, and it's an early warning indicator that the fabric of life that we depend on for freshwater and food and for clean air is unraveling."

Some 200 countries are gathering in Yerevan, Armenia over the next two weeks for COP17, the latest UN biodiversity summit, to advance commitments to reverse nature's unraveling by 2030. But progress toward those targets remains insufficient, with funding and implementation among the biggest challenges.

Take wetlands as an example. Some 85% of these vital ecosystems disappeared between 1700 and 2000. One study from Canada's University of Waterloo found that habitats like marshes and swamps in southern Ontario provide C$4.2 billion (€2.63 billion) worth of water filtration services each year, removing nutrients like phosphorus and keeping drinking water sources clean.

The study found that as they disappear, water quality worsens, which massively increases the cost of treating it.

Another example is the decline in pollinators like bees and bats. More than 75% of global food crop types rely in part on animal pollination.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

At the same time, soil and ecosystem degradation coupled with storms and heat waves linked to climate change are already damaging harvests. A recent UK government report stated that every critical ecosystem is on a "pathway to collapse," warning that nature's decline posed a grave threat to global food supply and geopolitical stability.

"The UK, like many other countries, relies on imports for much of the food and so is reliant on ecosystems around the world," said Louise McRae, a research fellow at the Zoological Society of London, who also contributed to WWF's Living Planet report. "This is why we need to care about global biodiversity."

Nature also provides the basis for many modern human medicines, with some 50% coming from natural compounds.

Penicillin, the first antibiotic, is produced by a mold and is estimated to have saved over 500 million lives. Before its discovery, a person could die from a simple cut. Around 70% of cancer drugs come from natural products or synthetic compounds "inspired by nature," according to the World Health Organization.

As biodiversity disappears, humans risk losing access to undiscovered treatments.

To return to the "nature as a team" metaphor, if a player disappears, sometimes a species with similar functions in the ecosystem can jump in as a substitute.

But not always, particularly if it's a "keystone species." They play a disproportionately large role in their environments, and their disappearance has significant knock-on effects.

The oyster is one such species. Wild oyster populations are facing massive declines, while 85% of their reefs have been lost worldwide. An adult oyster filters up to 50 gallons of water a day.

"No one would ever think they did anything but sit in a shell and be slimy," said Shaw. "But you lose oysters, you can lose water filtration and clean water, you can lose the habitat for many other species that we interact with or sometimes consume."

And, said Shaw, the humble oyster protects coastal communities from storm surges. If you lose it "you lose the coastal protection."

The loss of a single species can also lead to more disease. One study suggests a decline in red foxes in North America is linked to the spread of Lyme disease, a tick-borne illness that also affects humans.

Extinction is a natural process. But the planet has experienced five mass extinctions, when a large proportion of species globally disappeared over a short geological period. The rate at which species are disappearing today suggests Earth is experiencing a sixth event driven largely by human activity, according to scientists.

Both McRae and Shaw called the declines extremely worrying, but said they shouldn't provoke despair.

Though she acknowledges that the underlying global trend is moving in the wrong direction and cannot be ignored, McRae said "the statistics are there to just motivate us to action rather than to cause alarm."

And the Living Planet report also highlights conservation successes, showing that nature can recover.

The number of green sea turtles, for example, had fallen significantly, but has now bounced back. This is thanks to a massive worldwide effort to protect nesting beaches and changes to fishing practices that reduce accidental capture.

Sea otters are another example. Prized for their fur, in the 1800s they were hunted to near extinction on the US Pacific Coast. When they disappeared, it meant sea urchins had no predators, leaving them free to decimate kelp forests.

That matters because as well as providing habitat for other species, these giant underwater groves protect coastlines from storm surges and absorb carbon, making them important for climate protection.

Following a ban on commercial hunting, sea otters have also rebounded, helping kelp forests recover.

"You can see that ripple effect that really had an obvious and a measurable impact. But critically, it can be reversed," said McRae, adding that biodiversity loss and climate change are intertwined and exacerbate each other but have joint solutions.

"We're learning how to turn things around at very small scales," said Shaw. "Now the real challenge is to turn things around at very big scale so we can see it in the global indicators."

#487. Manifestations du 24 octobre : "C'est pas une voiture qui va nous arrêter !" À Albi, plus d'un millier de manifestants contre la vie chère bravent l'interdiction préfectorale

Article rédigé par Nawel Omara

l'essentiel Pouvoir d'achat, éducation, démocratie : la colère a dépassé la seule question de la vie chère dans les rues d'Albi (Tarn). Ce samedi 24 octobre 2026, plus d'un millier de personnes ont défilé dans les rues de la cité épiscopale. Une mobilisation marquée par le passage du cortège dans le centre historique, malgré l'interdiction préfectorale.

"On y arrivera, on ne fait pas ça pour rien !" Ce samedi 24 octobre 2026, dès 14 heures, les Albigeois se sont retrouvés au kiosque du Jardin national pour l'acte II de la mobilisation contre la vie chère. Les syndicats ont estimé la participation entre 2 000 et 3 000 personnes, contre environ 1 500 selon les renseignements territoriaux.

À Albi, entre 2 000 et 3 000 personnes étaient présentes selon les syndicats, tandis que les renseignements territoriaux en dénombraient environ 1 500. DDM - N.O.

Les revendications ont, quant à elles, largement dépassé la seule question du pouvoir d'achat. Éducation, conditions de travail, inquiétudes pour la démocratie et lutte contre le fascisme ont également marqué cette journée. Lycéens, étudiants, parents et mères de famille ont ainsi défilé côte à côte au nom de la "convergence des luttes".

Depuis le Jardin national, la foule s'est élancée pour un parcours d'environ quatre kilomètres. Mais au pied de la cathédrale, alors qu'ils devaient emprunter la passerelle, les manifestants en tête, majoritairement des lycéens, ont décidé de poursuivre dans le centre historique malgré l'arrêté préfectoral pris la veille. Celui-ci interdisait les manifestations dans plusieurs secteurs d'Albi, dont le centre historique et les Lices Georges-Pompidou.

Les manifestants ont défilé dans le centre historique malgré l'interdiction prefectoral. DDM - N.O.

"C'est pas une voiture qui va nous arrêter", a lancé l'un d'eux au mégaphone. Malgré la présence des policiers, le groupe a forcé le passage et pénétré dans le périmètre interdit, sans que la situation ne dégénère. Les manifestants ont ensuite changé une nouvelle fois d'itinéraire et renoncé à passer par le rond-point de l'Arquipeyre. Leur objectif : rejoindre la préfecture et contester l'arrêté.

Devant le bâtiment, ils se sont assis et ont chanté en chœur : "Même si Macron ne veut pas, nous, on est là." Le cortège a ensuite poursuivi sa route jusqu'au rond-point Jean-Jaurès, où les manifestants ont bloqué la circulation pendant quelques minutes. La mobilisation a finalement pris fin aux alentours de 16 h 30, place du Vigan, où les manifestants se sont dispersés.

#488. Eine Welt ohne Hunger rückt in weite Ferne

Kriege und Klimakrise betreffen vor allem in Afrika immer mehr Menschen. Die Folgen: Flucht, Vertreibung und Hunger. Zwei aktuelle Berichte liefern Fakten und Empfehlungen an die Weltgemeinschaft.

Der Zeitpunkt für die Veröffentlichung des Welthunger-Index und des Hunger-Reports ist kein Zufall, denn Mitte Oktober, am 16.10.1945, wurde die Ernährungs- und Landwirtschaftsorganisation der Vereinten Nationen (FAO) gegründet. Ihr Ziel: die weltweite Ernährung sicherzustellen. Darum aber ist es nach Einschätzung der Hilfsorganisationen "Welthungerhilfe" und der "Aktion gegen den Hunger" schlecht bestellt. Beide Nichtregierungsorganisationen beklagen in ihren Berichten massive Verschlechterungen.

"Ernährungssicherheit ist eine Voraussetzung für Frieden und Stabilität", sagt die Präsidentin der Welthungerhilfe Marlehn Thieme. Ihr Kollege, Generalsekretär Mathias Mogge, nennt im DW-Gespräch konkrete Beispiele: Somalia, Sudan, Kongo und die Sahel-Region. "Da gibt es mehr Hunger. Das sind häufig Länder und Regionen, in denen die Auswirkungen des Klimawandels ganz besonders stark sind. Da sehen wir einen ganz klaren Zusammenhang."

Der Welthunger-Index basiert auf vier messbaren Indikatoren: Unterernährung in der gesamten Bevölkerung sowie verzögertes Wachstum, Auszehrung und Sterblichkeit bei Kindern. Auf der Basis dieser Daten wurden die 122 erfassten Länder, in denen solide Daten vorlagen, in vier Hunger-Index-Gruppen eingeteilt: niedrig, mäßig, ernst, sehr ernst. Das Gesamtergebnis ist alarmierend: In 32 Ländern hat sich die Hungersituation verschlechtert.

Welthungerhilfe-Präsidentin Thieme spricht nach fast zwei Jahrzehnten deutlicher Fortschritte von einer alarmierenden Trendwende: Sicherheit werde zu oft nur militärisch gedacht. Während die Etats des deutschen Verteidigungsministeriums um 20 und mehr Prozent anstiegen, gingen die für Entwicklungszusammenarbeit und humanitäre Hilfe zum Teil um die Hälfte zurück. "Dabei gerät eine entscheidende Frage aus dem Blick: Wie sicher können Menschen leben, wenn sie nicht wissen, ob sie morgen genug zu essen haben?"

Trotz aller Rückschläge gibt es im Welthunger-Index aber auch ein paar Lichtblicke. Welthungerhilfe-Generalsekretär Mogge erwähnt Uganda, Kenia und Sierra Leone. "Verbesserungen sehen wir insbesondere dort, wo wir es mit einer stabilen Regierung zu tun haben, wo es keine oder nur sehr wenige Konflikte gibt. Und wo es eine klare Politik gibt, gegen die Auswirkungen des Klimawandels anzugehen."

Dort behalte man die Ärmsten der Armen im Blick, sagt Mogge, der sich durch zahlreiche Reisen in die betroffenen Länder und Regionen selbst ein Bild von der Lage vor Ort macht. Erfolge gebe es vor allem dann, wenn in ländliche Gebiete investiert werde: "in Landwirtschaft, Gesundheit, Bildung, aber auch in soziale Sicherungssysteme".

Im Gazastreifen, aus dem Mogge kürzlich nach fünf Tagen zurückgekehrt ist, kann davon nach seinen Einblicken überhaupt keine Rede sein. Die Vereinten Nationen (UN) haben im Jahr 2025 für dieses nach dem Krieg zwischen Israel und der islamistischen Hamas weitgehend zerstörte Gebiet eine Hungersnot festgestellt.

Inzwischen sei der Hunger dort nicht mehr so katastrophal, weil mehr Hilfsgüter nach Gaza reingekommen seien, sagt Mogge. Aber die Menschen seien auf engstem Raum zusammengedrängt, 90 Prozent müssten in Zeltstädten leben. "Die hygienischen Verhältnisse sind sehr schlecht, was dazu führt, dass insbesondere Kinder unter Hautkrankheiten und Durchfallerkrankungen leiden. Und sie sehen im Moment leider wenig Hoffnung auf Verbesserung."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Mogges frische Eindrücke decken sich mit einer offiziellen Einschätzung der Bundesregierung: Die humanitäre Lage in Gaza bleibe "katastrophal", heißt es in einer kürzlich veröffentlichten Antwort auf eine parlamentarische Anfrage der Linken im Deutschen Bundestag.

Als einer der größten bilateralen Geber habe Deutschland seit dem Terrorüberfall der Hamas am 7. Oktober 2023 bis zu 420 Millionen Euro für humanitäre Hilfe bereitgestellt. Außerdem setze man sich auf diplomatischem Wege gegenüber Israel "ohne Unterlass für eine Verbesserung der humanitären Zugänge ein".

Auch im Report der Aktion gegen den Hunger wird die Lage in Gaza als verheerend beschrieben: "87 Prozent der landwirtschaftlichen Flächen wurden beschädigt, 81 Prozent der Gewächshausinfrastruktur zerstört und rund 90 Prozent des Wassers ist nicht trinkbar." Auch sonst überwiegen die schlechten Nachrichten.

"Hunger konzentriert sich zunehmend auf wenige Länder, die gleichzeitig von Konflikten, Vertreibung, Klimaschocks und dem Zusammenbruch grundlegender Infrastruktur geprägt sind", bilanziert Geschäftsführer Jan Sebastian Friedrich-Rust. "Diese Krisen verstärken sich gegenseitig und treiben Millionen Menschen in die Not." Die Gesamtzahl der Menschen, die an chronischem Hunger litten, beziffert seine Organisation wie die Welthungerhilfe auf 645 Millionen.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Grundlage des erstmals auf Deutsch veröffentlichten Hunger-Reports sind Daten des "Global Report on Food Crises" (GRFC), Analysen der Welternährungsorganisation (FAO), des Welternährungsprogramms (WFP) und vor Ort gewonnene Erkenntnisse der Aktion gegen den Hunger.

Auch diese in 54 Ländern aktive Hilfsorganisation kritisiert die seit 2023 stark gesunkenen Etats für Entwicklungszusammenarbeit und humanitäre Hilfe. "Wir sind zunehmend gezwungen, lebenswichtige Programme einzustellen, während der Unterstützungsbedarf gleichzeitig wächst", beklagt Geschäftsführer Friedrich-Rust.

"Oftmals können wir nur noch lebensrettende Soforthilfe leisten, während wir langfristig angelegte Projekte beenden müssen, die Menschen dabei helfen, widerstandsfähiger zu werden und sich selbst zu versorgen", skizziert der Geschäftsführer der Aktion gegen den Hunger eine Kettenreaktion, die er als "Teufelskreis" bezeichnet.

In der Rangliste von zehn Ländern mit der höchsten absoluten Zahl von Menschen, die unter hoher akuter Ernährungsunsicherheit leiden, dominiert der Kontinent Afrika. An der Spitze stehen Nigeria, Kongo und Sudan. Der Südsudan ist erstmals im Ranking vertreten. Dort sind inzwischen mehr als 80 Prozent der Bevölkerung auf humanitäre Hilfe angewiesen.

Friedrich-Rust warnt zugleich davor, die von 197 auf 177 Millionen gesunkene Zahl von Menschen in dieser Rangliste falsch zu interpretieren. Denn aufgrund von Datenlücken hätten relevante Krisenländer wie Äthiopien dieses Mal nicht berücksichtigt werden können. Allein in diesem ostafrikanischen Land seien im Vorjahr rund 22 Millionen Menschen von hoher akuter Ernährungsunsicherheit betroffen gewesen.

Aus Sicht der Aktion gegen den Hunger steht außer Frage, wo der Hebel umgelegt werden muss: Die internationale Gemeinschaft müsse die Ursachen der Krisen angehen und die Voraussetzungen dafür schaffen, dass Menschen langfristig ein Leben ohne Hunger führen könnten. "Hilfe ist nicht nur eine moralische Verpflichtung", betont Friedrich-Rust.

Wer bei Entwicklungszusammenarbeit und humanitärer Hilfe kürze, handele kurzsichtig. "Wer heute spart, verschiebt die Rechnung nur auf morgen und macht sie am Ende sogar deutlich teurer."

#489. Wotan Wilke Möhring im Interview: "Perfektion hat bei der Urlaubsplanung nichts zu suchen"

Ich packe meinen Koffer und nehme mit: Geheimnisse, Misstrauen, Eifersucht und ein Zweithandy. Die Freundes-Clique aus Bora Dagtekins Kinoerfolg "Das perfekte Geheimnis" geht auf Reisen. Doch "Der perfekte Urlaub", den der Titel der Fortsetzung verspricht, wird es nicht - zur Freude des Kinopublikums. Denn auf Mallorca müssen Leo (Elyas M'Barek) und Carlotta (Karoline Herfurth), Pepe (Florian David Fitz), Eva (Jessica Schwarz) und Rocco (Wotan Wilke Möhring), Simon (Frederick Lau) und Neuzugang Maus (Diana Amft) schnell feststellen, dass sie neben Bikinis, Badehosen und Sonnencreme auch eine ganze Menge aufgestaute Emotionen im Gepäck mit sich herumschleppen. Im Interview mit ntv.de verrät Rocco-Darsteller Wotan Wilke Möhring, wieso es seiner Ansicht nach gar keinen perfekten Urlaub gibt, was für ihn der absolute Vertrauensbruch ist und was echte Männerfreundschaften ausmacht.

ntv.de: War für dich sofort klar, dass du für die Fortsetzung von "Das perfekte Geheimnis" zusagst?

Wotan Wilke Möhring: Irgendwie schon. Im Grunde war die Zusage ein No-Brainer. Aber natürlich musste die Fortsetzung auch stimmig sein. Im ersten Teil gab es einen Cliffhanger, zu dem Bora Dagtekin etwas Passendes einfallen musste. Dann musste ein Zeitpunkt gefunden werden, an dem das gesamte Ensemble wieder Zeit hat, alle sind ja sehr beschäftigt. Am Ende hat es sieben Jahre bis zu "Der perfekte Urlaub" gedauert. Zwischen den beiden Filmen sind aber nur vier Monate vergangen. Wieder zusammenzuarbeiten war dann ein Fest, weil alle Kolleginnen und Kollegen, die mitspielen, eben auch Freunde von mir sind. Und man sieht sich so selten.

Was macht das Ensemble so besonders für dich?

Das sind alles Menschen, mit denen ich privat gerne Zeit verbringe. Mittlerweile haben aber fast alle Familie oder gehen beruflich ihrer Wege. Und deswegen wird die Zeit, die man gemeinsam hat, meist während der Arbeit verbracht. Es war einfach schön, während der Dreharbeiten von "Der perfekte Urlaub" mal wieder ein paar Monate zusammen abzuhängen.

Der erste Film war eine Art Kammerspiel. In "Der perfekte Urlaub" habt ihr viel draußen auf Mallorca gedreht und konntet euch auch körperlich so richtig austoben. Wie viel Spaß hat das gemacht?

Mit noch mal vier Monaten im dunklen Studio hätte uns Bora nicht gekriegt. Egal, wie gut das Buch gewesen wäre. (lacht) Ich glaube aber, dass das auch ein guter Ansatz ist, um Neues über diese Gruppe zu erfahren. Wie verhalten sie sich in einem anderen Biotop, draußen in der freien Welt? In "Das perfekte Geheimnis" wollten ja alle eigentlich nur gemeinsam einen schönen Abend verbringen. Das geht dann total in die Hose. In "Der perfekte Urlaub" ist die Ausgangssituation anders: Keiner will mit dem anderen zusammen sein. Die Paare reisen getrennt an und lügen sich gegenseitig in die Tasche. Und als sie dann alle aufeinandertreffen, müssen sie mit sich und ihren Problemen klarkommen, die sie natürlich mitgenommen haben. Dabei wollen sie sich eigentlich nur aus dem Weg gehen.

Klingt nicht nach einem perfekten Urlaub?

Das Wort "perfekt" hat für mich eh nichts bei der Urlaubsplanung oder bei der Lebensplanung zu suchen. Ich glaube, perfekt ist nicht der Anspruch, den man haben sollten. Perfekt ist irgendwie tot. Für mich bedeutet ein guter Urlaub natürlich in erster Linie Ruhe und Erholung. Gleichzeitig möchte ich ganz nah bei meinen Kindern sein, intensive Zeit mit ihnen verbringen, mit meinen Lieblingsmenschen. Wenn man zurückkommt, sollte man denken: "Ach, das war so schön!" Oder gar nicht mehr wegwollen. Wenn man mit diesem Gefühl heimkehrt, hat man schon viel erreicht.

Du spielst hauptsächlich ernste Rollen. Was ist schwerer: Drama oder Comedy?

Ich glaube, für den Zuschauer sieht Drama schwerer aus und Comedy leichter. Aber in der Herstellung ist es ein ähnlicher Prozess. Beim Drama musst du viel mehr zurückhalten, weil du willst, dass der Zuschauer den Kreis der Trauer schließt. Bei der Komödie gilt es, die Leute mit Leichtigkeit anzustecken. Dabei ist völlig egal, wie es dir persönlich gerade geht. Das ist eine hohe Kunst.

Im Film gibt es ein paar echte Fremdschäm-Momente, auch für deine Figur Rocco. Kostet es Überwindung, solche Szenen zu drehen - oder machen sie erst recht Spaß?

Sie machen richtig Spaß! Aber du denkst in Bezug auf Rocco auch: "Was für ein Idiot!" (lacht) Aber dass du das denkst, ist ein gutes Zeichen. Denn du siehst zwar deine Physis, dein Gesicht, deine Gestik und Mimik, aber die Person auf der Leinwand ist einfach ein anderer Typ. Und das ist ein guter Hinweis darauf, dass du da auf dem richtigen Weg bist, diese Figur zu gestalten.

Gibt es etwas, dass du Rocco gerne mit auf die Reise gegeben hättest?

Eine aufs Maul? (lacht) Nein, im Ernst, vielleicht mehr Mut. Mehr von dem, was ich vielleicht bin. Die Dinge auszusprechen, wie sie sind. Wobei ich es nicht schlimm finde, wenn man ein Geheimnis hat oder eine bestimmte Wahrheit zurückhält, weil man versucht, den anderen zu schützen.

Warum vertraut Rocco sein Geheimnis Eva nicht einfach an?

Ich glaube, er wollte erst einmal die Wahrheit für sich selbst herausfinden. Dass er es Eva nicht erzählt hat, könnte auch daran liegen, dass er davon ausgegangen ist, dass sein Geheimnis sie als Frau anders trifft. Es hat ihn ja auch getroffen. Eigentlich ist es der richtige Weg, der Sache erst einmal auf den Grund gehen zu wollen. Doof ist nur, wenn der andere das Geheimnis vorher selbst herausfindet. Aber damit konnte Rocco nicht rechnen.

Ohne zu spoilern, aber eigentlich ist Evas Geheimnis viel schlimmer als Roccos, oder?

Das ist schon Hochverrat, absolut. Das kann man nicht miteinander vergleichen. Aber ist es nicht lustig, dass Eva, die so kontrolliert daherkommt, beinahe wirkt, als habe sie sich Roccos Geheimnis schlimmer gewünscht? Und dann versucht, diese Ungleichheit über eine erotische Abarbeitung zu nivellieren?

In das Handy des Partners zu schauen, erweist sich in "Der perfekte Urlaub" oftmals als kontraproduktiv. Wie stehst du dazu?

Absolutes No-Go! Selbst wenn da nichts Schlimmes steht, verstehst du ja oftmals gar nicht, wie etwas gemeint ist, weil du den Hintergrund nicht kennst. Das ist wie Briefe öffnen, man verletzt ein ganz persönliches Geheimnis. Das macht man nicht. Das ist ein Vertrauensbruch.

Es gibt eine Kernfrage in dem Film: Wie viel Wahrheit verträgt eine Freundschaft? Wie würdest du sie beantworten?

Ist die eigene Wahrheit, die jeder für sich persönlich auslegt, relevant für den anderen und für die Freundschaft? Hat sie unmittelbar Einfluss auf das Verhältnis zueinander? Dann ist sie relevant. Aber Wahrheit setzt ja immer eine Unwahrheit voraus, sonst würde man die Frage nicht stellen. Aber was, wenn es die vielleicht gar nicht gibt?

Und will man wirklich alles von dem anderen wissen? Wenn man die andere Person in- und auswendig kennt, dann ist sie meiner Meinung nach verschwunden. Dann weiß man ja alles schon vorher und braucht sich mit der Person gar nicht mehr auseinanderzusetzen. Teil des Geheimnisses menschlicher Beziehungen ist aber, eben nicht alles über den anderen zu wissen. Sicher zu sein, aber eben nicht zu sicher. Es gäbe sonst ja gar nicht diese Abstoßung und Anziehung unter Menschen, die Attraktion.

Deswegen ist die Wahrheit für mich gar nicht das verbindende Element. Das verbindende Element ist Liebe. Oder Verständnis. Den anderen so sein zu lassen, wie er ist. Selbst wenn er dir dabei nicht gefällt. Es ist allerdings nur dein subjektives Bild von diesem Menschen, das dann Schaden nimmt. Nicht die Person selbst ist schadhaft. Das zu unterscheiden, ist in einer Beziehung noch mal schwieriger. Deswegen ist es vielleicht leichter, mit Bekannten in Urlaub zu fahren als mit Freunden. Manchmal sollte man Freunde mehr wie Bekannte behandeln, glaube ich. Nicht alles auf sich beziehen, gar nicht so in die Tiefe gehen. Sich eben nicht fragen: "Wie hat er das jetzt gemeint?" Lieber denken: "Der ist halt so, fertig, aus." So eine Gelöstheit setzt aber viel Selbstbewusstsein voraus.

Unterscheiden sich Männer- und Frauenfreundschaften?

Ich glaube schon. Frauen haben andere Konfliktverarbeitungsstrategien als Männer. Ich bilde mir ein, dass Männer weniger sagen und mehr für sich behalten. Auch, weil sie eine simplere Kommunikationsform haben. Da reicht ein Blick, ein Wort. Oder man muss den ganzen Abend gar nicht reden und weiß trotzdem, wie es dem anderen geht. Um für das andere Geschlecht verständlich zu sein, müssen Männer lernen, Worte zu formulieren, die wir beim gleichen Geschlecht nicht sagen müssen, weil wir eh verstanden werden. Und Frauen müssen verstehen, und das machen sie im besten Fall ja eh längst, dass die wenigen Worte, die ein Mann sagt, auch reichen können. Es muss nicht immer der gewünschte Katalog sein.

Was denkst du, verbindet die Männer im Film?

Im ersten Teil haben wir erfahren, dass sie sich schon seit der Schule kennen. Ich glaube, dass die Jungs im Film nie befreundet wären, wenn sie sich nicht bereits in der Schulzeit gefunden und ihren eigenen Kosmos für sich abgesteckt hätten. Denn eigentlich sind sie zu unterschiedlich. Es gibt bestimmte Zeiten in deinem Leben, in denen du Freundschaften schließt. Vor allem eben in der Jugend. Das ist irgendwann später nicht mehr so, weil du viel zu wenig Zeit hast, dich um Freundschaften zu kümmern. Richtige Freunde sind Menschen, bei denen man sich gar nicht melden muss und die dich trotzdem verstehen. Die tolerieren, dass du dich änderst und nicht enttäuscht fragen: "Was ist denn mit dir los?" Ich erinnere mich noch gut an die Schulzeit, wenn man in den Sommerferien was Neues für sich probiert hatte und dann deswegen sofort von seinen Mitschülern niedergemacht wurde. Und das macht ein Freund eben nicht. Ein echter Freund ist auch nicht enttäuscht, wenn man mit einer Partnerin ankommt, die ihm nicht gefällt.

"Der perfekte Urlaub" läuft seit dem 22. Oktober in den deutschen Kinos.

Mit Wotan Wilke Möhring sprach Claudia Spitzkowski.

#490. Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya

Travellers are subject to temperature checks at Kenyan border crossing-points

Kenya has recorded its second death from Ebola as it handles its first ever outbreak of the disease.

A woman, aged 65, who was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, died after being placed in quarantine, the health ministry said.

Seven other Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities, it added.

All the cases were within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry said.

More than 4,000 people have died in Africa since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.

Kenya's latest victim had been under quarantine when she developed symptoms on 13 October, the health ministry said.

The first death, on 5 October, was that of a man who fell ill in September and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo before arriving in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, where he died a few days later.

Those still being treated are three other relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner.

The US has warned its citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.

Ebola is a rare but deadly disease, external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.

The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

The Bundibugyo species of Ebola is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.

Kenya has introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from DR Congo and nine other countries it considers to be at high risk: Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.

Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights and present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.

Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.

Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.

Is Ebola under control in Kenya after nine cases confirmed?

Woman with Ebola in Nigeria confirmed as wife of Swiss diplomat

'I buried my parents one day after the other' - Ebola mourners learn how to grieve safely

Nigeria's health minister said its sole confirmed case of Ebola appeared to be genetically related to a strain identified earlier in Kenya.

Prof Ali Pate said there was no evidence so far that the Kenyan patient had travelled to Nigeria, but that further testing was under way.

Health officials have been investigating whether Nigeria's first case crossed paths with Kenya's first patient. Both are believed to have travelled through Uganda's Entebbe airport earlier this month.

Uganda's health ministry announced on Friday that people who had travelled to DR Congo would no longer be able to transit via Uganda as part of its prevention measures.

#493. ‘Our third date was at Buckingham Palace’: Marlon James and Nicholas Boggs on life as a literary power couple

Shortlisted for the Booker and Baillie Gifford prizes respectively, the novelist and biographer talk about working and living together – and giving a voice to Black queer history

The literary power couple is a historically seductive concept. Two writers sharing a life, their private and creative worlds entwined, each becoming witness to and critic of the other’s work. Think Simone de Beauvoir and Jean-Paul Sartre, Joan Didion and John Gregory Dunne. Or, less auspiciously, Sylvia Plath and Ted Hughes.

Now, into this illustrious company steps a new pair: the novelist Marlon James and the biographer Nicholas Boggs, whose books have each been shortlisted for one of Britain’s most prestigious literary awards – James for the Booker prize and Boggs for the Baillie Gifford prize for nonfiction. Between them, they have produced two formidable books, each the culmination of years of work, and each concerned with the lives of Black queer men whose stories have often been overlooked.

“I’m not sure what to do with it,” James says, when I ask how they feel about the inevitable impending “literary power couple” label. “I have all these romantic notions that we were like Joan Didion and John Gregory Dunne or something – I don’t know. What do you think?” He turns to Boggs, who laughs. “It’s all very new,” he says. “We’re still getting used to it.”

It is a warm October morning in Williamsburg, the fashionable writerly enclave in Brooklyn, and I am sitting across from the pair at their apartment. They are relaxing on a chaise longue, looking comfortable enough to have been there all morning. Their exchanges have the easy rhythm of a long relationship, full of small corrections and private jokes.

James, the 55-year-old Jamaican-born novelist whose 2015 book A Brief History of Seven Killings won the Booker prize, is back on the shortlist this year with The Disappearers, a sprawling, dark reckoning with the brutality of Aids-era gay life and homophobia in Jamaica. Boggs, his 53-year-old partner of nearly nine years, has been shortlisted for the Baillie Gifford prize for his first book, Baldwin: A Love Story, a biography of James Baldwin that draws on two decades of research into the writer’s intimate life and creative relationships.

“The Baillie Gifford’s a prize I know well,” James says. “So when Nick was on the shortlist, I knew what a big deal it was.” Boggs remembers James’s reaction when the nonfiction shortlist was announced on 1 October. “His eyes got very wide. I don’t think I’ve seen his eyes get quite that wide before.”

James had the first taste of the excitement, when the Booker shortlist was announced in September. “You got shortlisted first, so the pressure was on!” Boggs jokes. “No matter how many times you do this, it’s always a great surprise,” James adds.

The pair have been together since 2018 and have lived in this apartment for a little under a year. Its walls form something of a shrine to their work and interests, crowded with art by African American and queer artists, from intimate, often erotic photography to paintings. At one point they rummage beneath the bed to retrieve an original 1938 painting by Beauford Delaney, the Harlem renaissance artist who became one of Baldwin’s mentors, and features heavily in Boggs’s book. A monumental horse sculpture dominates the room – or, as Boggs points out with a laugh, “it’s really just the horse’s ass, isn’t it!” Bought by James after his 2015 Booker win and christened “Booker” by Boggs, it stands alongside a similarly imposing gorilla.

Their romance began not in a rarefied literary salon, but through the very ordinary business of a dating app. “I was on the apps and was like, well, I’m only dating in my neighbourhood,” Boggs says. “He was three blocks away, so it was perfect.”

By then, they were both in their 40s. Boggs, who had never been out with a writer before – “it was mostly bartenders”, he jokes – knew of James’s work, but hadn’t read any of his books. James, for his part, didn’t know Boggs was a writer prior to their first meeting.

“It was a very chaste first date,” James says, with a twinkle in his eye. “We were gentlemen.” The relationship developed “healthily slowly” over a summer spent apart while Boggs was teaching in London, until they reunited when James invited Boggs to a Booker anniversary event in the capital. He was keen to set the bar high.

“Our third date was at Buckingham Palace,” James says, with a faux shrug. “I try to keep it classy, you know, gotta impress him. We actually made out in the queen’s bathroom.”

Their relationship may have brought them into the same orbit, but the worlds they each came from – and the experiences that inform their writing – are markedly different.

Growing up in Washington DC, where his father was a civil rights attorney, Boggs read Baldwin from a young age. While studying the writer at college, he came across a reference in a 1994 biography to an out-of-print children’s book by Baldwin, illustrated by a French artist, Yoran Cazac. Boggs had suspicions that there was a love affair behind the collaboration, tried to track down Cazac, but was told he was most likely dead. A few weeks later, the phone rang.

“It was Yoran saying, ‘I’m alive, I’m in Paris, come on over, I have many stories to tell you about Jimmy,’” Boggs recalls. “That was 23 years ago, and it began a realisation that there were these untold stories in Baldwin’s life that needed to be unearthed.”

For James, rampant homophobia shaped his upbringing and his storytelling. Growing up gay and closeted in 1980s Kingston, in the classroom he was “the school homo”; at church, he tried to become straight. He only began to build a more comfortable queer identity after moving to Minneapolis to teach in 2007, away from the scrutiny of family and friends in Jamaica. Unlike Boggs, his queer literary education came late. He picked up Baldwin’s Giovanni’s Room for the first time when he was 50. “The first thing I thought was I could never have read this at 20,” he says. “I was so in the closet.”

Across his fiction, James has repeatedly excavated Jamaica’s histories of violence and political upheaval, from his debut 2005 novel John Crow’s Devil (famously rejected 78 times by publishers), to the gang warfare and state corruption of A Brief History of Seven Killings, which made him the first Jamaican to win the Booker prize. The Disappearers, his sixth novel, grew out of a rumoured homophobic attack in a middle-class area of Kingston in the late 1980s.

“I first heard about it when I was 21,” he says. “I knew it happened, I just couldn’t prove it. It haunted me: the idea that that could happen – and in a posh neighbourhood – was one of the things that certainly pushed me firmly into the closet.”

He was unable to establish exactly what had happened until he began researching the novel, interviewing almost 20 people in Jamaica who helped him piece together the incident over several years. “I wanted to fill in the blanks,” he says. “I wanted to give those guys back some sort of agency and power.”

In different ways, both men are trying to recover Black queer histories that have been marginalised or lost. “We both respond to gaps,” Boggs says.

For James, one such gap became the starting point for The Disappearers. He wanted to build his novel around the production of a play, but couldn’t find one that would fit. The solution came, serendipitously, from Boggs: while researching his biography, he discovered Baldwin directed a 1969 production of John Herbert’s Fortune and Men’s Eyes in Turkey. He suggested James consider it for his novel.

“At first you were like, ‘no’,” Boggs recalls. “And I was like, ‘just read these 60 pages’. And I was right.”

It is no exaggeration to say that the play serves as the novel’s structural and emotional scaffolding, and is central to Boggs’s chapters on Baldwin’s life in Turkey, too. “I like to say I plundered his book with his permission,” James says, smiling. “It’s one way in which our books wouldn’t be possible or wouldn’t have ended up the way they did were we not together.”

Discover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to you

On a table in the couple’s living room there sits a 25 September edition of the New York Times. It contains a review now infamous in the literary world, in which the notoriously harsh critic Dwight Garner devoted an almost novella-length appraisal to The Disappearers, hailing it as “a masterpiece, the novel of the decade and possibly of the century”, placing it alongside the work of Salman Rushdie, Toni Morrison and William Faulkner.

“I still don’t quite believe it,” James says. The morning the piece came out, an author friend had emailed to alert him to what he described as a “stonking review” from Garner. “I didn’t know what stonking meant, I thought it was something bad!” he laughs. “So I’m like, ‘God, no. I’m not going to read this.’” But he clicked the link anyway, and saw the word “masterpiece”.

“I went to the newsstand to go find it, because I still didn’t believe it,” he says. “I was like, ‘if I leave this bed, I’m going to wake up.’”

He is wary of the idea that acclaim should ever become an expectation, or success a fait accompli. “There’s a part of me that still thinks I’m this underground, scrapping writer who got lucky,” he says. “For me, it’s still a genuine surprise. It still catches me off guard. I don’t know if I want to get to that point where I start to expect good reviews. I don’t know if I want that level of entitlement.” He laughs. “I know some writers who are like that – I’m not going to name any names,” he adds, with a mischievous look.

Joan Didion once described her collaboration with John Gregory Dunne as a process of creative osmosis: “One of us writes the first draft, and the other functions as really kind of a super-editor and writes the second draft. In the end, you can’t really tell who has done what.”

There is no such blurring of authorship in the James-Boggs household. The pair keep their manuscripts to themselves until the work is finished, even as they discuss the ideas and research behind it.

“People are always surprised to hear that,” Boggs says. “Marlon didn’t read my book until after it was finished, I finished his on the publication date.”

Their working habits are almost opposite, too. Boggs describes himself as a binge writer, while James writes every day and keeps regular hours. James needs music – “lots of free jazz” – while Boggs requires “perfect peace and quiet”. They work on opposite sides of the house, and Boggs also has a separate office a few blocks away. But living with James has helped Boggs reconsider his idea of what writing should feel like.

“Marlon has an incredible work ethic, and it was really a reminder that this is a job,” he says. “That was really helpful. It’s not screaming from the other room in frustration, or complaining about it at dinner every night.”

They insist there is no competition between them. “I think I really worried about that when we first met,” Boggs says. “But we write so differently, even stylistically. And because of the time that we’re living in, getting these stories told is so much more important than any individual anyway.”

Just this month, new research from PEN America found that the US saw almost 12,000 book bans in public schools during the 2025-2026 school year, the highest number in a single year. For James and Boggs, whose work is concerned with recovering the lives and histories that have been overlooked or suppressed, the stakes are difficult to ignore.

James refuses to censor himself in anticipation of a backlash, but he is not oblivious to the risks. “I do sometimes get this fear that the oppressors are coming, because they always burn the books first,” he says. “The forces stacked against me are immense. But then, when have the forces against us not been immense?”

I ask if they have thought about leaving the US altogether. “Yes, 100%,” James says, without skipping a beat. He is uncompromising in his diagnosis of the country’s downward slide. “For me, it’s weird seeing America become the type of country America has spent the past 60 years creating everywhere else. I think we’re becoming a banana republic, which, coming from the Caribbean, I know a lot about.”

He is not, however, a pessimist. “I have to have a pretty big sense of optimism to think that my big-ass books are going to sell,” he says. “Throughout all of this, I’ve never lost faith in the reader. Writing has always been an art form that had to struggle against oppression, that speaks truth to power. If you decide to be a writer, part of it is to say that you’re going to take this on.”

For all their independence on the page, Boggs and James are now embarking on a creative collaboration. Baldwin: A Love Story has been optioned for film by Anonymous Content. Higher Ground (Barack and Michelle Obama’s production company) will be co-producing. Boggs knew immediately with whom he wanted to write the screenplay: James, who has experience writing for the screen, including the television series Get Millie Black. Anonymous Content hired them to write the screenplay together.

So far, the process has been seamless. “I think even we are surprised how smooth it’s going,” Boggs says, laughing. “But we’re just so interested in each other’s work and interested in how one another thinks.”

I ask how it feels to be adding to the queer literary canon, in their shared and solo endeavours. They look at each other for a moment before Boggs responds. “Just to be alive is wonderful,” he says. “Something that Marlon and I both share is that when you grow up in the shadow of Aids, you don’t necessarily think that you have a future.”

“We lost so many great artists, gay artists,” Boggs adds. “So there’s a certain kind of responsibility to telling those stories. There are so many that still need to be told.”

#494. Brazil’s election and the battle for the Amazon – podcast

Our Latin America correspondent, Tom Phillips, heads to Roraima to hear what’s at stake for the rainforest and the communities that live there in the Brazilian presidential runoff on Sunday. Send your comments and questions to tif.questions@theguardian.com

For the Amazon and the communities who live there, the stakes in Sunday’s Brazilian presidential election runoff could scarcely be higher.

Our Latin America correspondent, Tom Phillips heads to Roraima, the country’s most northern state, to hear from voters, preachers and politicians in a region that heavily backed Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round.

He finds them all hopeful that the far-right candidate will bring back the mining that his father Jair so heartily encouraged when in power in an administration that oversaw the felling of 11m acres (4.5m hectares) of rainforest.

Tom also meets Indigenous activists determined to fight back even if the Bolsonaros take power again.

Helen Pidd asks what it will all mean, not only for Brazil but also for the climate crisis more broadly.

#495. A shark went astray and captured Korea's heart - will she finally make it back to sea?

Watch: BBC follows operation to rescue shark stranded in South Korean canal

As soon as a large shark was spotted in a canal in Busan - a bustling shipping hub and beach city on South Korea's south-eastern tip - marine biologist Kim Hyun-woo was drafted in to rescue it.

He got the call in mid-September, on his way home from a business trip tracking shoals of mackerel to aid fishing vessels. Despite being one of the country's leading shark experts, he never thought he'd be asked by the coastguard to actually save one.

South Korea is no stranger to sharks but one this size, in a shallow, concrete canal right by the world's seventh busiest port, was unheard of - until now.

With an excited crowd already gathering at the waterfront, his team from the National Institute of Fisheries Science had to move fast.

The first task was to determine the species.

Some sharks are more dangerous than others. The star of the 1975 blockbuster Jaws, the great white shark, is known to attack and kill humans.

The specimen in Busan was found to be a female dusky shark, a species linked only to two deadly attacks. Still, Kim feared someone in the crowd might jump or fall into the canal.

The dusky shark was first spotted in the canal in mid-September

A small coastguard ship made an initial attempt using an electrical deterrence device, which generates a weak current that sharks avoid.

They're usually used after sightings near popular beaches. But after five hours, officials determined this particular shark was too large and fast for the device.

Kim changed tack, deciding instead to wait for the shark to let herself out. But that did not happen.

As authorities looked for ways to guide her out of the canal, the stranded creature went viral.

Just hours after she appeared, the council had sent everyone in the city an emergency text alert, urging pedestrians and residents to "exercise caution for their safety".

People rarely visited the park along the canal but because of the message, the place was soon brimming with people eager to spot the shark.

Adoring fans named her Bukangi, from "buk hang", the Korean name of the nearby harbour. Within days, a business trademarked it and Bukangi pins, plushies and T-shirts began selling online.

City authorities joined in, livestreaming the shark and making her their official mascot.

A banner was hung at the entrance of the canal, asking the public to sign a petition "on behalf of Bukangi" to demand the national government's support for the construction of a new 30,000-seater baseball stadium by the canal.

Shark spotting became a team effort among locals and visitors. The unspoken rule was that children were given the front row, and whoever saw Bukangi had to point her out to newer arrivals.

Some self-appointed defenders even patrolled the canal at night to make sure no-one was shining torches or lasers at Bukangi.

A poster encourages support for a baseball stadium "on behalf of Bukangi"

More than 1.6 million visitors ultimately flocked to the canal.

The local mayor said the shark brought "the kind of publicity even billions of dollars cannot buy" to the port.

"It's really rare these days for people to come together," said Kim Joo-eun, who came to see the shark with her two nieces. "I feel that Bukangi brought us all together, cheering for herâ¦ It's a lot of fun."

But officials couldn't leave Bukangi in the canal.

As September drew to an end, she hadn't been seen feeding for days and was spotted with bloody abrasions on her snout from bumping into the concrete walls.

Prominent marine biology professor Choi Yoon told local media that experts were particularly worried about a "critical" injury around the shark's eye.

Kim Joo-eun and her nieces were among Bukangi's many visitors

At the end of September, Kim's team mounted another rescue attempt. The marine biologist looked back to a 2004 incident in Massachusetts, when water jets were used to drive a great white shark away from a shallow pond.

But when the team tried this on Bukangi, she kept circling back.

On 2 October, they decided to install a net spanning the width of the canal to stop her from returning. She managed to swim around the net and was back within hours.

At this point, Kim started thinking the shark might have problems with her snout's electromagnetic sensors, which she uses for navigation. Or she might have become confused by the loud noises emitted by ships in the harbour.

The reason Bukangi was even in the canal may be a sign of warming seas, the oceans ministry suggests.

It believes she may have followed plentiful fish to warmer waters. Some 50 large sharks were recorded off South Korea's east coast in the first half of the year; four times as many as last year.

The canal leading up to the Busan port where Bukangi was stranded

With each failed attempt some of Bukangi's newfound fans began demanding she be left in peace.

On Thursday, several showed up with placards and shouted "leave Bukangi alone" and "remove the net".

When a security guard told them to stop, one man cried: "I love you, Bukangi!"

"I am obsessed with her," said Jeong Yo-won, a woman in her 40s. She called the shark a "source of hope and joy" and insisted, "I don't think we should evict her mercilessly like this."

Jeong protesting against Bukangi's "eviction", alongside a man demanding officials "protect Bukangi's right to self-determination"

Others thought it was time for her to return home.

"I would stare at her for hours because I was so enamoured by her," a woman said after sighting the shark on her third attempt. "I hope Bukangi would stay, but I prefer that she lives a long and healthy life."

People joked the council should "make an official ID for Bukangi and give a pension", Shin Seungmin said.

"She brought so much fun with her. But she should go and live her normal shark life."

Bukangi became a sensation, drawing the curious and the concerned

Staying in the canal would seriously jeopardise Bukangi because of falling autumn temperatures, Kim explains. Usually this prompts sharks to migrate to warmer waters further south.

"This canal is far from something we can call a habitat," he adds. "A wild animal cannot stay in a space made strictly for humans."

Eventually, as public scrutiny grew, the oceans ministry took over the rescue operation from the fisheries institute. Around 40 personnel, including divers from Busan's aquarium, were mobilised. A vet was on standby, along with an ambulance in case the divers were attacked by Bukangi.

On Wednesday divers installed two layers of nets, and Bukangi was successfully herded out of the narrow canal into open water. But overnight, she swam back into the canal, diving under the outer net.

This left her trapped between the two layers.

Then on thursday, rescuers removed the outer layer, and Bukangi was seen swimming further and further towards open sea.

Although she did occasionally circle back, the rescue operation had ended.

Staying in the canal is dangerous for Bukangi, says marine biologist Kim Hyun-woo

There have been no sightings of Bukangi in the last few days, which experts say is a positive sign.

Prof Choi believes she may be adjusting to wider, deeper waters.

She is unlikely to have travelled far, he adds, and could reappear over the coming week.

But he is also worried about any injuries she may have sustained. Trapped in the canal, it "kept scraping against [the walls], stripping the skin off its snout and even its pectoral fins", he told local media.

For now, South Korea is holding its breath, hoping Bukangi can find her way back to her home - the open sea.

Additional reporting by Leehyun Choi in Seoul
