#496. Manifestations du 24 octobre à Auch : casques, garrots et sacs de secours... Qui sont Chat et Belette, ces mystérieux "street medics" présents dans les manifestations ?

Article rédigé par Salomé Dubart

l'essentiel Ce samedi, quelque 220 personnes se sont rassemblées sur la place de la Libération, à Auch, dans le Gers. Parmi elles, deux silhouettes se distinguent : Chat et Belette, des "street medics" chargés d'apporter les premiers secours en cas de besoin. Derrière leurs équipements, ces deux militants racontent leur engagement, marqué par des manifestations parfois violentes. Reportage.

Ils se font appeler Chat et Belette. Leurs vêtements ne laissent aucune place au doute quant à la raison de leur présence, ce samedi matin, sur la place de la Libération auscitaine. Pas plus que leur équipement, bien plus fourni que celui des autres manifestants. Casques sur la tête, sacs à dos solidement fixés aux épaules et remplis de matériel susceptible de sauver des vies, les deux militants se tiennent légèrement en retrait du rassemblement. Alors que quelque 220 manifestants ont investi le rond-point de la place, Chat et Belette gardent le regard vif, attentifs au moindre débordement, au moindre signe de détresse parmi la foule.

Quelques 220 manifestants se sont mobilisés ce samedi à Auch. SEBASTIEN LAPEYRERE

Au rythme des tambours, les chants s'élèvent. "Tout ce qu'on veut, c'est la grève générale", scandent les manifestants. Mais rien ne semble déconcentrer les deux silhouettes dont les vêtements portent une inscription bien particulière : "Street Medic 32". Car Chat et Belette sont des secouristes de rue. Des militants qui, au fil des mobilisations, ont choisi de se consacrer aux premiers secours pour venir en aide aux personnes blessées ou en difficulté lors des manifestations.

À lire aussi : Manifestation du 24 octobre à Toulouse : pas de mariages au Capitole, stations de métro fermées, marché du Cristal seulement jusqu'à midi, le point sur les perturbations dans le centre-ville

Leur présence pourrait presque paraître étonnante dans le Gers, où les rassemblements, malgré l'ampleur nationale des mobilisations, demeurent pour le moment plus calmes que dans les grandes métropoles. Pourtant, derrière leurs pseudonymes, ces deux street medics possèdent une expérience des mouvements sociaux et de leurs débordements qui les a convaincus de toujours se tenir prêts à intervenir.

Sous les parapluies et derrière les pancartes aux messages revendicatifs, un nouveau slogan retentit : "À bas l'État policier !" Chat et Belette acceptent alors de raconter leurs parcours, leurs expériences et les raisons de cet engagement qui, même au cœur des mobilisations gersoises les plus paisibles, conserve à leurs yeux toute son importance.

"Nous, on est une petite équipe de street medics auto-constituée dans le coin. On a un vieux parcours militant, antifasciste de base", explique Chat. Mais, au fil des années, son engagement a évolué. Désormais, lorsqu'il participe à une manifestation, il se consacre exclusivement aux secours. "Quand je viens sur une mobilisation, maintenant, je ne suis que médic. Je ne suis plus militant", précise-t-il, évoquant également des problèmes de santé qui l'ont conduit à adapter sa manière de s'engager.

Ancien conducteur d'ambulance, Chat a commencé à exercer ce rôle lors du sommet international anti-Otan à Strasbourg, en 2009. Un événement qui l'a profondément marqué. "On était deux, je crois, pour 20 000 personnes", se souvient-il. Pendant plusieurs jours, il raconte avoir assisté à des affrontements et à des scènes de violence. "J'ai vu les gens se faire abîmer, gazer. Je voyais les gens s'étouffer dans les gaz, moi compris. Je me suis dit : il faut quelqu'un pour aider." C'est à cette occasion qu'il découvre des formations destinées aux secouristes présents dans les manifestations. Une expérience qui ne le quittera plus.

À lire aussi : La manifestation internationale anti-Otan dégénère en violences

Pour Belette, le parcours est différent. Ancienne assistante dentaire et vétérinaire, elle a d'abord apporté les premiers secours de manière spontanée lors de rassemblements. "J'ai fait un peu mes armes en free party", raconte-t-elle. Habituée à conserver une trousse de secours sur elle, elle intervenait auprès des personnes qui en avaient besoin, sans appartenir à une équipe organisée.

Puis les manifestations contre les mégabassines de Sainte-Soline, en 2023, ont marqué un tournant. Pour des raisons de santé, Chat et Belette n'avaient pas pu s'y rendre, mais avaient prêté du matériel à des proches mobilisés sur place. "On ne pensait pas que ce serait si violent", confie Belette. Selon leur récit, plusieurs de leurs amis en sont revenus profondément marqués. "On s'en est beaucoup voulu de ne pas y être", poursuit-elle. Depuis, les deux militants cherchent à renforcer leur présence sur le terrain et à perfectionner leurs connaissances. Ils échangent notamment avec d'autres secouristes pour partager leurs expériences et leurs pratiques.

Sur la place de la Libération, leurs sacs à dos témoignent de cette préparation. Compresses, sérum physiologique, matériel destiné à prendre en charge les petites blessures ou à soulager les personnes exposées aux gaz lacrymogènes : chaque compartiment possède une fonction précise. Mais certains équipements sont réservés à des situations bien plus graves. "On a une poche, vraiment, qu'on espère ne pas ouvrir, pour les blessures graves", explique Belette.

À lire aussi : Manifestation de Sainte-Soline : une "logique de confrontation", des "manquements déontologiques" et un "langage ordurier" ont conduit à un "lourd bilan humain", dénonce la Défenseure des droits

À l'intérieur, des garrots, des pansements compressifs et du matériel permettant de prendre en charge des blessures importantes. Les deux secouristes disposent également d'un brancard pliable. Un équipement qui pourrait sembler disproportionné au regard du calme de la mobilisation auscitaine. Pourtant, pour Chat et Belette, mieux vaut être préparés à toute éventualité.

"On sait qu'à Auch, la mobilisation n'est pas très forte. C'est un département peu peuplé", reconnaît Chat. Mais pour les deux militants, la présence d'une équipe de secouristes participe aussi à l'organisation du mouvement. "C'est intéressant aussi de faire vivre les mouvements dans les plus petites villes, où on est vraiment plus proche des gens qui ne militent pas trop d'habitude", explique Belette. Selon elle, ces rassemblements permettent également à des personnes moins habituées aux manifestations de franchir le pas.

Au-delà des blessures, les deux secouristes souhaitent donc jouer un rôle de prévention et de réassurance. Leur simple présence peut suffire à rassurer certains participants, notamment les plus jeunes ou les personnes âgées.

Street medics autoproclamés! Aucune compétence particulière, sauf en matière de guérilla urbaine. Par contre, pour draguer la manifestante, un street médic , ça doit emballer sec !

#497. France: Young voters blase about Glucksmann's Socialists

Raphael Glucksmann wants to lead France's Socialists to power without working with the left-populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, who is particularly popular with young voters. How can the center-left candidate win them over?

The historically working-class Parisian neighborhood of Belleville has gentrified in recent years. It was here that Raphael Glucksmann, a member of the European Parliament for France's center-left Socialists, celebrated his victory in the party's presidential primary on October 11.

Two rounds of voting had been anticipated, but the 46-year-old son of philosopher and essayist Andre Glucksmann triumphed in the first round with a convincing 66% of the vote and will be the Socialist candidate in France's 2027 presidential election.

As he left the Cantine de Belleville restaurant, Glucksmann was flour-bombed by an unidentified assailant. The following morning, he called on his rival, the left-wing French populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, to condemn attacks carried out by his supporters, though it is not clear that the attacker was indeed a supporter of Melenchon's La France Insoumise (LFI).

The incident has highlighted the issue set to dog Glucksmann's presidential candidacy over the coming weeks: How can he win over Melenchon's supporters if he refuses to work with their candidate?

"Where do you stand on Melenchon?" That was the question that dominated much of the Socialists' primary campaign. Party leader Olivier Faure spoke in favor of leaving the door open for cooperation with the LFI, but Glucksmann called for a clear break with the far left. His decisive victory is therefore also seen as a vote in favor of a clear demarcation.

The other primary candidates questioned Glucksmann's political experience. Segolene Royal, a previous presidential candidate, compared his bid for the Elysee with that of an "intern" wanting to take charge of a company. She said Glucksmann had no experience in government or even running a local authority.

Despite Glucksmann's victory in the primary, his starting position is a difficult one. A poll by Toluna Harris Interactive, published the day after his win, projects that he would win 10–11% of the vote. The same poll put Melenchon on 18%, meaning the far-left man would be much more likely to reach the runoff. But the survey was conducted before Glucksmann won the primary, and so does not take into account any potential boost the nomination may give him. Still, 10% would be an improvement on the Socialists' performance in the last presidential election in 2022, when their candidate Anne Hidalgo won just 1.75% of the national vote.

There is also the complication that the Socialists are banking on a man who is not even a party member to lead them from irrelevance. Raphael Glucksmann actually belongs to a small center-left party called Place Publique.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Glucksmann has his work cut out for him — especially with young people. In an Ipsos survey in September, which posited Glucksmann as the social-democratic candidate and Edouard Philippe as the only candidate from the political center, Melenchon scored 41% among the under-25s. Meanwhile, 20% of this age group supported the far-right nationalist Marine Le Pen. France's young electorate is politically divided, but Melenchon still dominates on the left.

The 75-year-old is currently rallying alongside the students whose protests have drawn international attention. At a rally near Clermont-Ferrand in central France, he expressed solidarity with their movement and reiterated his calls for lowering the voting age to 16 and abolishing Parcoursup, France's national admissions procedure for higher education.

In an analysis for the Fondation Jean-Jaures, a Socialist-aligned think tank, the political scientist Antoine Bristielle distinguishes between a core group of committed LFI voters and the broader left. Melenchon's most loyal supporters, he says, are often young, educated city-dwellers, and many are under financial pressure. Four in 10 households in this group live on a net monthly income of less than €2,000 ($2,200).

Bristielle estimates that just under a third of the left-wing electorate in his study care more about a left-wing victory than their allegiance to any particular party. Almost half of the people in this group are younger than 35 and would consider voting for the Socialists, the Greens or LFI. Redistribution and an active government are important to them, but most would prefer politicians who are willing to compromise.

The pattern recently observed in Germany, where young women are more likely to vote for the left and young men for the right, does not apply in France. Political scientists Anja Durovic, Nonna Mayer and Noemie Piolat found that in the 2024 European and parliamentary elections, young French women were not significantly more likely to vote for the left, or less likely to vote for the far right, than men of the same age. It remains to be seen whether this pattern will be replicated in the 2027 presidential election.

Glucksmann says he would ease the burden on earned income by reducing France's CSG social security tax while increasing taxes on inheritances worth more than €2 million. He also presents himself as a committed supporter of European integration, while Melenchon has called the EU a neoliberal institution. Glucksmann's political profile combines social policy demands with foreign policy positions that could also appeal to voters from the camp of the current president, Emmanuel Macron.

France's Ukraine policy is one such issue. Glucksmann favors decisive support for Kyiv. Manon Aubry, a member of the European Parliament for Melenchon's LFI, says her party supports military assistance only under certain conditions, namely: The provision of aid to Ukraine must first be subject to democratic debate; it must not enable attacks deep inside Russian territory; and it must not weaken France's own defense capabilities. In 2024, LFI MPs voted against the French–Ukrainian security agreement.

The tension between the parties of the left was once again apparent in the aftermath of the flour attack in Belleville. The LFI MP Sebastien Delogu posted a declaration of support on X for the taxi driver who was going to have to clean his car.

Glucksmann must win over a lot of voters from Melenchon's camp if he is to have a chance of winning the presidency. This is likely to prove a much more difficult task than simply distancing himself from Melenchon.

This article was originally written in German.

#498. Frauenfußball boomt - aber viele verdienen kaum Mindestlohn

Auf den ersten Blick wirkt der Frauenfußball gesund wie nie zuvor - doch hinter dem Milliarden-Boom verbergen sich prekäre Gehälter, psychische Krisen und strukturelle Lücken. Was das für die Zukunft des Sports bedeutet.

Auf den ersten Blick wirkt der Frauenfußball so gesund wie nie zuvor. Ein aktueller Bericht der globalen Spielergewerkschaft FIFPRO prognostiziert, dass die weltweiten Einnahmen im Jahr 2027 die Marke von einer Milliarde US-Dollar überschreiten werden. Von der Weltmeisterschaft in Brasilien, die im Juni und Juli 2027 stattfindet, wird erwartet, dass sie das bislang meistgesehene und umsatzstärkste Frauenfußballturnier wird.

Gleichzeitig zeigt der Bericht aber auch, dass es für Frauen eine große Herausforderung bleibt, vom Fußball leben zu können. Laut FIFPRO verdienen viele Profifußballerinnen weltweit kaum den Mindestlohn, bei manchen liegt der Verdienst sogar noch darunter.

Eine Studie, die auf Umfragen unter Spielerinnen aus aller Welt basiert, ergab, dass nur 66 Prozent der Profis zwölf Monate im Jahr bezahlt werden. Ihre durchschnittliche Vertragslaufzeit bei Vereinen beträgt lediglich 1,6 Jahre.

Laut Studie liegt das weltweite Durchschnittsgehalt von Profispielerinnen bei 2600 US-Dollar (2322 Euro). Allerdings vermittelt dieser Wert ein schiefes Bild, denn wenige Spielerinnen liegen mit ihrem Verdienst teilweise sehr weit über dem Durchschnitt, sehr viele Fußballerinnen verdienen dagegen weniger.

"Im Frauenfußball verlaufen die Unterschiede nicht nur zwischen den fünf stärksten Ligen und dem Rest. Dieses Gefälle gibt es zwar, aber auch innerhalb der einzelnen Ligen selbst", sagt Frankie Brown, der FIFPRO-Forschungsleiter für Frauenfußball, gegenüber der Deutschen Welle (DW). "In manchen Wettbewerben gibt es Vereine, die professionell arbeiten und ihren Spielerinnen ein angemessenes Gehalt zahlen. Gleichzeitig spielen in derselben Liga Mannschaften, deren Spielerinnen Amateurverträge haben und gar nicht bezahlt werden."

In Osteuropa beträgt das durchschnittliche Monatsgehalt umgerechnet beispielsweise nur etwa 785 Euro. In Afrika liegt es sogar bei lediglich 385 Euro, während Spielerinnen in Nordamerika im Schnitt knapp 5360 Euro pro Monat verdienen.

Psychische Belastungen aufgrund wirtschaftlicher Unsicherheit und mangelnder beruflicher Absicherung sind laut Bericht inzwischen der zweithäufigste Grund dafür, dass Spielerinnen darüber nachdenken, den Fußball vorzeitig zu verlassen.

"Das ist einer der besorgniserregendsten Aspekte des Berichts", erklärte Alex Culvin, die FIFPRO-Direktorin für Frauenfußball, der DW. "Von den 49 Prozent der Fußballerinnen, die darüber nachdenken, ihre Karriere frühzeitig zu beenden, nannten 46 Prozent ihre psychische Gesundheit als Grund."

In Interviews hätten Spielerinnen berichtet, dass das Wachstum des Sports neue Belastungen mit sich bringe, darunter einen höheren Arbeitsaufwand und Missbrauch in sozialen Medien. Gleichzeitig fehlten in vielen Vereinen die notwendigen Schutzmechanismen, um mit diesen Veränderungen umzugehen.

"Wir möchten, dass Vereine und nationale Verbände verpflichtende Angebote zur psychischen Unterstützung schaffen, die sich am Wohlbefinden der Spielerinnen orientieren und unabhängig von sportlichen Leistungszielen sind", so Culvin.

FIFPRO fordert die FIFA deshalb auf, eine Art verbindliche Mindeststandards für den Frauenfußball einzuführen. Dadurch sollen grundlegende Vorgaben etwa bei Verträgen, Rentenansprüchen und der Gesundheitsversorgung durchgesetzt werden können. Als mögliches Vorbild gilt die 2026 vereinbarte Tarifvereinbarung der nordamerikanischen Basketballliga WNBA.

Kern des neuen Vertrags ist, dass die Spielerinnen künftig deutlich stärker am wirtschaftlichen Erfolg der Liga beteiligt werden, sodass ihre Einkommen automatisch steigen, wenn die Einnahmen der Liga wachsen.

Das lange ausgehandelte Abkommen sendete das Signal an Sportlerinnen weltweit, für bessere Bezahlung, bessere Arbeitsbedingungen und eine stärkere Beteiligung an den von ihnen erwirtschafteten Einnahmen zu kämpfen.

"Es ist positiv, dass die Durchschnittsgehälter für einige Spielerinnen steigen und mehr Frauen ein zufriedenstellendes Einkommen erzielen. Gleichzeitig darf man nicht übersehen, dass die Unterschiede bei der Bezahlung zwischen den einzelnen Regionen enorm sind", sagte Culvin.

"Auch bei den Arbeitsbedingungen gibt es große Ungleichgewichte, nicht nur weltweit, sondern auch innerhalb einzelner Regionen. In Europa beispielsweise sind die Unterschiede zwischen Ost- und Westeuropa gewaltig. Diese Kluft müssen wir dringend verkleinern. Das Wachstum in den fortschrittlichsten Märkten darf nicht vollständig vom Rest der Branche entkoppelt sein."

Mit großen Hoffnungen auf die Weltmeisterschaft 2027 in Brasilien und jüngsten Schritten zur weiteren Professionalisierung des heimischen Frauenfußballs möchte Deutschland ein Beispiel für strukturelle Verbesserungen werden. Die angestrebte Ausrichtung der Europameisterschaft 2029 schafft dabei zusätzlichen Anreiz, die Standards weiter anzuheben.

Die Gehälter zählen zu den höheren im internationalen Vergleich. In der Saison 2023/24 verdiente eine Spielerin der Frauen-Bundesliga im Durchschnitt rund 48.000 Euro Grundgehalt pro Jahr. Dennoch steckt die strukturelle Entwicklung des Frauenfußballs in Deutschland vielerorts noch in den Anfängen.

Eine neue Regel des DFB zeigt, dass selbst grundlegende professionelle Strukturen erst nach und nach aufgebaut werden. Erst seit der Saison 2025/26 sind Vereine der Frauen-Bundesliga verpflichtet, Assistenztrainerinnen und -trainer, Torwarttrainerinnen und -trainer sowie Athletiktrainerinnen und -trainer hauptberuflich in Vollzeit zu beschäftigen.

Als eine Art "Goldstandard" gilt seit einigen Jahren die englische Women's Super League. "Die Trainingsbedingungen und die personelle Ausstattung waren ein wichtiger Faktor", sagte Deutschlands Nationalspielerin Nicole Anyomi der DW zu ihrem Wechsel von Eintracht Frankfurt zu den London City Lionesses. "Hier haben wir mehr als 30 Mitarbeitende, während es in Frankfurt vielleicht sieben oder acht waren. Man kann von jeder einzelnen Person lernen, und jeden Tag kommt etwas Neues dazu. So entwickelt man sich als Spielerin schneller weiter."

Letztlich gilt: Je schneller der Frauenfußball wächst, desto dringender wird es, die bestehenden Lücken zu schließen.

Dieser Text wurde aus dem englischen Original "FIFPRO report highlights growing pains in women's football" adaptiert.

#499. Australian MP's condition improves after alleged car attack

Helen Haines had both her legs amputated after what authorities say was a deliberate attack

The condition of Helen Haines, the Australian MP hit by a car five days ago in north-east Victoria, has improved from critical to serious but stable.

The independent MP, 65, had both her legs amputated after what authorities say was a deliberate attack outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on Monday.

In the latest update on Saturday morning, the Alfred Hospital in Melbourne said Haines was in a serious but stable condition, the first improvement since she was airlifted there.

Her alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, was arrested shortly after the incident and has since appeared in court on three charges.

The politician's husband, Phil Haines, said on Wednesday that the "horrendous incident" had caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind" were "in good shape".

Shock and disbelief: How the attack on an Australian MP unfolded in a small rural town

Nugent, who was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the MP, appeared in court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.

Police said more charges might be laid, including attempted murder.

His lawyer said his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail.

Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established.

Investigators are looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident.

Nugent's family has said they were long-time friends with Haines.

Shortly after the alleged attack, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told ABC television that there had been a "rise in temperature" and "too much shouting, not enough discourse" in Australia.

Haines, known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action, entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife.

#503. The datacentre next door: on the frontline of tech’s latest David v Goliath battle

The AI boom is pitting local residents against corporate giants seeking to power their energy-hungry networks – but one Welsh city is fighting back

Dale Johnston opens the gate to his neat suburban garden on the western fringes of Newport in South Wales. There’s a trampoline and a slide on the lawn for his grandchildren, and chairs for him and his wife. He should be enjoying the light draining from the perfect autumnal sky – but almost his entire view is blotted out by a vast expanse of prefabricated panels.

The 23 metre-high grey hulk looming over him and his neighbours is a hyperscale datacentre. It is heralded by the area’s Labour politicians as a job creator, yet all Johnston can think about is what he has lost: “Before, the sun used to come around here and it was lovely.” The way residents have been treated is “disgusting”.

Johnston, who used to work for a chemical company in the city, worries what their lives will be like when the centre is switched on: the 36 sets of air blast coolers, needed to stop the chips inside overheating, most likely generate a constant drone, while regular testing of 60 back-up diesel generators, to prevent costly interruption to the flow of data, could produce harmful fumes. He already has to keep his bathroom window closed to stop the low hum from another facility on the rapidly expanding 46-acre datacentre campus that borders the small enclave of 27 houses. His wife, a nurse who works night shifts, can barely sleep already. He shakes his head in despair: “We just don’t know what’s going to happen.”

Johnston can talk about little else, but he feels no one in authority is listening. He’s invited councillors and MPs backing the development to visit his garden. But “they won’t come around here to see what they’ve done”.

This is the frontline of Britain’s datacentre boom, which is pitting residents against giant US tech firms seeking to build a network of facilities capable of providing the immense computing muscle for powerful AI models. There are 315 hyperscale datacentres waiting to connect to the national grid, which carries electricity from power plants to homes and businesses (hyperscale typically means facilities with at least 5,000 servers and 10,000 sq ft in size). Combined, these new centres will require 73GW of power, 28GW higher than the typical peak energy demand of 45GW on a cold winter’s day.

Wales is one of the main development hotspots outside London. It already has the largest datacentre capacity beyond the capital, with new hyperscale facilities planned for former industrial and urban sites. The Keir Starmer-led Labour government viewed this as an inevitable revolution, which the country must embrace or be left behind. It established five AI growth zones to push more datacentres through the planning system and speed up connections to the national grid. The new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has signalled little will change, turning down calls for a moratorium and insisting datacentres bring economic benefits. But anti-datacentre groups springing up in villages, towns and cities across the country see it rather differently: as the imposition of a resource-hungry, polluting industry that increases profits for often US big tech, with little tangible benefit to local people or the country as a whole.

Digital storage is nothing new. The first home PC users saved files on floppy discs and hard drives; businesses used their own server rooms in the 80s and 90s, then moved to off-site facilities as their needs grew. But the development of cloud computing services in the 2010s, such as Google Drive, and AI chatbots in the 2020s, like ChatGPT, led to even greater information and processing demands, which the tech industry insists can only be met by larger and larger datacentres. This has driven huge speculative bets on hyperscale hubs, which investors and tech firms hope will one day reap the rewards of an AI-led transformation of the economy. Globally, it is estimated spending on new facilities could reach $7tn by 2030 – more than double the cost of the New Deal, the Marshall Plan to rebuild Europe after the second world war and the Apollo space programme combined, even allowing for inflation.

The US is at the forefront of the boom, already hosting roughly half of the world’s hyperscale capacity. But the industry is facing a furious backlash, with three- quarters of Americans now opposed to datacentre development and blaming it for increasing energy bills, threatening water supplies in drought-hit areas and spewing out toxic fumes. More than 500 counties and municipalities have passed permanent or temporary datacentre bans.

Loudoun County in northern Virginia sits in what is known as Data Center Alley because it is home to more facilities than anywhere else in the world. Greg Pirio’s life was turned upside down when a gas-powered datacentre opened 150 metres from his home last year. “This neighbourhood was calm and peaceful, and it’s turned into this nightmare,” he says on a video call. “Our quality of life has been degraded so much.”

The noise from the centre’s eight gas turbines is “like being at an airport with all these engines roaring,” Pirio says. “It has given many of my neighbours headaches. It has kept children up at night.” Pirio, who used to work for the Voice of America radio station, has also developed health problems since it opened, including dry eyes and chest tightness. Once he had to leave his house because he was struggling to breathe: “I know whenever the diesel generators are on, because I feel it in my lungs.”

The UK has not yet seen the same level of opposition as the US. But anti-datacentre groups are gathering momentum. Residents in east London are waging a high-profile campaign against a new datacentre on Brick Lane, including protesting outside the offices of Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, who overturned a council decision blocking the scheme.

Seasoned campaigner Owen Espley, who works for environmental charity Global Action Plan, is helping scores of residents’ groups organise against planned datacentres. “This summer has been wild. Every other week a new group has popped up. Petitions are getting thousands of signatures in days,” he says. “Communities are in uproar, and most politicians are playing catch-up.”

Espley has been taken aback by the gulf between the government’s conviction that there is no alternative and ordinary people’s deepening understanding of the complex issues at stake. “There has been a real grassroots questioning of datacentres that connects British Bangladeshis in Brick Lane with Hertfordshire villagers and communities in Northumberland, who want good jobs to come back,” he says. “It is astounding.”

In fact, there are many alternative pathways to market-­led expansion – from tougher regulation to prioritising publicly-owned data infrastructure – which serve communal goals, such as the heart disease and dementia research powered by Bristol University’s new Isambard-AI facility. “First, we need strong standards for private datacentres,” Espley says. “Second, we need industrial strategy to deliver our own public computer, rather than an assumption that US big tech building and owning everything is the only way forward.”

On the deprived eastern edges of Cardiff, the early morning sunshine is warming a car park dotted with scraggly weeds. The perimeter fence is overgrown with brambles, with patches of singed, blackened grass from a recent wildfire visible just beyond. It looks abandoned but soon cars carrying doctors, nurses and other NHS staff start arriving. They are here to catch free buses to Cardiff’s Heath hospital, the largest in Wales.

Hundreds are said to use the park and ride every day, but it is under threat because Labour-controlled Cardiff council wants to sell the land to a property developer, Curtis Hall, to build a hyperscale data facility. The centre will use up to 150 megawatts (MW) of electricity a year, more than triple the demand of a city the size of Cardiff.

The development is one of the most controversial in Wales. Council meetings have been disrupted and more than 1,200 planning objections lodged. Last month, the new Plaid Cymru-led government ordered the council to put the application on hold while it considered whether to take the decision out of councillors’ hands.

Campaigners are determined to keep up the pressure on the Welsh government. Sue Elias, a retired librarian with seemingly endless reserves of energy, dashes back and forth reattaching her “Ditch the datacentre” banner to the car park fence and taping leaflets to the bus stop glass. “What is going to happen to all the people who use the park and ride? It’s bonkers,” she says.

Elias has leafleted the park and ride every Wednesday morning for six weeks. Today she is collecting signatures for an open letter to prove it is well used – so far she has added the names of 1,300 staff and patients. “I’ve not done anything like this before but I’m told I’m a natural,” she says with a mischievous smile, before breaking off to speak to staff arriving for the next bus.

She belongs to community-based union Acorn, which has campaigned against the scheme, and has taken part in protests, including bursting into a council planning meeting in July. “We’d sent emails, done petitions, but we’d had nothing back – tumbleweed. They’re our elected representatives … They should be talking with us.”

It is hard to find anyone in support of the plan in the queue for the bus, which runs three times an hour. “I use it every day. Without it, I probably wouldn’t continue working at the hospital,” says Ami George, a midwife. “Parking there causes that much stress.”

Across Cardiff’s Rhymney River, which curves around the proposed datacentre development, the area’s newest residents have only recently moved into 100 homes built under the city council’s flagship house-building programme. Nick Richards, a freelance filmmaker and skateboarder, and his wife arrived in November. “It felt like the stars had aligned because there is a brand new skate park up the road … the best in Cardiff. It’s amazing,” he says. “I never pictured myself living in suburbia but when we came we saw kids playing outside and thought, this is a really nice area.”

Like many other residents on the estate, Richards had no idea the council was planning to sell the park and ride to a datacentre developer. They moved in two months before the planning application was submitted. Instead of enjoying their new life, they now fear they will never be able to sell. Their home is 300 metres from what the plans describe as the temporary energy centre, which includes seven giant gas turbines. They are expected to power the facility around the clock for five years, according to documents filed by the developer. “I feel trapped,” Richards says, pacing his kitchen. “I couldn’t look prospective buyers in the eye and not say there’s going to be seven gas turbines right next to them.”

Richards has pored over the planning documents and leafleted every house on the new estate, including a care home, which will be just 150 metres from the turbines. “This datacentre will be powered by gas turbines,” he says. “They will pump nitrogen dioxide into our atmosphere. There will also be fine particulate matter and formaldehyde. All these toxins cause health conditions, such as asthma, COPD and heart disease.”

Air quality assessments commissioned by the developer estimate the emissions will be within safe levels. Curtis Hall says the scheme cannot proceed without 100% compliance with all environmental and public health regulatory requirements.

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

There are more than 100 other planned UK datacentres aiming to use gas turbines due to the long wait to be connected to the grid. Richards doesn’t want his estate to be a test case. “Within a mile of this datacentre are 30,000 people. But the people building this centre don’t live here ... They don’t give two shits about Welsh people.”

A stone’s throw away is Llanrumney Hall, once the home of privateer and slave trader Sir Henry Morgan, who gave his name to Captain Morgan rum. It is now a thriving community centre, with a cafe, recording studio and creche. Labour councillor Lee Bridgeman is vaping on an outdoor table, dressed in a hoodie and baseball cap. He ran the local youth centre until it was lost to austerity-era cuts, and though he’s a high-ranking councillor, jointly responsible for housing and communities, he does regular youth work shifts in the area, one of the poorest in Cardiff.

“Llanrumney runs through my veins,” he says. “I’m not your usual politician. I don’t go to conferences. I got into politics to help the community.”

Bridgeman is charming and friendly – but he is not afraid of a fight. He is one of the few public figures in the area who has spoken out in support of the development, sometimes clashing with anti-datacentre campaigners on local Facebook groups. “Some of the information being spread is scaremongering,” he says. “They are telling residents their electricity bills will go up … the river and reservoir will be drained … It’s false information.”

Many of these fears stem from the US, where the rapid expansion of hyperscale facilities has been linked to rising electricity bills, water shortages and toxic air pollution. Bridgeman argues that “planning processes are totally different in the UK. So whereas [US authorities] turn a blind eye to some of the environmental impacts of those monstrosities, that would never happen in the UK.” He “wouldn’t be comfortable” if the gas turbines were running for five years but thinks they might not be needed if the datacentre can connect to the grid sooner.

The backlash has caught him by surprise, but he blames outside activists. “I didn’t see it coming. I didn’t think there would be this much interference,” he says.

Emotions are running high in the city. Some residents say they have been blocked by councillors when trying to question them on Facebook. Planning committee members have received threatening emails, Bridgeman says. “Threats like ‘I will come after you ... we will make your life hell.’ That shouldn’t happen.”

Although the datacentre will employ only up to 125 people when it is built, Bridgeman believes it could encourage other big companies to east Cardiff: “I’m told the knock-on effect could lead to thousands of jobs.”

Later that day, residents squeeze into the local boxing club for a public meeting about the datacentre plan. It is standing room only, with people lining the walls. Bridgeman repeats his claim that few locals have complained: “I have hundreds of emails from residents ... So far I’ve had two emails with regards to the datacentre.”

Some in the audience react angrily. There are shouts of, “We don’t know you, that’s why” and, “Have you heard of social media?” One woman stands up and says, “Don’t tell me you haven’t been privy to the meetings … or things online.” In a show of hands, roughly three-quarters of the 80 to 100 people in the room indicate they are from Llanrumney, almost all opposed. There are cries of, “There you are … you don’t need emails!” and, “That’s every person!” Almost three weeks later, Bridgeman performs a sudden about-turn, submitting a formal letter of objection to the scheme, noting that he has heard from a large number of residents.

The UK hyperscale buildout has been focused on London, but datacentre developers are increasingly targeting areas outside the south-east, to escape severe electrical grid capacity limits. Wales already has the largest datacentre capacity of anywhere outside the capital. Many more could be coming: five of Wales’s largest new and proposed datacentres will consume more electricity than all Welsh homes put together. While the previous Welsh Labour administration welcomed the building spree, claiming giant tech firms’ investment would generate thousands of jobs, the Plaid Cymru-led government has been more circumspect, with ministers emphasising it must benefit Wales.

In the light and airy Welsh parliament building, which overlooks Cardiff Bay, opposition is growing. Plaid Cymru’s Nick Carter, who is the Senedd member for Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, which includes Cardiff East, worries that the surging market will benefit developers and US tech firms rather than the public. “As a party, we’re not going to want to see a proliferation of datacentres, haphazardly being built across the country, on what may be an opportunistic basis,” he says.

Carter, who has a background in commercial property, has examined the Cardiff plans in detail. He says the developer, Curtis Hall, has no track record in datacentres; “They could be a front for someone else: Google, Microsoft, whoever. I can understand why these operators need datacentres, but I’m not sure members of the public share the need.” In response, Curtis Hall says it never claimed it would operate the facility itself, adding it had been working on datacentre projects for five years.

Carter is glad the Welsh government has intervened in Cardiff. But he doesn’t believe Wales needs to follow Scotland by imposing a moratorium on new datacentres: “The Welsh government is developing a strategy for datacentres nationally. We’ll see what comes out of that.”

However, it is not clear how the Welsh government can meet its goal to reach net zero by 2040 without limiting datacentre expansion. Carter admits, “It’s massively problematic.” In Westminster, similar questions have been asked. The Department for Science, Innovation and Technology tells me the government will enable the development of datacentres by generating unprecedented amounts of clean power.

A soft autumnal dusk descends on the residents living beside the new datacentre in Newport. Its sleek industrial-grey walls cast shadows across the closest gardens and homes. Much of the anger and frustration that met the original proposals has given way to weariness and resignation. Some residents talk of moving away, while others are mollified by meetings with the US-based data campus operator, Vantage.

Yet their troubles may only just be beginning – right now, only one of the three Vantage datacentres is operational. Microsoft will be opening its own nearby soon. When all are running, there could be upwards of 500 air handling units working at the same time, with back-up diesel generators needing regular testing, so they can immediately fire up if there is a power cut.

Newport council’s chief scientific officer warned during the planning process that the fumes from all the generators had the “potential to cause unacceptable air pollution levels under use, and testing needs to be understood and mitigation proposed, if needed”.

The council tells me it doesn’t have a duty to monitor emissions from generators, but says its officers check air quality management plans, and ask managers to minimise the impact of generator tests. Vantage says all its facilities operate in accordance with noise and air quality controls. It says it will monitor impacts and investigate concerns when the new centre opens.

Some residents have already given up on democratic process. Johnston fought the proposals through the planning process but felt he was ignored. “We’ve been let down by all of them. I’ve had electoral roll cards come through my door. But I’m voting for none of them … I can’t trust them. They don’t care about any of us.”

Over the road are older homes, where staff working on a nearby wealthy estate once lived. Sonia Thomas, a retired teacher, has lived in the same housekeeper’s cottage since 1969. She can remember when orchards and fields fanned out in front of their gardens but now she doesn’t even know if the sun is shining. “From inside you see grey, not blue,” she says, glancing at the datacentre filling the sky. “It’s horrible.”

#504. Alberta welcomed migrant workers. Now, it wants to restrict their rights

‘Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living,’ Vanesa Ortiz says

When Vanesa Ortiz came to Calgary from Mexico, she found herself in a city gripped by winter. Outside the airport, it was -15C (5F).

“I would come to understand that this was not an extreme cold,” she said. “But in the moment it was terrifying.”

But she also found in those first moments an immense warmth. She was welcomed by elderly volunteers in white cowboy hats, and Ortiz soon felt that Calgary was a place she could one day raise a family. And yet when the teacher reflects on that moment a decade ago, she worries that the opportunities she had to put down roots could be soon closed to others.

This week, Alberta held a referendum, asking residents to weigh in on the province’s relationship with Canada – and the extent to which the province should restrict some newcomers’ access to healthcare, education and social support. It also asked about the need for constitutional reforms.

While unofficial results show both the separation and constitutional questions will fail, the ones on immigration are likely to succeed.

“I love Calgary and I love Alberta,” said Ortiz. “But when I hear people asking whether people should get access to these services – I mean, that was my daughter’s education. That was my family’s healthcare.”

The referendum amplified the grievances of fringe separatists, but it also exposed a central tension in Alberta’s approach to immigration. Even as the oil-rich province seeks newcomers to fill shortages in the job market, the provincial government wants to limit services available to some of those same workers.

The governing United Conservative party blames the rapid population growth for overcrowded and underfunded hospitals and schools. But critics say the proposed solution – restricting access to healthcare, education and social supports – could leave workers and their families more vulnerable without fully addressing the underlying causes of the crisis.

The referendum asked if the government should introduce a law ensuring only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and “individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status” can access healthcare and education. Another asked if newcomers should have lived in Alberta for 12 months before qualifying for certain social support programmes and allowing the province to charge some temporary residents fees for healthcare and education.

Earlier in the year, the Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, blamed the immigration policy of Justin Trudeau’s Liberal government for the resource strains in classrooms, emergency rooms and social support systems. And in a social media post, Smith said: “For every $1 of taxes a guest worker generates, taxpayers are covering $10 in services. This is not sustainable.”

Canada’s federal government has since trimmed immigration targets and placed restrictions on its temporary foreign worker program amid criticisms it was being abused by large companies. But the western province’s economy relies on workers from abroad to fill jobs in sectors, like agriculture, food services and tourism, where employers struggle to recruit or retain enough staff.

Ortiz, who works with the non-profit Asociación de Mexicanos en Calgary, worries mounting skepticism towards migrant workers will push workers into the shadows and make them more vulnerable to labor exploitation.

“I can’t imagine the scale of the harm that a policy like this might create,” she said, noting that thousands of farm workers in the province don’t receive healthcare.

Ortiz has seen views shift on immigration in recent years and says the results of the referendum reflect a population that is “squeezed” economically.

“Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living. That’s not going to fix our classrooms. They keep essential services open. In many cases, they are frontline workers. And now they’re being treated as disposable.”

For some residents, the proposals represent a sharp reversal from Alberta’s earlier efforts to attract newcomers. The UCP government invested in recruitment and expanded its provincial immigration nomination targets to address labour shortages. But as a growing number of Albertans sour on immigration, the government position has shifted.

Ximena González, a Calgary-based writer, said when the provincial government began its campaign to bring in more people, it “wanted more workers to exploit”, noting that most workers come from abroad on temporary permits.

“Now, the message feels more out in the open: ‘We wanted you to come, to exploit you. And now, we don’t need you any more – so we will punish you.”

The provincial government has claimed that temporary residents, who make up almost 6% of Alberta’s total population, contribute roughly $150m in tax revenues but cost the province more than $1bn annually in health, education and other social services.

But González argues that there is no data to back that claim.

Economist Gillian Petit notes that temporary residents also remit taxes to the federal government, which helps fund Alberta’s healthcare, meaning those residents probably contribute far more than the province acknowledges. If they contribute less in total tax dollars than other Albertans, it is because they earn less than the median resident. They are also less likely to use healthcare and education resources than the average Albertan.

“In all honesty, if I were a temporary resident and had to choose whether or not to stay, I wouldn’t,” said González, who came to Canada 16 years ago as an international student. “I would not feel wanted, and I don’t want to be treated like a third-class citizen.”

She says that media fixation on Alberta’s fringe independence movement meant the other questions in the referendum received little scrutiny and left voters uninformed.

“The media failed to help people to make an educated vote – instead of just voting based on racism.”

Economist Jim Stanford said hundreds of thousands of residents skipped over those questions on immigration, choosing to only answer the one on separation.

“This cannot remotely be interpreted as a mandate for the government to crack down on immigration,” he said, adding the province didn’t have the power to “unilaterally” act on these proposals. “This was a symbolic ideological exercise and gives a cast of legitimacy to some of these very rightwing nativist sentiments that are bubbling in the far right of Alberta politics.”

During a series of town halls over the years led by the government, more extreme views on immigration were clear. One resident received cheers after suggesting a policy of mass deportations and another said immigrants “harm” children and suggested she might seek asylum in the US.

For Ortiz, the government’s about-face reflects a “betrayal” of the workers who have helped build the province.

“We’re asking people if we should remove the right to access healthcare and education from taxpayers who are, quite literally, building our communities,” she said. “But I also worry that what gets lost in this debate is these people. They are not just labour. They work, study and raise their children here. They need to know they deserve the chance to build a life with dignity and with respect to feel safe and to feel welcome.”

#505. Why the charts are full of old songs - and so are your playlists

One of 2026's biggest hits is Zara Larsson's Lush Life, originally released in 2015

More music is being created than at any other time in human history. Every day, more than 100,000 songs, external are being submitted to streaming services.

And despite the deluge of AI music, external - Spotify says it has removed 75 million "spammy tracks" from its catalogue - real music still makes up most of our listening. The streaming service Deezer says AI accounts for just 0.5% of streams on its platform.

The problem for all those artists creating new music is that our listening habits increasingly show a love for nostalgia.

Luminate, an independent entertainment data and analytics company that tracks music, film, and television consumption first started tracking music streaming in 2008.

This year, it recorded that the streaming of current music (released less than 18 months ago) was significantly dwarfed by older music in both the UK and US.

In the first half of 2026, almost two thirds of the music played (about 60%) was released five or more years ago.

So, if we're stuck in a streaming rut, what's to blame?

In the UK, most of us seem to be shunning new songs.

Eighteen of the year's top 20 bestselling songs, external were released 12 months ago, or earlier.

The year's eighth biggest hit is Zara Larsson's Lush Life, which originally came out in June 2015. Michael Jackson's Billie Jean (1983) is in 22nd place. Fleetwood Mac's Dreams (1977) is 30th.

It's a sign that, with practically every song ever recorded available at the press of a button, people are increasingly seeking out the classics - or what the music industry categorises as "deep catalogue".

There, in the two most-played genres, R&B and Hip-Hop, external, about 60% of streams are old-school catalogue hits.

Even when current songs do break out, they themselves dominate streaming for weeks and even months.

Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's duet Rein Me In recently made UK chart history, spending a record-breaking 23 non-consecutive weeks at number one.

Olivia Dean and Sam Fender have broken chart history with Rein Me In, after 19 non-consecutive weeks at the top of the UK singles chart

Likewise, in America, Ella Langley's Choosin' Texas has become the longest-running number one in US chart history.

The reality, of course, is that hits need to achieve "millions of streams a day, external" to reach the top of the charts.

But according to the UK's Competition and Markets Authority, nearly two thirds of streams are of music recorded by "only the top 0.4% of artists, external".

As we increasingly cling on to our favourites, aspiring artists may be suffering.

Even after a song has gone viral, some musicians say it can be hard to promote subsequent releases and sustain a career. A platform like TikTok isn't set up to boost artists, it's there to create viral moments around a single song.

"It's easier [today] for folks to be passive fans," noted J Erving, the founder of Raye's distribution company, Human Re Sources, in a recent interview with Billboard, external.

"For you to consider yourself broken [as a mainstream artist], people need to care about you beyond the song. Where is the connectivity? Are people really dialled in in a deeper way?"

It's a problem the music industry is keen to tackle.

Oliver Schusser, the Head of Apple Music, says his streaming service is working to champion "tomorrow's artists" in its curation.

"You know, we do the Super Bowl halftime show, we need to make sure that we still have performers in 10, 20, 30 years," he tells BBC News.

"Because if you look back at the performers we had in the last four years, they all started somewhere before they got to the world's biggest stage."

Other organisations like Sofar Sounds work exclusively with grassroots musicians, putting on intimate pop-up gigs in cities across the globe.

This October, its Shoreditch Sofar Fringe festival showcased a whole host of artists like East London rapper J Casa.

Rapper J Casa is one of thousands of grassroots artists trying to cut through the noise on streaming platforms

In an age of content oversaturation, Casa thinks there's something unique about a live performance.

Rather than hearing more of what they already know, Casa says audiences form "a lasting connection" with a new artist and their music.

Sofar is also launching its Human Discovery Movement, external campaign that aims to put music curation and discovery "back into human hands."

Music lovers can now text a "mystery number" and receive voice notes from Sofar's tastemakers with recommendations for new music worldwide.

Artificial intelligence (AI) may also be playing its part in the so-called death of new music.

Musicologist Anna-Kaisa Kaila thinks "there absolutely is potential for bias" with AI-generative playlist technology.

"With AI systems, the bias can either come from the data or from the system itself. If there's not enough training data in a particular style that is perhaps not so commercially dominant, it will be that much harder for the system to pull up tracks in that style."

Others fear an algorithmic streaming bubble is to the detriment of genuine music, its discovery and creatives' livelihoods.

As Tim Garcia, London-based DJ and curator puts it: "They're based on everyone's listening behaviour and data, right? So, you're probably going to get given a very similar recommendation to an artist you're already listening to."

Dan Mackta, managing director at Qobuz, an online music platform that maintains a strict human-first approach to curation, agrees the technology "is never going to want to throw a curve ball at you".

London-based artist Chiminyo performs at his ongoing jazz-electronic NRG project

Chiminyo, a London-based independent artist, believes that auto-generated playlists are also misleading people into thinking they're listening to "hand-picked" tunes from bona fide artists - as opposed to digitally mass-produced sound-alikes created to catch streams.

Scrolling through a "relaxing jazz piano playlist" with over 370,000 saves on Spotify, he spots that top featured artists that rack up hundreds of thousands of monthly listens have unverified accounts.

Little - if anything - can be found about them online, he says.

To his trained ear, Chiminyo also says the different artists' tracks sound near identical, reason enough to conclude the compositions have been synthetically mass-produced.

"Its all the same: the same piano feel, the same microphone placement, the same tape machine, has been used on every single one of these tracks."

When asked, Spotify said it had rolled out platform-wide policies, external against impersonation and is working to the improve filtering out of AI-related issues on its platform. But it acknowledges AI's use in music production sits on a spectrum with some artists choosing to use it to varying degrees.

New music may not be dying out, but it's clear it has a lot to contend with in 2026.

#506. La célèbre villégiature du "Nid d'Aigle" d'Hitler en Allemagne ravagée par les flammes, un suspect arrêté

Article rédigé par Clément Périé

l'essentiel Situé dans les Alpes bavaroises en Allemagne, le refuge de villégiature du dictateur nazi Adolf Hitler a été ravagé par les flammes dans la nuit du 23 au 24 octobre. Plus de 200 pompiers ont été mobilisés pour éteindre l'incendie du Nid d'Aigle, situé sur un éperon rocheux à 1 800 mètres d'altitude. Une personne suspecte a depuis été placée en garde à vue, ont annoncé les autorités allemandes.

Il s'agissait d'un des lieux de villégiature préférés d'Adolf Hitler, le dictateur nazi ayant dirigé l'Allemagne de 1933 à 1945. Dans la nuit du 23 au 24 octobre, le refuge situé sur une hauteur des Alpes bavaroises a été en proie aux flammes. Plus de 200 pompiers ont été mobilisés pour éteindre le sinistre, situé à 1 800 mètres d'altitude, sur la commune de Berchtesgaden (Bavière, Allemagne). L'origine du sinistre dans ce refuge, reconverti en monument historique en 1952, reste pour le moment inconnue.

Chaque vendredi, retrouvez les affaires qui marquent notre région, les enquêtes qui font parler, les procès majeurs et les coulisses de l'actualité police-justice, décryptés par nos journalistes spécialistes.

Les pompiers ont expliqué que l'accès aux lieux du sinistre était particulièrement difficile alors que "le bâtiment était entièrement en feu". Même si aucune victime n'est à déplorer, les pompiers affirment qu'ils ne peuvent "pénétrer dans le bâtiment qu'avec un équipement de protection respiratoire lourd".

À lire aussi : Hitler aurait-il menti pour cacher son rôle dans la mort de sa nièce ? Des archives troublantes relancent les soupçons de meurtre et bousculent l’alibi du dictateur

#508. Is Germany's eight-hour workday under threat?

Would you work 12 hours straight? The CDU/CSU and SPD are locked in a dispute over reforms to the Working Hours Act. Workplace flexibility, collective bargaining agreements and worker protection rules are at stake.

The town of Leuna, in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, is one of the country's largest chemical industry hub, where more than 100 companies have established operations. Among them is the Finnish biotechnology group UPM, which has recently built a biorefinery for wood-based chemicals in Leuna. It's now hiring.

One of the job listings is for a chemical technician to oversee the rollout of new facilities. But to qualify, candidates must be willing to work 12-hour shifts. Is that legal? According to German law, standard working hours are limited to eight hours per day. It is permissible to extend this to ten hours, provided that workers receive compensatory time off for the overtime, and there must be at least 11 hours of rest between two shifts.

Business associations and the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties have long called for these rules to be made more flexible.

Rainer Dulger, president of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA), points to the European Working Time Directive, which allows for a maximum weekly working time of 48 hours. "The allowance is being taken advantage of almost everywhere else — except here," Dulger told the dpa news agency in August.

Companies say they often find the existing rules too rigid, particularly in industries with seasonal fluctuations — such as tourism — or in project-based work, or during irregular peaks in workload, such as in the restaurant industry. They could deploy their staff more efficiently, says Dulger: "The Working Hours Act dates back to the era of fax machines and rotary-dial phones. It knows nothing of laptops or daycare hours."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In their 2025 coalition agreement, the CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) agreed to reform the Working Hours Act. "In keeping with the European Working Time Directive, we want to allow for a maximum weekly rather than daily working time — also and especially to promote a better work-life balance," the agreement said.

The SPD would have preferred to leave the law unchanged, but had to accept the conservative parties' plans. The Social Democrats pointed out that longer working hours are already permitted in exceptional cases, such as in emergency services, the health care sector and security services. Workers in power plants, refineries and the chemical industry are also allowed to work up to 12 hours at a time.

Even Chancellor Friedrich Merz himself seemed unaware of this exception until quite recently. After visiting the UPM refinery in Leuna in September, he recounted to business leaders at the German Employers' Day in Berlin that he was "completely surprised" to learn that the facilities operate on a continuous 12-hour shift schedule, thanks to the approval of the works council.

Merz recounted the shift supervisor describing the work schedule as "really great" — with three-day work weeks. "He said we have plenty of time for our families — it's a great way to organize things." Merz went on to conclude that this demonstrates the benefits of relaxing the Working Hours Act.

"Working more than eight hours is not exploitation. Rather, it can be a good opportunity to organize working hours more flexibly — both for businesses and for the people working there," the chancellor said. "We should do it."

But there is resistance from within the SPD and from trade unions opposed to amending the Working Hours Act. The trade union Verdi argues that significantly longer workdays would have negative consequences for employees' health and would disadvantage people with family and caregiving responsibilities. In certain industries, employees could also be put under pressure to accept longer shifts.

An initial reform draft was drawn up in June 2026 by the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry, headed at the time by Bärbel Bas, an SPD politician who has since resigned for personal reasons.

The draft includes some conditions, including a collective bargaining agreement between employers and unions if any schedule changes were made, as well as health and safety regulations, and working hours to be tracked electronically.

Annika Klose, spokesperson for labor and social policy for the SPD parliamentary group, explained the thinking behind the idea. Flexibility, she said, is "not a one-way street." The coalition agreement explicitly aims to promote a better balance between family and work. "So that it's sometimes possible to take your child to football practice in the afternoon and then continue working afterward — but not that my boss tells me against my will: 'You're working the shift from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. tomorrow.'"

The CDU/CSU immediately rejected the draft. Businesses were also up in arms. "This draft must be withdrawn and completely revised," demanded Dulger in a statement, saying it was "steeped in mistrust." The German Confederation of Skilled Crafts (ZDH) spoke of a "breach of the commitments agreed to in the coalition agreement." The reform has been on hold ever since.

At the Employers' Day event, Merz held out the prospect of progress. "This is indeed long overdue. I believe we can accomplish this relatively quickly and create flexibility in the labor market."

It remains to be seen, however, whether the new SPD Labor Minister, Alexander Schweitzer, shares this view. In early October, his party released a paper on reforming working hours that read like a declaration of war against the CDU. "Self-determination, Not Deregulation" is the title of the seven-page document that was signed by the SPD working group on labor, the youth organization Jusos, the "60plus" working group and the women's wing of the SPD.

In the paper, the Social Democrats not only reiterate the points that already appeared in Bas' draft back in June. They also demand that, in the future, employers and employees should decide on working hours "jointly and by mutual agreement." They argued that it is not "in the spirit of a modern reform of working time law" if only employers can determine when employees finish work.

From a political perspective, the dispute over reforming work hours has long become more than just a debate over legal provisions. It is a fundamental dispute over how much flexibility workers should be expected to tolerate in the future and to what extent the state should protect them. And it is yet another stumbling block for the already beleaguered government in Berlin.

#509. Student movement takes Serbia's Vučić to the wire in neck-and-neck election

The Student List is Number 3 on Serbia's ballot paper, so the figure seen being hugged by this supporter has become a symbol of the movement's fight for change

If Sunday's parliamentary elections really are a battle for the heart of Serbia, then who better than a cardiologist to be one of the leading figures in the race.

Ilija SrdanoviÄ appears an unlikely opponent for Serbia's long-serving leader, Aleksandar VuÄiÄ, arriving for an interview by motorbike sporting a fluorescent yellow jacket emblazoned with pro-student slogans.

He has been selected as top candidate for an opposition movement posing the most serious challenge to VuÄiÄ since the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) entered government in 2012.

The Student List has emerged from almost two years of anti-corruption protests led by young Serbians, outraged by the deaths of 16 people when a railway station's canopy collapsed in Serbia's second city Novi Sad.

What you need to know about Serbia's pivotal election

Instead of running for office themselves, student-led assemblies at the country's university faculties have chosen 250 candidates to stand in the parliamentary election, with SrdanoviÄ, professor at Novi Sad University, heading the list.

"It is absolutely normal to stand with my students to help them in their fair struggle," SrdanoviÄ told the BBC.

Ilija SrdanoviÄ tops the Student List's 250 candidates but would not necessarily lead Serbia if they won

The Student List is up against a Serbian leader who has served successively as deputy prime minister, prime minister and president since 2012. When he called these snap elections last month, he stood down as president to run again for the role of prime minister.

Whatever VuÄiÄ's title, there has never been any doubt that he was the man in charge â an image enthusiastically promoted by Serbia's largely uncritical media.

He retains strong support among a significant section of Serbia's population. They view him as a strong leader who stands up for the country's interests. He can also point to significant economic growth over the past decade and numerous improvements in infrastructure.

VuÄiÄ has painted the student movement as foreign-backed and seeking to "bring down our state". "Let us always protect and defend it," he told supporters at a final campaign rally.

Just like the protest movement from which it developed, the Student List has no hierarchy or nominated leader. This makes it a proposition unlike any other in Serbia's relatively short democratic history.

Reliable polls are thin on the ground, but analysts are predicting an extremely tight vote.

A reported 150,000 supporters turned out for the final Student List rally in Belgrade's Slavija Square on Thursday night

Ilija SrdanoviÄ may head the list of candidates â but he is not the movement's leader and would not necessarily be first choice prime minister if they won.

SrdanoviÄ insists that the Student List has a clear vision: "We offer to our citizens the core values of civilised society, which this previous regime has taken away from our citizens for the last time."

The other candidates on the Student List range from academics to athletes â and economists to engineers. None of them has a political background. But the students who selected them believe that is a strength, rather than a weakness.

"We've gathered people who are actually the best in their fields, and we really think that they are competent enough to rule the country," says Aleksandra, a student at Novi Sad University who only wants to give her first name.

"All of them are gathered around the same vision of a country where the freedom of speech is ruling, where you can walk to your home in the middle of the night and you will not be beaten up by some hooligans," she adds.

The Student List and its supporters say that Aleksandar VuÄiÄ and the SNS dominate state institutions and media coverage.

At the last parliamentary election in 2023, the International Election Observation Mission noted "overwhelming ruling party advantage" due to "bias in the media" and "misuse of public office and resources".

The BBC approached leading figures in the SNS for an interview but was not offered a response.

VuÄiÄ continues to command strong support among sections of Serbia's population

For the past 18 months, there has also been a full-time, pro-SNS camp in the small park between the National Assembly and the Presidency building in the centre of Belgrade. Its residents have repeatedly attacked journalists and made the park a no-go zone for local people.

VuÄiÄ has called the camp "a symbol of resistance" against those who "cannot stand different opinions".

But his major challenge remains what happened outside Novi Sad railway station two years ago.

The station's renovation was a key part of his signature infrastructure project â the high-speed line linking Belgrade and Budapest. So it has been difficult for VuÄiÄ to distance himself from the disaster.

Aleksandar VuÄiÄ stepped down as president last month with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister

Protests followed, with participants accusing the authorities of corruption and having "blood on their hands".

"This is a problem for the government," says Magda Anastasijevic, the Eastern Europe analyst for the conflict monitor, ACLED.

"VuÄiÄ has survived this in the past, he was always able to find a scapegoat and blame whatever problems on them. This was not the case for the canopy."

On the diplomatic front, he has performed a delicate balancing act.

Membership talks with the EU continue, albeit fitfully, even as Serbia retains close ties with Russia and China â both countries that refuse to recognise Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia.

VuÄiÄ has warned those links could be severed if the Student List took power.

"When you ask them: will you impose sanctions on Russia? Silence, umming and ah-ing, but no answer," he told the audience at a pre-election rally.

"You know what the Chinese think, you've heard what Vladimir Putin said. So you decide. Think about who has our best interests at heart."

The final rallies of the campaign saw the SNS stage an event at Belgrade Arena, with Aleksandar VuÄiÄ as the only speaker. But on the other side of the Sava River, the Student List attracted a reported 150,000 people in Slavija Square to listen to a mixture of students and candidates.

The contrasting visions were clear to see: the strong, sole leader â or a collective approach. Now Serbia's electorate must decide which they prefer.

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Ferry and train services have also been halted as Storm Boelo hurtles towards UK bringing heavy rain and gales

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

More than 1,500 flights have been delayed and train services disrupted after Storm Boelo hit the UK with winds of up to 80mph, triggering “danger to life” weather warnings.

Flights to and from major UK airports, including London Heathrow, Manchester, Edinburgh and Glasgow, have been delayed by an average of two hours amid severe weather conditions.

The Met Office issued amber weather warnings for far north of England, Scotland and the north-east of Northern Ireland on Saturday night.

It said gusts of 60-70mph were expected widely, with winds potentially reaching 80mph in exposed coastal locations.

Scotland’s environmental watchdog issued 29 flood warnings and 11 less severe flood alerts as Storm Boelo brought heavy rain and powerful winds to the country.

Ferry services between Ireland and Pembrokeshire have also been halted, while more than a dozen rail services have been cancelled on Scotland’s west coast.

The travel chaos comes immediately after Storm Austen caused disruption on Friday, leaving thousands of homes without power in Cornwall and forcing schools to close.

Scotland's environmental watchdog has issued 29 flood warnings and 11 less severe flood alerts as Storm Boelo brings heavy rain and powerful winds to the country.

The Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa) has warnings and alerts in place across Scotland amid concerns over rising water levels and flooding.

A yellow rain warning covering central parts of the Highlands, including Inverness, came into force at 9pm on Saturday and is expected to remain in place until 3pm on Sunday.

“Very strong westerly winds associated with Storm Boelo are expected, with fairly widespread gusts of 60 to 70mph and gusts to 80mph in exposed coastal areas,” the Met Office said.

“The strongest winds will initially affect western Scotland and the far north of Northern Ireland on Saturday evening and then spread eastwards overnight and through Sunday.”

The latest warnings come just a day after Storm Austen brought heavy rainfall to much of the UK.

An amber weather warning for wind across Scotland and a yellow warning for rain for parts of the country have come into force in response to Storm Boelo.

The amber wind warning affects almost all of Scotland, with the exception of Orkney and the Shetland Isles, although Orkney still has a yellow wind warning in place.It came into force at 9pm, and is to remain in place until 9pm on Sunday.

The yellow rain warning that came into force concurrently affects central parts of the Highlands, including Inverness, and will be called off at 3pm on Sunday.It comes after Storm Austen brought heavy rain to much of the UK on Friday.

The Met Office has warned of potential injuries and danger to life from flying debris as well as a chance of damage to buildings, power cuts and travel disruption.“

Very strong westerly winds associated with Storm Boelo are expected, with fairly widespread gusts of 60 to 70mph and gusts to 80mph in exposed coastal areas,” the Met Office said.

“The strongest winds will initially affect western Scotland and the far north of Northern Ireland on Saturday evening and then spread eastwards overnight and through Sunday.”

Storm Boelo’s strong winds disrupted flights at Dublin Airport, where as of 4pm on Saturday, nine outbound and 10 inbound flights had been cancelled by airlines because of weather issues.

It also reported that six inbound flights performed go-arounds – five of which landed on the second attempt, with the other diverting to another airport before returning a short time later. A Dublin Airport spokesman warned “winds are forecast to remain strong for the rest of the day, which may lead to further disruption”.

The UK is braced for its second storm of the season just a day after Storm Austen passed.

Flights have been grounded after the Met Office issued fresh “danger to life” weather warnings ahead of Storm Boelo.

Dublin Airport announced several cancellations and delays on Saturday as this second storm hurtled towards the UK and Ireland, bringing heavy rains and gales.

But why have these storms been called Austen and Boelo? Why are storms named, and how does the naming system work?

Severe weather is disrupting a lot of train lines in the north of England on Sunday. Delays are expected on the journey between Crewe and Manchester Piccadilly, as well as the route from Leeds to Manchester Victoria.

Services in Stoke, Maccersfield, Blackpool, Preston and Wigan also face serious disruption tomorrow.

A man says he is "lucky to be alive" after a large oak tree came down during Storm Austen, crushing his car while he was inside it.

Pete Smith was waiting at a temporary traffic light in his black BMW 4-series in Swanage, Dorset, on Friday when the 75mph gusts blew down the 50ft oak tree.

The 63 year-old financier said he heard a "giant bang" and there was smashed glass and tree everywhere.

LNER train line has said that most trains operating to and from Aberdeen will be cancelled on Sunday due to Storm Boelo.

A reduced service will also be operating between Northallerton and Darlington, and Newcastle and Edinburgh on Sunday.

LNER said that “due to the severity of the weather and expected road closures, rail replacement coaches will not be available”. They added: “As other operators are also impacted, it will not be possible to travel with a different train company”.

Met Office chief forecaster Jason Kelly said: “Storm Boelo will be felt across the UK this weekend, with the strongest winds and greatest potential for disruption in the north.“

“Amber warnings are in place across mainland Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, where gusts of 60-70mph are expected widely, with the potential for 80mph in exposed coastal locations.

“Strong winds will also affect other parts of the UK, with gusts of 50-60mph possible in places. Heavy rain will provide an additional hazard, particularly in the north, bringing the potential for further impacts.

“People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies.”

People should secure loose items outside, plan ahead if they are travelling and keep an eye on the latest forecast and warnings, he advised.
