#512. Verschwörungstheorien: Wie prüfe ich, was stimmen könnte?

Verschwörungen gibt es und wird es immer geben. Die Frage ist, wie sich absurde von wahrscheinlichen Verschwörungstheorien unterscheiden lassen. Dabei hilft ein gewisses Maß an Misstrauen - auch sich selbst gegenüber.

"Birds aren't real", Vögel gibt es nicht. Das kritzelte der US-amerikanische Student Peter McIndoe auf ein Stück Pappe und mischte sich 2017 bei einer Demonstration unter die Anhänger des US-Präsidenten Donald Trump.

Auf seinen Slogan angesprochen erzählte er: Die US-Regierung habe alle Vögel umbringen lassen und sie durch Überwachungsdrohnen ersetzt. Vögel säßen auf Stromleitungen, um sich aufzuladen, Vogelkot sei ein flüssiges Ortungsgerät.

Das ist eine Verschwörungserzählung. Eine andere geht so: Der Ölkonzern ExxonMobil wusste bereits seit den 1970er-Jahren von der Bedrohung durch den Klimawandel. Vom Konzern bezahlte Forschende haben den globalen Temperaturanstieg ziemlich präzise eingeschätzt.

Die internen Analysen von ExxonMobil standen allerdings immer in heftigem Kontrast zu ihren öffentlichen Erklärungen, in denen der Klimawandel kleingeredet, Mythen verbreitet und Unwissenheit vorgetäuscht wurde.

Peter McIndoe erzählte der New York Times 2022, dass seine "Birds aren't real"-Verschwörung Satire gewesen sei. Er habe damit darauf aufmerksam machen wollen, wie schnell Menschen an erfundene Verschwörungserzählungen und Desinformationen glauben.

ExxonMobils Machenschaften wurden 2015 durch investigative Journalisten aufgedeckt, die Zugang zu internen Dokumenten und Forschungsberichten hatten. 2020 reichte der Generalstaatsanwalt von Washington D.C. Klage gegen ExxonMobil und weitere Ölkonzerne ein. Eine 2023 im Fachmagazin Science erschienene Studie wertete die internen Forschungsergebnisse des Unternehmens aus und bestätigte die Verschwörungserzählung: Exxon wusste seit Jahrzehnten von den Folgen des Klimawandels.

Es gibt also beides: wenig plausible und plausible Verschwörungserzählungen. Die Frage ist nur, wie sich die eine von der anderen unterscheiden lässt. Es gibt ein paar Prüfkriterien, die dabei helfen können.

Eine Voraussetzung dafür ist: innehalten und nachdenken. Nichts tun, außer sich selbst ein paar kritische Fragen zu stellen.

Eine dieser Fragen ist die nach der Logik, sagt Lotte Pummerer, Sozialpsychologin und Postdoc an der Universität in Mannheim, wo sie zu Verschwörungstheorien forscht.

Wie viele Menschen müssten eingeweiht sein und welche Motive sollten sie haben, die Verschwörung geheim zu halten? Um bei dem Beispiel mit den falschen Vögeln zu bleiben: Neben den Drahtziehern müssten alle Ornithologen und Vogelschützer Bescheid wissen und dichthalten. Und das seit Jahrzehnten. Ohne einen einzigen Whistleblower. Wie logisch ist das?

Auch die eigenen Motive sollten einmal unter die Lupe genommen werden, sagt Pummerer. "Kann es sein, dass ich gerade bewusst nur in eine bestimmte Richtung nach Informationen suche? Gibt es einen Grund, dass ich eine schnelle, befriedigende Antwort will oder wäre es okay für mich, zu dem Ergebnis zu kommen, dass ich diese Antwort aufgrund meiner derzeitigen Informationen nicht bekommen kann?"

Solche Fragen sollen mögliche kognitive Verzerrungen (cognitive bias) überprüfen, für die wir alle anfällig sein können. Es handelt sich dabei um systematische Denk- und Wahrnehmungsfehler, die unsere Entscheidungsfindung, Urteilsbildung und Wahrnehmung beeinflussen und zu falschen Annahmen führen.

Ein Beispiel für eine kognitive Verzerrung ist der sogenannte Bestätigungsfehler (confirmation bias): Wir bevorzugen tendenziell Informationen, die am besten in unser Weltbild passen und unsere ohnehin vorhandenen Annahmen bestätigen.

Aufgrund dieser kognitiven Verzerrungen sei es wichtig "mal ganz bewusst den Gegencheck zu machen", sagt die Sozialpsychologin. Und sich zu fragen: "Bin ich bereit, mich überzeugen zu lassen, wenn die wissenschaftliche Evidenz in eine andere Richtung weist?"

Pummerer nennt 9/11 als Beispiel. Die Verschwörungserzählung, dass die Anschläge auf das World Trade Center und das Pentagon 2001 von der US-Regierung inszeniert waren, hält sich hartnäckig. Die Türme können nur gesprengt worden sein, sie wären sonst nie zusammengefallen. Oder hätten zur Seite kippen müssen.

Umfangreiche Ermittlungen vieler unabhängiger Expertinnen und Experten haben ergeben: 9/11 war ein islamistischer Terroranschlag. Es war der Einschlag der beiden Flugzeuge, der die Türme zum Einsturz gebracht hat. "Da sind viele Leute, die in den entsprechenden Bereichen viel mehr Expertise haben als ich, angefangen von Bauingenieuren, Menschen, die Flugschreiber und Flugradare auslesen, bis hin zu Investigativjournalistinnen. Warum sollte ausgerechnet ich, die ich nicht dafür ausgebildet bin, zu der entscheidenden Erkenntnis kommen?", fragt Pummerer.

"Es gibt einen Wissensunterschied zwischen Leuten, die Experten sind und einem selbst, wenn man kein Experte ist", ergänzt Marlene Altenmüller, ebenfalls Sozialpsychologin und Juniorprofessorin für Wissenschaftsrezeption am Leibniz-Institut für Psychologie in Trier. Es sei wichtig, diesen Unterschied anzuerkennen, denn "wir leben in einer komplexen Welt und können gar nicht alles selbst durchdringen und verstehen."

Bedeutet auch: Ohne Vertrauen geht es nicht. Das heißt aber nicht, dass wir blind vertrauen sollten, im Gegenteil. Misstrauen sei wichtig und konstruktiv, sagt Altenmüller. "Misstrauen und Zweifel sind zentraler Bestandteil wissenschaftlicher Prozesse."

Sie bezeichnet Wissenschaft als "institutionalisierten Zweifel". Studien werden immer wieder von unterschiedlichen Forschenden kritisch geprüft und oft auch wiederholt, um frühere Ergebnisse abzusichern und besser zu verstehen. Aus diesem Grund, sagt Altenmüller, sei Wissenschaft "die beste Annäherung an die Wahrheit, die wir haben".

"Wissenschaftlicher Konsens" bedeutet, dass sich die Argumente durchgesetzt haben, deren Datenbasis einer wiederholten, kritischen Prüfung standgehalten haben. Der menschengemachte Klimawandel ist ein Beispiel für wissenschaftlichen Konsens.

"Dieses ständige Hinterfragen und der produktive Prozess des Misstrauens, der dann zum Konsens führt, sollte viel überzeugender sein als eine Einzelperson mit einer Meinung", sagt Altenmüller.

Es liegt in der Natur wissenschaftlicher Erkenntnisse, dass sie nie als absolut unumstößlich angesehen werden, sondern immer mit einer gewissen Unsicherheit behaftet sind. Ein Umstand, den sich ExxonMobil in seinen öffentlichen Stellungnahmen zum Risiko durch die globale Erwärmung zunutze gemacht hat: Unsicherheiten in Bezug auf die Klimawandelforschung wurden besonders betont und übertrieben.

Die Wissenschaftlerin Lotte Pummerer wünscht sich an dieser Stelle ein bisschen mehr selbstkritisches Hinterfragen und weniger Doppelstandards: Wenn von einer politischen oder wissenschaftlichen Institution eine lückenlose Beweiskette verlangt werde, wie könne dann gleichzeitig irgendeiner Person auf einem Sofa in einem YouTube-Video geglaubt werden, die beim Schminken was von geheimen Machenschaften erzähle?

#513. Older, calmer, but still playing the hits: Mourinho and Madrid primed for clásico

Once Bobby Robson’s translator at the Camp Nou, José Mourinho is tasked with bringing down Barcelona on Sunday

José Mourinho has done the por que?, the printout and the press conference no-show, and he’s been here only three months. The Real Madrid manager has played the classics without even playing a clásico. Not yet anyway, but it’s time: on Sunday night he returns to the stadium he first arrived at 30 transformative years ago as Bobby Robson’s talented young translator, and last visited in 2013 as the most famous manager in football.

The coach who once declared “today, tomorrow and always, Barcelona in my heart,” and claimed he would only ever go to Real Madrid to destroy them, has been entrusted with attempting to bring about the destruction of Barcelona. It is not the first time: if his return is about nostalgia, which it is, that’s wrapped up in their rivals too.

“The clásico is just another game in the championship but to say it’s a game like any other would be to lie, totally unreal,” Mourinho said on Wednesday, and he knows. As for Barcelona’s latest star, he’s looking forward to seeing Mourinho again. “I love the needle,” Lamine Yamal says. “The Mourinho-Guardiola era, I loved all that. That’s football. Sport is serious but I want a show and we have more fun.”

There are bigger things, sure; life beyond Barcelona. Madrid’s astonishing Champions League record since Mourinho was last here – following up the elusive decima, the 10th title which had evaded them for 12 years, with the 11th, 12th, 13th, 14th and 15th in 10 years – played out without Barcelona. There has not been a European clásico since the 2011 Champions League semi-final when the man Pep Guardiola had just called the puto amo, the fucking master, produced his por que speech, asking why Barcelona were favoured by the continent’s referees and accusing Uefa of fixing it for them.

Yet right now it doesn’t feel as if anything is bigger, this week’s Champions League matches framed around what they meant for the game that really matters, even with Barcelona going to Paris. The rivalry is always there; in Mourinho’s case it is at the heart of it. The day he got the Madrid job in 2010 was the day he won the Champions League with Inter but its genesis lay in the semi-final, when he had sprinted across the Camp Nou pitch, finger raised, celebrating. Madrid were relieved and grateful, spared the sight of Barcelona lifting the European Cup in their stadium and shown how to stop a team that appeared unbeatable. Mourinho, leaving the Santiago Bernabéu in Florentino Pérez’s car while his joyful players returned to Milan, was asked to repeat that with Madrid.

Pérez, who had presided over the galácticos’ failure and walked away, had returned in 2009 but won nothing. Instead, Barcelona dominated. They had the core of Spain’s World Cup 2010 winners: six starters in the final. Madrid needed a culture shift, to go to war, a manager to rule over the dressing room. “This year’s galáctico is José Mourinho,” the president said.

By the time Mourinho left, it had turned nasty, his enemies internal too. They had been, Mourinho later said, “three intense, almost violent years”. Yet Pérez had always felt drawn towards the only manager he has truly liked. Including when Mourinho was belligerent; especially when he was belligerent. Mourinho had, Pérez said, returned Madrid to their rightful place. After every subsequent success the president called to tell him he started this. And if Mourinho’s first clásico brought a 5-0 defeat, Barcelona going on to win the league and Champions League; if his final season had ended trophyless; and if Guardiola had won twice as many trophies, it was also true that of the four competitions Guardiola failed to win at Barcelona, three were taken from him by Mourinho.

Time has passed, things have changed, but the parallels are clear. Madrid have gone two years without a trophy. In the first of those, Barcelona won the league with two weeks to spare, completing a domestic treble. They had defeated Madrid four times, scoring 16 goals. Last season they wrapped it up with three weeks to spare via a clásico victory as incontestable as their superiority throughout a season when Madrid’s splits played out in public. Then Spain won the World Cup with eight Barcelona players in the squad. Madrid’s only representative, Marc Cucurella, joined the club after the tournament started.

If this was a crisis, it was time for Mourinho. A man whose flaws had been forgotten over time, nostalgia eclipsing all else. A man with the authority – a man afforded the authority – to impose on the dressing room. One with the personality to fight, go to war again. With just about everyone, and Barcelona especially. When you listened to Pérez’s extraordinary rant in May, the quiet part said out loud, all campaigning and conspiracy, politics and paranoia, it made sense.

When it comes to the still unresolved Negreira case, in which Barcelona paid the vice-president of the referees’ committee, José María Enríquez Negreira, more than €7m between 2001 and 2018, there is substance to Madrid’s complaints. Barcelona have denied corruption, saying Negreira worked as an adviser, but that case has become the centrepiece of Madrid’s discourse, unlike when the two clubs were still holding out in the Super League. It doesn’t help when the league president likens your TV channel to Joseph Goebbels’ propaganda.

Whether those complaints have validity now is a different question; whether the discourse of conspiracy does is another step again, even when decisions go against you. Every mistake – and decisions that are not even mistakes – is framed as a machiavellian plan, the insinuations constant – when they are not said outright.

When Mourinho arrived he said he was older, calmer, but here he is. In defeat, perhaps he was always likely to be. After losing to Betis, he asked por que? (Why? Because that’s the rule, the decision correct.) After losing to Atlético, he turned up with a printout. And then he didn’t turn up to the press conference after he had run on to the pitch to embrace Vinícius Júnior after the Brazilian scored against Villarreal only for the goal to be ruled out and Vinícius sent off for pulling Nathan Saliba’s hair. That led to a four-game suspension, the forward ruled out of the clásico.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The reason for the no-show was that Mourinho didn’t want to risk saying something that would earn him a suspension for the clásico, the game. And he is happier now, if only for a little while, something shifting. When last Saturday Barcelona made it 11 wins from 11, averaging more than four goals a game, most agreed they would win the clásico and the title would be done: they were flying, led by Lamine Yamal, while Madrid, beaten twice, hadn’t taken off. Mourinho’s team had not been very good, familiar problems still there. In short, there was not much football.

The previous Wednesday Madrid had delivered another of their seemingly inexplicable comebacks, from 3-1 down at Roma, to win 4-3 in the final seven minutes, but was there really anything to build on? It turned out there was something of an explanation. In those minutes Arda Güler played, Yan Diomande played, Fede Valverde played at right-back, and Vinícius didn’t play.

It seemed so obvious to everyone, including the manager. So he did it again, and Madrid scored four against Sevilla – three of them glorious – last Sunday and four more against Leipzig on Wednesday, Diomande belting in a wonderful volley once Vinícius had gone off. The night before, Barcelona conceded four at the Parc des Princes.

Hansi Flick admitted he prioritised the clásico over PSG, leaving out Rodri and withdrawing Pedri and Raphinha early to keep them fresh for a game that could be decisive and tends to shape a season. But he has injury concerns at the back and warned his players that 15 goals conceded is too many. Mourinho couldn’t resist complaining that Madrid have a day less rest for the clásico – something perhaps mitigated, much like any analysis, by playing at home against Leipzig rather than away at Paris Saint-Germain – which got the excuse in early, more evidence of how “they” have it in for his side.

“We need to cut the gap and we can only do that by winning,” said the Real Madrid goalkeeper, Thibaut Courtois, of the six-point deficit. “We’re going with confidence.” Yet things do feel a little better now, defeat for Madrid not inevitable, a title still there to played for and something like a team taking shape. “I had to get to know them,” Mourinho said on Wednesday night. “I’ve only been here 105 days; it’s not long.”

#514. Kim Jong-un crosses newly opened bridge into China

North Korean leader travels over New Yalu River Bridge to meet senior Communist party member

Kim Jong-un has visited China, inaugurating a bridge that connects the two countries and saying he hopes to expand cooperation with his neighbour.

The North Korean leader arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday after crossing the New Yalu River Bridge, according to South Korea’s unification ministry, which handles affairs related to North Korea, and China’s official Xinhua news agency.

He met Wang Huning, a member of the standing committee of China’s Communist party. The pair toured a car factory, and promised to strengthen the bilateral relationship.

Kim said his country “stands ready to work with China to carry forward their historical friendship and expand practical cooperation, thereby delivering tangible benefits to the peoples of both countries”, according to Xinhua.

Wang then accompanied Kim to the bridge to send him off, Xinhua said.

The visit appears to be timed to underscore the strength of Kim’s ties with Beijing ahead of the 25 October anniversary of China’s first major victory in the Korean war, which came days after Chinese troops crossed the Yalu River into North Korea in October 1950.

Japan’s Kyodo news agency said on Saturday that traffic controls had been imposed around the bridge and near a museum about China’s role in the war, and that hotel bookings nearby had been restricted.

Diplomatic sources told the agency the measures were linked to a visit by a senior North Korean official.

The 3km bridge opened in mid-October, 12 years after China finished building it, after being held up by delays on the North Korean side. In early September, North Korea and Russia opened the first road bridge across their own short border, leaving Pyongyang newly linked by road to its main backers.

The trip is Kim’s sixth visit to China and his first since September 2025, when he attended a military parade in Beijing alongside the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin. Xi visited Pyongyang in June, his first trip there in seven years.

Relations with South Korea, meanwhile, have deteriorated. Kim’s sister, Kim Yo Jong, has issued about 10 statements criticising Seoul since late September, a frequency South Korea’s unification ministry has called unusual, and has also announced plans to resume loudspeaker broadcasts at the border within days.

Xi will host the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on 18-19 November, which has fuelled speculation about a meeting between Kim and Donald Trump.

Reuters reported on Friday, however, that US and South Korean officials see little chance of Kim meeting the US president this year.

Associated Press contributed to this report

#515. Students like new tenancy freedoms - but landlords warn of higher rents

Eddie Lever was able to leave his tenancy more easily because of the Renters' Rights Act

When the Renters' Rights Act came into force in May it was described as the biggest change for tenants in England in a generation, giving more stability and security to the millions of people who rent from private landlords.

The legislation has also prompted a shake-up of the student rental market, which has posed challenges for landlords as it allows people to leave a tenancy rather than being tied in for the full academic year.

Eddie Lever had finished his first year at the University of Exeter when he decided the course wasn't for him.

The 20-year-old wanted to switch to studying international relations at the University of York but had already organised his house for the upcoming year.

But because of changes in the Renters' Rights Act, Eddie only had to give two months' notice before he could leave and stop paying rent.

The legislation ended fixed-term tenancies - where renters are tied in to contracts for a specific number of months. For students, previously contracts were generally for the full academic year.

Instead, properties are now rented on a rolling basis, which means tenants pay rent weekly or monthly with no fixed end date.

University-owned halls of residence and Purpose-Built Student Accommodation are exempt, external and can still offer fixed-term contracts so this change primarily affects students renting from a private landlord.

"If the Renters' Rights Act wasn't a thing, I don't think I would have been able to move universities because I would have been locked into the full [year] contract," Eddie explains.

What the Renters' Rights Act means for tenants and landlords

'I fought for change to remove student housing stress'

More students planning to live at home for university over 'insane' living costs

As he was signed up to a joint tenancy, when he left it ended the tenancy for the whole house.

Fortunately, Eddie had a friend who was looking for a room who was able to take his place so his housemates could sign a new tenancy.

He acknowledges the situation would have been more difficult for his housemates if there wasn't someone who could take his room.

However, Eddie thinks the benefits for students are worth this risk.

"If you were to fall out with your flatmates or if you decide that university is not for you, being locked into a full-term contract can be really prohibitive financially," he says.

"So without that flexibility, people can really be locked into situations that they don't necessarily want to be in."

Lewis Wilson, vice president for higher education at the National Union of Students, says this flexibility means students can also save money on rent by moving home for the summer.

While previously, many student rental contracts ran into the summer after courses had finished, students can now choose to move out earlier if they want.

Wilson says students also benefit from wider changes in the act, which bans landlords in England from evicting tenants without a reason.

Campaigners argue this gives renters greater security and confidence to ask for repairs, without fearing they could be evicted if they raise concerns.

Lewis Wilson from the NUS says the legislation has given students more freedom to move out when they want

However, greater flexibility for students to leave tenancies also means less certainty for landlords.

The act did introduce a specific ground, external for landlords to evict a group of students at the end of the academic year if they intend to re-let the property to students.

Chris Norris, chief policy officer at the National Residential Landlords Association, says the bigger problem for student landlords is if their tenants choose to move out earlier.

He argues this is a bigger risk for students - who may fall out with their housemates or drop out of university - than, for example, families, who are less likely to want to move out after just a few months.

Norris says the end of fixed-term tenancies means student houses could be left empty over the summer after courses finish - or even earlier.

He adds that it is now more difficult for student landlords to rent a house for just a few months as they don't know how long the tenants will stay and can't guarantee it will be available for students again in the autumn.

Norris says it's early days for the new legislation and many landlords are taking this year as a test to see how these issues play out in practice.

However, he warns that some may choose to increase the monthly rent they charge to cover the risk of their properties being empty over the summer.

In some cases, he says landlords may even sell up or stop renting to students, reducing supply and pushing up prices.

Sue Lawes thinks the changes mean many student landlords will put up their rent

Sue Lawes, who rents three shared houses to students in Norwich, is worried about the changes.

While Sue says she doesn't want to put up her prices, if her houses end up being empty over the summer because students decide to end their tenancy after their final exams she says she may have to.

She has already brought forward the start of her tenancy agreements to August instead of September to try and reduce the risks of this.

However, she says if her tenants move out earlier in the year she would struggle to make a profit, whilst covering costs including her mortgage, council tax and utility standing charges when the properties are empty.

She argues higher monthly rents would mean bigger upfront costs for students and higher overall costs for those who do choose to carry on renting over the summer.

Sue stresses that she supports the aim of the legislation to give tenants greater security and that students should be able to move out if their landlord is not carrying out repairs.

But she wants landlords to be allowed to offer fixed-term contracts to students in line with the academic year to avoid properties being left empty over the summer.

"Landlords are going to find it very, very hard to absorb those void periods," she says.

"Landlords will put prices up and students are going to pay."

#517. REPORTAGE. "Elle a mieux résisté à la chaleur que de nombreuses autres variétés" : face à la canicule, la pomme Juliet a tiré son épingle du jeu

l'essentiel Depuis début octobre, la récolte de pommes Juliet bat son plein à Saint-Vite, dans le Lot-et-Garonne. Malgré une récolte en baisse cette année, la pomme Juliet, produite notamment dans les vergers de Benoît Escande, a mieux résisté face aux fortes chaleurs que d’autres variétés. 23 000 tonnes sont prévues pour la récolte globale de 2026, avec une majorité destinée au marché français et européen.

Depuis la première semaine d’octobre, les ouvriers agricoles s’activent dans les vergers de pommiers de Benoît Escande, à Saint-Vite. C’est la période de la récolte de la pomme Juliet, une variété importée des États-Unis en Lot-et-Garonne par son grand-père dans les années 1970 et officiellement lancée en 1998 avec trois autres personnes : Jean-Noël Carles, Guilhem Sévérac et Jean-Paul Touchard. L’association des Amis de Juliet, créée en 2005, a contribué à structurer cette démarche.

À lire aussi : Fumel. Juliet, la pomme 100 % bio

Pour l’arboriculteur et pépiniériste lot-et-garonnais, les prévisions de la récolte 2026, qui devrait encore durer une semaine, illustrent les difficultés rencontrées cette saison, en raison notamment des fortes chaleurs.

"Si on arrive à 300 tonnes cette année, on sera content, confie l’agriculteur. Alors que normalement, il faudrait faire 500 tonnes, explique le producteur. Il y a moins de pommes cette année à cause des conditions climatiques. Car on a quand même eu quasiment 40 °C tous les jours pendant trois semaines cet été. Heureusement pour nous, Juliet a mieux résisté à la chaleur que de nombreuses autres variétés. Certains producteurs de pommes ont perdu jusqu’à 80 % de leur récolte. Pour nous, c’est aux alentours de 30 %."

La Juliet, qui est aujourd’hui exclusivement cultivée en France et en agriculture biologique, se distingue par sa capacité à mieux supporter les épisodes de fortes chaleurs. Un argument de poids dans un contexte où les arboriculteurs doivent adapter leurs pratiques aux évolutions du climat. Au-delà de son comportement face aux températures élevées, cette variété possède un autre avantage : sa capacité à s’inscrire dans une production biologique, grâce à ses résistances naturelles aux nuisibles, qui permettent de limiter le recours aux traitements.

"Cette pomme a une grande faculté de résistance naturelle aux bioagresseurs, c’est-à-dire les pucerons et les champignons. Elle a cette rusticité énorme pour elle, avec une pruine naturelle qui la protège." La pomme Juliet présente, en effet, cette fine pellicule naturelle qui recouvre la peau. Cette caractéristique visible fait partie des éléments distinctifs de la variété, même si elle ne suffit pas, à elle seule, à expliquer sa résistance aux fortes chaleurs.

À lire aussi : "Gustativement, elle a tout pour plaire" : la pomme Juliet, seule variété 100 % française et bio en pleine récolte dans le Tarn-et-Garonne

Pour autant, la Juliet n’est pas à l’abri de tous les aléas météorologiques. Le gel printanier reste une menace pour les vergers, notamment en raison d’une floraison relativement précoce, autour de début avril. "Il n’y a rien qui résiste à un fort gel. Un petit gel, ça peut aller", déclare le pépiniériste de Saint-Vite. Face au dérèglement climatique, la résistance à la chaleur ne dispense donc pas les producteurs de rester vigilants.

Actuellement, la pomme Juliet est présente dans plusieurs bassins de production français, du Sud-Est au Sud-Ouest, en passant par la vallée du Rhône, le Jura et l’Ouest. En Occitanie, il y a énormément de vergers dans le Tarn-et-Garonne. Cette implantation géographique permet d’élargir les zones de culture et d’assurer une présence sur le marché tout au long de l’année.

Sur les 23 000 tonnes prévues lors de la récolte 2026, 16 000 tonnes seront destinées au marché du frais et se retrouveront dans le panier du consommateur dès le 16 octobre. Le reste sera destiné notamment à la production de jus et aux compotes. Parmi elles, 10 000 tonnes alimenteront la France et l’Europe, avec un marché français qui reste prioritaire et majoritaire en volume. Les 6 000 tonnes restantes prendront la voie de l’export maritime, notamment vers l’Asie. Du Vietnam à la Malaisie, en passant par Singapour et Taïwan.

« On a une relative satisfaction, même si ça pourrait être nettement mieux, explique Benoît Escande. Après, tout dépend de si le marché nous paye les pommes au juste prix. Le bio coûte beaucoup plus cher à produire, il faut que le prix soit rémunérateur pour les producteurs. S’ils ne gagnent pas leur vie, c’est fini. Les producteurs de Juliet ont été très inquiets. On vient de traverser une grosse crise lors de ces deux dernières années. Avec l’après-Covid, il y a eu une envolée des prix et une baisse de la consommation en France en raison d’un pouvoir d’achat en berne. Sur les 3 ou 4 euros le kilo payé dans le commerce, seulement 50 à 70 centimes reviennent au producteur. Il faudrait être payé entre 80 centimes et 1 euro le kilo pour qu’on puisse bien gagner dignement notre vie. Ces 10 à 15 centimes de différence feraient vraiment gagner à la production. Ça nous permet aussi de réinvestir, de renouveler les vergers, de remplacer les arbres. »

#518. White House lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods as midterm elections loom

Canada and the US are currently locked in a tit-for-tat trade war

The Trump administration is lifting some of its 50% tariffs on Canadian goods two weeks before the midterm elections, after a Republican candidate in a key US Senate race said she had lobbied for the change.

From 30 October, tariffs will be eased on products including "plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment", the White House said on Friday.

Republican Senator Susan Collins, who is in a tight race to keep her seat in Maine, first announced the exemptions, saying they would help her state's agriculture industry.

The US imposed a 50% levy on $20bn (Â£15bn) worth of Canadian goods after trade talks between the two countries collapsed in August.

Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures in response to the US tariffs, which Prime Minister Mark Carney said were "necessary to protect our workers".

Last month, Carney matched the US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after the breakdown in talks. Trump had imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US car, dairy and alcohol exports.

The White House said that, while tariffs would be lifted from some items, including some packing crates and boxes, they would be introduced on other items such as carpets and "waste products".

It said the action reflected US President Donald Trump's "continued efforts to defend American workers and ensure fair trade".

Maine Senator Susan Collins is seeking to keep her seat in November's midterm elections

Trump "continues to address Canada's discriminatory treatment of US commerce", White House spokesman Matthew Middleton said.

Canada's internal trade minister Dominic LeBlanc said: "While we assess these latest steps, Canada stands ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada's interests."

The White House's announcement comes less than a fortnight before the US midterm elections, which will determine whether Trump's Republican Party or Democrats will control Congress, impacting the remaining two years of his term.

Collins said she had repeatedly asked senior Trump officials for tariff relief and that she would "continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally and largest trading partner".

She wrote on X that the tariff exemptions were on products that were "crucial to Maine's agricultural industries, including blueberry, potato, apple, and seaweed producers".

Collins' Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, responded: "Trump's trade wars have made life harder and more expensive for Mainers. Susan Collins enabled this chaos, voted to confirm the people behind it and now wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put out the fire."

Maine borders the Canadian provinces New Brunswick and Quebec. Its economy, as well as that of other border states, is deeply linked to Canada and they have felt the effects of the months-long trade war.

Michigan lawmaker Mike Rogers, also a Republican, has called on Trump to end the standoff after spending months supporting the policy in recent advertisements airing in his trade-reliant state.

Also on Friday, Trump said Canada was "working very hard" on a â trade âdeal with the US.

Carney, who has sought closer ties with Europe since the tariff war erupted, said that Canada was open to a mutually beneficial deal, but was willing to wait it out.

"We could sign it this afternoon if the US were there," he said on Friday, according to Canadian broadcaster CBC. "If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that."

LeBlanc confirmed on Thursday that a delegation met members of the Canada-United States Economic Relations Advisory Committee - the ninth meeting since April 2026. The committee members discussed the ongoing impact of US tariffs in Canada.

#520. How reliant is Ukraine on the US-controlled Starlink internet service?

Kyiv keeps issuing warnings that the satellite internet system Starlink is being restricted in Ukraine. How dependent is the country on the system, and what would happen if it went down?

Few technological systems have played such an important role in the war in Ukraine as Starlink, central to the communications, reconnaissance and drone operations of the Ukrainian armed forces. There are currently widespread concerns that Elon Musk's satellite internet service in Ukraine may be restricted or even switched off. In recent days, Kyiv has repeatedly reported disruptions and restrictions affecting its use.

Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has made extensive use of the satellite internet service, which is operated by the US company SpaceX. With it, military personell can continue to communicate and exchange data, even when infrastructure has been destroyed or cellphone networks are down.

According to the Center for Security Studies (CSS) at ETH Zurich, around 50,000 Starlink terminals were in use in Ukraine in 2025. These are the system's specialised receiving and transmitting devices, which enable communications on the battlefield. They are also used to relay orders between command levels and receive drone footage.

The importance of the Starlink network can in part be explained by events at the beginning of the war. According to a CSS analysis, the KA-SAT satellite system previously favored by Ukraine was targeted in a cyberattack just hours before Russia's invasion. Starlink quickly became a vital alternative.

When discussing current affairs, the terms "Starlink" and "Starshield" are often used interchangeably.

However, Starlink is SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, whereas Starshield is specifically designed for governmental and military use. While based on the same technological infrastructure, it is designed for security and defense applications.

This distinction matters, because the latest reports of restrictions seem to primarily concern systems used for military purposes. Elon Musk recently stated that Starshield systems are controlled by the US government, whereas Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX.

Alongside communications, Starlink is mainly used for drone operations. The system provides an internet connection for ground, naval and aerial drones.

This connection means video footage can be transmitted almost in real time, while drones can be controlled over long distances. Ukraine uses these systems for reconnaissance and attacks deep behind enemy lines.

According to ETH Zurich, images and GPS coordinates of Russian positions are also transmitted via these communication channels. The data is sent to artillery units and used to coordinate operations.

According to Ukrainian media reports, on Tuesday night, SpaceX temporarily introduced a speed restriction for Starlink terminals in Ukraine, limiting terminals in motion to a speed of about 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph).

Such a restriction has direct consequences for fast-moving Ukrainian drones, some of which travel at speeds of up to 300 kilometers per hour (186 mph). If the connection to the drone is lost, live video footage can no longer be transmitted, and the systems can no longer be controlled in real time. The drones effectively have to continue their mission while flying blind.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Restricting or even shutting down a Starlink network would therefore not only make communication more difficult. It would also affect Ukrainian drone operations, and other military activities.

However, Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, are only one essential component of Ukraine's defense system. Ukraine also receives reconnaissance data from western partners, including information about Russian air attacks, missile launches, troop movements and anti-aircraft positions, as well as potential routes to avoid them.

This information helps with air defense and offensive operations. Without this intelligence, it would be significantly harder for Ukraine to carry out long-range drone operations against targets in Russian territory.

The two elements are particularly effective when combined. Reconnaissance data provides information about potential targets and routes, while Starlink ensures that this data can be quickly relayed to units.

This is why reports that the US is limiting access to its reconnaissance data are as worrying as the possibility that Starlink might be throttled. Other NATO countries, such as the United Kingdom and France, can also provide reconnaissance data, but not to the extent as the United States.

Europe has several alternatives to Starlink, including Eutelsat/OneWeb. However, their ability to match Starlink's performance in wartime conditions has not yet been tested on a large scale.

The recurrent concern about possible restrictions makes clear that satellite communications have become a central component of Ukrainian defense. And while relying on a single provider simplifies operations, it also shows how dependent modern armed forces have become on private technology companies. Experts say this marks a fundamental change in warfare.

Meanwhile, Ukraine's successful use of Starlink has helped the system to achieve global recognition.

This article has been translated from German.

#521. At Aberfan, I saw fathers digging for their missing children. And the lessons society should have learned, it hasn’t | John Humphrys

Each of those 144 deaths was entirely avoidable, but nobody was held to account. We still don’t know how to get justice for ordinary people

Aberfan taught us a lot. Mostly, of course, that those in power cannot be trusted. Correction: must not be trusted.

I might have thought so until 60 years ago this week when I stood alongside mothers weeping and praying as they watched their husbands digging for the bodies of their children who lay crushed beneath the ruins of their little school.

The parents’ faces were black, save for the streaks of white from their tears. Two hours earlier those men had been digging coal from deep beneath the ground. With the coal, of course, came the waste that would have to be separated to become the great mounds that disfigured every mining valley.

My best friend’s father was a miner. I had been a reporter on the local paper and I once went down the mine to watch him at work. I begged to return to the surface after no more than an hour of breathing in the deadly coal dust. I tried to imagine every working hour trapped in that living hell and failed.

This, surely, was the most dangerous and demanding job in the land. Few miners escaped serious lung damage. I never once spoke to a Valleys mother who wanted her son to follow his father down the pit. But what I witnessed that day was something even the toughest miners, let alone their wives, could not have dreamed of in their darkest nightmares.

Every so often, one of the diggers would shout for silence. He thought he had heard a child cry out. We stood and prayed, hardly daring to breathe. Sometimes our prayers were answered. I watched a little girl handed to a policeman. She was unconscious but, thank God, she was breathing. She would live. Most did not.

I did my best to tell the outside world what was happening from a phone in the local pub overlooking the school. But what I failed to report until many hours later was the terrible truth that this was a disaster that need never have happened.

Correction: a disaster that should never have happened.

What every miner in that village and every miner’s wife had always known was that the massive waste tip that was to destroy their lives should never have been built. Or at least, should never have been built on that spot. This was not one of those disasters that might eventually be written off as part of the price society was reconciled to paying if we were to enjoy the benefits of what we once called “black gold”.

Every miner knew he faced danger from the moment he stepped into the cage that would drop him a couple of thousand feet below ground. Until the nightmare of Aberfan, the most painful job I was ordered to do as a teenage reporter on the Merthyr Express was knocking on the door of a miner’s cottage a few hours after his wife had been told she was now a widow.

The first time I was scared. Surely I would be ordered by the newly bereaved widow to clear off? But I learned quickly that they almost always wanted to talk about their dead husbands. And there was seldom any anger. They had always known – even if it was never talked about – that he might never come home. Accidents were inevitable.

But what happened in Aberfan was no accident.

It was the result of grotesque indifference on the part of the men who ran the National Coal Board (NCB) and were responsible for the location of every waste tip of every nationalised colliery in the land. Above all, of the man who chaired that board: Alfred Robens.

Such was his unbelievable disregard for the hell that had been visited on that little Welsh village that he couldn’t even spare a few hours to share their grief. While they were still digging through the filth that had choked the lives from so many children, His lordship was being chauffeured to a new university for a ceremony where he was to be made chancellor. And the year of the disaster, he also accepted an honorary degree for his services to the mining industry.

His “services”? Has ever the English language been more abused?

What Lord Robens had always known – if only because he would have been briefed by his team of senior officials – was that to build a massive tip on that particular spot on the hillside was the equivalent of lighting a bonfire in a dynamite factory.

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

I can state that as an absolute fact after all these years, because even as those brave miners and their wives were trying so desperately to deal with their grief, they were showing me copies of the letters they had written over and over again warning the NCB that it was criminally reckless to site the tip on that spot.

There was a simple reason that even an ignoramus such as me could understand. It rains a lot in the Welsh valleys and there are many springs beneath the surface of the hills. The spot the officials chose for the tip was notorious for its springs. But it was directly above the village. And Pantglas junior school.

Every morning two miners would trudge up the hillside of their own volition to examine the state of the tip. When they saw what was happening on 21 October 1966, they turned and ran down the hillside. But it was too late. Within minutes 100,000 tonnes of coal waste had hit the school at 80mph, killing almost everyone in its path.

It took a little more than a year for Robens and his henchmen to face a form of justice. I sat through the public inquiry when the scale of the disgrace was unveiled, day after agonising day, and Robens was the final witness.

The inquiry chairman treated his protestations of ignorance and innocence with richly deserved contempt and I remember leaping into my car to deliver a live broadcast with the sense that justice had finally been delivered.

But had it? Have we really learned anything as a result of Aberfan? The horror of the Grenfell Tower inferno suggests not. The inquiry found that the deaths of all 72 people in 2017 were “entirely avoidable”, resulting from systemic failures, deregulation and corporate dishonesty. It added: “There is still a great deal to learn.”

True, the last of the collieries in the Welsh valleys has long since gone, but can it really be true that no one deserved to face charges for criminal negligence?

What is true is the extraordinary spirit of those who suffered so much and, indeed, of those who survived.

I remember going to the home of a little girl who’d been one of the survivors and asking her mother why she hadn’t sent her to the new school. She answered with almost chilling simplicity: “Because I don’t want mothers who’ve lost their kiddies to see her in the street and be reminded of what they’ve lost.”

John Humphrys presents The Odd Couple podcast with Matthew Norman

#523. Typhoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to China

Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled

Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.

Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).

The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.

Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan.

Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.

Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.

Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.

Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.

#524. Warum steigen Krebserkrankungen bei Menschen unter 50?

Bei jungen Menschen wird weltweilt immer häufiger Krebs diagnostiziert, insbesondere Darmkrebs. Dafür gibt es verschiedene Gründe.

Die Zahlen sind erschreckend. Bei einigen Krebsarten hat sich die Zahl der Erkrankungen in den letzten 20 Jahren verdoppelt. Wobei allerdings nicht ganz klar ist, ob es tatsächlich zweimal mehr Erkrankungen gibt oder ob mehr Fälle im Frühstadium erkannt werden, weil sich das Bewusstsein, die Diagnose- und die Behandlungsmöglichkeiten in den Krankenhäusern verbessert haben.

Nehmen wir zum Beispiel Darmkrebs: In England wurde diese Krebsart 2001 bei einem von 26.000 Menschen unter 50 Jahren diagnostiziert. 2023 war es bei einem von 12.000 Menschen, also doppelt so viel wie um die Jahrtausendwende. Diese Zahlenstammen vom World Cancer Research Fund (WCRF), einem internationalen Netzwerk gemeinnütziger Organisationen, das Krebsregisterdaten aus England, den Vereinigten Staaten und den Niederlanden analysiert.

Die Zahlen haben sich zwar verdoppelt, meint Amy Berrington de Gonzalez, Professorin für klinische Epidemiologie am Institute of Cancer Research in London, insgesamt seien sie aber noch immer niedrig. "Bei jungen Menschen tritt Krebs weiterhin selten auf", sagt sie zur DW. "Dreimal eine kleine Zahl ist noch immer eine kleine Zahl." Dennoch will sie - wie auch andere Wissenschaftler und Wissenschaftlerinnen - wissen, warum die Zahlen steigen. Schließlich handelt es sich um eine weltweite Entwicklung. Ein typisches Beispiel ist Lateinamerika.

Für eine Studie aus dem Jahr 2025wurden die Registerdaten aus 50 Ländern und Gebieten bis zum Jahr 2017 analysiert. In 27 dieser Regionen war die Zahl der Darmkrebserkrankungen bei jungen Menschen gestiegen. In Lateinamerika war dies in Chile, Argentinien, Ecuador, Costa Rica und Puerto Rico der Fall. Der Anstieg in Chile gehörte mit fast vier Prozent jährlich zu den höchsten.

Marc Gunter ist Professor für Krebsepidemiologie am Imperial College London. Er geht davon aus, dass Lateinamerika in seiner Entwicklung den reicheren Ländern folgen werde, mit Ernährungsgewohnheiten, die sich zunehmend am westlichen Lebensstil orientieren und einem bewegungsärmeren Alltag. "Ich glaube, das passiert bereits", sagt er.

"Wir benötigen bessere Registrierungssysteme für Krebs", betont seine Kollegin Berrington de Gonzalez. "Insbesondere in Ländern wie Brasilien und Mexiko, wo auch die Adipositasraten gestiegen sind."

In einer weiteren Studie aus dem Jahr 2025, für die Daten aus 42 Ländern berücksichtigt wurden, verglich Berrington de Gonzalez Daten aus den Jahren 2003 bis 2017 von zwei Altersgruppen, 20- bis 49-Jährigen und Menschen über 50. In den meisten Ländern waren die Zahlen bei sechs Krebsarten (Schilddrüsen-, Brust-, Darm-, Nieren-, Gebärmutter- und Blutkrebs) unter jüngeren Menschen angestiegen. Bis auf Darmkrebs waren sie auch in der Gruppe über 50 gestiegen.

In der Tat waren die Zahlen für Darmkrebs außergewöhnlich. In etwa einem Drittel der Länder stiegen die Erkrankungen unter jüngeren Menschen stärker als unter älteren. "Es scheint die eine Krebsart zu sein, die bei jüngeren Menschen steigt, während sie bei älteren Menschen fällt", hebt Berrington de Gonzalez hervor.

Das hat Folgen für die Forschung. Steigt die Zahl von Krebserkrankungen in allen Altersgruppen, sind die Ursachen dafür vermutlich weit verbreitet. Würden für Studien nur junge Menschen herangezogen, sei das Risiko groß, dass komplizierten Erklärungen hinterhergejagt werde, ohne dies mit ausreichenden Daten überprüfen zu können, so Berrington de Gonzalez.

Eine Studie aus den USA zu Bauchspeicheldrüsenkrebs bei Erwachsenen im Alter von 15 bis 39 stellte fest, dass der Anstieg fast vollständig auf Tumoren im Frühstadium zurückzuführen war. Die Sterberate blieb unverändert. Die Autoren folgern daraus, dass nicht die Zahl der Krebserkrankungen nach oben geht, sondern dass sich die Früherkennung verbessert hat. Das ließe sich erklären durch das gewachsene Bewusstsein in der Bevölkerung und die größere Bereitschaft, zu Vorsorgeuntersuchungen zu gehen.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bei Darmkrebs zeichnen die Daten jedoch ein anderes Bild: Einige Studien aus den USA zeigen, dass auch die Zahlen bei fortgeschrittenen Stadien nach oben gehen. Dies lässt vermuten, dass die Zahl der Erkrankungen und nicht nur die Zahl der Diagnosen steigt.

Laut der Internationalen Agentur für Krebsforschung (IARC) der Weltgesundheitsorganisation gilt Adipositas oder Fettleibigkeit als erwiesene Ursache für mindestens 13 Krebsarten.

Eine 2021 durchgeführte Auswertung bestehender Studien zeigte, dass sich die Wahrscheinlichkeit für junge übergewichtige Menschen verdoppelt, vor dem 50. Lebensjahr an Darmkrebs zu erkranken. Gerade unter jungen Menschen hat sich Adipositas am schnellsten ausgebreitet. Seit den 1990ern leiden zweimal so viele Erwachsene unter Adipositas, bei jungen Erwachsenen sind es nach WHO-Angaben viermal so viele,.

Dabei hat die Ernährung einen großen Einfluss:

Auch hochverarbeitete Lebensmittel und Mikroplastik soll einigen Experten zufolge Krebs verursachen, doch die Beweislage sei nicht eindeutig, sagt Professor Gunter. "Es gibt viel Hype", warnt er und betont, dass weitere Forschung nötig sei. Berrington de Gonzalez stimmt ihm zu: "Die Ernährungsgewohnheiten haben sich geändert, aber wir wissen noch nicht, welche Rolle sie möglicherweise spielen."

Man sollte den Menschen nicht zum Vorwurf machen, dass sie in Gesellschaften leben, die auf Fertiggerichte und Bürojobs ausgerichtet sind, meint Gunter. Für eine nachhaltige Veränderung sei eine andere Gesundheitspolitik notwendig. Er betont jedoch auch, dass junge Menschen das Risiko, an Krebs zu erkranken, verringern könnten, indem sie auf ein gesundes Gewicht achten, sich mehr bewegen, mehr Ballaststoffe zu sich nehmen und weniger verarbeitete Fleischwaren essen.

"Einen Spaziergang machen, körperlich aktiver sein, mehr Obst und Gemüse essen, all diese Dinge mögen gerade nicht angesagt sein, aber sie sind wirklich wichtig", sagt er. Für alle 30-Jährigen, die dies lesen, hat Berrington de Gonzalez eine beruhigende Botschaft: Krebserkrankungen bei jungen Menschen sind noch immer relativ selten.

Adaptiert aus dem Englischen von Phoenix Hanzo.

#525. The Papers: 'Cops didn't share letter' and Burnham 'open' to EU free movement

A letter delivered to the Metropolitan Police and later passed on to the Duchess of Sussex detailing allegations about her father Thomas Markle feature on many of the front pages. "Cops didn't share letter" writes the Sunday Mirror, explaining the Met "did not pass on allegations about Meghan's dad to other police forces". It comes after "Meghan revealed its existence after fresh allegations her father had child abuse images," according to the paper. Thomas Markle strenuously denies the allegations.

Sources close to the duchess say she is "upset" about the "failure of the Met to act", the Sunday Telegraph writes, adding Scotland Yard is "now considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct". Elsewhere, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting "says Britain must be ready for war in 1,000 days", the paper's headline reports, "as Russia continues its hybrid warfare against Nato".

The Sunday Times leads with Prime Minister Andy Burnham's latest remarks, summarising that he is "open to adopting EU free movement". It comes as "PM calls for honest conversation, saying pre-Brexit migration not 'as difficult' as now", according to the paper. Coverage of the French protests continue on the front page, where a large rally in Marseille is pictured under the headline "France on the March".

The Sunday People carries a pre-Budget exclusive that the government is expected to announce a "boost for new social housing" in England, the paper says. "Extra Â£1bn for homes" reads the paper's headline.

The Sunday Express leads with remarks from Conservatives urging Prime Minister Andy Burnham to "come clean" on any mooted plans to lift the pension age to 68. It quotes campaigners who believe it would affect some six million people and bring hardship to those unable to keep working.

The Observer carries an interview with Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, who describes AI as an "evolutionary event". "'Like monkeys to humans', people will no longer be the most intelligent things on the planet," is the tech tycoon's verdict splashed on the front page.

Finally, an apparent resemblance between the late US pop icon Prince and the Prince of Wales fills the front page of the Daily Star on Sunday. "Purple Reign" quips the paper, as Prince William "claims he is often not recognised" and one time "a bloke thought he was pint-sized pop legend Prince" and wanted him to sign a copy of his record "Purple Rain". The comments came as the prince made an appearance on the BBC's Graham Norton Show.

#529. Two rescued after Nairobi building collapse with five still missing

Two people have been pulled alive from the rubble of a building that collapsed in Kenya's capital, Nairobi, on Friday, as a search continues for five still missing.

Police said on Saturday that a manhunt had been launched for the building's owner and the contractor responsible for the site.

Dramatic footage shows the bottom floor of the block, thought to have been 16 or 18 storeys, giving way before the rest of the building crumples, sending a plume of dust into the surrounding streets.

Dozens of builders had been working on the upper floors when it collapsed, but managed to emerge largely unscathed. Those missing were thought to have been in shops at the base of the building.

The incident has raised fresh concerns about construction standards and regulations in Kenya.

The block was under construction when it collapsed on Friday afternoon, with footage showing scaffolding still wrapped around the outside of the building. Officials said 11 shops had already opened on the bottom floors.

Interior ministry official Kipchumba Murkomen said 66 of the 67 construction workers in the building at the time had been able to get out unharmed, while the other had suffered injuries that were not life-threatening.

On Friday, Murkomen said that seven people had been reported missing and rescue teams had made contact with some of those trapped beneath the rubble.

The two survivors rescued on Saturday have been taken to hospital, police said.

Images from the scene, in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, show the concrete floors of the building piled on top of one another, as rescue workers saw through metal to get to those believed to have been stuck underneath.

Footage taken from nearby shows moments before (left) and moments after (right) the building collapsed

Questions have emerged about why the building suddenly collapsed and whether it met planning regulations.

Kenya's National Construction Authority said in a statement that it had identified the company behind the development, as well as the architect and structural engineer, but did not say whether the site had been inspected before Friday.

The National Police Service said it had launched an investigation to establish the cause of the collapse and determine whether anyone was criminally liable.

In a statement it warned that anyone found responsible for negligence or violating building regulations would "face the full force of the law".

Nairobi Governor Sakaja Johnson told local media that the owners of the building did not have the required paperwork for the building to be occupied.

He urged the national government to give local authorities greater powers to penalise "developers who disregard approved building plans and safety standards".

Building collapses are not uncommon in Nairobi, with poor construction or improper planning often cited as contributing factors.

#530. Healey’s first budget to include big devolution package to boost growth

Chancellor will build on Burnham’s promise that local leaders in England will no longer have to ‘come cap in hand to Westminster’

Andy Burnham has promised that local leaders in England will no longer have to come “cap in hand to Westminster” ahead of a fresh drive to devolve spending power in next week’s budget.

In his statement on Wednesday, the chancellor, John Healey, will include plans for a new £1.5bn borrowing facility, to be drawn up in collaboration with mayors over the next two years.

Regional mayors have long complained that they are constrained by their limited borrowing power – in contrast to local authorities in the US and some European countries, which commonly issue their own bonds.

The borrowing plan will form part of a big devolution package aimed at boosting regional economic growth. This will also include the allocation of an initial £285m “good growth” funding next year, to be spent on local leaders’ priorities – which could include housing, transport links or high street regeneration.

Amid fears in the Treasury about whether some local authorities have the capacity to administer increasingly large budgets, Healey will also announce £150m of support to help them scale up and build expertise.

Hailing the plans, Burnham said they would mean local leaders would no longer need to come to the Treasury for approval for each individual project. “I’m calling time on local leaders going cap in hand to Westminster. That is no way to run a country. When I became prime minister, I said that if a decision can be made closer to home, it should be.

“Today we’re putting that into practice, shifting power out of Westminster and into the hands of the people who know their communities best.”

The £285m in “good growth” funding is intended to tide local authorities over until a new system comes into force in 2028 whereby some income tax revenue will be handed directly to their areas to give them longer-term security – an idea first mooted by Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, earlier this year.

More details of how this will work will be announced at the budget. Local leaders are expected to be allowed to keep some of the additional revenues created by a stronger local economy, giving them an incentive to back pro-growth policies.

Tax and spending in the UK is more centralised than in many other leading economies, and Burnham experienced the constraints first-hand as mayor of Greater Manchester.

Healey said: “Mayors and local leaders know what their communities need to grow, which is why we are giving them more money, more power and more capacity to get projects moving, build homes and make the right decisions for their areas.”

The package has been drawn up in collaboration with No 10 North, which has been holding a weekly “situation room” meeting with local leaders, to ask them about the barriers to promoting economic growth.

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

This resulted in an announcement this week that the Treasury has called the “green book”, which gives guidanceon which projects taxpayers should fund. Under the new rules, projects that can be combined to boost growth – a housing and a transport scheme, for example – can be considered together.

A government white paper on “rewiring the state”, due to be published after the budget, will set out more details of how the civil service will be reshaped, as more powers are passed down from Whitehall.

Alongside the devolution plans, Healey’s first budget is expected to include support for poorer households hit by rising energy costs; and modest tax rises, including on banks. The chancellor has repeatedly said he wants to offer a “breathing space” to households and businesses that have struggled as the war in the Middle East has driven up bills.

These higher costs have also pushed up the interest rates on government borrowing, making it harder for Healey to balance the books.

He will set out how he plans to fully fund the four-year defence investment plan announced in the dying days of Keir Starmer’s premiership.

However, Healey is not expected to say when the UK will commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence – an issue that was central to his resignation from Starmer’s cabinet. This is likely to be delayed until a spending review due at some point next year.

#531. Populist Czech PM Babis goes empty-handed in Senate elections

Opposition parties still control the Czech Senate, in a major blow to Prime Minister Andrej Babis' and his governing coalition.

The ruling coalition of populist billionaire Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis has failed to win a single seat in elections in the Senate.

The result means pro-Western opposition parties control the chamber, the upper house of parliament.

The election on Saturday was the first electoral test for Babis after he won parliamentary elections in October 2025 that returned him to power after a break of four years since his first term as premier.

Final results from the two-day ballot showed that candidates directly linked to the opposition parties won 22 of the 27 seats up for grabs in the 81-member Senate, retaining a previous opposition majority.

The centrist ANO (or YES) movement led by Babis failed to win any more seats, leaving it with 14 Senate lawmakers.

"We certainly didn't expect that we wouldn't win a single Senate seat in this election," he said, but vowed to nonetheless go ahead with his government's agenda.

That includes an unpopular plan to revamp funding for the country’s public broadcasters.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

His euroskeptic coalition has also ended direct military support for Ukraine as it defends itself against a Russian invasion, and opposed European Union policies to combat global warming.

Although the lower house of the Czech parliament plays the main legislative role, the Senate has a big say in passing constitutional amendments and approving Constitutional Court judges.

#532. Protesters clash with police in Paris as demonstrations turn hostile across France

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Belgian police used pepper spray and tear gas during confrontations in Brussels with anti-government protesters on Saturday

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mass rallies drew hundreds of thousands of protesters across France on Saturday, with predominantly peaceful demonstrations giving way to evening skirmishes in Paris and Marseille despite an extensive security strategy deployed to head off a repeat of the previous week's unrest.

According to the interior ministry, 410,000 individuals joined demonstrations nationwide, though trade unions claimed the actual turnout was double that figure.

The main demonstration happened on the southeastern fringes of Paris, where at least 110,000 people turned out to denounce rising living costs and growing inequality.

Nearly 1,000 people were arrested as officers faced "an extremely elevated level of violence" from black-clad "ultra-left" people, interior minister Laurent Nunez claimed.

Two people were “seriously” injured, Mr Nunez said, with one man injured in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off, and another person in Clermont-Ferrand. He did not give details of either case.

The protests began in mid-September, when secondary school pupils took to the streets over staff shortages, deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms. The movement has since grown into a broader challenge to Emmanuel Macron’s government, drawing in teachers, parents and trade unions.

Conditions turned hostile following the conclusion of the rally on Saturday. Riot police deployed tear gas and water cannon against a crowd of roughly 500 masked youths, who eventually dispersed in the cold, wet conditions.

In Marseille, France's second city, young protesters set fire to rubbish bins to obstruct roads and threw stones and bottles at security officers. Police reported that several businesses, including two jewellery shops, were looted.

Confrontations were also reported in Lyon, Bordeaux, Grenoble, Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Rennes, Nantes and Toulouse.

"In almost every march we saw the formation of these high-risk groups. They broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence," said Mr Nunez, who blamed far-left activists and organised criminal groups for provoking the unrest.

Mr Nunez said 135 people had been arrested before the main marches began, with police seizing an assortment of weapons, including metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, improvised weapons, a katana sword and airsoft guns. Paris police later reported that 65 people had been arrested in the capital.

The demonstrations come as Macron approaches the final months of his presidency, with the growing movement exposing wider anger over living costs, public services and the government's handling of dissent.

A total of 70,000 police officers and gendarmes were deployed by authorities – 10,000 more than the preceding week – after officials admitted they had underestimated the extent of the unrest on 17 October.

Mr Nunez stated to reporters that the violence was less severe than the previous week, when vandals and looters engaged in widespread destruction. "What changed was anticipation," he said.

He added that far-right activists had attempted to confront leftist groups in the southern cities of Nice and Montpellier, creating a potential new dimension to the disorder.

Large parts of central Paris resembled a city under lockdown, with business owners shuttering premises, museums closing and more than 20 metro stations suspended.

Trade associations urged shopkeepers to keep their doors closed following damage or looting at thousands of commercial premises across France the previous weekend.

"There are hardly any customers, so it's not really worth staying open," said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris.

A number of the capital's prominent cultural locations, such as the Louvre, the Musee d'Orsay and the Paris Opera, opted to close as a preventative measure, leaving visitors disappointed.

"Everything's boarded up and we're not quite sure where we should be," said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from the US city of New Orleans.

The countrywide movement originated from minor student demonstrations in the Paris suburbs last month over school conditions. It quickly expanded into broader opposition to government economic policies, prompting similar rallies in neighbouring European nations.

Belgian police used pepper spray and tear gas during confrontations in Brussels with anti-government protesters on Saturday, while demonstrations also took place across several Italian cities for a second consecutive weekend, as well as in Albania.

Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who attended the Paris demonstration, suggested that rallies would persist until President Emmanuel Macron, whose term ends next year, addresses social discontent in France, one of the world's wealthiest nations.

"Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week. There is still time for (Macron) to give in. After that, the only thing left to him will be the exit door," Melenchon told reporters.

Numerous protesters accused the administration of an excessive response to the prior week's disruption, noting that military personnel were assigned to patrol the Champs-Elysees, a famous boulevard featuring high-end shops and restaurants.

"We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round," said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student.

"My friend and I almost didn't come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it's important not to let repression win," she added.

The day's initial approved march proceeded without incident in Orléans, roughly 120 km (75 miles) south of Paris, where marchers gathered to oppose Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally as it held a party congress in the city.

Tensions were heightened by a shooting west of Paris on Friday, in which a gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one individual and injured four others, including a 12-year-old girl.

"We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid," said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of Melenchon's France Unbowed party.

#533. Duchess of Sussex ‘deeply distressed’ over child sexual abuse image claims against father

Meghan reveals she was made aware of ‘disturbing allegations’ against him in 2018 by Met police

The Duchess of Sussex has said she is “deeply distressed” over accusations involving child sexual abuse images against her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr, and revealed she was made aware of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018 by the Metropolitan police.

Meghan issued a statement after the Sun newspaper published claims that her half-brother Thomas Markle Jr alleged he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.

In an interview with the Daily Mail, Markle Sr denied possessing child sexual abuse images, calling the accusations “sick lies”.

It is understood that authorities in the UK previously told Meghan that allegations made about her father in a 2018 letter sent to Scotland Yard, and subsequently shared with her by the police, were being investigated.

Meghan was informed by the Met of the allegations in the summer shortly after her wedding, it is believed.

In a statement through her spokesperson, Meghan said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection [Rasp]. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”

Sources said although Meghan was made aware of the allegations in 2018, she had been unable to speak publicly to avoid jeopardising any future investigation and because speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her.

The 2018 letter was understood to have been shared with Meghan by the Rasp unit within the Met police.

It is understood the Met has not previously investigated Markle Sr, nor is it currently doing so. The force said it was making internal inquiries regarding officers from Rasp being involved in the passing on of a letter.

A Met spokesperson said: “We are aware of media reports that officers from the Met’s royalty and specialist protection command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018. We are undertaking inquiries internally in an effort to confirm this.”

Markle Sr has been estranged from the duchess since he failed to attend her wedding to Prince Harry on health grounds, and he has never met his grandchildren Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.

The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke.

Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.

The FBI said in a statement: “The FBI is aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law.”

The undersecretary for the Philippines’ justice department, Nicholas Ty, told the BBC the matter was being investigated by a human trafficking and child sexual exploitation taskforce in Cebu.

The interior secretary, Jonvic Remulla, separately told the BBC that national police had secured Markle Sr’s computer to conduct a comprehensive digital forensic examination. Remulla said it would take “one week to get the forensic [results]”.

Meghan’s father has denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail that the accusations were “sick lies”.

He told the newspaper that the computers had not been in his possession since he left Rosarito, Mexico, with his son in January 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”.

Speaking from a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk with a prosthetic limb after his left leg was amputated because of a blood clot, he told the Mail: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.

“This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”

Meghan’s half-sister Samantha Markle has defended their father, accusing her brother Markle Jr of “making up lies” to make money.

She told the Mail: “There is no merit in these disgusting allegations whatsoever and my brother is disgusting for making them up. He wants to destroy our dad. Shame on him.”

She alleged her brother made the allegations days after their father cut off his funds, “and once the money stopped he made up the most outrageous lies he could to make money from the media”.

She alleged the computers were not in her father’s possession for two years and he could have been set up. “That leaves a lot of room for tampering,” she said.
