#534. Tigray: Eritrea schickt Truppen, Äthiopien Beschwerdebriefe

Äthiopien gibt Eritrea die Schuld an einer Eskalation in Tigray. Eritrea schickt Truppen. Das Bündnis gegen Premier Abiy rückt enger zusammen - die möglichen regionalen Auswirkungen sind kaum zu überschätzen.

Eritreische Streitkräfte haben die Grenze zu Äthiopien überquert: Das haben inzwischen mehrere Quellen bestätigt. Ein AFP-Bericht zitiert eine anonyme Sicherheitsquelle, die von 5000 bis 8000 Soldaten auf äthiopischem Gebiet ausgeht.

Am Donnerstag forderte die äthiopische Regierung in einem Schreiben an den UN-Sicherheitsrat den sofortigen Abzug eritreischer Truppen aus ihrem Hoheitsgebiet. Die Präsenz der ausländischen Truppen lasse Äthiopien "keine Wahl, als sich gegen Eritrea zu verteidigen", hieß es in dem Schreiben, das den Nachrichtenagenturen Reuters und AFP vorliegt.

Eritrea hat wiederholt rhetorisch Kontra gegeben. Informationsminister Yemane Meskel warf der Regierung von Premierminister Abiy Ahmed vor, "unaufhörlich die Kriegstrommeln zu rühren". Am Freitag veröffentlichte das Ministerium eine Erklärung auf der Landessprache Tigrinya. "Der souveräne Staat Eritrea ist durch Blut und Gesetz gebunden", hieß es dort: "Wehe denen, die ihn antasten."

Die offene Kriegsrhetorik ist die jüngste Entwicklung in einem Konflikt, der sich in den letzten Wochen rasch verschärft hat. Experten zufolge könnte Äthiopien die Eskalation bewusst herbeigeführt haben. Erst letzte Woche hatte das Land eritreische und ägyptische Diplomaten ausgewiesen - woraufhin Eritrea seinerseits die diplomatischen Beziehungen kappte.

Als Premierminister Abiy Ahmed am Montag für weitere fünf Jahre vereidigt wurde, bezeichnete er den Zugang zum Meer als Priorität. Das schürte neue Gerüchte, dass Abiy bereit sein könnte, Eritreas strategisch wichtigen Hafen Assab mit Gewalt einzunehmen.

Für Abiy läuft es gerade eigentlich nicht schlecht: Die äthiopische Armee (ENDF) erobert mit Unterstützung der Miliz "Tigray Peace Force" in großem Tempo besetzte Gebiete zurück - darunter die Landeshauptstadt Mekelle. Doch der Widerstand gegen die Regierung in Addis Abeba findet neue Kanäle.

Einer davon ist die Tsimdo-Bewegung (Tigrinya für "Engagement"). Die hat schon mehrere Metamorphosen hinter sich, berichtet Jalale Getachew Birru, Ostafrika-Analystin beim US-Krisenmonitor ACLED. "Das Tsimdo-Konzept tauchte erstmals im Rahmen grenzüberschreitender Friedensinitiativen auf, an denen Aktivisten, religiöse Persönlichkeiten und lokale Gemeinschaften in den Grenzdörfern von Tigray und Eritrea beteiligt waren", schreibt Jalale der DW. Heute zählen sich verschiedene ethnische Gruppen dazu, die teils schon lange mit der Bundesregierung im Konflikt stehen.

Aus dieser Bewegung ging die im September ausgerufene "Allianz der äthiopischen Volkskräfte für das Überleben" (Englisch kurz: Alliance for Survival) hervor. Laut Jalale zielt dieses Bündnis darauf ab, die derzeitige Regierung abzusetzen und einen Verfassungsdialog anzustoßen.

Für Analyst Abdurahman Sayed vom Londoner Thinktank "Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration" sagt das Bündnis viel über Äthiopiens zahlreiche ungelöste Konflikte. "Die Kämpfe in Äthiopien haben nie aufgehört", sagt Sayed der DW. "Was die Oromo Liberation Army betrifft, dauern sie schon seit Jahrzehnten an, bei den Amhara sind es mindestens drei Jahre."

Die Volksbefreiungsfront von Tigray (TPLF) wiederum - eine der zentralen Konfliktparteien im Tigray-Krieg von 2020 bis 2022 - habe sich vom Pretoria-Abkommen, das damals die Kämpfe beendet hatte, enttäuscht gezeigt. Denn das habe keinen nachhaltigen Frieden gebracht.

ACLED stellt jedoch fest, dass von den sieben Gruppen der Allianz bisher nur drei an den jüngsten Kämpfen beteiligt seien: die Tigrayan Defence Forces (TDF), die Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM) und eine relativ neue Gruppe der Afar-Ethnie namens Ugugumo. Der Erfolg der "Alliance for Survival" hängt laut ACLED zu einem großen Teil von der Unterstützung ab, die sie durch externe Akteure erhält.

Zu diesen externen Akteuren gehört ein loses Bündnis der Nachbarländer Sudan, Ägypten, Eritrea und Somalia. "Alle diese Länder hegen Vorwürfe gegen die Regierung von Premierminister Abiy Ahmed", betont der Londoner Analyst Abdurahman Sayed. In Ägypten gehe es um die Nutzung des Nilwassers: Seit Jahren gibt es Streit um einen Mega-Staudamm auf äthiopischer Seite. Im Sudan sorge es für Unmut, dass Äthiopien die Rapid Support Forces unterstütze, die im Bürgerkrieg den Regierungstruppen gegenübersteht.

Im Falle Somalias geht es - wie auch in Eritrea - um einen Hafen: 2024 hatte Äthiopien mit dem selbstverwalteten Gebiet Somaliland Vorabsprachen über eine Nutzung des dortigen Hafens in Berbera getroffen. Obwohl Somaliland schon seit Jahrzehnten autonom regiert wird, ist es bisher international (mit Ausnahme von Israel) nicht anerkannt. Somalia sah durch die Verhandlungen seine Souveränität verletzt, erst eine türkische Mediation konnte die Lage etwas beruhigen.

"All diese Nachbarländer sind der Ansicht, dass sie der von Äthiopien ausgehende Bedrohung gemeinsam begegnen müssen", folgert Sayed.

Ein Gipfeltreffen der vier Länder am vergangenen Sonntag und eine gemeinsame Abschlusserklärung sprechen Bände: Zwar wird Äthiopien nicht erwähnt, doch die Botschaft ist deutlich.

So betonen die Staatschefs die Bedeutung des Völkerrechts, "insbesondere die Achtung der Souveränität, Unabhängigkeit und territorialen Integrität der Staaten der Region". Und sie erklären, dass "die Verwaltung des Roten Meeres in der alleinigen Verantwortung der Anrainerstaaten liegt". Immerhin enthält die Erklärung auch ein Bekenntnis, "friedliche Lösungen für Konflikte" zu fördern. Doch die Realität vor Ort könnte dieses Bekenntnis schon bald obsolet machen.

#535. From Russian cages to Irish sanctuary: The five-year rescue journey of Bu and Tyapa

Tyapa (left) and Bu (right) were previously kept in small cages in the Republic of Dagestan in Russia

After years in cramped cages, two brown bears are adjusting to their new life following a remarkable rescue mission that spanned multiple countries, was disrupted by two major conflicts and involved more than 100 people.

For Bu and Tyapa, the five-year rescue journey from the Republic of Dagestan in Russia to the Irish countryside was anything but straightforward.

One bear had spent their life forced to perform in a circus, while the other was confined to a cage so small they could not stand upright.

Today, the bears are now adjusting to a totally different world among the trees and grass at Wild Ireland, a sanctuary for rescued animals in County Donegal.

Tyapa is slowly settling into her new surroundings in Burnfoot, County Donegal

Wild Ireland founder Killian McLaughlin first learned about Bu and Tyapa in 2021 and committed to bringing them to safety in Donegal.

The sanctuary, located in Burnfoot, opened in October 2019 and provides a safe space for animals, including brown bears, monkeys, wolves, and lynx.

Wild Ireland founder Killian McLaughlin says the bears' health improvements since their arrival have been remarkable

McLaughlin said the two bears were in extremely poor health when they were first rescued.

Former circus bear Bu had spent years confined to a small indoor cage after being forced to perform.

McLaughlin said Tyapa had lived in a cage measuring just 2.5m by 2.5m by 2m, which was too low for him to stand upright and had no roof, which left him exposed to the harsh winters and blistering summer heat.

The bear had no water dish and relied on a hose for drinking water. McLaughlin said he was being raised to be killed for an eventual taxidermy display.

When the bears were rescued, both were severely malnourished and showed signs of psychological trauma.

Blood tests also revealed serious kidney problems associated with prolonged dehydration.

Russia's invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 made the original transport route through Ukraine impossible, said McLaughlin.

An alternative route through the Middle East was then explored, but plans were disrupted again in February 2026 when the escalating conflict involving Iran led to airspace closures and flight disruptions across the region.

More than 100 people were involved in the rescue operation, including volunteers, lawyers, veterinarians, animal transport specialists, cargo teams and officials in Russia, the United Arab Emirates and Ireland.

The bears travelled from Moscow via Abu Dhabi to Dublin, arriving in the Republic of Ireland on 3 August 2026

In late October 2025, Dima and Yana Kim, who work at Tiger House, a sanctuary near St Petersburg that cares for former circus tigers, embarked on a 36-hour drive to Dagestan to rescue the bears.

Bu and Tyapa had to be cut out of their rusting steel cages, sedated and placed in secure transport crates for the journey back to Tiger House, where they received veterinary treatment and underwent quarantine.

After months of preparation and repeated delays, the bears eventually travelled from Moscow via Abu Dhabi to Dublin, arriving in Ireland in August.

Since arriving at Wild Ireland, McLaughlin said both bears have gained weight, their coats have improved, and follow-up blood tests have shown that their kidney function has returned to normal.

He said their habitat provides woodland, water and room to explore, as well as sheltered areas where they can retreat or move out of public view if they would like some privacy.

"These bears have suffered trauma and the first step of that recovery process is get them back out into the forest, get their paws into the soil and on the grass and get them exploring.

"We hope they can now have a full and happy life."

Working with bears is certainly not your everyday job, but for Wild Ireland team member Chloe McElhatton, it's one she absolutely relishes.

Chloe has been working at Wild Ireland for just over a year. She studied zoology at Queen's University Belfast, completing a four-year degree before joining the team.

"This is obviously a very unique job, and it's quite different from what most people would do," she said.

Chloe McElhatton is part of the bear team at Wild Ireland and says looking after bears is not your average 9-5 job

"We've done a lot of work hiding food around the bear habitats, encouraging them to search and forage for it themselves and this promotes their natural behaviours and helps them become more comfortable in that new open space," she said.

"Over time, we've seen their confidence build, and you can see great changes, both physically and mentally, in both of them."

Liam, who is from France, says the two bears are big and impressive

Liam, who is from France, said the bears were one of his favourite animals to see when visiting the park.

"Very big and very impressive," is how he summed up Bu and Tyapa.

"I saw chickens, some wolves and some monkeys and then the bears which were definitely my favourite."

Chris Roberts is a regular visitor to Wild Ireland and came to visit hoping to see a glimpse of the two new bears

Chris Roberts is from Manorcunningham, about 20 minutes from Wild Ireland, and has been visiting the site ever since it first opened in 2019.

"I've lost count of how many times we've been here, but we really wanted to come down today to see if we could catch a glimpse of Bu and Tyapa.

"It was fantastic to see them in the flesh.

"We absolutely loved it and are delighted to see them doing so well, especially considering their backstory and the awful conditions they were once kept in."

#537. Fusillade à Trappes : trois personnes de l'entourage du principal suspect également placées en garde à vue, celle du principal suspect prolongée

Article rédigé par Clément Périé

l'essentiel Selon les informations de BFMTV auprès du parquet national antiterroriste, trois membres de l'entourage du principal suspect de la fusillade raciste à Trappes (Yvelines) ont été placés en garde à vue ce 24 octobre. La mère du suspect s'est présentée elle-même auprès des forces de l'ordre. La garde à vue du principal suspect a, quant à elle, été prolongée.

Le principal suspect, Kévin T., 39 ans, à l'origine de la fusillade a vu également sa garde à vue prolongée. #539. Trump administration sues to block certification of upcoming Alaska election

Senator Dan Sullivan, right, is in a tight race with Democratic contender Mary Peltola.

The Trump administration wants to block the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses, arguing that another candidate with the same name may confuse voters.

The justice department said in a federal lawsuit filed on Thursday that the inclusion of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot could lead some to mistakenly cast their votes for the wrong candidate.

Polls suggest the race between Senator Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is tight, with Peltola holding a narrow lead in the final days before the 3 November vote.

The US government wants the judge to bar the state from certifying the results if Senator Sullivan loses by a margin less than the other Sullivan.

"I'm the one that said do it," US President Donald Trump told reporters when asked for his thoughts on the lawsuit after he landed in Florida for a campaign rally on Friday.

Trump has referred to the second Sullivan's candidacy as a "scam" and said his administration was looking at "powerful legal options" to end it. The retired teacher previously denied his candidacy had an ulterior motive.

Previous efforts to remove that Sullivan, a retired teacher, from the ballot have already been rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court.

For the 3 November midterm election, the senator will be listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent.

Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box.

In court documents, the justice department said Alaska "will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its elections" if it includes "any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J Sullivan".

The second Sullivan, who was also a US Forest Service worker, was reportedly once a member of the Alaska Independence Party before registering as a Republican earlier this year.

In the filing, Associate Attorney General Stanley E Woodward Jr asserted that the sole purpose of his candidacy was to benefit Peltola's campaign by reducing the number of votes for the senator.

"Given the substantial likelihood that the inclusion of Dan J Sullivan will confuse or mislead voters looking to cast a vote for Senator Sullivan and thus distort the will of Alaskan voters, there is a substantial likelihood that a certification of the election will reflect an electoral process that lacked integrity," Woodward argued.

Dan J Sullivan has repeatedly denied those claims, telling the local Petersburg Pilot newspaper earlier this year that he "wouldn't even know who to speak to" in Peltola's campaign.

He said separately to Courthouse News that it was his "sincere hope that people know who and what they are voting for but, ultimately, choice is good and voters' intent will be as varied as the candidates who are running".

In the event Peltola wins, and the margin of loss suggests possible confusion, the lawsuit calls for certification to be delayed pending an investigation into whether voters were mixed up on the names as well as any "necessary and appropriate" steps to determine what would have happened had the second Sullivan been kept off the ballot.

Neither candidate has so far commented on the lawsuit.

The Senate race in Alaska - which Trump won by 14 percentage points in 2024 - is among the most closely watched in the upcoming midterm elections.

The president's approval ratings in the state have been badly hit by voter disapproval of rising prices and the war in Iran.

#540. Storm Boelo: Travel disrupted and events cancelled as UK hit by wind and rain

Fresh deluge of wet weather comes after Storm Austen brought strong winds to many regions on Friday

Amber weather warnings have come into force as the worst of Storm Boelo could be set to hit parts of the UK.

Storm Boelo’s winds will peak from Saturday evening, leaving areas in the warning zone, including Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, braced for gusts of 60-70mph and even 80mph in exposed coastal spots, the Met Office said.

The forecaster’s amber warnings came into force on Saturday at 9pm.

Maximum gust speeds of 75mph have already hit South Uist Range, Western Isles, Highland and Eilean Siar, Scotland on Saturday, according to the Met Office, which has also issued several yellow warnings for rain.

Storm Boelo follows Storm Austen, the first named storm of the season, which brought strong winds to parts of the UK on Friday.

Gusts of 76mph were recorded at St Mary’s airport in the Isles of Scilly, with 74mph at Aberporth in south-west Wales and 71mph at Culdrose in Cornwall.

Heavy downpours since 8am on Saturday have already seen rainfall totals of 72mm in White Barrow, Wiltshire, along with 43mm in both Cwm Dyli, just south of the Snowdon range in North Wales, and Inveruglas on the west shore of Loch Lomond, Scotland.

Hundreds of homes were still without power in south-west England after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday where the National Grid said power had been restored to 131,225 properties by Saturday at 7pm.

An amber wind warning, the Met Office’s second most severe, is active across Scotland, the north of England down to Carlisle from 9pm on Saturday to the same time on Sunday.

A further amber warning runs from 9pm on Saturday to 10am on Sunday in the north-east of Northern Ireland.

Storm Boelo, the second named storm of the season, will bring a danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves and people should stay indoors as much as possible, the forecaster said.

The amber warning sits within wider yellow wind warnings which extend south into parts of England and North Wales and cover the whole of Northern Ireland.

The Environment Agency had issued 58 alerts for spots across England where flooding is possible by 8pm on Saturday, as well as 12 warnings stating that flooding is expected.

Met Office chief forecaster Jason Kelly said: “Storm Boelo will be felt across the UK this weekend, with the strongest winds and greatest potential for disruption in the north.

“Amber warnings are in place across mainland Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north of England, where gusts of 60-70mph are expected widely, with the potential for 80mph in exposed coastal locations.

“Strong winds will also affect other parts of the UK, with gusts of 50-60mph possible in places. Heavy rain will provide an additional hazard, particularly in the north, bringing the potential for further impacts.

“People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies.”

People should secure loose items outside, plan ahead if they are travelling and keep an eye on the latest forecast and warnings, he advised.

Storm Boelo has already caused widespread disruption.

Boelo’s strong winds disrupted flights at Dublin airport, where as of 4pm on Saturday, nine outbound and 10 inbound flights had been cancelled by airlines because of weather issues.

It also reported that six inbound flights performed go-arounds – five of which landed on the second attempt, with the other diverting to another airport before returning a short time later.

Network Rail shared images of a trampoline beneath a train and a shed by the tracks, in a call for those living near rail lines to secure their garden furniture firmly.

Visit Liverpool announced that the region’s River of Light event, featuring illuminated artwork, had been cancelled “in the interests of safety”.

London’s annual Diwali on the Square celebrations this Sunday were also cancelled on independent health and safety experts’ recommendations in light of the storm.

Other attractions closed on Sunday include Edinburgh Castle and the Fountains Abbey estate in North Yorkshire, which was due to host its Fountains by Floodlight event.

#541. Magnitude-7 earthquake hits Tibet, killing at least 16 and destroying hundreds of homes

Search and rescue efforts under way after quake strikes region’s north, with at least seven aftershocks recorded

A magnitude-7 earthquake has hit Tibet, killing at least 16 people, injuring 54 and destroying hundreds of homes in the northern regional city of Nagqu, official media have said.

Search and rescue efforts continued after at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds collapsed, the Nagqu media office said, citing city government officials. It was the biggest quake in the region in the past five years, according to China’s national broadcaster CCTV.

More than 1,600 people from the local county were deployed to help rescue efforts. Supplies were also sent into the region, including 1,000 prefabricated housing units, about 3,000 tents, folding beds, torches and winter clothing.

The US Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10.33pm local time on Thursday, with its epicentre 119 miles (191km) east-north-east of Nagqu, in a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet. It put the earthquake’s depth at 11 miles.

The agency recorded at least seven aftershocks of magnitudes between 4.3 and 5.2, all of them with a depth of 6 miles. Videos posted by CCTV showed workers running out of restaurants and objects falling off shelves at supermarkets when the quake struck.

China’s official Xinhua news agency said on Friday that communication in some areas hit by the quake was down. Local railway authorities had taken emergency actions to stop trains passing through the region.

More than 300 police officers were dispatched for relief work while the regional fire and rescue services had sent almost 350 personnel to the affected areas, Xinhua reported. Rescue workers clambered through damaged buildings, some with collapsed roofs, footage on CCTV showed.

The earthquake caused rockfalls, forcing local authorities to close a section of national highway 317, allowing only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles through as crews worked to clear debris, according to Xinhua. Intermittent snow was expected in the region over the next three days, Xinhua said.

China’s president, Xi Jinping, called for an all-out effort in the rescue operation and medical relief work.

Nagqu is more than 185 miles north of Tibet’s capital, Lhasa. Earthquakes are relatively common in China. In January 2025, at least 126 people were killed in one in Tibet’s rural Tingri county.

In August, a disastrous flood hit the border of Tibet and Nepal. China’s tight grip on information prevented international media from visiting the affected regions on the Tibetan side, obscuring the scale of the damage.

In December 2023, a quake in remote Gansu province in north-west China killed at least 134 people, state media said. That quake was China’s deadliest since 2014, when more than 600 people died in the south-western province of Yunnan.

Tibet is a particularly seismically active area. The high-altitude region was taken under Chinese control in the 1950s and its people, who are predominantly ethnic Tibetans, have had a tense relationship with the authorities in Beijing since. As well as being one of the poorest regions in China, many Tibetans reject Beijing-imposed controls on their culture and religion.

#542. As the US and China form AI blocs, countries are increasingly torn between them

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

With the two leading AI powers, the United States and China, forming their own AI blocs, other countries are maneuvering to harness the strengths of both groupings and avoid losing out.

As the rivalry intensifies, experts say the window for countries to be able to choose freely between the two AI superpowers may be narrowing, forcing them to at one point pick between the U.S.-led Pax Silica and the China-inspired World AI Cooperation Organization.

That could put many countries in a dilemma: Do they go with the U.S.’s most advanced chips and AI technologies, or join China’s more affordable, open-source AI systems?

Kazakhstan, a Central Asia nation of about 21 million people, is a rare example of a country that has sought to bridge that gap.

Just three weeks after its AI minister Zhaslan Madiyev visited Washington in June to join the U.S. group working to strengthen AI supply chains, he headed to Shanghai for a signing ceremony making the Central Asian country a founding member of China's initiative to shape the global AI agenda.

Being in Pax Silica means more technological partnerships, high-tech manufacturing jobs and a place in global AI supply chains. At the same time, as part of China’s World AI Cooperation Organization alongside 28 other initial founding countries including Pakistan and Russia, Kazakhstan hopes to also have a voice in setting regional and global AI standards.

“Everyone is hedging,” said Dana Masalimova, a former Kazakhstan diplomat and independent scholar and center associate at the Kathryn W. and Shelby Cullom Davis Center for Russian and Eurasian Studies at Harvard University.

“We don’t want this binary choice,” Masalimova said.

Kazakhstan among countries hoping to harness the best of both blocs

Kazakhstan is benefiting from both U.S. and Chinese investments, but is in a “very precarious spot,” she said,

It has rich critical mineral resources essential to AI development and has cheap electricity to power data centers, which have become politically fraught in the U.S.

Earlier this year, Kazakhstan's government signed an investment deal worth up to $10 billion involving Nvidia to build a “data center valley” in the country.

Meanwhile, more Chinese companies are investing in Kazakhstan. Local officials say Chinese foreign direct investment in Kazakhstan reached a record $2.8 billion in 2025. Chinese leader Xi Jinping met with Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in July to expand cooperation under China’s global infrastructure building Belt and Road initiative.

Washington’s pressure campaign versus Beijing’s courtship

Both China and the U.S. are leveraging access to AI to increase their global influence.

President Donald Trump insisted last month that “whoever wins AI, wins.” U.S. officials and AI companies have accused China of large-scale “distillation,” or extraction of capabilities, from frontier American models.

Beijing has rejected those claims and says the U.S. is pursuing an AI monopoly while restricting China’s access to some of the world’s most cutting-edge AI chips and chipmaking machinery.

Washington has signaled that Pax Silica — with China as its implicit target — is only for the trusted.

“Countries can’t be trusted partners in Pax Silica while substantively engaging in initiatives that advance a competing vision for super intelligence,” the U.S. State Department said, using the Trump administration’s new preferred term for AI.

For its part, Beijing touts the openness and inclusiveness of its World AI Cooperation Organization. “As both major countries in AI, China and the United States should leverage respective strengths in AI rather than guarding against each other,” the Chinese embassy in Washington said in a statement. “AI should not be owned by major countries.”

The two AI powers have different messaging largely because Beijing needs to court third countries in its bid to build an alternative coalition, whereas Washington already has a powerful network of allies, said Kyle Chan, a fellow at The Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center.

That lends power to what he described as “swing countries.”

Indonesia, Singapore may also be caught between China and the US

Like Kazakhstan, Indonesia has resources vital for AI and other technologies, such as nickel and copper. It's also seeking to make the most of both AI powers, having joined China's World AI Cooperation Organization.

Indonesia wants to benefit from both, Mari Pangestu, Indonesian National Economic Council's vice chair, told reporters at a University of Hong Kong Business School event. “We should be able to be part of both, put it that way. And choose the best system.”

U.S. AI firms are bringing investments to other countries like Singapore, where Anthropic is setting up its latest Asia office. The city-state says it is also considering joining China’s AI organization.

In Saudi Arabia, the AI startup Humain unveiled in September a platform built on an open model by a Chinese AI company. The kingdom also has a deal with Nvidia to expand AI computing with its advanced chips.

France, one of the most ambitious AI developers aside from the U.S. and China, is attempting to go its own way with its startup Mistral, whose new model released this month outperforms some advanced Chinese models.

Japan is closely aligned with the U.S. on strategic and security issues, including advanced semiconductors, trusted AI and standards. But it will not reject the more affordable Chinese AI models for “lower-risk applications,” said Takahiro Tsuchiya, a professor at Kyoto's University of Foreign Studies.

Difficult to challenge the two leading powers

For countries like the U.K. and Germany which have substantial economic and military capacity but no self-developed powerful frontier AI models of their own, aligning with the U.S. may be vital for their access to data centers and chip deals with U.S. companies, said Anton Leicht and Sam Winter-Levy at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Essentially, their access to advanced AI systems “depends on the whims of policymakers in Washington and Beijing,” they said, while those countries may have limited influence over AI’s future.

China, meanwhile, has been closing the technology gap with the U.S. when it comes to chipmaking and advanced AI capabilities, but it still trails top U.S. technological capabilities, at least for now.

Also, Beijing's open-source approach allows countries to be less reliant on the U.S., and China has been providing funding for developing countries to develop their own AI ecosystems, said Alberto Lemma, a research fellow at the think tank ODI Global.

To date, China has provided official sector grants and loans for project and activities that use or enable AI technologies in at least 77 low- and middle-income countries, according to the AidData research lab at William & Mary, a public university in Virginia. Some top recipients include Nigeria, Zambia, Ghana, Bangladesh, Senegal, Cameroon, and Kenya. Public perceptions are also changing. Recent study results from Pew Research Center have shown that people in middle-income countries are becoming more positive and trusting of China when it comes to AI and the technology’s regulation.

All things considered, many countries “don’t want to pick a side ... because there are advantages and disadvantages to each technology stack,” said Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

Most countries may eventually lack a good option since they cannot compete on building AI frontier models, but “every country in the world in some way or another is thinking about AI sovereignty," he said. After all, “maybe no other country than the U.S. and China can really build these very large, powerful models.”

#543. Obama attacks Trump as he campaigns for Democrats ahead of midterm elections

Watch: US midterms are 'last best chance to rein in' Trump administration, Obama says

Former President Barack Obama has attacked the Trump administration over the Iran war and high consumer prices as he hit the campaign trail for Democrats ahead of the US midterm elections.

"This election is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration," Obama told crowds in Ohio on Saturday.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump touted his administration's immigration and tariff policies at a rally in Georgia, telling supporters "we're in the golden age of America".

The midterm elections on 3 November will decide which party controls Congress for the rest of Trump's term, and therefore how easy it is for the president to carry out his plans.

Early voting has already begun and Trump cast his ballot on Saturday in Florida alongside his wife First Lady Melania Trump.

Speaking on Saturday in Ohio and Michigan, Obama targeted Trump and his cabinet members, at one point mocking the president's attempt to redecorate the White House.

"After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, 'enough is enough,'" the former president said in Cleveland.

Obama said he sympathised with voters who rejected Democrats in 2024 over economic and inflation concerns following the Covid pandemic. But he said Trump had only himself to blame for the current state of the economy.

"If you thought everything was too expensive before 'you know who'," he said, referring to Trump without using his name, "everything is more expensive now".

Trump, meanwhile, acknowledged that oil prices were "temporarily high" but said "our country is getting stronger and stronger all the time, and those pump prices are going to come down".

The Republican president has faced significant pressure to lower fuel prices, which have jumped due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

Talking up the economy, Trump told the crowd in Perry "we're taking in massive amounts of money through tariffs", and repeated his pledge to offer every adult American a $5,000 (Â£3,700) payout if Republicans win both chambers of Congress.

He also took aim at the Democrats, telling the crowd they would "loot your wealth" and "annihilate your borders".

Using derogatory language, he accused the Democrats of trying to open up immigration from Libya, Yemen, Haiti and Somalia - countries which he described as "terror-infested".

Describing a previous meeting with several senators, he recalled: "I said, 'Why do we always have to take people from shithouse countries? Why can't we take people from, like, well... Norway, Sweden? Why not Denmark?'"

Trump cast his ballot in West Palm Beach in Florida on Saturday, before going to support Republican candidate Mike Collins in Georgia

In Ohio, the current president faced an attack from his predecessor over the war in Iran, with Obama telling Democrat supporters the conflict had given Tehran "veto power" over the Strait of Hormuz.

When asked about the war earlier in the day, Trump said: "I've done it very effectively and I may have to finish it off, or maybe they'll make a deal, but I'm not sure. Either way, we win."

He was also asked whether Melania Trump would would visit Ukraine after the White House announced she secured a ceasefire in a Russian-occupied city. "We will see," he said.

At his afternoon rally, Obama also took a swipe at Trump's efforts to renovate the White House.

"What's with all the gold? He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened up a Cheesecake Factory," Obama joked.

Obama's rally in Ohio was to show support for ex-Senator Sherrod Brown, who is running to unseat incumbent Republican Senator John Husted, and Amy Acton, who is running for state governor against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy.

In his remarks, Obama criticised Ramaswamy for a campaign ad released last week in which Acton's estranged mother was featured calling her a liar. The ad didn't mention that the woman's husband was charged with raping Acton when she was a child.

The rise of AI election ads in US midterms campaign

"In recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross. No low he will not sink to try to get in the limelight," Obama said. "I mean, think about this latest ad he ran."

Acton also spoke at the campaign rally before Obama to argue that Ramaswamy "has chosen to exploit my childhood" to "save his struggling campaign".

#545. Englische Schülerinnen fordern Verbot von Schuluniformen in Pornos

Kurze Röcke, Kniestrümpfe, weiße Bluse: Schuluniformen sind ein weit verbreitetes Kostüm in pornografischen Videos. Das wollen englische Schülerinnen jetzt ändern - mit einer Petition.

Aylin und Mae, beide 15 Jahre alt, gehören dem Little Feminist Book Club (dt. "Kleiner feministischer Buchclub") ihrer Schule im englischen  Bicester, Oxfordshire an. Bei einer Gruppendiskussion erfuhr der Club davon, dass Jugendliche anderer Schulen versuchten, den Verkauf von Schuluniformen in Sex-Shops verbieten zu lassen. In pornografischen Videos sind Schulmädchen-Verkleidungen weit verbreitet. "Wir waren uns alle einig: Wir wollten einen Schritt weiter gehen", erzählt Aylin im DW-Interview. "Wir wollen Schuluniformen komplett aus der Pornografie verbannen." Um Aufmerksamkeit für das Thema zu schaffen, starteten sie eine Petition.

Viele ihrer Mitschülerinnen, so ist es ist es in der Petition zu lesen, haben bereits schlechte Erfahrungen mit dem Tragen ihrer Uniformen gemacht. Einige berichteten, dass sie schon im Alter von elf Jahren belästigt worden seien. Viele dieser Erlebnisse hätten sie verängstigt, ihnen große Scham bereitet und sie verunsichert. "Außerhalb der Schule trage ich meine Schuluniform nicht", erklärt Mae gegenüber der DW. "Ich mag es nicht, sie draußen anzuhaben."

Die Mädchen beziehen sich in ihrer Petition auch auf eine Umfrage der Hilfsorganisation Plan International aus dem Jahr 2018. Demzufolge hatten 35 Prozent der 1004 Befragten im Alter von 14 bis 21 unerwünschte sexuelle Aufmerksamkeit erfahren, während sie eine Schuluniform trugen. Acht Prozent gaben an, dass sie von einem Fremden ohne ihre Erlaubnis gefilmt oder fotografiert worden seien oder dass jemand ein Foto unter ihren Schulrock aufgenommen habe (bekannt als "Upskirting").

"Etwas, das eigentlich rein sein sollte, etwas, das eine Gemeinschaft symbolisieren soll, ist in der Gesellschaft mittlerweile in Verruf geraten", sagt Mae. "Und unsere Wahrnehmung dessen, was eine Schuluniform ausmacht, wurde durch diese widerwärtigen Medien verzerrt."

Schuluniformen gibt es in vielen Ländern weltweit. Sie sollen finanzielle Unterschiede der Familien weniger sichtbar machen, dadurch Mobbing verhindern und das Gemeinschaftsgefühl stärken. Im Vereinigten Königreich sind sie an fast allen Schulen und Vorschulen Pflicht, das heißt, praktisch alle Kinder im Alter von vier bis 16 Jahren tragen sie. Und sie haben nicht die Chance, sich außerhalb der Schule unerwünschten Blicken zu entziehen. "Wir wollen einfach nur verhindern, dass irgendjemand auf diese Art und Weise über Kinder und Schuluniformen denkt", sagt Mae. "Hoffentlich können wir das Verbot tatsächlich gesetzlich verankern lassen."

Bis dahin ist es noch ein weiter Weg, doch die Mädchen sind optimistisch. Die Petition hat bis jetzt (Stand: 09.10.) rund 27.000 Unterschriften gesammelt und dank eines Artikels in der "Times" auch große mediale Aufmerksamkeit erregt. Jetzt hoffen Mae und Aylin, dass das Parlament sich mit dem Thema befasst. Zwei Abgeordnete haben ihnen bereits ihre Unterstützung zugesagt.

Doch den Mädchen ist auch bewusst, dass manche Menschen der Meinung sind, man könne das Problem durch eine Verlängerung der Röcke lösen. "Ich halte das für falsch", erklärt Aylin. "Wir sollten nicht den Opfern die Schuld geben. Wir sollten diejenigen zur Verantwortung ziehen, die es in Ordnung finden, die Opfer zu sexualisieren."

#546. How big is Russia's threat against Germany?

Experts believe that, so far, Germany has been ill-prepared — both militarily and mentally — for Russian provocations. They also warn against the idea that ending support for Ukraine would make Germany safer.

Warnings keep mounting about Russia's threat to Germany. On October 12, Sinan Selen, president of Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, said that Russia's covert attacks and destabilization efforts against Germany and other European countries are "not a temporary development but a long-term hybrid attack."

Even if the war in Ukraine were to end, said Selen, the Russian threat would not disappear. "For Russia, this is about completely redrawing the map of Europe and redefining its own role within Europe and in global politics."

He added that Russia's aggression would continue to be felt not only in Ukraine, but also in the Baltic states, in Poland and in Germany.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has described the threat situation as one in which "our country is not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare." Russia's goal, he said, is not to defeat Germany militarily "but to subdue us politically and socially."

Security experts, however, are not so sure that Russia is only interested in exercising political and social influence. Last year, political scientist Carlo Masala told the political talk show Maischberger that "Russia is preparing for a major war." And he didn't mean just a cyberwar. Inspector General Carsten Breuer, the Bundeswehr's highest-ranking officer, agreed.

For now, though, Russia remains tied up in its war against Ukraine. According to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, there is no immediate military threat to NATO territory. But according to military experts, European intelligence agencies, and the German Defense Ministry, Russia will have the personnel and equipment to wage a conventional war against NATO by 2029. The Russian defense industry is running at full speed, and Moscow plans to expand its armed forces to 1.5 million soldiers.

At the moment, Russia has other objectives, believes Stefan Meister, an expert on Eastern Europe at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP): "I don't think Russia has any interest in a direct military conflict with NATO right now. It wants to test NATO and also display its capabilities," he tells DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An example of Russia's hybrid war might be the failed attack with an explosive-laden drone against a Ukrainian transport aircraft at Leipzig-Halle Airport in August. Soon after, the German government stated that it was certain Russia was behind the attack.

Security expert Nico Lange told DW at the time that Germany was very lucky the explosives did not detonate: "Honestly, it was pure coincidence and not the result of German defensive measures."

As for why Germany was targeted specifically, Lange said: "I believe that Germany has always been a primary target of Russian influence and hybrid warfare. Russia believes that Germany is the key to European decision-making. Germany is now leading the way in supporting Ukraine."

Moscow swiftly responded to the German government's accusation with an angry denial. Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said it was "the beginning of a real war," though there was no immediate further escalation.

Nevertheless, there is always the risk that things could spiral out of control following a Russian provocation and subsequent response, according to Stefan Meister: "Accidentally shooting down an aircraft that they were trying to intimidate would trigger a counter-reaction. But I don't believe that Russia is currently aiming for a direct war but rather for provocations, polarization, and sowing uncertainty among the population."

Not everyone shares the assessment that Russia poses a threat to Germany — some believe that the threat can be averted.

Despite the war in Ukraine, politicians from the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the populist left-wing Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) want to improve relations with Russia, resume Russian energy supplies and end support for Ukraine.

AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla said in early September, "People are fed up with this escalation against Russia, with the billions being squandered there on a system that is actually funded by German taxpayers' money."

The message appears to have resonated among the population, especially in eastern Germany. The AfD saw strong gains in all three state elections in September. In Saxony-Anhalt, it became the strongest party by far and may even run the government there soon, which would be the first time that a far-right party has held power in Germany since the end of WWII.

The CDU's security policy expert Roderich Kiesewetter disputed the claim made by the AfD and BSW that ending aid to Ukraine would mean greater security and more money for German schools and infrastructure: "Spending on education, social policy, and infrastructure is only possible if we live in freedom and democracy — and, above all, in peace and security. Anyone who believes that we'll have more money for social programs if we stop supporting Ukraine and let Russia have its way is either gravely mistaken or is making themselves a tool of Russian propaganda."

The perceived security threat has led the German military, the Bundeswehr, to fast-track significant modernization through substantial investment. But it is struggling to find enough recruits for its planned expansion. Many young Germans have taken to the streets to protest against plans to reintroduce conscription. Defense Minister Boris Pistorius faced criticism from inside his own party, the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), for saying that Germany must become "capable of waging war." Many found the statement to be too militaristic.

Is Germany prepared for a military threat? "Not at all. Germany is not well prepared militarily or in the civilian sector, and the population isn't mentally prepared for it either," said Meister. "Just look at the demonstrations against conscription and the military that continue to take place, even though Germany needs a draft. For decades, we've grown up in this culture of pacifism, in a comfort zone. I believe there is very limited societal resilience, but above all, we are not at all mentally prepared for war."

Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) are under increasing political pressure — especially from the far right — to scale back support for Ukraine. But Merz never tires of emphasizing that Ukraine will continue to receive support under his chancellorship, calling it a matter of Germany's security. He recently visited Kyiv once again and, together with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, surveyed the destruction caused by Russia.

But this also means that the threat from Russia will continue and even intensify, says Stefan Meister: "I believe we will see a massive increase in attacks such as the one in Leipzig, of provocations involving drones. We will see attacks on infrastructures and possibly also on specific individuals within the military-industrial complex. I believe this is the real, concrete danger facing Germany in the coming months."

#548. Minneapolis withdrawal was 'surrender', Trump's ex-border patrol chief tells BBC

Watch: Trump's ex-border patrol chief challenged over Minneapolis operation

The former US border patrol chief who became the public face of the highly controversial deportation drive in Minneapolis earlier this year has defended the operation, describing the withdrawal of agents from the city as a "surrender" by the Trump administration.

Greg Bovino also told the BBC that he was "not responding" to a lawsuit filed by the family of a woman shot dead during the operation. He appeared to dismiss the legal action, praising the officers deployed to Minneapolis and saying "people do lawsuits all the time".

Bovino, 56, was removed from his role shortly after the fatal shootings of US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January.

The two shootings, which were captured on video, triggered a bipartisan backlash and widespread protests. US President Donald Trump then said he was "going to de-escalate a little bit" and withdrew hundreds of immigration agents from the city.

Earlier this month, Good's family filed two civil lawsuits against the Trump administration over her killing, alleging wrongful death and a conspiracy to interfere with the civil rights of protesters.

One of the lawsuits names several top officials, including Bovino and Jonathan Ross, the agent who shot Good, "for their respective individual roles in the operation that led to Renee's death". It alleges that the government's operation in Minneapolis created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence".

Asked about Bovino's remarks, the family's lawyers said he was "spewing propaganda" and could not be "judge, jury and executioner". They added: "Our legal team looks forward to the depositions of Mr Bovino and all of the defendants in this matter".

A White House spokeswoman previously called the lawsuits "baseless".

Watch: Renee Good's partner speaks publicly for first time since her death

Speaking in Detroit, where he was campaigning for tougher immigration enforcement, Bovino said the administration "threw the towel in" and called for more deportations, which he said were now at a "virtual standstill".

He added that he regretted "not going harder in Minnesota and arresting even more illegal aliens".

Bovino said his agents in Minneapolis were the "real victims" of what he called "the most violence that any law enforcement mission ever in the history of the United States has been up against".

Challenged by the BBC over how immigration agents handled both shooting incidents, Bovino rejected suggestions that video evidence undermined his claim that Good and Pretti had intended to harm the agents.

"The evidence is that violence was perpetrated against agents of the US government, and this is a society of laws and people need to follow the law. If not, there are consequences," he said.

Trump initially blamed Good's own actions for her death, saying just hours after she was killed that she "violently, willfully and viciously ran over the ICE officer". Weeks later, he called her death a "tragedy" and said agents were sometimes "going to make a mistake".

The withdrawal from Minnesota, which saw some 700 immigration agents leave the state, also saw Bovino removed from his post. The operation was taken over by the White House 'border tsar' Tom Homan.

When asked why he was removed, Bovino told the BBC: "You'd have to ask the administration. I still haven't gotten the final word on that."

Bovino recently addressed a rally by activists in Michigan who are calling for authorities to deport Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed

Kristi Noem, who was Homeland Security secretary at the time of the operation, was fired by Trump in March.

Bovino has since retired from the US border patrol. He has become known for his hardline stance on immigration, often going further in his statements than Trump's own officials and claiming without evidence that 100 million people are illegally in the US and should be deported.

He has called for "total spectrum immigration enforcement" with support from the US military involving "cruise ships packed to the gills, cars, planes, trains, automobiles, all headed out of the United States packed with illegal aliens".

Renee Good: Family of US woman killed by ICE agent sues Trump officials

The ICE raids are over, but some Minnesotans say they still live in fear

Analysing the Minneapolis shooting frame by frame

Newly released video undermines ICE account of Minneapolis migrant shooting

When asked about Bovino's comments about Minneapolis, a White House spokesperson said "the president has delivered the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history".

"He stopped the invasion of our country and as a result of his policies more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the US," they said.

Bovino has also floated "exploring" a presidential run in 2028. "If politicians aren't going to step up and do their job then you might see something happen," he told the BBC when asked about his intentions.

Bovino recently addressed a far-right rally by activists in Michigan who are calling for authorities to deport Abdul El-Sayed, a US citizen and Democratic candidate running in the state's tightly fought race for a Senate seat.

American-born Sayed would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate if he wins the seat against Republican Mike Rogers.

#550. North Korea prepares to restart propaganda loudspeakers as ties sour with South

Kim Yo-jong, sister of Kim Jong-un, issues warning after inspecting border fortifications against backdrop of rising tensions

Propaganda loudspeakers aimed at South Korea will be ready to restart within days along the entire border, Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, has said amid a worsening of ties between the two countries.

The statement, carried by the state news agency KCNA on Thursday, came a day after she said the loudspeakers would be in operation along the whole border from some time in October.

Both North and South Korea have historically used giant loudspeakers to broadcast propaganda across the border, with the North in recent years playing haunting bestial howls, and the South opting for K-pop music ​and news criticising Pyongyang.

If the broadcasts resume, they would be the first loudspeaker exchange across the border in 16 months. South Korean president Lee Jae Myung suspended broadcasts from the southern side just days into his presidency in June 2025 to ease tensions with Pyongyang, and the military dismantled the speakers that August.

At a briefing on Thursday, a defence ministry spokesperson in Seoul said that if North Korea went ahead, “naturally there would have to be a proportional measure”, but made clear no decision had been made.

The joint chiefs of staff said routine maintenance of the North’s loudspeakers had been observed before Kim Yo-jong’s statements.

Tensions between the two Koreas have risen since September, when a landmine blast south of the military demarcation line injured three South Korean soldiers, two of them seriously.

Seoul and the UN command – which oversees the 1953 armistice that halted but did not end the Korean war – concluded it was a North Korean anti-personnel mine and an armistice violation. Pyongyang denied responsibility and called the incident a “self-staged farce”.

The loudspeaker threat comes as North Korea continues to fortify its side of the border. Since Kim Jong-un declared that the two Koreas were “two states hostile to each other” in December 2023, North Korea has laid mines, strung barbed wire and erected anti-tank barriers along the border.

On Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong inspected several fortification points along the border with Pak Jong-chon, a marshal and adviser to Pyongyang’s defence ministry.

The border had been “clearly blocked and turned into a fortress more thoroughly”, she said, adding that Kim Jong-un had told her it “should be a permanent line never to be crossed”.

Seoul says North Korean troops have repeatedly crossed the military demarcation line, the 250km line dividing the two Koreas, during the construction work, prompting South Korean soldiers to issue warnings over loudspeakers and fire warning shots.

North Korea has called the warning shots and broadcasts provocations by “armed rogues”.

#551. Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi ‘sounds strong’ but is isolated, son says

Kim Aris tells the Guardian chance to speak with detained Nobel laureate was ‘public relations’ move from military leaders

Myanmar’s former democratic leader Aung San Suu Kyi appears to be in good physical and mental health but is living in near-complete isolation, her son has said after the first call with his 81-year-old mother in more than five years.

“She still sounds certainly all there mentally, and physically she sounds strong,” Kim Aris said. “I don’t think she has anybody outside of the military or the police around her, so essentially she’s been held in solitary confinement from what I gather.”

After being deposed in a 2021 military coup, the Nobel Peace prize laureate has been moved to an unspecified location in the capital. “I’m still not entirely sure where she is,” said Aris. “I think it’s a residence in Naypyidaw, which is fenced off and it has a scrubby bit of land around it.”

Aris, who has lived in the UK most of his life and whose late father was a British historian, was allowed to speak to his mother on Thursday at the Myanmar embassy in London. While he welcomed the chance to talk, he said the invitation was part of a “public relations” campaign by the country’s military leaders.

The former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing has sought to rebuild international diplomatic ties, and in April switched his military fatigues for civilian clothes after elections that were widely condemned as a sham.

Activists have long demanded “proof of life” for Aung San Suu Kyi, as well as scores of other political prisoners. In August, she was finally photographed during a Red Cross visit. Last week, a government spokesperson published images of her smiling in a wood-panelled room as officials delivered two gardening books given to her as gifts by Britain’s King Charles. A paper calendar on the wall behind her showed the date.

Aris said these photo-ops were well-known stunts that the regime had used before to pretend his mother, a national icon, was being treated fairly. The daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San has spent much of her life since the late 1980s in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements.

“She remains completely shut off from the rest of the world. I think she’s unaware of what’s happening outside of where she is because she’s not allowed any newspapers or radio or television,” Aris said. “She’s been locked up for five years on trumped-up, politically motivated charges and she should be free.”

Ruled for decades by generals and suffering from western sanctions, Myanmar experienced a brief democratic moment after Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to run in a 2015 election that her party overwhelmingly won. She took up the role of “state counsellor” under a civilian-military power-sharing agreement.

Her international reputation was soon tarnished after the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims. Aung San Suu Kyi flew to the international court of justice in The Hague, where she said she acknowledged military units might have used “disproportionate force”, but defended the government against accusations of genocide.

Aris said that his mother was never “silent” on the Rohingya crisis and what she said on the issue “could fill volumes”. Under her leadership, Myanmar launched a domestic inquiry and appointed the former UN chief Kofi Annan to head a commission.

He added that as state counsellor, Aung San Suu Kyi was “always walking on a tightrope”, knowing the military could strip her of her fragile power at any moment.

“The very hard-won nascent democracy that she was trying to lead was holding on to things by a thread,” he said. “The military could have taken over at any point, and they were doing their best to make my mother’s situation a lot more difficult and to undermine her position. And I think in that respect they did a pretty good job.”

The 2021 power grab by the military triggered a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to conflict monitors.

Aris said the level of public global support for his mother had “dwindled incredibly” since the Rohingya crisis and that the whole country was now suffering from a lack of international attention. While many governments have called for Aung San Suu Kyi’s release, she is not treated as the beloved international figure that she once was.

“Never mind my mother, the fact that people ignore what’s happening in Burma shouldn’t be down to what was being done to the Rohingya,” he said, using the country’s former name. “And that seems to be the case sometimes, that people say: ‘Oh, well, look how the Rohingya were treated. We can ignore what’s happening in Burma.’”

#553. Don't fall for this - how to protect yourself from AI scams

Be careful where you buy from, shoppers are being warned as criminals use AI to supercharge scams.

Some fraudsters have made websites for fake retailers that claim to be family-owned firms selling quality UK-made products. Images may show a UK High Street with Union Jack flags in shot.

If you order you're likely to find a product either never arrives, or is a cheap, mass-produced item from a country such as China, trading standards officers say.

AI-generated images like this, as well as voice cloning and deepfake videos are increasingly being used to trick people out of their money, according to National Trading Standards.

For the first time, it has drawn up an AI scam watchlist, external highlighting some of the tools and techniques criminals are using.

Cloned or new websites that look polished and professional in rapid time and at a low cost

Romance scams in which AI is used to remember victims' personal details and keep conversations going over weeks or months

AI-generated deepfake videos and voice-cloned audio is used to impersonate family members or close friends asking for money in an "emergency"

Error-free, personalised phishing emails, text messages and social media posts can be generated by AI on a huge scale

Some of the old scam-avoidance techniques may now be less successful due to the benefits of AI.

Typos or grammatical errors can no longer be relied on to spot scams, says consumer group Which?.

Some of the ways to protect yourself, according to trading standards, include:

Never sending money, gift cards or personal or financial information to someone you have not met in person

Doing your research - such as checking whether a shop's address is real, using the Financial Conduct Authority's Firm Checker, external, to ensure a company is authorised to give financial advice, and contacting a business directly to check whether a job advert is real

Not assuming someone is genuine just because you've heard their voice or seen them on a video call

In general, they say stop and think before paying, sharing personal information or taking action. You should be especially wary of pressure or urgency because criminals want you to act before you have time to think.

Fraud and scams can be reported to Report Fraud, external or by calling on 0300 1232040, or you can call the Citizens Advice Consumer Helpline on 0808 223 1133 for advice.

#555. Finnland: Dämmerung über dem glücklichsten Land der Welt

Die Finnen könnten zufrieden sein - doch die Schulden des Landes drücken. Russlands Krieg in der Ukraine hat die fiskalische Belastung noch weiter erhöht. Kann der nordische Staat also einen weiteren Schock verkraften?

Sorgen in Finnland - in jenem Land, das neun Jahre in Folge als das glücklichste der Welt galt. Ein vielleicht sehr kalter Winter steht bevor, und dazu steht den Finnen der härteste Sparhaushalt seit Jahren ins Haus.

Vor den im April anstehenden Wahlen dreht sich die Debatte nicht mehr darum, wie stark gekürzt wird, sondern darum, welche Dienstleistungen, Sozialleistungen und Renten die größten Einschnitte hinnehmen müssen.

Finnlands Verschuldungs- und Defizitbilanzen sind so schlecht wie seit den 1990er Jahren nicht mehr. Damals hatten ein Bankenzusammenbruch und der Zerfall der Sowjetunion - eines wichtigen Exportpartners - das nordische Land in eine schwere Wirtschaftskrise gestürzt.

Im vergangenen Monat bestätigte das Statistikamt Finnlands, dass die Staatsverschuldung im zweiten Quartal 90,3 Prozent des Bruttoinlandsprodukts (BIP) erreicht hatte. Vor der Pandemie lag dieser Wert gerade einmal bei etwa 65 Prozent.

Auch hier liegt die Ursache wieder im Osten. Finnland erhöhte seine Verteidigungsausgaben, nachdem das Land der NATO beigetreten war. Diesen Schritt machten die Finnen ein Jahr nach dem umfassenden russischen Einmarsch in die Ukraine. Zudem sah sich Helsinki, das zuvor rund ein Drittel seiner Energie aus Moskau bezogen hatte, mit deutlich höheren Kosten konfrontiert, als es auf andere Lieferanten umstellte.

Doch die finnische Regierung gibt bereits seit der weltweiten Finanzkrise von 2008/2009 mehr Geld aus, als sie einnimmt - bedingt unter anderem durch die alternde Bevölkerung und das schleppende Wirtschaftswachstum. Im vergangenen Monat prognostizierte die staatliche Finanzverwaltung, dass das Haushaltsdefizit im Jahr 2026 bei 4,2 Prozent des BIP liegen werde.

Brüssel setzt Helsinki unter Druck, die Neuverschuldung zu verringern, weil die Regeln der Europäischen Union von den Mitgliedstaaten verlangen, eine Defizitgrenze von drei Prozent des BIP einzuhalten. Im Januar leitete der Europäische Rat daher ein Verfahren ein und setzte Finnland eine Frist bis Ende 2028, um das angestrebte Ziel zu erreichen.

Die im Juni 2023 ins Amt getretene Regierung unter Ministerpräsident Petteri Orpo hat sich zum Ziel gesetzt, in der laufenden Legislaturperiode rund neun Milliarden Euro einzusparen. Doch wer auch immer die nächste Wahl gewinnt, wird weitaus tiefer greifende Kürzungen vornehmen müssen, warnen Ökonomen. "Die derzeit geschätzten Summen liegen zwischen acht und elf Milliarden Euro", sagte Jarkko Kivisto, Berater in der Abteilung für Geldpolitik und Forschung der Finnischen Zentralbank, gegenüber der DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bereits zu Beginn des Jahres hatten sich - von einer Ausnahme abgesehen - alle politischen Parteien darauf verständigt, eine Schuldenbremse zu unterstützen, bei der sich die künftige Regierung verpflichtet, das Haushaltsdefizit des Landes bis 2031 auf zwei bis 2,5 Prozent des Bruttoinlandsprodukts zu begrenzen.

Orpos konservative Sammlungspartei (Kokoomus) ist bislang die einzige Partei, die weitere Einsparungen in Höhe von neun Milliarden Euro in Aussicht stellt, sollte er eine zweite Amtszeit gewinnen. Neben weiteren Kürzungen in den Bereichen Gesundheit, Pflege und Sozialwesen plant Orpo auch Maßnahmen bei der betrieblichen Altersvorsorge, ohne jedoch die laufenden Auszahlungen zu kürzen

Während die Sozialdemokraten die Reformlast auf Ausgabenkürzungen und Steuererhöhungen verteilen wollen, strebt Orpo sein Ziel ohne Steuererhöhungen an. Das würde bedeuten, dass die öffentlichen Dienstleistungen die Hauptlast tragen müssten. Kivisto gab jedoch zu bedenken: "Das Defizit ist so groß, dass ein Maßnahmenpaket erforderlich wäre, das sowohl Steuererhöhungen als auch Ausgabenkürzungen umfasst."

Zwar liegt die Armutsgefährdungsquote in Finnland unter dem EU-Durchschnitt, doch die Arbeitslosenquote ist höher als in jedem anderen Mitgliedsstaat des Blocks. Im August lag die Arbeitslosenquote in Finnland laut Eurostat, der Statistikbehörde der EU, bei 10,3 Prozent und damit knapp über dem Wert von 10 Prozent in Spanien. Die Jugendarbeitslosigkeit erreichte 23,3 Prozent, verglichen mit einem EU-Durchschnitt von 15,4 Prozent.

Angesichts der bereits rückläufigen Konsumausgaben der Haushalte warnte Lauri Olappa, Direktor des Finnischen Zentrums für neue Wirtschaftsanalysen, dass eine neue Sparrunde einen schweren Schlag für die Binnenwirtschaft bedeuten würde. "Mehr als ein Viertel der Bevölkerung ist im öffentlichen Sektor beschäftigt; wenn diesen Arbeitnehmern also Entlassungen drohen, wird die Sparquote steigen und die privaten Ausgaben werden erneut zurückgehen", so Olappa gegenüber der DW.

Eine Abfolge von Belastungen - von der COVID-Pandemie über höhere Zinsen bis hin zu den Auswirkungen zweier Kriege - hat die Bemühungen erschwert, die wachsende Lücke zwischen Einnahmen und Kreditaufnahme zu verringern. Der Haushaltsentwurf für 2027 sieht weiterhin eine Finanzierungslücke von 12,4 Milliarden Euro vor.

Bereits vor dem Ukraine-Krieg hatte sich Finnland zum Kauf von 64 F-35A-Kampfjets für rund 8,4 Milliarden Euro aus den USA verpflichtet. Während des mittlerweile mehr als vier Jahre andauernden Krieges Russlands in der Ukraine hat der nordische Staat seine Militärausgaben von 4,5 Milliarden auf über acht Milliarden US-Dollar pro Jahr erhöht. Dies geht aus Daten des Stockholmer Friedensforschungsinstituts SIPRI hervor.

Im April kündigte die Regierung an, die Verteidigungsausgaben weiter auf 3,2 Prozent des Bruttoinlandsprodukts (BIP) anzuheben und damit nahe an das NATO-Ziel von 3,5 Prozent heranzurücken.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Angesichts der Ölpreise, die infolge des Iran-Konflikts bei fast 100 US-Dollar pro Barrel verharren, hat die Regierung dem Druck zur Erhöhung von Kraftstoffsubventionen bislang widerstanden. Dies geschieht, obwohl die Finnische Zentralbank in den ersten Monaten des Iran-Konflikts einen Anstieg der Kosten für Energieimporte um 50 Prozent verzeichnete.

Zwar haben der Umstieg auf erneuerbare Energien und die Inbetriebnahme des Kernreaktors Olkiluoto 3 im Jahr 2023 eine schlimmere Energiekrise abgefedert, doch warnte die Zentralbank im Sommer: Anhaltend hohe Öl- und Gaspreise würden im kommenden Jahr ein "geringeres Wirtschaftswachstum und höhere Inflation" zur Folge haben.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ein weiterer Lichtblick ist der florierende finnische Exportsektor, der von einer starken Auftragslage in der Metall- und Schiffbauindustrie profitiert. Olappa verglich die Dynamik mit den "Boomjahren von Nokia", als der einstige Marktführer im Mobilfunkgeschäft das finnische Wirtschaftswachstum maßgeblich trug. "Es besteht die Möglichkeit, dass der Exportsektor uns aus dieser Rezession führen kann", sagte er der DW - vorausgesetzt, die Nachfrage aus dem übrigen Europa bleibt stark.

trotz zahlreicher Hindernisse bei der Senkung des Haushaltsdefizits fiel die Reaktion der Märkte auf Finnlands Schuldenproblematik bislang verhalten aus. Die Ratingagenturen haben den Ausblick für das Land stabil gehalten - mit Ausnahme von S&P, das den Ausblick im April auf "negativ" setzte, ohne jedoch das Rating selbst herabzustufen.

Am 6. Oktober lag der Zinsaufschlag, den die finnische Regierung gegenüber Deutschland für zehnjährige Anleihen zahlen muss, bei 38 Basispunkten. Zum Vergleich: Bei Frankreich lag dieser Wert bei 128 und bei Italien bei 107 Basispunkten. Mit anderen Worten: Investoren stufen finnische Staatsschulden weiterhin als eine der sichersten Anlagen in Europa ein.

Dies gilt allerdings nur, solange der nächste Schock nicht in einem länger anhaltenden Ölpreisanstieg, einer erneuten Eskalation durch Russland oder einer Schuldenkrise im Euroraum mit Schwerpunkt in Frankreich besteht.

Im kommenden März könnte Finnland zum zehnten Mal in Folge zum glücklichsten Land der Welt gekürt werden. Wie lange das Lächeln anhält, sobald einen Monat später die Rechnung für die jahrzehntelange Kreditaufnahme ins Haus flattert, lässt sich nur schwer vorhersagen.

#556. China's influence in the gaming industry is growing

Home to more than 700 million gamers, China is the world's largest gaming market — but it's also one of the most tightly regulated. The effects reach far beyond China, impacting players around the world.

In a dark underground hideout, dim light spills from a handful of oil lamps. A comrade fiddles with a rifle. A red flag hangs on one of the roughly hewn stone walls, bearing a hammer and sickle on a white star — the symbol of the ChineseWorkers' and Peasants' Red Army. Weapons are scattered on the ground. One is picked up, and soon the action moves into the snowy forest, where gunfire erupts among the trees.

Such a scene could fit in a new installment of "Call of Duty," the popular first-person shooter game that transports players to battlefields past, present, and future. But it is actually from "The Defiant." The game is currently being developed by the Chinese studio Hoothanes Technology in Hangzhou. It tells the story of Chinese forces fending off the Japanese army in the 1930s and 1940s.

Developer Connor Xu tells DW the weapons featured in the game are unique. They were used only in Asia and are therefore unfamiliar to many Western players, he says. The same goes for the story, which Xu says has never before been told in a video game.

"The Defiant" is also designed to appeal to an international audience. In just a few years, China has emerged as a major player in the global gaming industry despite strict regulations, censorship and a former ban on video game consoles.

More than 700 million people in China regularly play video games. According to market research company Newzoo, most consider gaming an important part of their lives. Many use games to stay in touch with friends.

"Games make life more interesting," developer Xu says. "I can try different roles, different stories, different characters, because we only have one life to live, but we can play a role in another story. That's really attractive, I think, to Chinese users."

People in China primarily play games on PCs and smartphones, while consoles are much less common. There are historical reasons for that: While gamers in Europe and North America debated whether PlayStation or Xbox was the better console in the early 2000s, the devices were not officially sold in China between 2000 and 2014. Chinese authorities said the restrictions were intended to protect children and teenagers from becoming addicted to gaming.

Minors in China are currently allowed to play online games for no more than three hours a week. There are no such limits for adults, but gaming is subject to strict controls. Anyone who wants to play must register using their real name and a personal identification number. That effectively allows the state to track who plays what and when, as well as whom they communicate with.

There is also a gray area that the Chinese government appears to tolerate. Some players log in using VPNs, giving them access to games that are not officially available in China. Some younger players use their parents' accounts to get around the limits on gaming time.

Despite its strict controls on underage gamers, China has become increasingly receptive to video games in general, having recognized the industry's enormous economic potential. Early on, games released for Chinese players often appeared to be copies of Western titles. At the same time, Chinese tech companies such as Tencent and NetEase invested in numerous Western gaming companies.

One distinctive feature of the Chinese market is its licensing system. "Unlike a lot of the other big video games markets in the world, China has a tightly regulated and licensed official video games market," George E. Osborn tells DW. The journalist advises NGOs and governments on video games and spoke at the Gamescom congress. In his book "Power Play," he describes how authoritarian states use video games to pursue political objectives.

The rule for all games in China is simple: No license, no sales. "That system essentially forces developers who want to release their video games to go through multiple layers of approval from China's Ministry of Propaganda, Ministry of Culture," Osborn says.

Games are prohibited from containing material that threatens China's unity, sovereignty or territorial integrity, among other restrictions. Pornographic content and gambling are also banned. Games may not incite crimes that threaten national security or spread information authorities believe could disrupt public order.

"The whole point around this criteria is that it's deliberately designed to be pretty vague," Osborn says. Whether a game violates the rules is a matter of interpretation. Sometimes games are altered even after release. In the 2025 action role-playing game "Wuchang: Fallen Feathers," for example, enemies based on famous Chinese figures from the Ming Dynasty suddenly could no longer be killed. Instead, they would collapse from exhaustion.

The Chinese action role-playing game "Black Myth: Wukong" became an unexpected international hit in 2024. By then, it was clear Chinese developers could do more than cater to the domestic market — they could create successful games for a global audience as well. The game was inspired by the 16th-century Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West."

Osborn sees nothing wrong with bringing Chinese culture to audiences around the world. The question, he says, is how much the state actually intervenes in the games themselves. "I think in general, video game players are actually quite deeply skeptical of these kinds of things. They are generally very good at spotting when someone might be selling to them or someone might be propagandizing. And so I think if it's too obvious, it won't work," he says.

Because of the licensing system, Western developers also have to comply with government requirements if they want to sell their games in China. And they do want to, Osborn says, because the market is too big to ignore. "But I think when you start thinking about the potential impact this has on creative standards around the world, I think it's really important that developers ask themselves the question of what will we or won't we compromise on here?"

He fears the real danger lies in self-censorship. That could lead developers, for example, to leave queer characters out of their games. That would represent a major step backward, he says, because games help many people explore their identities.

China is not the only country where games are modified to comply with national regulations. In Germany, for example, symbols that violate the country's constitution, such as the swastika, may not be shown in games unless the game in question explicitly contributes to the country's culture of remembrance. Depictions of extreme violence also have to be removed from German versions.

Glorifying violence is prohibited in China, too, yet Xu's team is still allowed to develop a war game. How does this add up? Xu explains it this way: "I think in this game, the most important thing is not violence. The most important thing is to tell history."

Xu says the team is committed to delivering a historically accurate product. Whether it succeeds will be for historians to judge.

This article was translated from German and edited by Sarah Hucal.
