#558. White House says Melania Trump brokered truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster'

These residents were able to get out of Oleshky in spring this year

US First Lady Melania Trump has "successfully secured" a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, the White House has said.

It said the truce in the "front-line war city on the brink of disaster" without medicine, food and clean water would begin on 29 October.

Ukraine and Russia confirmed the deal was agreed to evacuate residents and deliver aid. They both said their forces would stop firing at 01:00 GMT on 27 October.

Oleshky was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Trapped between Ukrainian positions across the Dnipro River and Russian forces to the east, residents have recently resorted to eating garden weeds to survive.

Trump: First lady's 'initiative' led to truce for Ukraine city

The White House statement said Melania Trump and one of her representatives had worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire".

"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she is quoted as saying.

"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive co-ordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."

Melania Trump added that Oleshky residents "have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks" and that "without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible".

The statement did not say how long the ceasefire would be in place for.

Davyd Arakhamia, a Ukrainian MP who heads President Volodymyr Zelensky's party in parliament, later said "an operation to unblock the settlement of Oleshky and its surroundings will begin in the near future".

"To achieve this goal, a ceasefire will be achieved in the near future, as announced by the First Lady of the United States, Melania Trump," he said.

In Russia, President Vladimir Putin's spokesman confirmed that, "those who wish to do so will be able to leave this settlement".

Oleshky has been without gas or electricity since 2023, so residents have had to find other solutions

Last month, some of the remaining Oleshky residents told the BBC harrowing accounts of how they were surviving in the city that was being constantly shelled and cut off from food and water.

They said that children remaining in wider Oleshky were suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services and were "degrading" without access to education.

Many also told the BBC there was only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.

The local population was living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.

Ukraine says it has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.

The Kremlin in September acknowledged that Oleshky was facing "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.

The Pope had been among those urging a ceasefire in the city, calling for "dialogue and peace".

Oleshky was home to 24,000 people before Russia's full-scale invasion. Now Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.

It is also one of a number of settlements where thousands of people lost their homes to a massive flooding caused by the collapse of Nova Khakovka Dam in 2023. Ukraine and its allies accused Russia of blowing up the dam, while Russia blamed Ukraine.

Melania Trump worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to agree the ceasefire, the White House said.

While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.

In August 2025, Melania Trump penned a letter to Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".

Although she did not mention Ukraine by name, just days later at the White House Zelensky handed over a letter from his wife Olena, thanking her for her efforts on children.

In a rare public appearance in October the same year, the US first lady said that Putin had answered directly in writing and that her representatives were working with the Russian president's team to repatriate Ukrainian children from Russia and vice versa.

Some 34 children have reportedly been returned since 2025, including five this July.

According to US President Donald Trump, his wife has also privately expressed scepticism about Putin and his desire to achieve peace.

"I'd get home, I'd say, 'First lady, I had the most wonderful talk with Vladimir. I think we're finished'," Trump said in July last year.

"And then I'll turn on the television, or she'll say to me one time, 'Wow, that's strange because they just bombed a nursing home.'"

#559. AFP boss says politicians’ heated rhetoric is fuelling threats against MPs

Commissioner Krissy Barrett says women are more often singled out, often with threats of sexual violence

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australia’s top federal law enforcement official has drawn a direct link between politicians’ rhetoric and threats and abuse being directed at leaders.

The safety of elected representatives at all levels has been thrown into the spotlight after independent MP Helen Haines was allegedly deliberate attacked outside her Wangaratta electoral office.

Haines remains in a serious but stable condition at the Alfred hospital in Melbourne, following her double leg amputation.

The Australian federal police commissioner, Krissy Barrett, said there was no doubt the threat environment had changed for politicians.

“When I start work every morning, one of the first things I do is read a report … [that] summarises all of the threats that have been reported to the AFP over the last 24 hours,” she told the ABC’s Insiders program.

“Now, some days that report is pages and pages long.”

The commissioner said she wasn’t interested in policing free speech or intervening in political discourse.

“But I would challenge any Australian to read some of these threats and some of the abuse that is reported to us from federal parliamentarians and for anyone to argue that that is free speech or political discourse,” she added.

The move from the sending of physical hate mail to online threats had played a significant role in the increasing volume of worrying material, while also highlighting the influence of inflammatory political imagery and language.

“We do see where there is particular political conflict or discourse occurring … it does have a direct correlation to what we see in terms of threats and abuse, and sometimes it’s very immediate,” Barrett said.

Past One Nation cartoons depicting political figures, including the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, being hit by cars or buses have resurfaced in the days since the alleged attack on Haines.

The AFP commissioner said there was “a reaction amongst the community” to material such as the cartoons.

The policing agency, which is responsible for protecting federal politicians and office-holders, has held a number of emergency safety briefings with parliamentarians since Monday.

Male and female MPs were targeted equally with threats and abuse, Barrett said, but women were more often singled out individually, often with threats of sexual violence.

“My hope is that this really causes people to pause and have a think about what’s happening in this country and the impact of that,” she said.

“And if this is not the incident, then what is?”

Federal MPs from across the political spectrum have acknowledged the difficulty in balancing their personal security and access to voters.

“As a local MP, I don’t want to stop going to community events,” Liberal frontbencher Ted O’Brien told News24 on Sunday.

“That open access is a cornerstone of democracy. We’re particularly good at it in Australia. We can’t take away grassroots politics.”

Labor minister Catherine King said she has been contending with the deteriorating safety for some time.

“It is when, not if, that something will happen to one of us and we’ve been saying that certainly for the last five years or so,” she said.

“I had a mobile caravan for almost 25 years. I don’t use that now because it doesn’t have a second exit point.

“If someone did kick off and I’m trapped in the van, it’s very hard to deal with that.”

#560. " La racaille doit payer" : ils avaient mis le feu dans un parc en tirant des mortiers d'artifice, trois mois après, leurs parents reçoivent la facture de plus de 400 000 euros, de la part du maire

Article rédigé par La rédaction de La Dépêche du Midi

l'essentiel Le maire de Neuilly-sur-Marne, dont le parc avait été touché par un incendie en juillet, réclame près de 400 000 euros aux familles des trois enfants, à l'origine du feu. Une décision, et une méthode, qui font réagir les avocats des familles. En effet, le maire avait déclaré dans une vidéo publiée sur Facebook : "La racaille doit payer".

En juillet dernier, alors que la France connaît une sécheresse record et des températures caniculaires, trois enfants de 10 et 11 ans ont déclenché un incendie, à l'aide de mortiers d'artifice. Le feu avait détruit plusieurs hectares dans la commune de Neuilly-sur-Marne (Seine-Saint-Denis), endommageant un parc, une passerelle et l'espace canin, selon nos confrères du Parisien.

Chaque vendredi, retrouvez les affaires qui marquent notre région, les enquêtes qui font parler, les procès majeurs et les coulisses de l'actualité police-justice, décryptés par nos journalistes spécialistes.

Trois mois plus tard, Zartoshte Bakhtiari, le maire Divers droite de la ville dit avoir envoyé la facture aux parents de ceux qu'il qualifie de "pyromanes". "Les enfants ont été auditionnés en présence de leurs parents. Ils ont reconnu être les auteurs de cet incendie", indique l'élu. S'appuyant sur le Code civil, qui prévoit, selon lui "la responsabilité des parents du fait des enfants", Zartoshte Bakhtiari réclame 415 000 euros pour les frais engendrés par l'incendie volontaire.

Interrogé par Le Parisien, Me Hugo Guagenti, l'avocat d'une des familles conteste la méthode, assurant que ces clients n'ont rien reçu et dénonçant la volonté de "faire de la com", plutôt que celle de "vouloir réellement régler un différend". Les mots choisis par le maire de Neuilly-sur-Marne ont également fait réagir.

En effet, Zartoshte Bakhtiari, avait publié un message, avec une vidéo, publiée sur Facebook, dans lequel il déclarait que "la racaille doit payer".

#561. Met says it shared allegations about Meghan’s father with her but not other forces

Scotland Yard says it shared letter about Thomas Markle Sr allegations in 2019 but did not pass claims to other agencies

The Metropolitan police have confirmed they gave a letter to the Duchess of Sussex in 2019 concerning “alleged offending” involving her father, after accusations arose on Friday about Thomas Markle Sr having child sexual abuse images.

Scotland Yard said it had received a letter in January 2019 making a number of allegations about offending outside Britain.

The police force said it had passed the information on to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s office, but it did not pass it on to “other law enforcement agencies”.

The Sun newspaper published claims that Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, claimed he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.

On Friday, Meghan said she had been made aware of these allegations by the Met, and that she was “deeply distressed” by them.

The duchess, who is estranged from her father said in a statement she had broken off contact to protect her children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five. He has never met them.

Meghan and Prince Harry recently moved back to the UK from the US.

Meghan’s father has denied the allegations and told the Daily Mail the accusations were “sick lies”.

The Met said it was considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) to review its actions.

In a statement, a Metropolitan police spokesperson said: “Following a thorough review of Met police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019, we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom. It was sent to the MPS (Metropolitan Police Service) Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.

“The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies.

“The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach.”

In a statement on Friday, issued through her spokesperson, the duchess said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection [Rasp]. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”

She later said she had misremembered the year the Met had contacted her, and confirmed it had been 2019, not 2018 as she said on Friday.

A spokesperson for the Duchess of Sussex said: “In recalling events from more than seven years ago, without the benefit of a diary entry or contemporaneous record, it is understandable that she may have been mistaken by a few months.

“If the MPS holds a time-stamped record confirming that the letter was reviewed in 2019, that should be treated as the accurate reference point for when it was received and shared with the duchess.

“I think it is reasonable to recognise that she is doing her best to recall the precise timing of events that were not diarised at the time, and that any discrepancy of a few months is an understandable consequence of that passage of time.”

Sources said that although Meghan was made aware of the allegations in 2019, she had been unable to speak publicly to avoid jeopardising any future investigation and because speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her.

The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke.

Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.

#563. When to switch your clocks back as British Summer Time comes to an end

Smartphones will often change automatically but analogue watches and clocks will need to be manually changed

British Summer Time (BST), also known as Daylight Saving Time (DST), will come to an end this week as the clocks go back an hour.

The change happens on Sunday 25 October at 02:00 BST meaning you may get an extra hour in bed.

Sunset will move forward an hour as well and initially you may notice the sun coming up earlier too.

The clocks don't go forward again until on Sunday 28 March 2027.

Changes to the clocks have been taking place for more than a century.

The first country to make use of DST was Germany in 1916.

It was intended to save fuel consumption during World War One. Making the most of the evening daylight in spring and summer meant less heating and lighting was needed.

Many other countries followed suit, such as the UK where it became known as British Summer Time.

Here the time shift has continued ever since, despite a short period in World War Two where the clocks went forward two hours for British Double Summer Time, and a spell from 1968 to 1971 when the UK experimented with all-year-around BST.

Once we go back to GMT sunsets will occur earlier

In the United States earlier in 2026 there was a bill to make daylight saving time the new standard time called the Sunshine Protection Act.

With a 308-117 vote, members of both parties approved the bill, which would remove the need for Americans to change their clocks twice a year and put the US under time currently observed between March and November - known as permanent standard time.

The idea of winding our clocks forward permanently has been a talking point in the past. Arguments for keeping summer time include a potential boost in economic productivity as well as a possible reduction in evening road accidents.

However, it would also mean some darker winter mornings, especially in Scotland. In some parts the sun rises around 08:45 GMT in the second half of December, which would equate to 09:45 BST.

Currently there are no plans in the UK to get rid of the biannual clock change.

This year most of Europe turns their clocks back on the same day as the UK - Sunday 25 October.

In Asia, Oceania, South America and Africa there are only a few places that follow DST.

In Egypt DST comes to an end on Friday 30 October.

In North America, however, the clocks go back on the first weekend of November which this year will be the first of the month.

US Congress takes next step to make daylight saving time permanent

#564. El Salvador’s Bukele says bodies found in Haiti are not those of missing Salvadorans

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele on Saturday denied that human remains handed over to his military teams at Haiti ’s airport were the bodies of the four Salvadorans reported missing after coming under attack by gangs on Oct. 18.

An official with El Salvador ’s government, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the matter, confirmed that the bodies found were not those of the missing aviation technicians.

The four missing Salvadorans are members of a gang suppression force established by the U.N. Security Council to combat organized crime in the Caribbean nation. Bukele has clarified that the Salvadorans are aviation technicians, not troops trained for combat.

On X, Bukele wrote that a nongovernmental organization handed over the remains of a child, a man “of considerably greater height than that of our air technicians," and another person wearing a uniform different from those worn by Salvadoran personnel.

He did not directly mention a fourth body, but wrote that “among the remains, identification cards and military uniforms from other countries were also found.”

“They are not our men,” Bukele wrote, adding that the organization that handed over the bodies claimed they belonged to the four aviation technicians.

Another official with knowledge of the investigation, who also spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the matter, told The Associated Press on Saturday night that four bodies were recovered but that there was no confirmation they were the Salvadoran aviation technicians.

The New York Times, citing a humanitarian aid organization, reported that the four bodies found could be those of the Salvadorans, but noted they were “severely burned” and that autopsies were needed to identify them.

El Salvador deployed more than 100 special forces troops to Haiti on Oct. 22 to help rescue the Salvadorans, a day after announcing a military operation and warning the criminals of a more forceful response if the Salvadorans are not released alive and unharmed.

Haiti’s government described the incident as a kidnapping and said the search for the technicians was its top priority.

#565. Iran: Mehr Druck auf Frauen ohne Hidschab

Immer mehr Frauen in der Islamischen Republik widersetzen sich der Hidschab-Pflicht. Hardliner setzen zunehmend auf sozialen Druck - statt auf die "Sittenpolizei" auf der Straße.

Frauen, die in der Öffentlichkeit ohne Hidschab unterwegs sind, gehören inzwischen in vielen Teilen Irans zum alltäglichen Straßenbild. Es ist eine der sichtbarsten gesellschaftlichen Veränderungen seit den Protesten der Bewegung "Frau, Leben, Freiheit" im Jahr 2022. Ausgelöst wurden diese nach dem Tod der jungen Frau Jina Mahsa Amini in Polizeigewahrsam, die wegen eines angeblich nicht korrekt getragenen Kopftuchs festgenommen worden war.

Den Behörden ist es bislang nicht gelungen, das Ausmaß an Straßenkontrollen aus der Zeit vor den Protesten wiederherzustellen. Der teilweise Rückzug der berüchtigten "Sittenpolizei" bedeutet jedoch nicht, dass sie die Durchsetzung der Hidschab-Pflicht für Frauen aufgegeben haben.

Behörden und konservative Kreise suchen nach neuen Wegen, den gesellschaftlichen Wandel einzudämmen, ohne die offenen Konfrontationen auf der Straße wiederzubeleben, die 2022 maßgeblich zu den Protesten beigetragen hatten. Justizchef Gholamhossein Mohseni Ejei forderte kürzlich ein härteres Vorgehen gegen das, was er als gesellschaftliche "Abweichungen", "Unsittlichkeit" und "Nacktheit" bezeichnete. Staatsanwälte sollten dabei enger mit Polizei, Geheimdiensten und staatlichen Institutionen zusammenarbeiten.

Gleichzeitig werben Unterstützer der Hidschab-Pflicht in Online-Kampagnen dafür, Geschäfte von Frauen zu meiden, die sich nicht an die staatlichen Kleidervorschriften halten. Stattdessen sollen Kundinnen und Kunden gezielt bei Frauen einkaufen, die den Hidschab tragen. Die Folge ist eine stärker zersplitterte Form der Kontrolle, die sich zunehmend von Polizeipatrouillen hin zu Arbeitsplätzen, Unternehmen und alltäglichen Dienstleistungen verlagert.

Die Initiatoren der Online-Kampagnen sprechen von "bewusstem Konsum" und rufen dazu auf, gezielt Anbieterinnen zu unterstützen, die den Hidschab tragen. Eine Anwältin aus Teheran erklärt gegenüber der DW unter der Bedingung der Anonymität, solche Kampagnen könnten gesellschaftliche Spaltungen vertiefen, statt die Einhaltung gesellschaftlicher Normen zu fördern. "Dies ist ein gezielter Versuch, Menschen über ihre Identität zu kategorisieren und gegeneinander auszuspielen", sagt sie.

Wirtschaftlichen Druck allein aufgrund des äußeren Erscheinungsbildes auszuüben, gehe über das Recht des Einzelnen hinaus, frei zu entscheiden, wo er einkaufen wolle. "Wenn gegen es selbst (das Regime) Sanktionen verhängt werden, spricht das Regime von Druck, Ungerechtigkeit und Wirtschaftskrieg", sagte die Juristin. "Wenn dieselbe Logik jedoch im eigenen Land angewendet wird, um einen Teil der Gesellschaft zu einem bestimmten Verhalten zu zwingen, heißt es plötzlich: Unterstützung von Werten".

Zugleich stellt sie die Annahme infrage, dass Frauen, die sich an einen bestimmten Dresscode halten, automatisch die gesellschaftlichen Werte Irans verkörpern: "Die iranische Gesellschaft ist wesentlich komplexer als das."

Berichte iranischer Frauen in sozialen Medien deuten darauf hin, dass die Kontrolle von Kleidungsvorschriften mittlerweile auch bei Alltagsdienstleistungen eine Rolle spielt. Einige Frauen sagen, ihnen sei wegen fehlenden Kopftuchs der Zugang zu Kliniken oder Banken verweigert worden.

Shirin Shams, iranische Exilaktivistin und Leiterin der Organisation Women's Revolution Organization, sieht in den aktuellen Kampagnen den Versuch, gesellschaftliche Gräben wiederherzustellen, die während der Bewegung "Frau, Leben, Freiheit" überwunden worden seien.

"Die Islamische Republik versucht seit Jahren, Frauen anhand ihrer Kleidung gegeneinander auszuspielen", sagt die in Deutschland lebende Aktivistin der DW. Für sie stellt die Hidschab-Pflicht eine der wichtigsten ideologischen Grenzlinien des iranischen Staates dar. Die große Zahl von Frauen, die inzwischen ohne Kopftuch in der Öffentlichkeit erscheinen, zeige jedoch, wie weit sich die gesellschaftliche Realität von den offiziellen Vorstellungen entfernt habe.

Die aktuellen Kampagnen seien deshalb weit mehr als eine Debatte über Kleidung. Es gehe darum, die Trennlinie zwischen Frauen, die sich den Vorgaben fügen, und jenen, die dies nicht tun, erneut zu etablieren.

Auch der in Frankreich lehrende Soziologe Saeed Paivandi sieht darin einen grundlegenden Konflikt um gesellschaftliche Kontrolle. Der Professor der Universität Lothringen erklärt gegenüber der DW, die Behörden hätten über Jahre hinweg zwischen "korrekt verschleierten" und "schlecht verschleierten" beziehungsweise unverschleierten Frauen unterschieden. "Die Regierung macht den Körper von Frauen erneut zu einer sozialen, moralischen und sogar sicherheitspolitischen Frage", sagte Paivandi.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Eine Frau ohne Kopftuch werde nicht lediglich als jemand wahrgenommen, der eine individuelle Entscheidung trifft. Teile des politischen Establishments betrachteten sie vielmehr als sichtbare Herausforderung für die ideologische Ordnung des Staates.

Während Präsident Massud Peseschkian wiederholt die Bedeutung gesellschaftlichen Zusammenhalts und nationaler Einheit betont hat, fordern konservative Richter und Politiker weiterhin eine strengere Durchsetzung der Kleidervorschriften. Dadurch entsteht ein Spannungsfeld innerhalb des iranischen Machtapparats. Ein Teil des Establishments scheint sich bewusst zu sein, dass eine Rückkehr zu großflächigen Konfrontationen zwischen Polizei und Frauen erhebliche gesellschaftliche und politische Kosten verursachen könnte.

Andere wiederum wollen die zunehmende Normalisierung des Auftretens von Frauen ohne Hidschab nicht akzeptieren. Das Ergebnis ist weder eine Rückkehr zum früheren System flächendeckender Straßenkontrollen noch das Ende der verpflichtenden Kleidervorschriften. Stattdessen zeigt sich der Druck punktuell und auf unterschiedlichen Ebenen: vor Gerichten, am Arbeitsplatz, in Unternehmen, bei Behördengängen oder durch gesellschaftliche Kampagnen.

Nach Ansicht Paivandis hat die direkte staatliche Repression ihre Grenzen erreicht. Deshalb suchten Befürworter der islamischen Kleidervorschriften nach alternativen Möglichkeiten, gesellschaftliche Konformität durchzusetzen. Dadurch werde ein Teil der Verantwortung von staatlichen Institutionen auf die Gesellschaft selbst verlagert.

Bankangestellte, Klinikmitarbeiterinnen, Arbeitgeber, Geschäftsinhaber oder Kunden könnten so zu Akteuren der Kontrolle werden, selbst wenn kein Polizist anwesend sei. Die Grenze zwischen Gesetz, persönlichem Ermessen und ideologischem Druck verschwimme dadurch zunehmend.

Zugleich warnt Paivandi, dass die Verbindung von Religion mit Ausgrenzung, Erniedrigung und Zwang besonders junge Iranerinnen und Iraner weiter von religiösen Institutionen entfremden könnte. Auch Frauen, die sich freiwillig für das Tragen eines Hidschabs entscheiden, könnten in einen Konflikt hineingezogen werden, den sie selbst nicht gewählt haben, wenn ihre Kleidung zunehmend als Zeichen politischer Loyalität interpretiert werde.

Dieser Beitrag wurde aus dem Englischen adaptiert.

#567. Russia wants blackout in Ukraine as winter comes — Zelenskyy

Ukrainian President Zelenskyy says Russia is trying to cut electricity and heating to civilians ahead of winter. He also called the US president's waiver of new sanctions on Moscow a boost for Vladimir Putin.

Russia is stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure in a bid to cut electricity and heating in the country as winter approaches, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Saturday.

His remarks come as Moscow intensifies its attacks on civilian targets in the capital, Kyiv, and elsewhere, with key observers saying its objective is to render the country virtually unlivable.

In a post on social media platform X, Zelenskyy said Russia had just carried out one of its biggest attacks on Ukraine's energy sector since it began its full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.

"More than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities were targeted across different regions of Ukraine," he wrote.

"Restoration work is ongoing, with all necessary services and all available resources of Ukrainian energy companies involved," he added.

Zelenskyy said that Russia was planning to leave Ukrainian citizens in the cold this winter.

"Russia is trying to cause a blackout in Ukraine — right before winter. Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating," he wrote, calling on allies to put pressure on Moscow to stop this happening.

He said Russia had "expanded ‌its campaign ​against the energy system" and was trying "to stretch ⁠Ukraine's ​reserves ​and repair ​capacity as ‌thinly as possible." ​

The Russian Defense Ministry, for its part, said on Saturday that its forces had attacked several infrastructure targets in Ukraine overnight.

Among those named was an electricity substation in the northwestern city of Zhytomyr.

However, it also said Ukraine's largest steelworks, in the city of Kryvyi Rih, had been hit, saying the facility supplied steel products to the Ukrainian military-industrial complex.

It said another steel plant in ​Zaporizhzhia, a city near the front ​line, had also been struck.

Ukrainian authorities have also said that one person — an ambulance driver — was killed ​and ‌19 others injured, including a child, in a Russian airstrike on Kherson in southern Ukraine.

Russian state news ​agency TASS has also reported the death of one woman as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes in Russia's Belgorod region that also injured a man.

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy also reacted to US President Donald Trump's decision to waive a package of new sanctions on Moscow, saying the move would only encourage Russian leader Vladimir Putin.

"A US sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking," Zelenskyy said.

On Friday, Trump signed an executive order that waived sweeping US sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia's energy revenues, two days before they were due to take effect.

The waiver has been hailed by a Russian presidential envoy as a "historic moment."

"The Trump administration's suspension of the [Lindsey] Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev said on social media.

Dmitriev said the act, named for the late US senator who sponsored the bill, "would have caused "serious damage first and foremost to the US economy and global markets."

Trump's move came as he increasingly criticizes Zelenskyy, fueling speculation that the US leader is siding with Moscow in the conflict.

#568. Seven shot dead by gunmen at church funeral in Jordan, officials say

Watch: CCTV footage appears to show gunmen near church

Seven people have been killed in an attack on a funeral in central Jordan, officials have said.

At least 34 others were injured as gunmen opened fire on a church in Hmoud, in the Karak governorate on Friday.

The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car, entered the church and opened fire before fleeing. No-one has admitted carrying out the attack.

In a news conference, Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said authorities were working to apprehend the perpetrators which he described as a "group of extremists".

Jordan's King Abdullah II said authorities would "confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties".

Initial reports indicated seven people had been killed in the attack. A government spokesperson later said six people had died, before officials again revised the death toll to seven.

CCTV footage, verified by the BBC, appears to shows three gunmen making their way from a road toward the church.

Two of the attackers are seen making their way on to what appears to be a vehicle entrance to the church grounds, before retreating briefly and returning with a third man. All three appear to be armed with handguns.

Separate footage believed to be from the aftermath of the attack appears to show several dead and wounded bodies on the ground amid chaotic scenes.

Between 150 and 200 people were in the church at the time of the shooting, according to one witness

Witnesses have described scenes of panic inside the church as people threw themselves under pews searching for cover, moving away from the windows.

Prayers and screams could be heard throughout the building as some tried to flee.

Khalid al-Mdanat was at the church and told BBC Arabic the attack lasted around 15 minutes with "people trying to flee while the shooting was still active".

"People began pushing and throwing themselves to the ground," he said.

"Some were taking cover, some were cradling the dead, others were holding their sons close, some were grabbing their children and fleeing, while others were holding onto their friends who were with them at the church."

He said the gunmen left through the church doors and fled in a pickup truck "firing as they went".

Another witness said: "I heard something as if a war had just started.

"I thought it was an electrical short circuit. I looked, people lying on the ground, wounded. The scene was catastrophic."

A woman in the church said explosions rang out seconds after a prayer.

"The sound of machine guns started, and the sound of glass. We began to realise that something was happening.

The witness described how the situation "continued to escalate for 10 continuous minutes". Once she ran out the church she said "bodies were all in the courtyards".

Al-Faraya has described the incident as "painful and horrific" and "unparalleled in the history of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan".

There was a heavy security presence at the entrance to a hospital treating people injured in the incident in Karak, amid an atmosphere charged with anger among residents of the governorate, particularly the families of those injured and killed.

Many looked distressed as roads were closed around the facility and people were forced to park their cars and continue on foot.

Security measures were also tightened ahead of the visit by King Abdullah II to check on the injured.

The atmosphere around the hospital remained tense as the sound of crying and shouting was heard as families mourned their loved ones.

Many people appear shocked, frightened and angry. Some expressed frustration at what they described as "a failure to take a tougher approach towards terrorists".

Karak has a sizeable Christian community in the majority-Muslim Jordan.

Such violence is rare in the country, but deadly attacks have been carried out in the past.

Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun, a Christian head of state, said the "heinous terrorist attack" on the church "violated the sanctity of death and funeral mourners, contradicts all religious and humanitarian values," according to Lebanese media.

Additional reporting by Majdi Gousous, BBC Arabic.

#569. ‘Horrific’: woman, 19, shot in head in drive-by shooting outside boxing event near Brisbane

Offenders still at large after shots fired from vehicle outside licensed premises in Loganholme

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Four people have been injured after a drive-by shooting outside a venue hosting a boxing event, including a 19-year-old woman who was shot in the head.

Queensland police Detective Inspector Ian Galpin said a group of people were gathered at the passenger drop-off zone outside Fitzy’s Loganholme, south of Brisbane, about 8.18pm on Saturday when a Mitsubishi pulled up.

Galpin said police would allege a “number of shots” were fired from the front window of the pub where two males wearing balaclavas and gloves were sitting, striking four people.

A Jimboomba woman, 19, was shot in the neck and head. She has undergone surgery and remains in a critical condition.

Speaking on Sunday, Galpin described her as an “innocent bystander”.

“It’s horrific. It’s something that her family should never have to go through.”

Three others were injured and remained in serious but stable conditions: a Browns Plains man, 38, shot in the abdomen and arm, a Salisbury man, 37, shot in the abdomen, and a Cornubia man, 27, shot in the abdomen.

Galpin alleged the Mitsubishi was set alight on Maloney Road at Waterford West, which was declared a crime scene, while a second car collected the occupants of the Mitsubishi and departed.

“It is possible one of these persons from the Mitsubishi was injured or burnt during this process,” Galpin said.

Galpin said it was too soon to say whether it was related to organised crime.

“This is a horrific event in a public space where adults and children were simply trying to enjoy a sporting event and this incident, it’s clearly not acceptable. We will not tolerate it.”

Speaking on Sunday morning, Logan’s mayor, Jon Raven, described residents in the area as frightened.

“This has sent a shock wave through Logan. We’ve never seen something like this in Logan before,” Raven told the Today show.

“Our hearts go out obviously to the victims and the staff and the people at this boxing event.

“I’ve been to one of these events before, they’re [a] really family friendly environment, and I know there’s lots of children who were there, and this will impact them for the rest of their lives.”

The deputy commander of Queensland police, Chris Stream, described the scene as “confronting”.

“A number of people had suffered gunshot wounds,” he told Today.

Raven said the event had been organised to help children steer clear of violence.

“[The organiser] will be devastated this has happened because he loves boxing and uses it as a tool to empower and reconnect young people who might be going off the rails, and this is the opposite of what he’ll want to see,” Raven said.

Logan City Titles shared a statement on social media on Sunday morning.

“We are heartbroken about the incident that occurred at the fight night,” it read.

“Logan City Titles was a family event, an event for our community, showcasing local talent, hard work and everyone’s skills inside the ring.

“These types of incidents have no place in the boxing community or any part of the broader community.”

The offenders were still at large on Sunday but police said they did not believe there was an ongoing threat to the public.

Police were urging anyone with information to contact them.

#570. Andy Burnham says he wants ‘honest discussion’ about freedom of movement with EU

Prime minister is considering different options for new relationship with Brussels ahead of summit in November

Andy Burnham says he wants an “honest discussion” with the British public about the possibility of a return to free movement between the UK and the EU as part of his plans for a new relationship with the bloc.

The prime minister has been open about his desire to revisit the relationship between Britain and Brussels. He has said a new deal could mean the UK goes “all the way” and rejoins the EU.

Other options discussed by Burnham include joining the single market, which would require signing up to free movement, or being part of the customs union. Both would require an element of agreeing to rules set by the EU.

In an interview with the Sunday Times, he said: “I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this.”

The prime minister has previously committed to the red lines in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

It means any fundamental change in the relationship is likely to have to wait until after a general election, expected by 2029.

The prime minister acknowledged freedom of movement “had very significant challenges associated with it”, but suggested that European migration had changed in the past decade.

“It was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now],” he told the Sunday Times.

“Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different.

“The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”

Burnham will meet EU chiefs at a summit in Brussels on 20 November.

He argued that there had been reciprocal benefits of free movement for Britons, particularly for young members of the population wanting to experience living in Europe.

The issue of migration was one of the dominant debates during the 2016 Brexit referendum campaign.

In the 12 months to June 2016 – the month of the Brexit leave vote – net migration was at a near-record high of 335,000, according to the Office for National Statistics.

Decisions made after the Brexit result would lead to higher levels of migration, however.

Net migration peaked at a record 944,000 in the year to March 2023 due to a surge of foreign workers encouraged to come to the UK by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government as the UK emerged from the Covid pandemic.

It has fallen sharply since then, with net migration dropping to well below pre-Brexit levels. It stood at 171,000 last year, almost half of what it was in 2016.

Burnham has said he will take the opportunity around the summit with EU leaders in November to lay out to the British public different options for the future relationship with the bloc.

But Burnham added that he could not imagine recommending that the UK join the Schengen Area, in which border controls have been abolished, or ditching the pound to adopt the euro.

Nigel Farage said the prime minister’s comments were a “total betrayal” of voters who backed Brexit, including in Burnham’s Makerfield constituency.

The Reform UK leader added: “He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty.”

Chris Philp, the Conservative shadow home secretary, said: “Andy Burnham knows full well that a return to EU free movement would mean handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe.

“The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it.”

#571. Nouveaux coups de feu à Toulouse : les tireurs débarquent sur une trottinette et ouvrent le feu, un homme blessé par du gros calibre au visage à La Reynerie

Article rédigé par Jean Cohadon

l'essentiel EXCLUSIF. Un homme a été blessé par balle dans la nuit de vendredi à samedi, quartier de La Reynerie à Toulouse. C'est la deuxième victime de la semaine après une fusillade mercredi soir où un garçon de 17 ans a été grièvement blessé. Des violences sur fond de guerre entre bandes et quartiers pour la maîtrise des points de deal.

De nouveaux coups de feu ont secoué le quartier de La Reynerie pendant la nuit, à Toulouse. Les services de police ont été alertés par des habitants réveillés peu après 4 heures, samedi matin, par des rafales de ce qui pourrait être une arme automatique.

Chaque vendredi, retrouvez les affaires qui marquent notre région, les enquêtes qui font parler, les procès majeurs et les coulisses de l'actualité police-justice, décryptés par nos journalistes spécialistes.

Sur place, policiers et secours ont découvert un homme blessé au niveau du visage. Pris en charge par les pompiers et une équipe du Smur 31, il a été évacué en urgence vers l'hôpital Purpan. Il souffre notamment d'une plaie très importante au visage.

Pas d'autres victimes identifiées mais les tireurs auraient tiré une dizaine de fois avec du gros calibre. Les violences ont eu lieu cheminement Auriacombe, au cœur du quartier. Un lieu désormais aussi connu pour son point de deal que pour ses blessés, et meurtres, par balle.

À lire aussi : Nouvelle fusillade à Toulouse dans un quartier sensible, un garçon de 17 ans entre la vie et la mort

Le parquet a saisi la division de la criminalité organisée et spécialisée, déjà en charge d'une autre fusillade qui a eu lieu juste à côté dans la nuit de mercredi à jeudi. Cette fois les tireurs étaient arrivés devant une épicerie-bar sur une moto électrique avant d'ouvrir le feu.

À lire aussi : Fusillade à Toulouse : le mineur grièvement blessé à La Reynerie va mieux

Une trentaine de balles ont traversé le commerce, blessant quatre personnes à l'intérieur. Un garçon de 17 ans, grièvement blessé, a été évacué en urgence absolue par les secours. Pendant 24 heures son pronostic vital est resté engagé mais vendredi, les nouvelles de sa santé étaient rassurantes.

Cette série de coups de feu s'inscrit dans un contexte de lutte entre les équipes du quartier de La Reynerie et de Bellefontaine sous fond de trafic de drogue. Ces derniers mois, les incidents violents se succèdent. Les policiers de la division de la criminalité organisée et spécialisée ont déjà une dizaine d'affaires en portefeuille, qui concernent des tirs entre habitants des deux quartiers. Et rien ne semble pouvoir arrêter cette fuite en avant.

#572. My dream of being a paramedic helped me save a life at 15

Ethan has wanted to be a paramedic from a young age

When aspiring paramedic Ethan ordered three resuscitation manikins so he could teach CPR to others, he had no idea how quickly he would put his training into practice and help save a life.

Just two weeks after the dummies arrived at his home in Mansfield Woodhouse, in Nottinghamshire, the 15-year-old found himself performing CPR on a man he found collapsed in the street.

Ethan, who had completed a one-off CPR course with East Midlands Ambulance Service (EMAS) last year, said he went through "a million and one emotions" as he realised he was about to apply his knowledge to a real-life emergency.

"It was adrenaline like never before, but I knew I had to stay calm, and not think too hard about the immense pressure of putting someone's life in your hands," he added.

The teenager was on his way home from a casual gardening job at about 14:30 BST on 18 September when he saw a 75-year-old man slumped over "half in the road and half on the pavement" on Ley Lane.

Ethan described the man as being unresponsive with a "raspy-sort of breathing" known as agonal breathing, and he was in cardiac arrest.

Having completed his course with EMAS, and watching countless TV programmes about front-line emergency workers, Ethan's training kicked in.

Ethan, a Year 10 pupil at The Manor Academy, said a lady who was on the phone to 999 was happy for him to take control as she did not know how to do chest compressions.

Together, they moved the man to a safe, flat surface, where Ethan knew the CPR would be more effective.

He said: "Even though I've spent ages preparing for this moment, to put it into practice was completely different."

Ethan was soon joined at the scene by an off-duty carer from King's Mill Hospital and a teacher from a nearby primary school, who took turns with the compressions.

He said it was a "massive sense of relief" when the paramedics arrived and prepared a defibrillator, and he felt a sense of hope once he saw the man had a "shockable rhythm".

According to Resuscitation Council UK (RCUK), an expert organisation on resuscitation, survival rates for cardiac arrests outside hospital "remain low", with one in 13 people surviving in the East Midlands.

The organisation said the statistic highlighted a need to improve confidence in CPR and using defibrillators in the region.

Ethan told the BBC he was thrilled to hear from the man's family that he was making a steady recovery.

The man who Ethan helped wishes to remain anonymous while he continues his recovery but his daughter, Erica, said: "As a family, we are so grateful for the bravery that Ethan showed and our gratitude for assisting saving his life.

"If it wasn't for Ethan and other passing public, there would have been a very different outcome.

"It is incredibly important that people know at least the basics of life saving and we support Ethan totally on his journey [to becoming a paramedic] and will help where we can."

Ethan bought three resuscitation manikins so he could share his training with others

Ethan became interested in learning basic life-saving skills from the age of 11 while helping to care for his grandparents.

He bought the Â£60 resuscitation manikins with the aim of running free life-saving sessions, particularly for young people, and has already led training at local scout groups.

He believes young people are reluctant to learn CPR because they feel awkward about "putting their hands on someone else".

He said: "There needs to be awareness that people performing CPR are protected by the Sarah Act."

The Sarah Act is also known as the the Social Action, Responsibility and Heroism Act 2015, which is designed to protect people who help others or intervene in emergencies.

Robert Gladwin, head teacher of The Manor Academy, said he would now look at investing some money to help more pupils learn life-saving skills.

He added: "Quite often young people get a bad reputation but, actually, this shows we generate students who have a real community value.

"It is absolutely critical that a Year 10 boy took charge of a situation that most people wouldn't know what to do with, and actually made a difference to the family and the wider community."

Jay Astles, clinical improvement manager for out of hospital cardiac arrest at EMAS, praised "Ethan for stepping forward to help in what must have been a very stressful situation".

He added: "We would encourage people of all ages to learn CPR and how to use a defibrillator.

"As Ethan's experience shows, having the confidence to act in an emergency could help save a life."

#573. New York's archdiocese and survivors of clergy abuse agree to $800 million legal settlement

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The Archdiocese of New York and attorneys for about 1,300 parishioners who said they were sexually abused by clergy have agreed to an $800 million settlement of their legal claims, the second-largest involving a Catholic archdiocese in the U.S.

Archbishop Ronald Hicks sent an email Saturday to clergy confirming the settlement after attorneys for the survivors of alleged abuse announced it. Hicks said the agreement will not be final until the parties sign it, an action scheduled for the week of Nov. 6.

The only larger settlement over sexual abuse claims in the U.S. was by the Archdiocese of Los Angeles, which agreed in 2024 to pay $880 million to 1,000 abuse victims, in addition to $740 million in claims it had paid previously. In June, the Archdiocese of San Francisco agreed to a $395 million settlement over about 500 lawsuits filed over clergy abuse, and in December 2025, a federal judge approved a settlement in which the Archdiocese of New Orleans agreed to pay at least $230 million to abuse victims.

The agreement with the New York archdiocese would end more than seven years of lawsuits. The parties agreed to a framework for an agreement in May that required everyone who filed a claim to sign off.

“The unanimous agreement of survivors who filed claims against the Archdiocese of New York marks a powerful moment in the pursuit of justice,” Jeff Anderson, an attorney representing people who filed more than 1,000 of claims against the Catholic Church in New York state, said in a statement. “Through their courage, sacrifice, and determination, survivors have helped bring about a reckoning and a meaningful step toward accountability.”

The Archiocese of New York covers the city's boroughs of the Bronx, Manhattan and Staten Island as well as seven counties to the north of New York City and is home to about 300 churches, more than 150 parochial schools and 2.5 million Catholics.

In his email to clergy, Hicks said that if church members ask about the settlement, “please let them know that much progress has been made.”

“We are on the verge of being able to, please God, bring some measure of healing and reconciliation to all victim-survivors,” he wrote. “This agreement will also allow the archdiocese to turn its full attention once again to its mission of preaching the Gospel, healing the sick, caring for the poor and needy, welcoming the stranger, and educating our children.”

A New York law enacted in 2019 allows survivors of child sexual abuse to file lawsuits against their abusers and institutions that shielded them until they turn 55. People who had already had turned 55 when the law was enacted also were given until August 2021 to file lawsuits, no matter when the alleged abuse occurred.

“This is an extraordinary achievement for the survivors,” said Trusha Goffe, an attorney in Anderson’s firm. "The survivors remined resolute through years of litigation to reach this monumental settlement.”

#575. Clash of the presidents: Obama and Trump lock horns in explosive midterm showdown as savage barbs fly and campaign battle reaches fever pitch

By JAMES GORDON, US NEWS REPORTER and SAMANTHA LOREN, US POLITICAL REPORTER

Published: 23:36 GMT, 24 October 2026 | Updated: 05:33 GMT, 25 October 2026

Barack Obama and Donald Trump have erupted into an extraordinary war of words ahead of the midterms, with the president unleashing a furious 1am tirade against his predecessor after a day of savage insults on the campaign trail.

Speaking in Ohio the former Democratic president ridiculed Trump's lavish White House renovations, compared his taste in gold to Saddam Hussein's and accused him of enriching his family and political allies.

But Trump fired back from a packed campaign rally in Georgia, mocking Obama's ability to attract supporters while declaring that his controversial tariffs were delivering billions in investment and thousands of American jobs.

The extraordinary presidential showdown unfolded across three battleground states, with Obama campaigning in Ohio and Michigan while Trump attempted to rescue Republican fortunes in Georgia.

With control of Congress hanging in the balance ahead of November 3, the increasingly bitter exchanges offered a glimpse of the political warfare gripping the country.

The bitter feud then escalated dramatically in the early hours of Sunday morning when Trump unleashed a furious Truth Social tirade, branding Obama a 'grossly incompetent President' and attacking the Democratic candidate he was campaigning for in Michigan.

In the extraordinary post, published shortly before 1am, Trump accused his predecessor of repeatedly backing losing candidates, citing Hillary Clinton's defeat in 2016 and Kamala Harris's loss in 2024.

'Obama was a grossly incompetent President!' Trump declared.

Former President Barack Obama speaks during a campaign rally at Cleveland Public Auditorium in Cleveland on Saturday

Trump is seen returning to the White House after another day of campaigning and unleashing a furious tirade against Obama online

It was just before 1am when Trump laid into Obama after hearing of the former president's jibes

'He said that Crooked Hillary Clinton was going to WIN, he campaigned hard for her, and she lost in all directions and ways. He then campaigned full out for Kamala, and likewise, she lost.'

The president then turned his fire on Michigan Democratic Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed, making a series of inflammatory and unsubstantiated accusations about his religion, political beliefs and professional background.

'Now he's campaigning for a Muslim Brotherhood Jihadist, who hates Jews and Blacks and AMERICANS and TRUMP, and he is going to lose, also,' Trump wrote.

'He's a Fake Doctor, who runs what is considered to be the WORST CLINIC IN AMERICA.'

He went on to boast about his record in Michigan, claiming he had revitalized the state's automotive industry and created jobs.

'Michigan doesn't want an arrogant, Open Borders, Fake Doctor, Jihadist, whose reputation will only get worse as more information is revealed - And there's plenty,' he continued.

The president ended his tirade with an emphatic endorsement of El-Sayed's Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.

At a rally earlier in the day, Obama, 65, delivered some of his sharpest attacks in Detroit, where he appeared alongside Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

Obama delighted in mocking the amount of gold that now adorns the walls of the White House comparing it to if Saddam Hussein has opened a cheesecake factory

Gold coasters bearing Trump's name grace side tables and even the button he presses to summon his favorite tipple, Diet Coke, is now gold and sits on the desktop in a wooden box bearing the presidential seal

Former President Barack Obama is joined by Democratic nominee for US Senate Abdul El-Sayed, right, and Democratic gubernatorial nominee and Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson greet supporters during a campaign event at Cass Technical High School in Detroit

Ohio. Obama is campaigning for Ohio Democratic candidates including Senate candidate, former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-OH) and gubernatorial candidate Dr. Amy Acton

The former president accused Trump of obsessing over decorating the White House while ordinary Americans struggled with soaring living costs.

'He is very focused on home renovation. He should be on HGTV,' Obama joked, drawing laughter from the crowd.

He then turned his attention to Trump's elaborate gold decorations and ambitious construction projects.

'What's up with the gold?' Obama demanded. 'I mean, he's got the one that's looking like Saddam Hussein opened a cheesecake factory.'

But Obama's criticism quickly turned from mockery to accusations of corruption and of Trump of using the presidency to benefit himself, his family and his allies.

'The one thing that the current president is focused on other than home improvements is enriching himself and his family and his cronies,' Obama said.

He pointed to Trump's cryptocurrency ventures and government contracts involving his children's businesses as examples of what he described as a pattern of self-enrichment.

'We have lost count of all the deals he and his family have done. You can't keep up. Meme coins, taxpayer-funded contracts for his kids' companies,' Obama said.

He also alleged that financial dealings involving Trump associates showed a wider culture of favoritism at the top of the administration.

'This is a culture that's set at the top,' Obama said.

Obama also mocked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing the administration of focusing on the appearance and masculinity of American troops rather than more pressing military matters.

'He's focused on important matters like the jawline and the testosterone levels of our troops,' Obama said, before criticizing the live-streaming of executions as a way to cultivate what he described as a 'manly warrior spirit.'

He then delivered a personal jibe at Hegseth, asking, 'How much time do you think this man spends in front of the mirror every day?'

From left, Democratic Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, left, former President Barack Obama, center, and Ohio Democratic candidate for US Senate Sherrod Brown, right, attend a campaign rally on Saturday in Cleveland

Former President Barack Obama, left, greets Democratic Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, right, at a campaign rally in Cleveland

Democratic Ohio gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton arrives for a campaign rally on Saturday

But hundreds of miles away in Perry, Georgia, Trump was delivering his own blistering performance before Republican supporters.

The president repeatedly referenced Obama's Michigan appearance, dismissing the former president's crowd size.

His assertion came despite reports of a packed high school gymnasium in Detroit, where Obama had been campaigning for El-Sayed.

Trump instead sought to turn attention toward the economy, announcing a major investment by German automaker Volkswagen in a new Audi manufacturing plant in Georgia.

The president claimed the $4.2 billion project vindicated his aggressive tariff policies, which have faced criticism amid stubbornly high consumer prices.

'Think of that. 200,000 cars a year. That's incredible,' Trump told supporters.

Georgia has emerged as a particularly important battleground, with Republican Senate candidate Mike Collins attempting to unseat Democratic incumbent Jon Ossoff.

Polling averages currently show Ossoff ahead by more than eight percentage points, while the Cook Political Report rates the contest as likely Democratic.

Trump's appearance marked his second visit to Georgia in two weeks, underscoring the importance of the race to Republican hopes of maintaining control of the Senate.

Trump's second visit to Georgia in just two weeks underscores the state's crucial importance in the midterms, with Republicans fighting to unseat Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff

President Donald Trump greets Gernot Döllner, CEO of Audi AG, at a campaign rally at Guardian Centers of Georgia, in Perry, Georgia

President Donald Trump dances at a campaign rally at Guardian Centers of Georgia

But even some of the president's supporters expressed doubts about his increasingly combative campaigning.

'I love Trump to death, but sometimes he should keep his mouth shut,' Chris Capp, 55, a former Army National Guard employee, told Bloomberg.

'That's awesome, I want jobs to come to Georgia,' said Richard Motes, 61.

'I'm dead red,' he added. 'If they let me push a button to vote all Republican, I'd push the button.'

Hours earlier, Obama was in Ohio and seized on what he described as 'cruelty and indecency' coming from President Donald Trump and his Republican allies.

Obama stepped into one of the nation's ugliest midterm fights as he worked to rally Democratic voters in the battleground state.

He took specific aim at Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, who has doubled down on an advertising campaign featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton.

Trump looked exhausted as he returned to the White House on Saturday evening

Obama had the crowd in the palm of his hand as he campaigned for Democratic candidate for Senate, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed

Trump and Vice President JD Vance have also defended the ad, even as Republican leaders across Ohio, including Gov. Mike DeWine, have called for its removal.

'In recent days, we've seen there is no line he will not cross, no low he will not sink to,' Obama said of Ramaswamy, noting that Acton has 'spoken movingly about her painful childhood and all she's experienced: abuse, neglect and homelessness.'

'There's a decency we should expect out of our public officials,' Obama continued. 'And I don't know what's happened where the standards of behavior are so low that somebody could run an ad like that.'

Obama, 65, remains the Democratic Party's best motivator nearly a decade after leaving the White House.

He was set to campaign in Michigan later on Saturday night, lending the Democratic Party his star power in midwestern battlegrounds that will help determine the balance of power in American politics next week.

Obama shared the stage with Acton and former three-term Ohio Senator Sharrod Brown who is looking to unseat Republican Senator Jon Husted.

Although Ohio has become more reliably Republican, it has been a hotly contested battleground this year.

Trump and Vance have both visited the state in recent weeks to drum up support for Husted and Ramaswamy. And the controversy over Ramaswamy's ad has ratcheted up the already high temperature.

Ramaswamy has defended his decision to press ahead with the ad as fair game.

Trump aggressively defended the ad, which has emerged as a national flashpoint in the midterms' final days, as he voted in West Palm Beach on Saturday.

'This is a disgrace,' Trump said. 'The mother said that Amy Acton is a liar and she's no good. And you know what? I don't think you can get a better reference on that.'

He added that if his own mother had said anything bad about him, it would be front and center.

The Ramaswamy campaign video features Acton's birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her 'a liar' and insinuating she has mental health issues.

Democratic Ohio Senate candidate Sherrod Brown speaks during a campaign rally on Saturday

Republican Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy sparked outrage with an ad featuring his Democratic rival Amy Acton's estranged mom, who accuses her daughter of lying

Vivek Ramaswamy has refused to withdraw the controversial attack ad despite criticism from fellow Republicans, including Ohio Governor Mike DeWine

Acton, Ohio's COVID-19-era health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child.

Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather, Arthur's husband, was indicted on a charge of rape involving Acton.

The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur failed to show for a court appearance and became a fugitive. Donna Arthur remained married to him until his death in 2004.

Appearing before Obama, Acton spoke as if addressing Ramaswamy directly.

'My opponent has chosen to exploit, intentionally, my childhood to save his stumbling campaign, but it's not going to work,' she said. 'Decency still matters.'

She added: 'Mr. Ramaswamy, you are not just out of touch, you are out for yourself and you are a danger to my state. Apparently there is no low to which you won't stoop.'

In Ohio, Obama also called out Trump's inability to lower costs, a key campaign promise, noting that the president has instead focused on building a new White House ballroom and helipad on the South Lawn.

'I don´t know if you've noticed, but he seems very focused on home renovation,' he quipped. 'He should be on HGTV.'

He went on: 'There's gold everywhere. He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.'

The former Democratic president acknowledged that the nation has Trump for another two years, until his term ends. But voters are not stuck with Trump's allies, he said.

'We're not stuck with a spineless Congress and Republican governors who are handling lawlessness and carelessness and cruelty and indifference for working people,' Obama said.

'After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence ... you get a chance to say enough is enough.'

#576. Argentina drops investigation into President Milei over crypto fraud

Javier Milei had denied crypto fraud allegations

A criminal investigation into Argentine President Javier Milei and his sister's links to a cryptocurrency scandal has been dropped.

The case against Milei and his sister Karina Milei was dismissed by federal judge Marcelo Martinez de Giorgi at the request of prosecutors, court records show.

The Argentinian president had denied promoting the newly launched cryptocoin $Libra, which collapsed shortly after he mentioned it in a social media post in February 2025.

He said he had acted "in good faith" when the cryptocurrency rose in value, before crashing and causing huge losses for the majority of its investors. Milei is yet to respond to news of the case being dropped.

Dismissing the case, the judge said "the reported events do not fall under a legal category" and concluded that no "criminally relevant deception" had been proven.

Accusations of fraud arose when Milei posted on X, formerly Twitter, about the $Libra coin, which he said at the time would help fund small businesses and start-ups.

The cryptocurrency's price subsequently shot up when the Argentine president shared a link to buy it.

But, within a few hours, he deleted his post and the crypto nosedived in value, losing investors most of their money.

It led opposition members of Congress to plan impeachment proceedings, while some online accused Milei of a "rug pull" - in which promoters of a cryptocurrency draw in buyers only to stop trading activity and make off with the money raised from sales.

The Argentinian president, though, insisted in an interview with Todo Noticias: "I didn't promote it, I merely shared it."

The presidential office insisted that Milei was in no way involved in the development of $Libra and announced that the Anti-Corruption Office would determine whether the president had acted improperly.

Milei himself defended deleting his post, saying that at the time he did not know "the details of the project and after learning about it, I decided not to continue promoting it".

He insisted in a TV interview that those who had invested in $Libra had done so "voluntarily" and knew of the risks.

#577. Pest-Verdacht in Sibirien: Was bisher bekannt ist

Nach dem Tod einer Labormitarbeiterin wächst die Sorge vor der hochansteckenden Lungenpest. Während Russland einen Ausbruch dementiert, fordern internationale Behörden Aufklärung. Was über den Erreger bekannt ist.

Russland stellte am Montag (05.10) klar: Der Tod einer Labormitarbeiterin sei nicht auf einen Pesterreger zurückzuführen. Die 28-Jährige sei an einer "Lungenentzündung unbekannter Herkunft" gestorben, zitiert die russische Nachrichtenagentur Interfax die russische Seuchenbekämpfungsbehörde Rospotrebnadsor.

Demnach seien in Proben der Toten keine Mikroorganismen nachgewiesen worden, "die mit ihrer beruflichen Tätigkeit in Zusammenhang stehen". Damit widerspricht die Behörde bisherigen Informationen.

Lokale Medien hatten zuvor berichtet, dass die Mitarbeiterin eines Instituts zur Bekämpfung von Pesterkrankungen ein Reagenzglas habe fallen lassen. Kurz danach sei sie am vergangenen Freitag im Kreiskrankenhaus der Stadt Schelechow bei Irkutsk in Sibirien gestorben.

Die US-Nachrichtenseite Axios hatte als einer der ersten über den vermeintlichen Vorfall berichtet. Dort wurde ein Mitarbeiter der Trump-Regierung mit den Worten zitiert, man sei sich der Lage bewusst, "beobachte den Ausbruch und prüfe Optionen". Axios hatte auch berichtet, dass rund 200 Menschen unter Beobachtung gestellt wurden, die mit der Verstorbenen in Kontakt gekommen waren. Auch Donald Trump hat sich mittlerweile zu der Situation geäußert und Russland Hilfe angeboten.

Die Weltgesundheitsorganisation (WHO) stuft die Pestgefahr in Irkutsk derzeit als moderat bis niedrig ein , fordert aber Aufklärung. Ähnlich sieht es auch das Europäisches Zentrum für die Prävention und die Kontrolle von Krankheiten ECDC. In einer am 6. Oktober 2026 veröffentlichten Mitteilung erklärte die Organisation jedoch, dass "auf der Grundlage der derzeit nur begrenzt verfügbaren Informationen keine Berichte über Sekundärfälle vorliegen und es keine Hinweise auf eine anhaltende Mensch-zu-Mensch-Übertragung gibt."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Offiziellen russischen Angaben zufolge wurden zwei Krankenhäuser und eine Kinderklinik unter Quarantäne gestellt. Die Mitarbeiterinnen und Mitarbeiter des Instituts befanden sich örtlichen Berichten zufolge an ihrem Arbeitsplatz in Quarantäne. Es habe keine weiteren Infektionen gegeben.

Dennoch herrscht weiter Misstrauen, was die russische Informationspolitik angeht. Auf einem russischsprachigen Social-Media-Kanal der DW schreibt eine Nutzerin:  "Es würde mich nicht wundern, wenn es dort jetzt zu einer Katastrophe kommt, sowohl was die Ausbreitung als auch die Quarantänemaßnahmen angeht." Wie sich die Situation tatsächlich entwickelt, bleibt abzuwarten.

Die Lungenpest ist eine von drei Pestformen - Beulenpest, Pestseptikämie und Lungenpest -, die alle durch dasselbe Bakterium verursacht werden. Das Bakterium nennt sich Yersinia pestis und kommt üblicherweise in Nagetieren vor. Flöhe dienen als sogenannte Vektoren und können das Bakterium dann auf den Menschen übertragen.

Die Weltgesundheitsorganisation (WHO) beschreibt die Lungenpest als die aggressivste Form der Pest. Ihre Inkubationszeit kann bei nur 24 Stunden liegen, und sie ist die einzige Form, die leicht von Mensch zu Mensch übertragen wird. Das geschieht vor alle durch Atemwegspartikel, die beim Husten eines erkrankten Patienten freigesetzt werden. Deshalb könne die Lungenpest schwere Epidemien auslösen.

Die Symptome treten schnell auf: hohes Fieber, Kopfschmerzen und Schwäche, gefolgt von einer sich rasch verschlechternden Lungenentzündung mit Atemnot, Brustschmerzen und einem Husten, der häufig Blut hervorbringt.

Eine Person kann sich mit Lungenpest infizieren, indem sie die Bakterien direkt einatmet, oder die Krankheit entwickelt sich, wenn eine andere Form der Pest, meist die Beulenpest, auf die Lunge übergreift.

Der Unterschied liegt darin, wo sich die Infektion im Körper festsetzt.  Das bestimmt, wie sich die Krankheit ausbreitet und wie tödlich sie ist. Die Beulenpest ist die häufigste Form und jene, bei der die meisten Menschen an den Schwarzen Tod des Mittelalters denken, der etwa 25 Millionen Menschen das Leben gekostet hat.

Sie wird meist durch einen Flohbiss verursacht. Die Bakterien wandern zum nächstgelegenen Lymphknoten, der sich zu einer schmerzhaften Schwellung - einer Beule -  entwickelt. Bleibt die Beulenpest unbehandelt, können sich die Bakterien weiter im Körper ausbreiten. Gelangen sie in den Blutkreislauf, entwickelt sich die Pestseptikämie.

Diese kann Blutungen unter der Haut und Organversagen verursachen. Erreichen die Bakterien die Lunge, entsteht die Lungenpest - die Form, die von Mensch zu Mensch über die Luft übertragen werden kann. Die Pestseptikämie und die Lungenpest können sich auch direkt entwickeln, ohne dass zuvor eine Beule auftritt.

Unbehandelt tötet die Beulenpest laut WHO zwischen 30 und 60 Prozent der Patienten. Die Pestseptikämie und die Lungenpest sind ohne Behandlung immer tödlich.

Die Lungenpest ist heilbar - aber nur, wenn die Behandlung schnell beginnt. Die WHO warnt, dass sie ohne Behandlung innerhalb von 18 bis 24 Stunden nach den ersten Symptomen tödlich enden kann. Gängige Antibiotika können die Infektion heilen, und die Heilungsraten sind hoch, wenn Patienten innerhalb von etwa einem Tag nach Erkrankungsbeginn behandelt werden.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ärzten wird geraten, nicht auf eine Laborbestätigung zu warten, sondern mit der Antibiotikagabe zu beginnen, sobald der Verdacht auf Pest besteht, so die US-amerikanischen Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Die eingesetzten Medikamente sind handelsübliche, weit verbreitete Antibiotika, und Patienten benötigen in der Regel eine Behandlung von bis zu zwei Wochen. Um eine Ausbreitung der Infektion zu verhindern, werden Patienten isoliert. Laut WHO hilft auch das Tragen von Masken.

Personen, die engen Kontakt zu einem Patienten hatten, werden auch behandelt, selbst wenn sie keine Symptome zeigen. Sowohl die WHO als auch die CDC empfehlen für enge Kontaktpersonen von Lungenpest-Erkrankten eine siebentägige vorbeugende Antibiotikabehandlung.

Laut dem Robert-Koch-Institut (RKI) kommt die Pest noch in Ländern Afrikas, Amerikas und Asiens vor. In Deutschland hingegen nicht. Das Risiko der Einreise eines mit dem Pesterreger Infizierten sei gering. Auch gebe es wirksame Maßnahmen, um eine Ausbreitung zu verhindern. Der Artikel wurde am 07.10 aktualisiert.
