#578. France: Protesters clash with police in nationwide protests, amid rising social polarization

Unrest broke out in parts of France as students, trade unionists and Yellow Vest activists took to the streets to protest high prices and inequality. Police arrested over 1,000 people amid chaotic scenes.

Police and protesters clashed amid mass rallies across France on Saturday, over high prices and social inequalities and the state of the education system.

France's Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said some 1,200 people had been arrested across the country and that 150 police officers had been injured.

"It's a miracle the toll wasn't higher," Lecornu said while visiting officers deployed in Paris on Saturday evening.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 110,000 people took part in the demonstrations in Paris alone, while 110 marches had taken place across the country.

The Interior Ministry said some 550,000 people turned out for the nationwide demonstrations.

The ministry said the arrests were made following violent incidents in Paris, Marseilles, Rennes, Toulouse, Angers and other cities across the country.

"Such actions include attempted looting, confrontations with law enforcement, the setting of fires to street furniture and the targeting of seats of power and media outlets," the ministry said, blaming the unrest on what it described ​as the "hard-left."

In Paris and Marseille, police fired tear gas at protesters as violent clashes took place.

AFP reported that dozens of shops were looted in Paris, Marseille, Nice, Bordeaux and Lille.

The windows of the offices of French broadcasters CNews and Europe 1 in western Paris were also broken by protesters, and AFP journalists reported seeing several parked cars torched.

French President Emmanuel Macron condemned the violence in a post on X and warned: "Those who have broken, attacked the prefectures as well as businesses, looted even our town halls, will be prosecuted and punished."

In Lyon, situated in central France, the city's tourism office was set alight with flames and black smoke seen billowing from the building.

In the city of Limoges, the town hall was set alight as unrest broke out. The blaze spread from a wing of the building and eventually reached the roof, where it continued burning as crowds stood watching.

The historic building was largely destroyed by the blaze, despite attempts by firefighters to douse the flames.

Meanwhile, in the northern city of Lille, protesters smashed their way into the city hall and vandalized the premises before leaving, according to an AFP photographer.

Riot police within minutes confirmed that all the protesters had left.

The protests come on the heels of an initial wave of demonstrations that began last month over the situation at schools in the country, with pupils complaining about teacher absences and run-down facilities.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In the French capital, police had banned rallies around the Elysee presidential palace, the prime minister's office and the Champs-Elysees avenue, along with other key locations.

A march through the center of the city was also banned.

Reports began emerging late on Saturday morning of riot police clashing with protesters in the Saint-Denis area on the outskirts of the capital, as well as near the Gare du Nord train station, among other areas.

In Paris, DW correspondent Jack Parrock said unrest was playing out in small pockets of the city.

"The videos circulating on social media of the violence in France don’t paint the full picture," Parrock said.

"The significant percentage of the people we met out on the streets of Paris were teachers, nurses, students, and workers, who want no part in the unrest, but do also seem to understand why the outbreaks are happening," Parrock explained.

"Amongst those people, we did still witness a collective rage against a government they don’t feel is listening to them," said Parrock.

On the matter of how police were responding, Parrock said they had seen police "seemingly try to show some restraint — clearly intending to de-escalate some of the recent tension."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Students have been joined by trade unionists and remnants of the Yellow Vests ("Gilets jaunes") movement, which staged mass weekly protests from November 2018 to June 2020, initially against rising fuel prices. They later morphed into protests against the high cost of living and economic inequality in general.

The student protests over the past weeks have been backed by Jean-Luc Melenchon, the leader of the hard-left France Unbowed ("La France insoumise", or LFI), who marched in one demonstration on Tuesday.

The government has blamed the LFI for pouring fuel on the fire of widespread public discontent, an allegation the party has denied.

#579. Embattled Greens senator Jordon Steele-John confirms leave from parliament after allegations against him made public

WA politician says he considered attending Senate estimates virtually but was told it would be ‘unacceptable’

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

Jordon Steele-John has confirmed he will not attend parliament next week as the embattled Greens senator apologises for publicly releasing the letter outlining the claims against him.

On Saturday afternoon, Steele-John removed a social media post containing a three-page letter marked as “confidential” sent to the Greens leader, David Shoebridge, earlier this month. The letter urged an investigation into allegations he had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.

Steele-John has denied all allegations made against him.

The Western Australian senator said he’d heard the full letter had been circulating online and “didn’t want to be seen as hiding from it”.

“I’m now not sure that was the right call and I’ve taken it down. I am really sorry for any additional stress it caused,” he said on social media.

After days of confusion following historical complaints about alleged misconduct were publicly aired in the media, the now-deleted statement posted to social media late Friday night said he considered attending Senate estimates virtually but was told it would be “unacceptable”.

He would instead focus on seeing through an independent investigation to its conclusion, he said.

“Over the past few days there has been a growing chorus calling on me not to attend parliament next week. I have explored attending digitally but have been informed that would also be unacceptable,” Steele-John said.

Steele-John said a precedent of keeping parliamentarians out of parliament after “allegations of allegations” were made had now been set.

“Had an allegation or complaint been made against me, I would have taken these actions immediately,” he said.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

The 32-year-old senator’s attendance in parliament for the remainder of the year had been uncertain after a public stoush with Shoebridge over whether he was on leave during the investigation.

The complaints are now subject to an independent investigation commissioned by the WA Greens and have been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission.

Shoebridge claimed Steele-John had requested leave and he accepted it last week after seven party members penned a letter to the leader urging an investigation into the claims.

Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you

The three-page letter sent on 13 October, and first published by the Nine newspapers, said the authors had been “made aware of multiple allegations of serious misconduct” against Steele-John about his “behaviour in the presence of women”.

The letter referred to an allegation of sexual harassment at a Greens campaign event in 2024 that the alleged victim had not reported out of fear of backlash. The letter provided no further detail.

In another, the authors referred to an allegation of “serious sexual misconduct” in 2025. Steele-John later responded this was alleged by a former partner and was investigated by Western Australian police with a finding of “no charges”.

Guardian Australia has confirmed the WA police told Steele-John the investigation was closed in May with no charges.

Also contained in the letter was a reference to a disparaging nickname for Steele-John – “feels on wheels” – which the authors said implied he had a reputation for acting inappropriately.

“To be clear, all signatories to this letter know that an allegation does not equate to a fact and/or guilt. We simply believe that it is in the party’s best interests to ensure that every allegation is investigated thoroughly, in alignment with community and member expectations,” the letter’s authors wrote.

Steele-John was defiant in a lengthy statement last Sunday, rejecting the allegations against him, denying he agreed to take leave from parliament and accusing an internal faction within the Greens of playing “nasty political games” in their decision to release the letter to the media.

Steele-John said any claims of his alleged behaviour should be investigated “fairly and thoroughly” but accused an “unofficial faction” within the WA branch of releasing the complaint letter to the media in a bid to oust him from the Senate.

#580. Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv targets Russian-occupied Crimea as UK and France conduct joint military exercise

Crimea strikes cause water and power cuts; war game designed to show how Nato countries could be defended amid fears of Russian aggression. What we know on day 1,705

A Ukrainian attack led to water and power cuts in occupied Crimea on Saturday, as a barrage of drones in several regions inside Russia left several dead, according to Russian authorities. Sergei Aksyonov, the Moscow-installed head of the Crimean peninsula, wrote on Telegram that due to the drone attack on local power grids “restrictions on the supply of electricity and water have been put in place”. He did not specify how many households had been affected in Crimea, which is home to more than 2.5 million people. The peninsula, which was seized from Ukraine by Russia in 2014, is a regular target for Ukrainian attacks.

A separate Ukrainian strike in part of the north-eastern Kharkiv region held by Russia killed at least three people and gravely wounded another on Saturday, the Moscow-backed authorities said.

Drones also rained down inside Russia. The country’s defence ministry said 616 of them had been shot down overnight across more than 20 regions of the country. During the day, drones hit Russia’s south-western Bryansk border region, killing at least three people, regional acting governor Yegor Kovalchuc said on Telegram.

In Ukraine, authorities said that at least five people died in several Russian drone and missile strikes in the country’s east. Dnipropetrovsk regional governor Oleksandr Ganzha on Saturday evening said three people were killed and at least 12 wounded when a Russian drone strike hit the town of Synelnykove, setting the fourth floor of a high-rise building on fire. Authorities in Sumy meanwhile said a Russian drone hit a farm, killing a 31-year-old woman and injuring four others.

Thousands of British and French troops have taken part in a military training exercise that included one of Britain’s largest airborne operations in two decades, the UK government said on Sunday. The war game is designed to show how Nato countries could be defended against a modern-day attack and comes during fears about Russian aggression in Europe amid Moscow’s war against Ukraine.

About 2,500 troops were involved in the seven-week exercise, in which 600 British and French paratroopers dropped from four RAF A400M Atlas transport aircraft over Germany. The exercise called Rhino Titan, held at the Sennelager military training centre in Germany, has been testing British troops’ ability against an enemy equipped with drones and electronic warfare. “The threats we face in the 21st century require an updated, modern approach to warfare – and our adaptable armed forces are preparing accordingly,” British defence minister Wes Streeting said in a statement.

Ukraine’s military has a “stable connection to Starlink”, the Ukrainian government said, 10 days after its ability to use the satellite communications system was suddenly restricted. But hours after the announcement, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, whose company owns Starlink, accused the Ukrainian military of violating ⁠the company’s terms. Neither Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield using Starlink technology, took responsibility for imposing the curbs.

Bulgarians will vote ​in presidential elections on Sunday as Russia’s war in Ukraine spreads to the waters off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast. Polls place acting president Iliana ⁠Iotova and ex-caretaker prime minister Andrey Gyurov as leaders in a race of 27 candidates. While the presidency is largely ceremonial, Sunday’s vote has taken ⁠on added significance after a series of drone attacks on merchant ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea ​coast that likely killed about two-dozen international ‌seafarers.

#581. Watch: Moment fin whale swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding

Videographer Rhys Morgan captured footage of the world's second largest whale lunge feeding

This is the moment the planet's second largest living creature opens its giant jaws and swallows thousands of gallons of water during feeding.

The fin whale was filmed by videographer Rhys Morgan off the Pembrokeshire coast in Wales, and it shows the mammal's expandable pleats take in up to 18,000 gallons of water and krill.

Morgan said "it was complete luck" that he captured the whale feeding and swimming with dolphins on his drone while fishing with a friend.

Second only to the blue whale, the fin whale is one of the largest animals ever to have lived, reaching up to 24m in length and weighing up to 70 tonnes.

Despite its enormous size, the fast-swimming creature is elusive and spends much of its life in the open ocean and often surfacing only briefly before disappearing beneath the waves.

The mammal can be found all over the world's oceans but is most at home in cooler waters.

The fin whale is about 24m (79ft) in length and weighs up to 70 tonnes

Morgan, from Houghton, Pembrokeshire, works at an oil refinery by day, and said he was "brought up on the water", but became interested in marine videography after using his friends drone to capture footage of sea creatures across the surface of the ocean.

"It's pretty incredible really," Morgan said.

"It makes you feel very small out there."

Rhys Morgan said he was "brought up on the water" and has been going out on boats since he was a young

To avoid causing harm to the whales while recording out at sea, Morgan said: "We do what we can to keep our distance in the boat but unfortunately nature can have a mind of its own sometimes.

"There's been times when we've been anchored up fishing with nothing happening in the area and a whale has popped up next to us.

"The wildlife will approach you sometimes."

Dr Marianna Chimienti is a lecturer in marine top predator ecology at Bangor University and said Morgan experienced a "rare and fortunate encounter".

Chimienti, who specialises in animal behaviour added: "It is normal that the fin whale comes and feeds at the surface, as it is part of the species foraging strategy but being in the coastal water is quite spectacular.

Little is known about fin whale migration but their movements are believed to be quite different from other baleen whales such as blues and humpbacks.

Scientists have found that fin whales are more abundant in higher latitudes in warmer months of the year, and more numerous in lower latitudes during colder months, but this can vary.

Fin whales have a pretty simple diet which is usually made up of krill, small schooling fish and squid.

Due to the small size of its prey, fin whales have to eat a lot to survive and can spend several hours each day feeding, consuming up to 2,000 kilograms of food.

#582. REPORTAGE. Manifestations du 24 octobre : "Il faut faire converger les luttes !" À Gaillac, d'anciens Gilets jaunes ressortent les banderoles pour l'acte II de la mobilisation contre la vie chère

Article rédigé par Nawel Omara

l'essentiel À Gaillac (Tarn), plusieurs dizaines de manifestants ont investi le rond-point Taillefer, ce samedi 24 octobre 2026, pour "l'acte II" de la mobilisation contre la vie chère. Parmi eux, quelques anciens Gilets jaunes, mais aussi des citoyens mobilisés autour de plusieurs enjeux : pouvoir d'achat, lutte contre le fascisme, soutien aux lycéens et aux étudiants. Un même mot d'ordre les rassemble : faire converger les luttes.

Il est 10 heures. Les premiers manifestants arrivent. Aux abords du rond-point Taillefer, à Gaillac, les automobilistes klaxonnent et encouragent ceux qui prennent part à "l'acte II" de la mobilisation contre la vie chère, en ce samedi 24 octobre 2026. "Tiens, je t'ai amené des piquets pour accrocher les banderoles", lance Maxime, dit "Milou", à Alain. Ce dernier est un Gilet jaune de la première heure. Pour l'occasion, le retraité a ressorti une vieille affiche de 2018. Le tissu a légèrement jauni et porte des taches qui ressemblent à des éclaboussures provoquées par le passage des voitures. Mais l'inscription, tout comme la motivation de ceux qui la brandissent, reste parfaitement intacte : "On est là, même si Macron ne veut pas !"

Ce samedi 24 octobre 2026, environ 60 présentes, selon les forces de l'ordre, étaient présentes au rond-point Taillefer à Gaillac. DDM - N.O.

Pour lui, le gilet qu'il arbore fièrement aujourd'hui relève davantage du symbole que d'une réelle volonté de faire revivre le mouvement. "Ce n'est plus la même chose. Mais c'est quand même important de se rassembler, au vu de tout ce qu'il se passe." S'il regrette d'abord le manque d'affluence, "parce que Macron a foutu la trouille avec son discours", les habitants gagnent peu à peu le terre-plein en face du rond-point. Parents venus avec leurs enfants, jeunes actifs, retraités...

Les profils se mêlent et les préoccupations se rejoignent. Pouvoir d'achat, lutte contre le fascisme, contre les violences policières, soutien aux lycéens et aux étudiants... Les sujets de mobilisation ne manquent pas et les manifestants entendent faire front commun. "Il faut faire converger les luttes !", martèlent plusieurs d'entre eux. Pour une jeune maman, le contexte politique renforce même la nécessité de se rassembler : "La répression que l'on vit actuellement donne encore plus envie d'être là. C'est peut-être la dernière fois que l'on peut."

Les manifestants ont distribué des tracts aux automobilistes. DDM N-O.

Si le mécontentement est palpable, la manifestation se déroule dans une ambiance sereine. Une vingtaine de membres des forces de l'ordre, policiers et gendarmes confondus, veillent à son bon déroulement. Selon eux, environ 60 personnes sont présentes. La situation reste calme et la circulation n'est pas interrompue, malgré quelques ralentissements au moment de la distribution de tracts syndicaux, qui dénoncent "les annonces sécuritaires du Président" ainsi que les "atteintes au droit de manifester".

Le rassemblement de Gaillac était le seul déclaré auprès de la préfecture du Tarn. Un point de rendez-vous au rond-point de l'Arquipeyre, à Albi, dès 8 h 30, figurait sur les cartes interactives, mais personne n'était présent sur place. Dans la cité épiscopale, une mobilisation doit avoir lieu à 14 heures, au départ du kiosque du Jardin national.

Face à ces initiatives spontanées, la préfecture a pris des mesures préventives, avec notamment l'interdiction de manifester dans les centres historiques et commerçants d'Albi et de Castres, ainsi que le déploiement d'un dispositif renforcé des forces de l'ordre.

#583. Explosion and fire erupt at Quaker Oats plant in Cedar Rapids, Iowa; no injuries

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

An apparent explosion caused a fire Saturday at a Quaker Oats plant in Iowa that the company touts as the largest milling facility in the world. No one was hurt, fire officials said.

The Cedar Rapids Fire Department said firefighters responded to the call at about 4:45 p.m. Video and photos posted to social media showed black smoke over the downtown of the city of about 140,000.

The fire evidently began with an explosion, the department said via Facebook.

All workers got out safely and were accounted for without any injuries, Mayor Tiffany O’Donnell said in a Facebook video.

The fire happened in an area of the building that handled products, O’Donnell said.

“It’s not heavily populated with employees and team members. Which of course in this case was a blessing,” O’Donnell said.

There was no immediate information on what caused the fire.

PepsiCo Foods US said in a statement that fire responders went to the scene of the blaze and how it started would be investigated.

The Quaker Oats brand, by way of the Quaker Mill Company, turns 150 years old in 2027. It is owned by PepsiCo.

The Quaker Oats facility is the largest milling facility in the world, processing over 2 million pounds (900,000 kilograms) of oats daily, according to the company’s website.

#585. Deadly shooting near Paris is a 'racist terrorist attack', Macron says

Watch: Emergency services at the scene of shooting near Paris

French President Emmanuel Macron has labelled a gun attack in a Parisian suburb that killed one person and injured five others "a racist terrorist attack".

Macron said the attack was a "turning point in the life of our Republic and our nation" - the first time there had ever been a random racial killing like this.

The attack unfolded over some 15 minutes, with the attacker opening fire from his car - first in Trappes, to the south-west of Paris, and then in nearby La VerriÃ¨re - appearing to target people of migrant origin. He was subsequently arrested.

Three of those injured, including a 12-year-old girl, remain in a serious condition.

Macron said while visiting the scene of the attack that people had been targeted over their skin colour or religion and urged the public not to give an inch in the face of what he called "ideologies taking root".

The exact motive remains unclear, but the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said the incident appeared to be "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise".

The suspect has been named in French media as Kevin T who, according to PNAT, had four previous convictions that had been "automatically expunged".

The 39-year-old was known to police but not to France's intelligence services, local media report.

He was not on a list of individuals considered to be a serious threat to French security, the national anti-terrorism prosecutor's office told BFMTV.

A member of the suspect's "immediate family circle" was also taken into custody on Friday, it added.

French police inspect the scene of the shooting in Trappes, near Paris

French firefighters and police were seen at a petrol station in the area

The gunman had driven through several neighbourhoods in a grey Renault Clio, according to witnesses.

The mayor of Trappes, Ali Rabeh, said he had "fired randomly" with the seeming intent of causing "as many casualties as possible", adding: "He wanted to cause carnage."

Rabeh said people had been targeted at a petrol station, a medical centre and a playground in Trappes before the attacker had driven on to La VerriÃ¨re.

A police union official said the suspect had been detained in La VerriÃ¨re on the main road that runs through the town.

The mother of the injured 12-year-old told French broadcaster RTL that her daughter suffered eight gunshot wounds and required surgery.

"How could anyone do this to a child?" she asked.

The mother said her daughter had been wearing a headscarf and questioned whether this was why she was attacked.

"She's a child who was born in France, in Trappes. She has the right to live in France, to make her life in France."

A big deployment of police and emergency services has been present at the scene

A local police chief told BFMTV that the suspect had used "an older-style semi-automatic weapon". Le Parisien reports that the gun dated back to World War Two.

PNAT said its investigation also included "possession of a Category A weapon" - which covers military-grade weapons or weapons capable of firing in bursts.

The anti-terrorism office also said its investigation was looking into "conspiracy with a terrorist group for the purpose of preparing crimes against persons".

#586. Manhunt launched for violent prisoner after he absconds from London medical facility

Published: 18:59 GMT, 24 October 2026 | Updated: 05:19 GMT, 25 October 2026

A manhunt has been launched for a violent inmate after he escaped a medical institution.

Anthony Lloyd, 38, was last seen at around 4.10pm on Friday after forcing his way out of the unit in Lewisham in South London and heading in the direction of Catford.

The Metropolitan Police said he 'poses a risk both to himself and the public'.

Lloyd, around 5ft 8in, of medium build with short dark hair, was wearing a grey-blue t-shirt, black tracksuit bottoms and white trainers, police said.

The force has warned members of the public not to approach him.

It is understood the prisoner was convicted in 2025 of Actual Bodily Harm (ABH) relating to an incident in Nottinghamshire involving three emergency workers.

He received a 12-month custodial sentence, which he was serving in prison.

In September, he was transferred to the Lewisham medical facility.

Anthony Lloyd, 38, was last seen at around 4.10pm on Friday after forcing his way out of the unit in Lewisham in South London and heading in the direction of Catford

Detective Superintendent Melanie Pressley, who is leading the manhunt, said: 'We are conducting various significant inquiries to find Lloyd and return him to custody.

'We are concerned he poses a risk both to himself and the public, and would urge anyone who sees him to call 999 immediately. Do not approach him.

'If you have any information – however small – that could help us locate Lloyd, please get in touch with police as a matter of urgency.'

Officers believe Lloyd could be anywhere in London, and he also has links to Surrey, Sussex, Thames Valley, Hampshire, Nottinghamshire, Derbyshire and Merseyside.

#587. Helen Haines’s condition improves days after losing both legs from alleged attack

Independent MP now serious but stable, according to update from Melbourne’s Alfred hospital

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Independent MP Helen Haines’s condition has been downgraded to serious but stable after she lost both legs following an alleged attack near her electorate office in north-east Victoria on Monday afternoon.

The Alfred hospital in Melbourne provided an update on Haines’s condition on Saturday morning.

“The patient is in a serious but stable condition at The Alfred on Saturday morning,” a spokesperson for the hospital said.

Haines, the federal MP for the Victorian seat of Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was struck by a car in Wangaratta on Monday afternoon. Surgeons were trying to save her right leg but both legs had to be amputated due to the seriousness of her injuries.

The MP’s husband, Phil Haines, provided an update at the Alfred hospital on Wednesday, saying “both her heart and her mind are in good shape.”

“I think when we reflect and talk about and think about Helen, the two most important parts of Helen for us as a family are her heart and her mind,” he said.

“Her heart is huge. She is a very compassionate, caring, loving person. Incredibly supportive of all around her – her family, her community, anybody she comes across. And her mind. She has the sharpest intellect.”

Police on Tuesday charged Brendan Nugent, 43, from nearby Tarrawingee with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official. Police have since charged him with two additional offences – cultivating and possessing cannabis – according to court documents.

Nugent appeared at the Wangaratta magistrates court on Wednesday and did not apply for bail.

On Friday, an update on Haines’s social media accounts said her staff were working to reopen her electorate offices next Thursday. “What happened on Monday has deeply affected Helen’s family and all of her staff. Many of us witnessed the incident and some were among the first to come to her aid,” the post read.

“As Helen takes the time she needs to recover, we will take time to look after ourselves and one another, too. Healing will take time, and we ask for your understanding as we navigate the days and weeks ahead.”

Haines’ staff said they had been overwhelmed with kindness shown by the local community in Indi and across Australia and the globe. They said more than $730,000 had been raised for Save the Children in Haines’ honour after her husband directed people to donate to the special appeal as his wife recovered.

“We are deeply moved by the extraordinary generosity of so many people,” the post read.

The alleged attack on Haines has reverberated through Australian politics, prompting conversations about the temperature of political debate, security risks for MPs and mental health services in regional Victoria.

WA Police charged a 56-year-old man after allegedly threatening staff and wielding nunchucks at the electoral office of the the state’s local government minister, Hannah Beazley, days after the alleged attack on Haines.

A community vigil was held for Haines in Wodonga on Wednesday evening after it was revealed the MP had lost both her legs following Monday’s alleged attack.

Haines’s predecessor as the federal member for Indi, Cathy McGowan, said on the sidelines of the event the community was grappling with “mixed emotions”.

#588. Ukrainian President Zelenskyy speaks at EU summit amid spat with Donald Trump

EU leaders reaffirmed support for Ukraine at the Brussels summit. But souring relations with the US over Russia and Starlink and a big hole in the budget will make for a difficult winter for Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was applauded by EU leaders when he appeared at this week's summit in Brussels. But getting what he needs from Europe will be tough, and a public dispute with US President Donald Trump has put him in a very difficult position.

Speaking to press at the summit, he said that "Putin wants to destroy us" and that Ukraine must prepare for a hard winter.

Experts view the upcoming cold season as a rough one for Ukraine as well.

"Ukraine is arguably entering the most difficult winter since [Russia's] full scale invasion," Olena Prokopenko, a senior fellow at the German Marshall Fund of the United States, a nonpartisan think-tank, told DW.

Three painful topics were on the table at the summit for discussion between Zelenskyy and EU leaders: US relations with Russia, Starlink ― and money.

Zelenskyy's visit to Brussels comes at a time when he needs European support more than ever. That's because his relationship with the US is worsening. Worries are growing in the EU and Ukraine that the US is growing more sympathetic to Russia.

President Trump told US news channel Newsmax: "I think I find Zelenskyy to be more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin."

Trump struck a deal to buy Russian diesel on October 12, which signifies a step back from sanctions placed on Russia and a blow for Ukraine.

When Zelenskyy ordered Ukrainian forces to conduct fresh strikes on Russia's oil refineries, Trump labelled the Ukrainian leader's decision as "a disgrace."

At the press conference at the summit on Friday, Zelenskyy told reporters that he knows that US-built missiles "are being sent to the Middle East, so it is no secret that we are not a priority."

He is asking Europe instead to supply the military power Ukraine needs to get through the winter.

Since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the US has been the biggest military donor to Ukraine. But the relationship between the two countries has become more difficult since the start of Donald Trump's second term in the White House.

Ukraine uses Starlink, a satellite Internet service developed by tech billionaire Elon Musk. The country also uses Starshield, the military-grade version, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-occupied territory and interceptor drones, though not for long-range strikes in Russia.

At the summit, Zelenskyy spoke of his "deep and unpleasant" surprise upon finding out that Ukraine was experiencing disruptions to the systems. He said this has hobbled Ukraine's ability to defend itself.

Both Elon Musk and the White House say they are not responsible for the slowdown.

The EU's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas told the press at the summit before the talks began: "Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine and unfortunately in [the] short term Europe can't replace this capability."

Prokopenko said that this was the reason "why Ukraine's most credible medium-term solution here is to continue relying on the US. And the EU is critical in this context in terms of backing Ukraine's requests for the US administration to keep those technologies on offer" for Kyiv.

Speaking to journalists at the summit, Zelenskyy said the speed of Starlink had still not been fully restored but had improved. He said Ukraine is cooperating with various countries, including France, to search for a partial solution.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Zelenskyy urged EU leaders Friday to keep backing Kyiv financially as well, asking for nearly $80 billion (€70 billion) more next year.

"This is a realistic amount and I ask you to find this support," Zelenskyy said. "It will help us hold Russia back."

The EU gave Kyiv an approximately $100 billion (€90 billion) loan last year, making the EU Ukraine's biggest international backer. But the Ukrainian government is saying it needs more.

"The war is becoming objectively more expensive, and the Ukrainian economy is increasingly affected by the Russian strikes, leading to a drastic decline in tax and customs revenues," Prokopenko said. "So the needs will continue growing."

So will Ukraine get what it needs? Closing the summit, President of the European Council Antonio Costa said that Ukraine "remains a priority" and asked the European Commission to come up with a proposal to pull together more funds for the country in 2027.

Essentially, it looks as though the EU will try to find a way to meet Ukraine's cash demands ― though it is not yet clear how.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised the EU will "continue to lead" but urged international partners to step up as well.

Zelenskyy will leave Brussels without concrete promises or numbers, but with renewed commitments for support from Europe.

The Ukrainian president concluded his press conference with an emotional statement: "We will keep living and fighting with dignity."

#589. Chemie-Nobelpreis geht an Forscher aus Frankreich und Japan

Der Chemie-Nobelpreis würdigt in diesem Jahr zwei Forscher für grundlegende Entdeckungen zur Entstehung asymmetrischer Moleküle. Ihre Arbeit ist auch für die Entwicklung von Arzneimitteln wichtig.

Der Franzose Henri Kagan und der Japaner Kenso Soai werden mit dem Nobelpreis für Chemie ausgezeichnet für die Entdeckung nichtlinearer Effekte und der Autokatalyse in der asymmetrischen organischen Synthese. Das gab die Königlich-Schwedische Akademie der Wissenschaften in Stockholm bekannt.

Ihre Forschung half dabei, ein lange bestehendes Rätsel der Chemie zu lösen. Viele Moleküle, darunter Aminosäuren, können in zwei Varianten vorkommen. Diese verhalten sich zueinander wie Bild und Spiegelbild. In lebenden Organismen findet sich jedoch jeweils nur eine dieser Formen. Lange war unklar, wie eine solche chemische Asymmetrie entstehen kann.

Kagan von der Université Paris-Sud und Soai von der Tokyo University of Science lieferten mit ihren Arbeiten wichtige Erklärungen dafür. Nach Angaben der Nobel-Akademie waren ihre Entdeckungen entscheidend für Chemiker, die Grundlagen für die Herstellung von Arzneimitteln entwickeln.

Der Chemie-Nobelpreis gilt als renommierteste Auszeichnung des Fachs. In diesem Jahr ist er mit insgesamt zwölf Millionen schwedischen Kronen dotiert, umgerechnet rund einer Million Euro.

Die Nobelstiftung hatte das Preisgeld anlässlich des 125-jährigen Bestehens der Nobelpreise um eine Million Kronen erhöht. "In diesem Jahr feiern wir das 125-jährige Bestehen des Nobelpreises. Aus diesem Anlass freuen wir uns, das Preisgeld um eine Million erhöhen zu können", sagte die Geschäftsführerin der Nobelstiftung, Hanna Stjärne.

Auch bei der Bekanntgabe gibt es im Jubiläumsjahr eine Premiere. Erstmals werden die Namen der Nobelpreisträger für Physik, Chemie und Wirtschaftswissenschaften von einer Frau verkündet.

Ellen Moons ist seit Anfang 2026 Generalsekretärin der Königlich-Schwedischen Akademie der Wissenschaften. Die gebürtige Belgierin ist die erste Frau auf diesem Posten seit Gründung der Akademie im Jahr 1739.

Im vergangenen Jahr hatten Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson und Omar Yaghi den Chemie-Nobelpreis erhalten. Sie wurden für die Entwicklung metallorganischer Gerüstverbindungen ausgezeichnet. Die Strukturen können unter anderem Wasser aus Wüstenluft gewinnen, Kohlendioxid abscheiden oder chemische Reaktionen katalysieren.

Seit 1901 wurde der Chemie-Nobelpreis an 198 verschiedene Forscher vergeben. Zwei von ihnen erhielten die Auszeichnung zweimal. Unter den Geehrten waren bislang acht Frauen. Dazu gehören Marie Curie, die 1911 ausgezeichnet wurde, sowie Emmanuelle Charpentier und Jennifer Doudna. Sie erhielten den Preis 2020 für die Entwicklung einer Genschere.

Die diesjährige Nobelpreis-Woche hatte am Montag mit der Medizin begonnen. Ausgezeichnet werden die Deutschen Peter Hegemann und Georg Nagel sowie der US-Forscher Karl Deisseroth für ihre Entdeckungen in der Optogenetik. Mit dieser Methode lassen sich Zellen mithilfe von Licht gezielt an- und abschalten.

Am Dienstag wurde der Physik-Nobelpreis dem belgisch-amerikanischen Forscher Francis Halzen zugesprochen. Gewürdigt wurden seine Beiträge zum Neutrino-Observatorium "IceCube" in der Antarktis, mit dem erstmals hochenergetische kosmische Neutrinos nachgewiesen wurden.

Am Donnerstag und Freitag werden die Nobelpreise für Literatur und Frieden bekanntgegeben. Am kommenden Montag folgt der von der schwedischen Reichsbank gestiftete Wirtschaftspreis.

Die Auszeichnungen werden traditionell am 10. Dezember überreicht, dem Todestag des Preisstifters Alfred Nobel.

#590. Hundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policing

Almost 1,000 arrested as police charge crowd in Paris and teargas used to stop protesters reaching other city centres

Hundreds of thousands marched in cities across France on Saturday in largely peaceful protests to support schoolchildren’s demands for more teachers and repairs to dilapidated buildings, as Emmanuel Macron faces a social and political crisis in his final months as president.

In Paris, at least 110,000 people marched along the eastern edge of the city, according to government estimates. They supported high schoolers but also complained of the high cost of living and the government’s heavy policing, saying riot police had been sent to target school protesters over the past month, instead of the government offering political solutions.

The mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government’s policing, saying: “Oppression breeds rebellion” and “The right to protest”.

But at the end of the Paris demonstration, at Porte de Vincennes on the city’s eastern edge, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged who had not appeared to have taken part in the peaceful march. Some groups of masked men threw glass bottles and stones at police, who responded with teargas, water cannon and stun grenades. A bin was set alight and fireworks were set off towards police.

Riot police also charged a larger crowd of protesters at the end of the Paris march, using batons against them.

Police fired teargas to prevent protesters in Lyon, Lille, Montpellier, Nantes and Toulouse from reaching city centres. In Marseille, some bin fires were lit amid clashes with police. At least two people were seriously injured, one in Clermont-Ferrand and another in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off.

The government estimated that at least 400,000 people had marched across France. Trade unions estimated the number at double that. The interior ministry said there had been almost 1,000 arrests.

Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, said that at various street marches across France there were what he called “high-risk groups” who “broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence”.

More than 70,000 police were on the streets of French cities, with shops boarded up and many museums closed. The government had feared a repeat of last Saturday, when, despite peaceful protests taking place, France saw one of the most violent days of unrest in years, with public buildings burned, hundreds of shops destroyed and looted and at least 2,700 people arrested in cities across the country.

At Saturday’s protests, there was widespread anger at Macron for banning non-union demonstrations that his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.

At the Paris march, Nadège, a 43-year-old communications worker, said she had been teargassed last weekend at a peaceful demonstration. “I’m out again peacefully today to support everyone who is brave enough to demonstrate. It does take courage. People are afraid now. We have to keep our rights alive … In France, it’s our legal right to protest in the street and I’m here to defend that.”

A 21-year-old student from a Paris science faculty that is now blockaded by demonstrators said: “We feel in France that we are increasingly living in an authoritarian regime that is trying to stop our democratic right to protest in the street.”

The radical left presidential candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who took part in the Paris rally, said Macron must “give in” and address France’s social malaise or face repeated protests. “Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week,” Mélenchon said.

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

The government has been facing a crisis since the start of high school demonstrations in mid-September, when children aged between 15 and 18 began protesting against staff shortages at their schools, leaking and crumbling buildings, and a lack of chairs in overcrowded classrooms. It grew into the biggest youth movement in years, with trade unions, teachers and parents joining. Police investigations are under way after some children and protesters were maimed and injured by explosive police weaponry.

At Saturday’s march there were some people dressed in yellow vests who had taken part in the gilets jaunes anti-government protests of 2018 and 2019. Standing amid demonstrators, Jérôme Rodrigues, a key figure from the gilets jaunes protest, said: “Today the government is afraid; that is why they are pushing demonstrators to the edge of the city, away from places of power. It’s not police shields that will provide an answer to French people struggling and unable to make ends meet.” He said it was likely that demonstrations would continue.

Pierre, 60, a retired banking consultant, said he was demonstrating in support of school students. “I have an eight-year-old granddaughter. I want her to have a brighter future than the sombre times we are facing today. There is a complete refusal by the government to listen to people’s demands.”

Jesse, 40, a charity worker from the north of Paris, carrying a sign saying “Free Hugs”, said: “I’m so angry. I’m here to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions. I’m so proud of them, and we have to stand together.”

She said: “I know I’m not going to war by coming out to demonstrate peacefully. But at times it really does feel like a war … This is the first time I’ve prepared so carefully for a peaceful march, wearing old clothes in case they are gassed or torn.”

In Orléans, thousands shouting anti-fascist slogans marched against a congress held by Marine Le Pen’s far-right anti-immigration National Rally party. Protesters criticised Le Pen, a frontrunner in next year’s presidential election, as well as Macron, who steps down from power next year. “Macron, resign. Le Pen in prison,” the crowd shouted.

#592. British and French paratroopers in largest airborne drill for decades amid Russia fears

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Overall, roughly 2,500 personnel took part, which included 600 French and British paratroopers dropping from four RAF A400M Atlas aircraft

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Thousands of service members from Britain and France have joined forces in a military wargame intended to demonstrate the defence of Nato territory against potential foreign aggression.

The drills featured a major airborne operation, among the largest conducted in two decades, with British and French paratroopers leaping from RAF transport aircraft over German soil.

The joint drills come amid heightened security fears across Europe driven by Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine, as Russian troops probe Nato frontiers and the Kremlin faces accusations of directing arson, sabotage, and assassinations within European countries.

Conducted at the Sennelager military training area in Germany, Exercise Rhino Titan pushed the UK’s 16 Air Assault Brigade to respond to adversaries armed with electronic warfare systems and drone fleets, reflecting the tactical capabilities Russia is anticipated to employ.

Overall, roughly 2,500 personnel took part, which included 600 French and British paratroopers dropping from four RAF A400M Atlas aircraft.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "The threats we face in the 21st century require an updated, modern approach to warfare – and our adaptable armed forces are preparing accordingly.

"Alongside our French and German allies, this large-scale training exercise shows we can deliver rapid, large-scale airborne power anywhere it’s needed to defend Nato territory.

"This combination of troops and specialised equipment is what is required to deter our adversaries and keep Britain and our allies safe."

Brigadier Ed Cartwright, commander of 16 Air Assault Brigade, said: "We have been given a realistic challenge to defend Nato territory and pitted against an enemy using drones and electronic warfare, which is what we would face on the modern battlefield."

#593. Manifestations du 24 octobre : "Quand je vois des étudiants qui ne mangent pas à leur faim, je trouve ça révoltant...", dans le Lot près de 800 personnes réunies pour l'acte II

l'essentiel Dans le Lot, plus de 800 personnes se sont mobilisées. Près de 200 personnes ont défilé à Cahors, samedi 24 octobre, pour dénoncer la privation des libertés et les inégalités sociales. Parmi les manifestants, des Gilets jaunes et des lycéens unis pour réclamer plus de moyens. À Figeac, plus de 600 personnes ont exprimé des revendications similaires, dans un climat pacifique. Une nouvelle mobilisation est prévue le 31 octobre. Reportage.

Au son des djembés et tambours, ponctué par des claquements de mains et des slogans scandés en chœur, près de 200 personnes ont investi les rues de Cahors, ce samedi 24 octobre, dans une ambiance à la fois festive et revendicative. Au milieu de la foule en mouvement, les pancartes brandies au-dessus des têtes donnent le ton : "La France et la démocratie nous manquent" ou encore "Après une politique sans queue ni tête, une répression sans yeux ni mains."

Près de 200 manifestants se sont réunis place François Mitterrand ce samedi 24 octobre. DDM Juliette Rigaud   Ils ont animé la manifestation ce samedi 24 octobre. DDM Juliette Rigaud

"C'est un ras-le-bol général", souffle Léa. La trentenaire, Gilet jaune de la première heure, a choisi de battre à nouveau le pavé. "Il y a une privation des libertés, je trouve ça hallucinant", poursuit-elle. Dans les mots qu'emploient les manifestants, l'amertume transparaît. Pour beaucoup, la sensation d'une coupure entre le gouvernement et le peuple.

À lire aussi : REPLAY. Manifestations du 24 octobre : entre 410 000 et 800 000 manifestants en France, des heurts dans plusieurs villes

Dans le cortège, encadré par une vingtaine de policiers, plusieurs Gilets jaunes. Parmi eux, Christiane et Bernard. "Je suis là pour trois raisons : contre la vie chère, pour soutenir la jeunesse et pour les retraites et les salaires", résume la sexagénaire. Voir les lycéens se mobiliser pour leur avenir, c'est ce qui a motivé les retraités à se mobiliser à nouveau, huit ans après le début de leur mouvement.

Bernard ancien sellier-bourrelier touche 900 euros de pension de retraite. DDM Juliette Rigaud

"Ce monde marche sur la tête. Quand je vois des étudiants qui ne mangent pas à leur faim, des jeunes qui se prostituent pour payer leurs études, je trouve ça révoltant", lâche Christiane. Comme Bernard, un chiffre la crispe : celui du nombre de personnes vivant sous le seuil de pauvreté monétaire en France. En 2024, ils étaient 9,8 millions. "Les inégalités sont de plus en plus présentes. On est dans un pays qui lamine ses citoyens", martèle le septuagénaire, ancien sellier-bourrelier qui touche 900 euros de pension de retraite.

Les pancartes étaient nombreuses dans le cortège, ce samedi 24 octobre. DDM Juliette Rigaud

En retrait, les deux retraités écoutent attentivement les jeunes se succéder au micro. "Nous sommes le peuple qui s'est soulevé. Le peuple qui souffre et qui désormais se bat pour ne plus souffrir", lâche un manifestant. Parmi les revendications, la lutte contre l'extrême droite figure également.

Aux alentours de midi, le cortège a regagné la place François-Mitterrand (le parcours avait été déclaré en préfecture par la CGT). L'heure est désormais à organiser la prochaine mobilisation, samedi prochain. Derrière, un groupe dont la plupart sont en classe de terminale au lycée Gaston-Monnerville a également choisi de battre le pavé. "Je suis là parce que j'espère un meilleur avenir pour moi, pour ma sœur, pour ma mère, souligne une lycéenne. Pour ne plus avoir la boule au ventre." Les jeunes dénoncent également les violences qui ont pu avoir lieu dans d'autres villes en France. "C'est une honte de pleurer du matériel et de ne pas parler des manifestants qui ont subi des violences", soutient-elle.

Un groupe de lycéens dont la plupart est à Gaston Monnerville était dans le cortège cadurcien. DDM Juliette Rigaud

Le groupe l'assure : ils continueront de se mobiliser tant qu'ils n'auront pas obtenu "de réponses dans notre sens." "Il faut rénover les bâtiments, revoir nos emplois du temps, aménager le temps de travail, réformer Parcoursup...", glisse-t-il. Ces revendications ce sont les leurs, mais pas question pour les cinq lycéens d'oublier celles portées par les Gilets jaunes. "Ils sont là en soutien pour nous et on est là en soutien pour eux." Ensemble, ils reviendront déguisés samedi 31 octobre pour, à nouveau, faire entendre leurs voix.

"Jeunesse fâchée, pas facho", "Professeur, espèce en voie de disparition" : ce samedi matin, les pancartes racontaient les inquiétudes et la colère d’un cortège de plus de 600 personnes dans les rues de Figeac. L’école, l’avenir des jeunes, les services publics et le droit de manifester traversaient les messages brandis par les participants. "Trop jeune pour être écouté, assez grand pour être gazé", pouvait-on lire, ou encore : "On nous apprend la liberté d’expression sauf quand on l’exerce" et "Macron casseur pilleur".

À Figeac, plus de 600 personnes se sont mobilisées. DDM Sophie Mitrani

Lors d’une prise de parole, une militante d’"Indignons-nous" a résumé cette colère : "Qui sème la misère récolte la colère !" Dénonçant la précarité, la dégradation des services publics et le sentiment de ne pas être entendus, elle a réclamé des réponses concrètes à "la crise sociale, la fin des violences policières et la démission d’Emmanuel Macron". "La démocratie ne peut pas se résumer à voter tous les cinq ans", a-t-elle affirmé, défendant l’accès de chacun à la santé, à l’éducation et au logement.

À lire aussi : Manifestations du 17 octobre : "Un ras-le-bol qui touche tout le monde" Gilets jaunes, retraités, lycéens... la mobilisation rassemble près de 1000 personnes dans le Lot

Le cortège est resté parfaitement pacifique (la manifestation avait été déclarée en préfecture). Plusieurs commerçants rapportent pourtant avoir reçu, le matin même, un appel les avertissant de risques de casse sur le parcours. L’origine de ces appels reste à préciser, la préfecture assure ne pas en être à l'origine.

Enfin, certains participants avaient prévu de défiler dans d’autres communes, notamment à Villefranche-de-Rouergue, où, selon leurs témoignages, la manifestation avait été interdite. Une décision qu’ils évoquaient avec un vif agacement. La manifestation s’est prolongée par une assemblée générale aux jardins de l’hôpital.

Vous souhaitez suivre ce fil de discussion ?

Souhaitez-vous recevoir une notification lors de la réponse d’un(e) internaute à votre commentaire ?

Ces jeunes sont bien dans l'évolution de la société , travailler moins demander plus. Faites un tour sur les parkings des FAC avec de très nombreux véhicules, le dernier portable, les jeudis soir en ville etc alors la vie n'est pas trop moche tout de même pour eux.

Merci à toutes ces personnes qui prennent du temps et des risques pour défendre notre dignité de citoyens et de citoyennes, les services publics et l'intérêt général. Les commentaires négatifs des égoïstes et des frustrés me dégoutent.

Il faut aller vers une alimentation moins chère et meilleure pour la santé : préférer les rognons de porc à la pizza, la sanguette de poulet au kebab, ramasser les noix et noisettes, faire de la compote avec des fruits dégradés.

#595. Freed US citizen was tortured in Russian jail, former Ukrainian prisoners say

Stephen Hubbard (second from left in the first row) was flown back home on a US plane earlier this week

Ukrainians held alongside freed US prisoner Stephen Hubbard have said they witnessed him being beaten and humiliated by Russian guards during his four-year detention.

Dmytro Khyliuk first met Hubbard at the Novozybkov prison in Bryansk, not far from Russia's border with Ukraine, in September 2022.

"We heard it from the guards. They came during inspections and were asking: in which cell is the American? And then they used obscene words. They threatened him, they mocked him from the first days."

Ihor Shyshko also remembers Hubbard's arrival at the jail and says his nationality marked him out to the officers.

"It attracted such attention because they mocked him, forced him to learn the Russian language, sing the national anthem and repeat the rules of the prison schedule, which he could not read."

Hubbard was captured in April 2022, when Russian soldiers occupied the eastern city of Izyum, where he was living with his Ukrainian partner.

He was accused of serving in Ukraine's armed forces and convicted in a trial in Moscow before being sentenced to six years and 10 months. Shyshko and Khyliuk were held alongside Hubbard as he awaited trial.

Ihor Shyshko alleges that Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of Russian prison staff

Shyshko said he witnessed and heard Hubbard being beaten by prison guards and electrocuted with a stun gun.

"They beat him on the legs, on the back, on the arms," he said. "Of course, they didn't give him food, they didn't give him medical care. They kept him in the cold.

"He was always treated more harshly, because he was an American. They claimed he was a mercenary, and said 'let's beat him'."

Shyshko, a captured Ukrainian soldier, alleges Hubbard was subjected to sexual humiliation and abuse for the entertainment of the prison staff.

Accounts from the two former Ukrainian prisoners corroborate statements made by Hubbard's family that he was tortured in prison.

The 74-year-old was released by the Kremlin after four-and-a-half years, on the day US special envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg to discuss the war in Ukraine.

Witkoff praised the Russian President as a "humanitarian", despite the ongoing full-scale invasion and daily Russian attacks across Ukraine.

US President Donald Trump said he had asked Putin to free Hubbard during a phone call the week before.

Dmytro Khyliuk says Hubbard was hidden in a Russian prison to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors

Khyliuk, a journalist, was held in the earliest days of the invasion, when Russian troops advanced towards the capital Kyiv.

He said he knew Hubbard's health was declining over the months they were initially held in nearby cells because he heard his complaints and the guards calling him more often to see the prison doctor.

Khyliuk described broken windows and biting cold, with detainees using time out of their cells to huddle together in the bathroom for warmth.

"It was very difficult conditions in Novozybkov, worse than in the next prison. It was very cold there in winter, terribly cold," he said.

Both men encountered the retired English teacher again at their next prison, Pakino, where Shyshko says Hubbard's condition worsened.

"There was not a single spot on his knees or on his feet without rot," he said.

"Everything was rotten. We all had scabies. It was very, very difficult for him. I even bandaged him once at the medical centre, because the doctor didn't want to do it. He just couldn't do it himself, and I had to help. He was quite weak then and he almost couldn't move."

They detailed a harsh regime and a meagre diet of porridge, bread and potatoes, with a daily routine of beatings and humiliation, being forced to run or hold stress positions.

"There's a handler with a dog, who lets go so it can bite you on the buttocks, on the elbow, or bite your leg. Then these wounds fester very badly," Shyshko said.

Khyliuk claimed that soon after their transfer to Pakino, Hubbard was hidden to conceal his condition from a team of International Red Cross visitors.

"I would like to say that an international humanitarian organisation that receives a lot of funding could do better. They saw only what was shown to them and they were happy with that," he said.

Hubbard was sentenced to almost seven years in a penal colony in 2024, accused of serving in a defence unit in eastern Ukraine

The International Committee of the Red Cross said in a statement that "in any situation where the ICRC has been granted access, we request to see every individual and assess the conditions they are held in. We continue our discussions with parties to the conflict on this issue."

Khyliuk said Hubbard disappeared from the prison in 2024 and he thought he must have been released. Khyliuk was returned to Ukraine in August 2025 in a prisoner exchange.

He likened their treatment to the regime of Soviet leader Joseph Stalin.

"Russian captivity is a torture machine. From the first second of your detention, they do everything to suppress you, to intimidate you. This is torture in all its manifestations, from psychological to physical. Beatings, hunger, cold, lack of any information, lack of the opportunity to communicate even with other prisoners".

Khyliuk said he was pleased to see Hubbard finally released and heading to the US.

"I understand what it is like to be in terrible captivity. Moreover, it was not his war. He ended up in the wrong place and at the wrong time," he said.

But he described the timing as "shameful PR of the US president, who is losing votes in elections to Congress".

Shyshko said he hoped one day their torturers would face justice.

"Evil must be punished, and so it will be. I have hope for that".

#596. Thunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding predicted for much of Australia

Parts of Queensland, Victoria and South Australia can expect severe storms on Saturday, moving into NSW and Tasmania by Sunday

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Severe thunderstorms and heavy rain will sweep across most Australian states this weekend, adding to the deluge in an already drenched Queensland.

Flash flooding in south-east Queensland this week prompted hundreds of SES callouts and the closure of multiple schools. On Saturday morning, the Bureau of Meteorology had nine flood warnings in place for south Queensland.

The BoM is now warning of severe thunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding across South Australia, Victoria, NSW, Tasmania.

Senior meteorologist at the Bureau of Meteorology, David Crock, said severe thunderstorms and heavy rain were forecast across multiple locations in central and eastern Queensland on Saturday, including Rockhampton, Gladstone, Bundaberg, the Sunshine Coast hinterlands and Roma.

Severe storms could also sweep through parts of Victoria, including Melbourne’s eastern suburbs and central and eastern South Australia. Heavy rain is expected to develop in Tasmania overnight into Sunday morning.

“There’s plenty of rain across the south-east, as well as plenty of showers and storms and rain across much of Queensland as well, after what’s already been a really wet week,” Crock said.

The cold front will move across NSW on Sunday, bringing severe thunderstorms to the west of the state as well as north-eastern Victoria, Sydney and Brisbane.

“Tomorrow is a threat for thunderstorms right across eastern Australia, with severe thunderstorms likely through a wide part of inland eastern Australia,” he said.

This week, multiple areas in Queensland were hit by more than twice their average October rainfall across a few days.

“It was an incredibly wet week in Queensland. Much more typical of summer or January or February than this time of year,” Crock said.

The Sunshine Coast hinterlands and Caboolture were hit by flash flooding and recorded a seven-day rainfall total of 300-400mm of rain, with some areas reaching 450mm.

“It’s been notable how persistent this weather pattern has been, how much moisture has pumped in … then how those rainfall totals have accumulated across seven to 10 days through Queensland and northern New South Wales,” Crock said.

On Thursday, torrential rain in south-east Queensland caused flash flooding, water rescues and hundreds of calls for help while several schools were forced to close on Friday.

Thursday’s heavy rain stretched from Caboolture down to the Border Ranges, with some places copping well over 200mm falls.

The Queensland fire department carried out more than 16 swift-water rescues, including using a raft to retrieve an elderly man clinging to the roof of his vehicle at Caboolture.

#597. Manhunt under way to find prisoner who absconded from medical facility

Met police say Anthony Lloyd, 38, was last seen on Friday in south London, and ‘poses a risk to himself and the public’

A manhunt is under way to locate a prisoner who police say “poses a risk both to himself and the public” after he absconded from a medical facility in London.

Anthony Lloyd forced his way out of a health unit in Lewisham, in south-east London, shortly after 4pm on Friday, the Metropolitan police said.

The force warned the public not to approach Lloyd, but instead to contact 999 if he is spotted.

Lloyd was seen heading in the direction of Catford, police said in a statement on Saturday.

Lloyd was convicted in 2025 of actual bodily harm, according to the Press Association, relating to an incident in Nottinghamshire involving three emergency services workers.

He received a 12-month custodial sentence and was sent to prison. In September he was transferred to the medical facility in Lewisham.

The 38-year-old is white and about 5ft 8in, of medium build with short dark hair.

He was wearing a grey-blue T-shirt, black tracksuit bottoms and white trainers when last seen at about 4.10pm on Friday, police said.

Det supt Melanie Pressley, who is leading the manhunt, said: “We are conducting various significant inquiries to find Lloyd and return him to custody.

“We are concerned he poses a risk both to himself and the public, and would urge anyone who sees him to call 999 immediately. Do not approach him.

“If you have any information – however small – that could help us locate Lloyd, please get in touch with police as a matter of urgency.”

Officers believe Lloyd could be anywhere in the capital. He also has links to Surrey, Sussex, Thames Valley, Hampshire, Nottinghamshire, Derbyshire and Merseyside.

Anyone with information is asked to call 999, quoting the reference CAD4739/23Oct.

#598. Emma Thompson goes under cover... hiding beneath a heavy canoe as she films new Apple TV thriller in London

Published: 01:07 GMT, 25 October 2026 | Updated: 04:01 GMT, 25 October 2026

She won a best actress Oscar playing an elegant intellectual in costume drama Howards End, set in an Edwardian country house.

Now Emma Thompson has found herself in grittier surroundings – hiding beneath an upturned kayak beside Regent’s Canal in London for her latest role as a private investigator.

The actress, 67, was pictured running along the towpath while filming the second series of Apple TV thriller Down Cemetery Road.

Wearing a long black leather coat, grey T-shirt, blue jeans and heavy boots, Dame Emma was spotted sprawled on the leaf-strewn ground as the heavy green boat rested on top of her.

For another shot, she was seen clinging to the concrete edge of the canal before dropping to her knees with her arms outstretched.

The pictures appear to show her character, Zoe Boehm, trying to escape from a man dressed in black. Crew members including her stunt double, wearing an identical outfit and matching grey wig, helped Dame Emma to her feet.

The first series of Down Cemetery Road – written by Slow Horses author Mick Herron – premiered last October. It followed Zoe and art conservator Sarah Trafford, played by Luther actress Ruth Wilson, as they investigated the disappearance of a young girl after a house exploded in Oxford.

The second series is based on The Last Voice You Hear and Smoke And Whispers, written by Herron. It begins with a woman falling in front of a train. Zoe is called in to investigate, but she and Sarah are drawn into the black market for art and antiquities and cross paths with a serial killer.

Apple announced last week that Doc Martin star Martin Clunes and Sherlock’s Amanda Abbington had joined the cast.

#600. MAGA candidate reveals how he feels about Trump constantly talking about his rear

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Jon Husted is currently behind in the polls to Democrat Sherrod Brown

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The Ohio senator who has been the subject of President Donald Trump’s constant praise for his physique has revealed how he feels about the comments.

Twice in recent days, Trump took time during rally speeches to talk about Republican Jon Husted’s “ass.” While appearing Saturday on Fox News, Husted was asked about his reaction to Trump’s comments.

“Well, I have to tell you, when I woke up the next morning after hearing that, I told my wife, I’m like, ‘Hey, I think I got to get down to the gym and keep up my reputation! So, I gotta keep working out,'” Husted said.

The Republican in a tight race added that he is part of an athletic family, as he played college football and his wife runs marathons.

“Well, it got you a lot of headlines. Maybe some that you didn’t expect, but certainly a lot of press,” Fox host Aishah Hasnie quipped.

At rallies in North Carolina and Ohio, Trump talked about Husted’s body.

“But I looked at his ass, and then I looked at his legs,” Trump said. “I said, ‘His ass, s***, it’s like, it’s like a pile of muscle. Then I looked at his legs, and I said, ‘Man, his feet are big.’ Then I looked at his shoulders, and I tapped him on the shoulder, and it actually hurt my hand. He’s like a piece of steel. I said, ‘This guy’s a monster!’”

Trump comments were mocked both online and by TV pundits. CNN’s Anderson Cooper ran a montage of the president talking about other officials’ bodies during one show this week.

The clips included several politicians. At one point, it showed Trump calling Georgia Republican lieutenant gubernatorial nominee Greg Dolezal a “good-looking guy.”

“You’re not allowed to say that about women or men anymore. It’s the end of your political career. But he is a good-looking guy,” Trump said.

Cooper then ended with a quip of his own about Husted and Trump’s comments.

“As for Senator Husted, his ass may be hard, but his polling is soft. According to the latest CNN poll of polls, he’s down five points,” Cooper said.

Husted is running against Democrat Sherrod Brown in a competitive Ohio race. A Cook Political Report poll released this week found Brown up on Husted, 49 percent to 43 percent.

#601. Offensive gegen Huthi: Kampf um Zukunft des Jemen

Jemens Regierungstruppen gehen gegen die Huthi in die Offensive. Doch die Erfolge am Bab al-Mandab sind umstritten. Entscheidend ist, ob die zerstrittenen Gegner der Huthi ihre Kräfte koordinieren können.

Die Bündnispartner haben zugesagt: Im Rahmen des Anfang August gegründeten Mekka-Pakts wollen die Türkei und Pakistan Truppen nach Saudi-Arabien schicken, um das Königreich vor weiteren Angriffen der pro-iranischen Huthi zu schützen. Derweil nimmt die Miliz erneut Ziele in Saudi-Arabien ins Visier. Zugleich verstärkte die von Riad geführte Militärkoalition ihre Luftangriffe im Jemen. Die jemenitischen Regierungstruppen starteten eine groß angelegte Offensive und erzielten nach eigenen Angaben erste Geländegewinne an der strategisch wichtigen Meerenge Bab al-Mandab. Die Huthi weisen dies zurück und konnten zugleich um die im Südwesten des Landes gelegene Stadt Taizz nahe des Roten Meers offenbar weiter vorrücken.

Das Bild bleibt damit widersprüchlich: Während die Regierung am Bab al-Mandab einen Teilerfolg reklamiert, geraten ihre Kräfte bei Taizz selbst unter Druck. Von einem strategischen Durchbruch kann bislang keine Rede sein.

Die beiden jemenitischen Akteure ringen um die politische Macht und territoriale Kontrolle in dem Land. "Letztlich geht es um die Frage, wer die politische Vormachtstellung im Jemen und die Souveränität über das Staatsgebiet und die Bevölkerung ausübt", sagt Philipp Dienstbier, Leiter des Regionalprogramms der Golfstaaten der Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung in Jordanien, im Gespräch mit der DW.

Das Problem der Regierung ist ihre innere Zersplitterung. Zu den Anti-Huthi-Kräften gehören Gruppen mit teils völlig unterschiedlichen politischen Zielen - so etwa der Südliche Übergangsrat, der einen unabhängigen Südjemen anstrebt. Auch in der Region Hadramaut im Osten des Jemen wurden Autonomieforderungen laut.

Diese Fragmentierung erschwert die militärische Koordination erheblich. Die verschiedenen Kräfte seien sich keineswegs wohlgesonnen und verfolgten unterschiedliche Interessen, sagt Jens Heibach, Experte für die Golfregion beim German Institute for Global and Area Studies (GIGA) in Hamburg, im DW-Interview. Darin lägen auch die militärischen Rückschläge der vergangenen Jahre begründet.

Die Huthi hingegen begnügen sich nicht mit territorialen Eroberungen. Raketen, Drohnen, Angriffe auf Schiffe und politische Kommunikation sollen Unsicherheit und Kosten erzeugen und stärkere Gegner - wie etwa Saudi-Arabien - zu Reaktionen zwingen. Mehr als auf taktische Erfolge einzelner Angriffe setzten sie auf deren jeweilige politische und wirtschaftliche Wirkung, schreibt dervom US-Kongress geschaffene Thinktank Irregular Warfare Center.

Besonders wichtig ist dabei der Kampf um Taizz. Die Stadt liegt an wichtigen Verkehrswegen zwischen dem Roten Meer und dem Süden des Landes. Nach Einschätzung des Sana'a Center versuchen die Huthi deshalb vor allem, die Verbindungen zwischen Taizz und den von der Regierung kontrollierten Gebieten zu unterbrechen. Sie müssen dafür nicht unbedingt die Stadt selbst erobern, sondern vor allem die umliegenden Höhenzüge und Verkehrswege kontrollieren.

Damit wollen sie zugleich ihre jüngsten Gewinne an der Küste absichern. Durch die Eroberung des Gebiets am Bab al-Mandab konnten sie in den vergangenen Wochen den Verkehr auf einer der wichtigsten internationalen Schifffahrtsrouten beeinflussen. So konnten sie erheblichen regionalen und internationalen Druck erzeugen, heißt es in einer Studie des britischen Think Tanks Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies (RUSI).

"Die Fähigkeit der Huthi, den Schiffsverkehr zu beeinträchtigen, ist durchaus groß", sagt Heibach. Für diesen Zweck hätten sie die zuletzt eroberten Küstengebiete nicht einmal zwingend benötigt. Die neuen Stellungen erleichterten ihnen allerdings die Überwachung und Kontrolle der Schifffahrt, ergänzt Heibach im Gespräch mit der DW.

Umso mehr gilt es für die Regierung, Taizz zu halten, die Verkehrswege zu sichern und zugleich zu versuchen, die Huthi von der Küste zurückzudrängen. Eine erfolgreiche Gegenoffensive erfordert daher mehr als Luftangriffe. Ohne eine koordinierte Bodenoffensive lassen sich die strategisch wichtigen Höhenzüge und Verkehrswege kaum dauerhaft zurückgewinnen, heißt es in einer Studie des jemenitischen Think Tanks Sanaa Center for Strategic Studies.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Womöglich könnten die Regierungstruppen ihre militärischen Erfolgschancen verbessern, sagt Dienstbier. Saudi-Arabien und die jemenitische Regierung hätten seit Monaten versucht, die bislang stark zersplitterten Regierungskräfte besser zu koordinieren und ihre Kommandostrukturen zu vereinheitlichen. Zusammen mit der saudischen Luftunterstützung könne eine besser funktionierende Bodenstreitmacht nun tatsächlich eine neue Dynamik entwickeln.

Allerdings sei dies nicht der erste Versuch, die vom Iran unterstützten Huthi militärisch zurückzudrängen, sagt Heibach. Bereits im vergangenen Jahr seien Waffen geliefert und Kräfte ausgebildet worden, um eine Offensive vorzubereiten. Die Anti-Huthi-Koalition sei dennoch erneut auseinandergebrochen, während die Huthi selbst in die Offensive gingen. An der grundsätzlichen Ausgangslage habe sich seitdem nicht viel verändert, sagt Heibach.

Auch die bisherigen Erfahrungen sprechen gegen einen schnellen Durchbruch. Selbst die massive amerikanische Operation "Rough Rider" konnte die Huthi trotz wochenlanger Angriffe nicht besiegen. Deshalb hält Heibach wenig davon, die bisherige Strategie aus Luftangriffen und Unterstützung der Anti-Huthi-Kräfte einfach fortzusetzen und auf ein anderes Ergebnis zu hoffen.

Der Mekka-Pakt erweitert zugleich die regionale Dimension. Für Riad geht es damit nicht nur um den Ausgang des jemenitischen Machtkampfs, sondern auch um den Schutz des eigenen Territoriums und der internationalen Handelswege.

Der aktuelle Kampf um Taizz und Bab al-Mandab könnte deshalb ein entscheidender Test sein: für die Fähigkeit der Regierung, ihre Kräfte zu einen - und für die Fähigkeit der Huthi, ihre militärischen Erfolge in dauerhaften politischen Einfluss zu verwandeln.
