#603. Hijab ban at schools in Azerbaijan: What's behind the rare wave of protests?

Girls wearing headscarves have been turned away from schools in Azerbaijan, triggering unusual protests involving children. The government rules do not mention hijabs. Why are schools enforcing unwritten rules?

A dispute over Islamic headscarves in Azerbaijani schools has triggered protests at home and an unusual exchange of criticism between politicians in Azerbaijan and Turkey, two countries whose leaders routinely describe their relationship as that of "one nation, two states". The row has raised questions about religious freedom, sovereignty and the limits of Turkish and Iranian influence in the south Caucasian country.

The unprecedented protests have been taking place across Azerbaijan for a nearly week. Children have demonstrated against the headscarf ban introduced at schools. Among those rallying outside of schools are girls who wear Islamic headscarves; others, including boys, have joined classmates in solidarity.

Rallies in general are rare in a country where police routinely disperse any public protests. But demonstrations involving children are unprecedented in Azerbaijan. As the videos showing the protests started spreading on social media, access to Instagram and TikTok was disrupted in the country, indicating how seriously the authorities are taking the issue. Internet monitors documented blocks; the authorities have not explained their cause.

The dispute follows a series of legal changes. On July 7, Azerbaijan amended its general education law, reinforcing the principle of secular education and requiring pupils and teachers to comply with dress codes. On September 21, the government adopted Resolution No. 309, tightening school uniform rules.

The resolution prohibits additional clothing that disrupts the standard uniform or conflicts with secular education. It does not explicitly mention the hijab ― a Muslim headscarf covering the hair and neck ― or instruct schools to exclude pupils wearing one. But some school administrators have interpreted the rule as applying to hijabs and turned girls covering their heads away. The regulation gives each school's pedagogical council responsibility for resolving compliance issues.

A separate decision on October 6 set dress requirements for teachers. Reports followed of women wearing headscarves being prevented from teaching.

Azerbaijan is a predominantly Muslim country, but Article 18 of its constitution separates religion from the state and requires state education to be secular. Articles 42 and 48 protect the right to education and freedom of conscience.

Supporters of the schools' actions say the same dress rules should apply to all pupils. Critics argue that excluding girls because of religious clothing violates their rights. The dispute cuts across conventional political divisions: some government critics support the restrictions, while some non-religious Azerbaijanis oppose them. School headscarf restrictions also prompted protests in 2010 and subsequent years.

A Baku literature teacher with 40 years of experience, said that girls wearing headscarves were not admitted to classes at the teacher's school. Some removed their scarves; others went home or wanted to study at home. The teacher, who didn't want to be identified by name and provided only the initials M.C., supported enforcing the uniform rules, arguing that children were too young to make decisions about religious dress.

A parent identified as D.A. told DW this was not a nationwide hijab ban, but a matter of school uniforms. Another parent who opposed the restrictions withdrew an interview before publication.

Facebook user Sarraf Cabbarov from Baku posted on his social media account that his daughter Sevil, a primary school teacher in Azerbaijan's capital, was dismissed for refusing to remove her headscarf. He also published a school order issuing her a written warning under the new dress regulations.

On October 12, the Interior Ministry said 37 people had been detained in connection with the protests. According to the ministry's statement, the group had confronted school staff, damaged property and attempted to obstruct school activities and traffic. A criminal case was opened under Article 233, concerning disruption of public order. The ministry did not identify those detained or say whether they included children.

Artist and activist Ilkin Huseynov went missing after launching a project linking volunteer tutors with pupils affected by the restrictions. Local media later reported, citing people close to him, that he had been given 30 days of administrative detention for allegedly disobeying police orders.

Some observers linked the introduction of the new rules for school uniform to the attempts by the Azerbaijani government to counter the influence of neighboring Iran and the growing strength of religious groups within the country. This interpretation is, in essence, echoed by government officials as well, although they stop short of explicitly naming Iran.

Fazil Mustafa, who chairs the Committee for Public Associations and Religious Institutions at Azerbaijan's parliament, said the authorities were concerned about religious groups influenced from abroad and defended the school rules. Allahshukur Pashazade, head of the Caucasus Muslims Office, also warned of outside interference but called for a peaceful solution. The alleged foreign involvement has not been independently established.

Amnesty International condemned the exclusion of girls wearing hijabs and called for the release of anyone detained solely for protesting peacefully.

The controversy has also drawn criticism in Turkey, Azerbaijan's close ally. Protesters gathered outside Azerbaijan's consulate in Istanbul on October 3. Oktay Saral, an adviser to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, criticized the restrictions,saying it's unacceptable to deny education to students wearing headscarves. Azerbaijan's ruling New Azerbaijan Party replied that close relations did not justify interference in its internal affairs.

For affected families, the immediate question remains whether children can attend school without removing their headscarves.

#604. Prix des carburants : "Cette baisse est attendue à compter du 1er novembre", Sébastien Lecornu annonce la signature du décret visant à réduire le prix du litre de gazole de 18 centimes

Article rédigé par Clément Périé

l'essentiel Le Premier ministre Sébastien Lecornu a annoncé ce samedi la signature d'un décret "permettant la libération de 10 millions de barils de gazole". Un décret qui pourrait rapidement avoir des effets sur le prix à la pompe, avec une baisse de 18 centimes envisagée selon le chef du gouvernement.

18 centimes : c'est la baisse du prix annoncé ce samedi 24 octobre par Sébastien Lecornu après la signature d'un décret "permettant la libération de 10 millions de barils de gazole", soit un volume de 1,6 million de m3. Présentée par le chef du gouvernement sur son compte X, cette baisse est attendue "à compter du 1er novembre". Ainsi, sur un plein de 50 litres, cette diminution du prix du gazole représente une économie de 9 euros par rapport aux prix actuels.

Le décret permettant la libération de 10 millions de barils de gazole vient d’être pris. Ces stocks seront mis sur le marché à leur prix d’acquisition, près de quatre fois inférieur au prix actuel du marché. Ils permettront ainsi une baisse du prix du gazole pouvant atteindre 18 centimes par litre. Cette baisse est attendue à compter du 1er novembre. Une garantie : l’intégralité de cet avantage financier devra être répercutée sur le prix payé par les consommateurs. Cette mesure bénéficiera également aux consommateurs de gazole non routier, de gazole pêche, de fioul domestique et de gazole en Outre-mer.

Concrètement, le décret impose aux distributeurs de répercuter intégralement la baisse du prix sur les consommateurs et d'informer ces derniers sur cette baisse. Le décret prévoit par ailleurs une transmission régulière aux autorités de bilans des ventes et des répercussions de la baisse par les distributeurs.

Cette mesure annoncée par le Premier ministre concernera également les "consommateurs de gazole routier, de gazole pêche, de fioul domestique et de gazole en Outre-mer".

À lire aussi : VRAI OU FAUX. Prix des carburants : les 10 millions de barils de gazole libérés par la France feront-ils vraiment baisser les prix "entre 12 à 18 centimes" à la pompe ?

Après cette annonce de libération des stocks stratégiques par Sébastien Lecornu, Patrick Pouyanné, le patron de TotalEnergies, s'était engagé à baisser d'environ 10 centimes le prix du litre de gazole pour les particuliers et de 20 centimes pour le litre de GNR (Gazole non routier).

En parallèle, un autre décret distinct a été publié ce samedi concernant la prolongation du guichet d'aide pour l'achat de gazole non routier pour les travaux agricoles. Pour rappel, il s'agit d'une baisse à hauteur de 15 centimes par litre.

Ces mesures cherchant à diminuer le prix du baril de gazole annoncées par le gouvernement tentent ainsi de répondre aux revendications des manifestations contre la vie chère.

#605. Oil spill washes up on UAE beaches after tanker strike

An oil spill from a tanker attacked near the Strait of Hormuz is spreading along the United Arab Emirates (UAE) coastline, forcing the closure of some beaches and coastal areas.

Satellite images from Monday show the beginnings of the oil spill from a ship matching the location and dimensions of Gem No.2, which was damaged between 9 and 10 October during a record surge of vessel strikes by Iran.

The slick of oil had spread more than 35km (22 miles) from the tanker by Wednesday, the satellite imagery showed.

UAE authorities said on Thursday that the incident is affecting beaches near the northern city of Umm Al Quwain and verified video from Friday shows the oil washing ashore, colouring the water black.

The UAE's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Thursday that it "immediately began containment" in order to "limit environmental impacts".

Prof Steve Widdicombe, director of Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre in the UAE, told BBC Verify it was "inevitable that there will be an impact", but researchers caution it is too soon to assess extent of the damage.

Initially a much smaller oil leak could be seen emerging from the ship on 19 October.

But the slick appears to have rapidly spread over two days, according to radar satellite imagery reviewed by BBC Verify and intelligence firm MAIAR.

Oil spills can cause immediate deaths of marine animals and other organisms, for example by physically trapping turtles, smothering the feathers of seabirds or damaging the gills of fish.

They can also cause longer-lasting damage, Prof Widdicombe said, if species remain exposed to toxic compounds from the oil which could impact their ability to reproduce.

Researchers have cautioned the environmental impact at this stage is very uncertain, as it depends on factors including the volume and type of oil spilled, how quickly it evaporates or breaks down and the effectiveness of the clean-up operation.

But the spill does extend towards Siniyah and Khor Al Beidah islands, a globally recognised Key Biodiversity Area containing habitats like corals, seagrasses and saltmarshes, as well as species including green turtles and the critically endangered Halavi guitarfish.

The proximity of the spill to this area is the "most concerning environmental angle", according to Eoghan Darbyshire, a scientist at the Conflict and Environment Observatory.

BBC Verify analysis of the dimensions and location of the ship indicate they match a crude oil tanker called Gem No.2.

Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard reported the Panama-flagged tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile" on 9 October, just north of the town of Al Jazeera Al Hamra, causing a fire on board that was later extinguished.

Verified footage first posted on social media on 10 October showed the crew running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rose over the ship.

Iranian state media shared footage of a ship matching Gem No.2 which appeared to show the vessel on fire with burning oil spilling into the sea.

The ship had been attempting to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an "unauthorized and dangerous route", according to state media.

All 22 Indian crew members were rescued, the Indian consulate in Dubai said on 11 October.

Gem No.2 is one of a record number of ships that reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz at the start of October.

Security experts told BBC Verify this was part of an Iranian effort to assert greater control over the strait, in response to the US military successfully escorting more vessels through the vital shipping lane.

Tankers and other commercial vessels have come under attack from both Iranian and US forces in and around the Strait of Hormuz amid the conflict between the two countries.

Another major oil slick washed up on the shores of Iran's Qeshm Island in August, which experts said threatened wildlife, protected ecosystems and fishing communities.

#606. Ukraine’s military says Starlink satellite connection stable after recent restrictions

But Elon Musk, whose company SpaceX owns Starlink, accuses Ukrainian military of violating ⁠the company’s terms

Ukraine’s military has a “stable connection to Starlink”, the Ukrainian government said, 10 days after its ability to use the satellite communications system was suddenly restricted.

But hours after the announcement, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, whose company owns Starlink, accused the Ukrainian military of violating ⁠the company’s terms. Neither Musk nor the US government, which operates Starshield using Starlink technology, took responsibility for imposing the curbs.

“Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for ⁠offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week,” Musk said in a social media post.

Serhiy Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian presidential adviser, said on the Telegram app that the country is “physically unable” to use Starlink for long- and medium-range attack drone operations.

Ukraine’s general staff and defence ministry did not immediately comment.

The Starlink satellite terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations. Sudden speed restrictions on the terminals, which capped operations at speeds of 160km/h (99mph), led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions earlier this month.

The military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones was hampered and some Ukrainian operations to strike behind enemy frontlines were cancelled. Russia was able to launch ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US.

The speed restrictions coincided with the announcement by Donald Trump of a US deal to buy Russian diesel, although the US president initially denied that his administration was behind the decision to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

“I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said, referring to Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive.

However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to throw suspicion on Musk when he defended Trump last Wednesday. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk,” Rubio said. “That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.”

Musk was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus [president of the United States],” he wrote.

The US vice-president, JD Vance, backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blamed both parties: “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed … And technically, SpaceX did it.”

There were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in EU countries and that they applied only to Ukraine, he added. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”

A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day

He said the decision would “bring a lot of human losses … of course people would die”.

Announcing the restoration of the system on Saturday in a diplomatic video address on the Telegram app, Zelenskyy expressed his gratitude to his US allies, including Trump and the US state department, for resolving the operational issue: “The most important development for ‌today is that Starlink ‌and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the ‌level we need.”

The restoration began overnight. “By this morning, the speeds were already sufficient for operational use,” Zelenskyy said. “This is very important and significant for our frontline logistics and for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shaheds.”

On Thursday, Trump had claimed the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning.

When asked by reporters whether he would tell Musk to stop “messing around” with Ukraine’s access to Starlink on Friday, the US president said: “I’ve not spoken to him. I might have to … I’ve heard it was fixed. But if it’s not, I’ll speak to him … If there is a problem, I’ll get it straightened out.”

He then described Musk as a “very brilliant” and “very good” person.

#607. ‘Bolso shows all signs of fascism’: the journalist who predicted Brazil’s future – and paid the ultimate price

Dom Phillips warned that Jair Bolsonaro would make life more dangerous for reporters and the Amazon rainforest, and that his sons were even more extreme

“Bolso shows all signs of fascism, as do his supporters,” the murdered British journalist Dom Phillips told me before his death. “His sons are all more extreme if anything.”

These words were written in 2018 by the Guardian contributor shortly before the election of the far-right former army captain Jair Bolsonaro as president of Brazil – a prospect that Dom viewed with dread.

As he predicted back then, this would lead to more mortalities, more destruction of the Amazon rainforest and more danger for journalists. His own life and death were to prove the prescience of this foresight.

Dom was killed four years ago alongside the Brazilian indigenous expert Bruno Pereira, but his views feel alarmingly relevant once more as Brazil braces for a presidential runoff this Sunday in which a member of the far-right Bolsonaro clan is once more a favourite to win – despite all the dangers that poses to the environment and those who seek to protect it.

Polls suggest Flávio Bolsonaro – the son of Jair Bolsonaro – is narrowly ahead of the Workers party incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Although the difference between them is within the margin of error and Lula appears to have gained momentum, the possibility of another Bolsonaro administration is likely to fill any friends of Dom and Bruno with alarm.

Dom was no diehard political leftist. In an earlier election, he shocked me by expressing support for the centre-right challenger Aécio Neves because he felt the then Workers party administration had become too entangled in corruption. But while Dom eschewed ideology, he had clear ideas about the importance of sound, considerate government in the interests of people and the planet.

He saw the Bolsonaro family as a menace to both. Looking back through our exchanges of WhatsApp messages, I am struck by the prescience of his observations.

Some may be inclined to normalise Flávio as just another candidate, or to assume that all politicians are as bad as each other. That was certainly not how Dom saw things – and he came to pay the ultimate price for his efforts to address those concerns.

“I don’t think I have ever been so negative about Brazil’s future. Spent a week in Manaus, everyone seemed to be voting for Bolsonaro,” he wrote ahead of the first-round vote in 2018. “ If he wins, what would it be like living here? It’s like a ‘carte blanche’ to attack anyone his mob disagrees with.”

Two weeks later, he observed the creeping hostility towards the media at a Bolsonaro press conference, which he said was packed with rightwing supporters who loudly booed a journalist that they considered unfriendly.

This followed a physical attack on the organiser of an anti-Bolsonaro women’s group. “Chilling times here,” he wrote on 12 October of that year.

“I agree that Bolso shows all signs of fascism, as do his supporters.

“This is a very dark and worrying period and it is only going to get worse. My sense if [sic] that it is also going to become more dangerous for journalists.”

He detailed the changes he was already seeing – the proliferation of lies, a hardening of discourse online and a rising sense that violence was acceptable. He predicted more people would die as a result of Bolsonaro’s policies, and the wider environment would also pay a heavy price.

Over the following years, Dom’s reports for the Guardian confirmed his worst fears. Bolsonaro’s mismanaged response to the Covid crisis contributed to more than 704,000 deaths – the second highest toll in the world after the US.

His four years in power saw the highest level of Amazon deforestation of any presidential terms. Orwellian misinformation campaignsincluded efforts to blame environmental groups for forest fires and to boast – contrary to all the evidence – that his government was saving the Amazon.

In August 2019, Dom told me these claims were “staggering even by Bolsonaro standards, especially given Flávio Bolsonaro’s bill to get rid of legal reserves”, the latter a reference to a proposal by the then president’s son – and now presidential candidate – to remove one of the greatest protections for the rainforest.

Dom also came under social media attack after he politely asked the president about Amazon deforestation at a press conference. Bolsonaro snapped back, “the Amazon is Brazil’s, not yours, OK?” – a reply that was instantly spread across networks to suggest the nationalist had bested the foreigner.

Dom felt he had been set up. “The smile doesn’t last for long,” he observed. “Wonder how much of the Amazon will be gone by the end of Bolsonaro’s first term?”

That answer to that question would be 45,000 sq km (17,400 sq miles) over Bolsonaro’s 2019-2022 period in office, roughly equivalent to the loss of more than a million trees a day, and 59.5% higher than the previous four years.

Dom never got to report on that. He too was cut down, murdered alongside Bruno on 5 May 2022 close to the Javari Valley indigenous territory while he was researching a book titled How to Save the Amazon.

The man who confessed to their killing was a fisher named Amarildo da Costa de Oliveira, who is now on trial. He apparently resented Bruno’s efforts to prevent him invading the indigenous territory, incursions that were illegal but encouraged by the president’s weakening of protections, rhetoric against environmental groups and tacit acceptance of lawlessness. As Dom had foreseen, Bolsonaro had made life more dangerous for journalists and the forest.

Jair Bolsonaro lost office later that year and was then convicted for attempting a military coup to overturn the election results. Dom had also anticipated this: “He is a criminal and I sincerely hope one day I see him being arrested by those federal police guys in the balaclavas in black,” he wrote in 2021.

I am sure Dom would have been cheered by last week’s government announcement of record low deforestation in the Amazon and the neighbouring Cerrado savanna thanks to strong enforcement during Lula’s current four-year term.

Such gains look precarious now that one of Bolsonaro’s “more extreme” sons is frontrunner in the presidential runoff and has promised, if he wins, to free his father and give him any job of his choice in the government.

Is there time for Lula to turn this around? How much worse could a second Bolsonaro family administration be? How much life – people, trees and other species – will die if they return to power?

I wish Dom were still around to discuss that.

#608. Obama unloads on Trump over the Iran war and mocks the president’s diplomatic strategy

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Obama bashed Trump for causing fuel prices to surge and what he saw as the unnecessary deaths of service members in a war that has raged on for nearly eight months

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Former Democratic President Barack Obama has unloaded on Donald Trump for the Iran war, mocking the Republican president’s diplomatic strategy.

“These are not serious people. They’re not serious people. And the problem is you end up having to pay the price for their lack of seriousness,” Obama said Saturday while stumping for Democrats in Ohio.

The U.S., alongside Israel, started launching strikes against Iran in late February, with Trump claiming that Americans were in imminent danger over the Middle Eastern country’s nuclear ambitions.

But Obama argued that the issue had already been dealt with under his administration — until Trump unraveled it.

“Let’s think about this Iran war. The original rationale was, we’re going to go in there and get them to give up their nuclear program, their nuclear weapons,” Obama said. “Now, the thing was, Iran didn’t have nuclear weapons, because I put a deal in place that everybody acknowledged — kept them from getting nukes. And I didn’t have to fire a missile to do it; I just had to engage in diplomacy.”

Obama was referring to the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action, commonly called the Iran Nuclear Deal, which the Middle Eastern country signed in 2015 and Trump withdrew from during his first term.

The deal restricted Iran’s nuclear program to ensure it was only using those materials for peaceful purposes in exchange for sanctions relief.

But Trump argued when withdrawing from the deal in 2018 that it “allowed Iran to continue enriching uranium and — over time — reach the brink of a nuclear breakout.”

Trump has insisted throughout the war that it would be a quick operation, but it has now dragged on for nearly eight months. Soon after the strikes began, Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, blocking oil tankers from passing through the vital passageway and causing fuel prices to skyrocket.

A total of 21 American service members have been killed and 865 wounded in operations related to the war, according to the Pentagon.

“So seven months later, how’s that war going?” Obama asked.

“Our allies and our bases have been attacked; Americans have been killed; hundreds of Americans have been wounded; we have, we’ve run down our stock of missiles,” the former president said, though Trump has denied reports of munitions shortages. “And Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz, where oil goes through to the world market.

“This is the reason why the price of oil is up. Nobody disputes that. This is reason the price diesel is up. This is why the reason the just about everything is up.”

Trump is hosting daily rallies across the country to boost Republicans’ chances of keeping control of Congress in November’s midterm elections — all while dealing with his deeply unpopular war.

Forty-seven percent of Democrat voters and 56 percent of Republican voters think ending the war in Iran should be one of the highest priorities for the next Congress, according to a new AP/NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll.

Obama was in Cleveland Saturday to support Amy Acton, who is running for Ohio governor against Trump ally Vivek Ramaswamy, and former Senator Sherrod Brown, who is running against Republican Senator Jon Husted.

Ramaswamy saw his betting odds plummet over a controversial ad using his opponent’s mother, whom Acton has accused of abuse, to call her a “liar” and urge Ohians not to vote for her.

Acton has an 83 percent chance of winning the race compared to Ramaswamy’s 18 percent on the prediction market Polymarket as of Saturday evening.

Ramaswamy was also trailing Acton by seven points in a traditional poll. Acton had 50 percent of support among likely Ohio voters compared to Ramaswamy’s 43 percent, according to a recent survey conducted by Marist Poll before the campaign ad was released.

In that same poll, Brown was up four points with 48 percent of voter support compared to Husted’s 44 percent.

#611. Fireworks and tear gas as protesters and riot police clash in Paris

Police have clashed with protesters in Paris as some demonstrations in France turned violent on Saturday.

A largely peaceful day of protests turned into unrest after nightfall, as protesters were seen throwing objects and fireworks at police.

Around 70,000 officers were deployed across France for a second consecutive weekend and used tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds.

The Interior Ministry estimated around 400,000 people took part in Saturday's demonstrations, with nearly 1,000 arrests made.

Europe correspondent Nick Beake reports from Paris, where he says there are few signs the unrest will ease soon.

#612. Serbien: Droht Vucic ein Schicksal wie Milosevic?

Vor 26 Jahren stürzten Serbiens Bürger den Autokraten Slobodan Milosevic. Nun stehen entscheidende Wahlen bevor. Der heutige starke Mann des Landes, Aleksandar Vucic, möchte eine Wiederholung dieser Geschichte vermeiden.

"Es kommen Zeiten, in denen der ganze gesellschaftliche Bodensatz, der ganze Schlamm, alles Schlechte in einer Gesellschaft an die Oberfläche steigt", sagte Aleksandar Vucic einmal über den 5. Oktober 2000. "Diese Lektionen haben wir durchlebt und gelernt. Deshalb besiegen wir sie."

Der 5. Oktober 2000 ist und bleibt das größte politische Trauma des Langzeit-Herrschers Serbiens. Damals zwangen Bürger auf den Straßen den Autokraten und Kriegsherrn Slobodan Milosevic, seine Wahlniederlage anzuerkennen. Besiegt wurde er von einer bunten Koalition demokratischer Splitterparteien.

Vucic stand im Jahr 2000 auf der anderen Seite: Als Mitglied von Milosevics Koalitionspartner, der extremistischen Serbischen Radikalen Partei und Informationsminister der Regierung in Serbiens Hauptstadt Belgrad war er vor allem zuständig für Zensur.

Was Wunder, dass die demokratische Wende Serbiens vor 26 Jahren für den heutigen Strongman des Landes ein wunder Punkt blieb. Umso mehr, weil Vucic heute selbst in Milosevics Lage geraten könnte. Vor Kurzem trat er als Präsident zurück. Bei den am 25. Oktober anstehenden Wahlen will er nun als Spitzenkandidat seiner Serbischen Fortschrittspartei ins Amt des Ministerpräsidenten gewählt werden.

"Diese Wahl ist ein Referendum", sagt der Politikwissenschaftler und Meinungsforscher Dusan Lj. Milenkovic. "Für Serbien gibt es in den kommenden Jahrzehnten nur zwei Wege: entweder die Befreiung von der autokratischen Herrschaft Aleksandar Vucics oder Jahrzehnte unter Repression und Diktatur."

Diesmal kommt die Herausforderung für Vucic nicht von einer geeinten demokratischen Opposition. Sie kommt von Studenten. Die "Studentenliste" ist aus einer großen Protestbewegung gegen Machtmissbrauch und Korruption hervorgegangen. Monatelang blockierten die Studenten die großen Universitäten des Landes. Auslöser war der Einsturz des Vordachs am frisch renovierten Bahnhof von Novi Sad Ende 2024, bei dem 16 Menschen starben.

Als Kandidaten wählten die Studenten angesehene Professoren, Aktivisten und bekannte Persönlichkeiten. Berufspolitiker sucht man auf der Liste vergeblich. Nach Jahren, in denen eine zerstrittene Opposition Vucics Macht nicht einmal ankratzen konnte, scheint die Strategie aufzugehen: Eine der jüngsten Umfragen sieht die Studenten bei 44,4 Prozent, Vucics Lager bei 41,7 Prozent. Inzwischen haben sich die meisten Oppositionsparteien aus dem Rennen zurückgezogen und unterstützen die Studenten.

Andere Umfragen, erstellt von regierungsnahen Instituten, sagen dagegen einen komfortablen Sieg Vucics voraus. Doch in Serbien, wo das Vertrauen in Institutionen und Medien einen historischen Tiefstand erreicht hat, glaubt man auch Umfragen nur bedingt.

Der frühere Ministerpräsident Zoran Zivkovic spricht von einer "Referendumsstimmung". Er gehörte 2000 zur siegreichen Koalition. 2003 übernahm er das Amt des ersten demokratischen Ministerpräsidenten Zoran Djindjic, nachdem dieser bei einem Attentat ermordet worden war.

"Damals gab es eine echte, gut organisierte Opposition", sagt Zivkovic der DW. "Leider sieht die Opposition in Serbien heute aus wie Dinosaurier im 21. Jahrhundert. Entweder existiert sie nicht mehr oder sie hat sich an das Regime verkauft. In jedem Fall trägt sie nicht dazu bei, dass Serbien wieder ein Staat der Ehrlichkeit und des Rechts wird."

Die Enttäuschung über die Opposition ist ein Grund für den Aufstieg der Studentenbewegung. Der andere liegt bei Vucic selbst: Dem Machthaber, der das Westbalkanland zwischen Europäischer Union, Russland und China navigiert, werden Kontrolle der Medien, der Ausverkauf natürlicher Ressourcen und Verbindungen zur organisierten Kriminalität vorgeworfen.

Die heutige Protestbewegung hat jene von 2000 lange übertroffen. Damals gingen die Bürger zwei Wochen lang auf die Straße. Milosevic gab seine Niederlage erst zu, nachdem ihm Armee und Teile der Polizei die Gefolgschaft verweigert hatten. Sein Machtapparat zerfiel.

Das heutige Serbien ist allerdings nicht mehr das Land von damals. Es ist nicht das Serbien nach einem Jahrzehnt blutiger Kriege beim Zerfall Jugoslawiens, nach Kriegsverbrechen, Sanktionen, galoppierender Inflation und den NATO-Bombardierungen von 1999 auf dem Höhepunkt des Kosovo-Konflikts.

Erst nach dem 5. Oktober 2000 wurde das damalige Rest-Jugoslawien - bestehend aus Serbien und Montenegro - wieder Mitglied der Vereinten Nationen. Löhne und Renten wurden wieder regelmäßig ausgezahlt. Ein großer Teil der Auslandsschulden wurde erlassen.

"Vucic hat sich immer bemüht, all diese Errungenschaften des 5. Oktober zu verneinen", sagt Milenkovic der DW. "Das war politisch opportun. Wie viele Politiker mit so viel Macht will er seine Sicht der Dinge im serbischen kollektiven Gedächtnis verankern."

Dabei beschwören nicht nur die Gegner der Regierung die Erinnerung an den 5. Oktober. Auch Vucic selbst greift seit Jahren auf die Rhetorik der Milosevic-Ära zurück. Kritiker nennt er "ausländische Söldner", "Terroristen" und "Faschisten". Den Aufstand gegen ihn bezeichnet er als vom Westen importierte "Farbrevolution". Über die großen Boulevardmedien und fast alle Fernsehsender Serbiens werden diese Begriffe immer wieder unter die Bevölkerung gebracht.

Doch die klassischen nationalistischen Narrative und Fragen wie die nach Serbiens Weg nach Osten oder Westen, also in die Europäische Union oder in ein Bündnis mit der "orthodoxen Mutter" Russland spielen für die Studentenliste keine Rolle. Sie vereint Liberale und Nationalisten, Linke und Rechte. Die Liste ist ein Vehikel für den Machtwechsel. Ihre Themen: der Kampf gegen Kriminalität und die Achtung des Gesetzes.

Ex-Ministerpräsident Zoran Zivkovic hat einen Rat: "Schon jetzt müssen die Mitglieder der neuen Regierung bereit sein und wissen, was sie am Tag nach der Machtübernahme tun, sieben Tage später, einen Monat später. Innerhalb eines Jahres müssen alle Reformen umgesetzt werden. Danach muss es echte demokratische Wahlen geben, bei denen jeder sein eigenes Programm anbietet."

Besonders wichtig sei die Lustration - also der Ausschluss all jener aus der Politik, die am alten Regime beteiligt waren. "Diejenigen, die heute an der Macht sind, sollten sich nicht einmal für den Verwaltungsrat ihres Wohnhauses zur Wahl stellen dürfen", sagt Zivkovic.

Die Studenten führen ihren Wahlkampf vor allem über soziale Netzwerke und von Tür zu Tür. Und sie machen keinen Hehl daraus, wie sie sich Vucics Schicksal im Falle eines Sieges vorstellen. In einem ihrer viralen Spots ist ein einsamer Vucic zu sehen. Dazu hört man seine Selbstlobreden. Dann ein Schnitt: Ein Mann, dessen Gesicht nicht zu sehen ist, schrubbt einen Gefängnisflur.

Bis zu einem Prozess gegen Aleksandar Vucic ist es noch ein weiter Weg. Vorerst fürchten die Gegner der serbischen Regierung Wahlmanipulationen. Vielleicht auch offene Gewalt, wie sie Polizei und regierungsnahe Schläger während der Proteste immer wieder angewandt haben.

Jovo Bakic, Soziologieprofessor in Belgrad und Kandidat der Studentenliste, sagt, er sei vom Sieg überzeugt. Ebenso überzeugt sei er davon, dass Vucic eine Niederlage nicht anerkennen werde - genau wie einst Milosevic. Doch die Studenten hätten auch für diesen Fall einen Plan, sagte Bakic dem Magazin Vreme. Welchen? Er lachte. "Das kann ich nicht verraten."

Offenbar bereitet sich ein großer Teil der Regierungsgegner bereits auf die Zeit nach den Wahlen vor: auf den Kampf um eine faire Auszählung der Stimmen und die Anerkennung des Ergebnisses. Gewiss ist derweil nur eines: Serbien steht vor der am wenigsten vorhersehbaren Urnengang seit dem Jahr 2000.

#613. Elle payait ses courses et ses factures avec l'argent d'une ligue de sport pour enfants : après avoir détourné plus de 65 000 euros, elle est licenciée par la ville qui l'employait

l'essentiel Une femme a reconnu avoir détourné près de 73 000 dollars, soit un peu plus de 65 000 euros, d'une association organisant des activités sportives pour les enfants, dont elle se servait pour régler différentes dépenses personnelles, comme ses courses et ses factures en passant par diverses commandes en ligne. Pendant plus d'un an, elle semble avoir profité d'une faille étonnante dans la gestion du compte bancaire de l'association, qui était censé avoir été fermé. Employée au service des espaces verts de sa ville, elle a été licenciée suite à ses aveux.

Heather Spier a fini par avouer son crime. Cette résidente d'Huntsville (Alabama) a reconnu avoir détourné, sur une période de seize mois entre fin 2022 et début 2024, la somme de 73 000 dollars (un peu plus de 65 000 euros) du compte de la Huntsville Eastern League, une association qui organise des activités sportives pour les enfants.

Les relevés bancaires du compte de l'association font apparaître des dépenses variées, ne correspondant évidemment pas à celles que pourrait avoir une ligue de sport pour enfants. L'enquête a notamment mis au jour plus de 11 000 dollars de dépenses sur le site du géant du commerce en ligne Amazon, 4 000 dollars consacrés à des factures d'électricité ou d'assurance, 600 dollars de commande de repas dans différents restaurants, 30 000 dollars retirés dans des distributeurs automatiques et même un billet de cinéma. "Cela ne ressemble pas au compte bancaire d’une association. Cela ressemble à un compte personnel, comme celui que vous ou moi pourrions avoir" a déclaré Macky Outlaw, un enquêteur privé cité par WAFF. L'association fonctionne en partie grâce à de l'argent public, puisqu'elle reçoit des subventions de la ville d'Huntsville.

Comment Heather Spier a-t-elle pu détourner tout cet argent pendant si longtemps ? Selon les premiers éléments de l'enquête, il semble qu'elle ait été la seule personne à avoir eu accès au compte de l'association, qui était supposé avoir été fermé en 2022. Le conseil d'administration avait décidé d'en ouvrir un nouveau et de vider l'ancien, ce qui n'a vraisemblablement pas été le cas. Il se pourrait même que Heather Spier ait détourné plus que 73 000 dollars : sur la période, 245 000 dollars ont transité via le compte de l'association. "Si nous avions pu prouver qu’elle avait pris davantage d’argent, le montant aurait été plus élevé, mais c’est ce que nous pouvions prouver" a déclaré Tim Gann, procureur adjoint du comté de Madison. Plus étonnant encore, à ce jour, rien ne relie Heather Spier à l'association sportive.

Ces dernières années, Heather Spier était employée par la ville d'Huntsville, au service des espaces verts. Si elle a conservé son poste durant la procédure judiciaire, elle a été immédiatement licenciée après son plaidoyer de culpabilité, le 21 octobre. Inculpée en 2024, Heather Spier a pu conserver son emploi durant la procédure, notamment pour mettre de l'argent de côté et rembourser l'association en cas de condamnation. Ce qui a donc été le cas. Heather Spier a été condamnée à deux ans de probation, 46 mois de prison avec sursis et le remboursement des 73 000 dollars à l'association dans les sept jours suivant le verdict, ce qui a bien été fait, ont confirmé les procureurs.

#614. The Bundestag has debated the genocide Germany carried out in Namibia a century ago. But will it spur progress on addressing colonial crimes?

Opposition parties have forced a debate in the Bundestag on the early-20th-century genocide Germany carried out in Namibia. Will this finally spur progress in addressing colonial crimes?

Gaob Daniel Timotheus Frederick was sitting in the front row of the visitors' gallery in the Bundestag this week. Wearing a suit and hat, he had traveled all the way from Namibia to see this parliamentary debate unfold. For almost 120 years, his family had been waiting for the return of human remains of their ancestor, Cornelius Frederick (sometimes spelled Fredericks), who had led the Nama resistance against German colonial rule and died on Shark Island in Germany's first concentration camp.

In the name of his great-grandfather and as a member of the Nama Traditional Leaders Association (NTLA), Frederick was there to demand an "unconditioned apology" from Germany.

Sitting next to him, in uniform and white gloves, with a carved lion on the handle of his walking stick, was the head of the Ovaherero Traditional Authority, Paramount Chief Mutjinde Katjiua. Speaking before the Bundestag debate, the chief said: "We call upon the Bundestag to recognize unequivocally the genocides committed against the Ovaherero and Nama peoples."

Many people wonder why the German parliament hasn't already done this — and why the government has not yet issued an official apology. There is a draft joint declaration with Namibia in which the German government acknowledges that "from today's perspective, [it] would be called genocide." But there is no German-Namibian reconciliation agreement. The evidence is overwhelming: From 1904 to 1908, the German Empire waged a war of extermination against the Indigenous people of southwestern Africa, including the Ovaherero (also known as the Herero), the Nama, the Damara and the San. At least 100,000 people were killed, and just as many displaced. Many were subjected to forced labor and forced prostitution. The land seizures and expropriation carried out at the time continue to affect their descendants today.

Jürgen Zimmerer, a professor of history at the University of Hamburg whose research focuses on Africa, told DW that the Bundestag and government lack the will to confront this era in German history. "There are Bundestag resolutions on the Armenian genocide, one on the Holodomor [in Ukraine], and one on the genocide against the Yazidis [by the "Islamic State" in Iraq]. But there is no recognition of the genocide against the Herero and Nama by the German Bundestag." If there were any political will to do so, Zimmerer said, it could happen very quickly.

The socialist Left Party initiated the Bundestag debate by drafting a resolution calling for full recognition and compensation in collaboration with representatives of the descendants. The goal: "restorative justice." Paramount Chief Katjiua has rejected the existing agreement between the Namibian and German governments. "Development aid cannot substitute for comprehensive reparations," he said.

Since 2021, the governments have been negotiating a joint declaration that pledges €1.1 billion ($1.24 billion) in reconstruction aid to Namibia over 30 years. Once the agreement is signed, Germany's president is set to issue a formal apology.

But the Foreign Ministry warned: "Legal claims to compensation cannot be derived from the recognition of genocide. With these negotiations — which are unique worldwide — Namibia and Germany have broken new ground and are pioneers in confronting their colonial past."

Political scientist Andreas Mehler, the director of the Anton Bergstraesser Institute at the University of Freiburg, said the government's plan sounded like "checkbook diplomacy."

Zimmerer also said there was a financial calculation: "If we were to recognize an obligation to provide reparations to the families of those killed — given the millions of victims of World War II, the victims of the Germans — it would ruin us."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Four lines in the 144 pages of the coalition agreement of the current German government — between the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU)/Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — summarize the extent of the government's commitment to reconciliation with Namibia.

"We will intensify our efforts to come to terms with colonialism," the text reads. "This includes transnational research into artifacts and the restitution of cultural property in dialogue with the countries of origin. Particular attention will be paid to establishing a dignified memorial site and the repatriation of human remains."

Compared with the efforts to address colonialism led by the SPD-led government from 2021 to 2025, "the issue has lost visibility," said Alexander Stroh-Steckelberg, a professor of political scientist at the University of Bayreuth who specializes in Africa.

Zimmerer has an even more critical take: "I wouldn't even call it a stalemate anymore. I believe this government is rolling back the progress that has been made in terms of raising awareness of colonial injustices."

Much remains to be done, as far the descendants of the Ovaherero are concerned: The remains of tens of thousands of people are believed to still be in Germany. Gaob D. Timotheus Frederick and other descendants of the victims have been fighting to heal these wounds for generations.

In March, Germany established a coordination council, headed by the Foreign Ministry, which stated that the government did not wish to "dictate to the countries and societies of origin which cultural artifacts and human remains they should reclaim, what priorities they should set or how restitutions should be handled."

Serap Güler, a state minister in the Foreign Ministry and the chair of the coordination council, defends the government's actions so far. Recounting her own official trips — she has already been to Togo, and next week she plans to travel to Rwanda and Burundi — she said: "Everywhere I go, I receive recognition for our sincere and trusting approach to the past — as well as for our determined commitment to a future of freedom, security and prosperity."

Zimmerer said Germany "has earned a reputation as a country that takes a critical view of its own history and learns from its mistakes" — which gives it "enormous cultural capital" on the world stage. But he is concerned that this capital is currently being squandered.

The government's memorial policy does not appear to address colonialism. Zimmerer even detects an attempt to "marginalize German colonial crimes" in the recent proposal by Minister of State for Culture Wolfram Weimer to create a dignified memorial site in Bremen. He notes that victim groups have not been included in Weimer's proposal and said the colonial capitals of the German Empire — Berlin and Hamburg — must also become sites of remembrance.

Ninety-five percent of the colonial troops set sail from Hamburg's Baakenhafen, including Commander Lothar von Trotha, who issued the orders to exterminate the Ovaherero and Nama. According to Zimmerer, the fact that a new opera house — rather than a memorial site — is being built at Baakenhafen constitutes a staggering case of "art-washing of history." Mehler also hopes that a productive debate on memorial sites will still take place and that, overall, "many more places will come to terms with colonial history."

Meanwhile, Gaob D. Timotheus Frederick continues to call for a collective effort to come to terms with the past: "Let us give opportunity to the affected communities that are being represented by us to have a seat on the table to discuss with them the rest of the way."

This article was originally written in German.

#615. I paid to have my son's tonsils removed when the NHS refused. It's saved him from the misery of repeat infections. Hospitals now say it's too expensive and unnecessary - despite doctors' concerns for children. Here's what you need to know

Published: 01:00 GMT, 25 October 2026 | Updated: 04:00 GMT, 25 October 2026

It was once one of the most common operations performed in Britain. For much of the 20th century, tonsillectomies – in which the tonsils, two fleshy mounds at the back of the throat, are cut out to stop repeated infections – were practically a rite of passage for children.

The legendary James Bond actor Sir Roger Moore recalled in his autobiography how, as a boy growing up in 1930s London, doctors decided to remove his tonsils after a bout of mumps and a ‘raging sore throat’. ‘I wasn’t really too sure what this would entail,’ said Sir Roger, ‘but was promised that when I woke up I would be fed ice cream.’

Sir Roger was one of some 200,000 patients – the vast majority of them children – who at the time went under the knife every year.

Today, fewer than 27,000 patients have their tonsils removed on the NHS each year – in large part because it now classes the operation as a ‘low clinical priority intervention’.

Experts agree not every child who suffers tonsillitis needs surgery. For most, the infections become less frequent with age – peaking between the ages of five and 15. And the operation is not without risk – bleeding afterwards is common, and in very rare cases it can be fatal [see panel on right].

However, a growing number of experts argue that the NHS rules are now far too strict, and that, in some parts of the country, many patients who do qualify are being turned away. They say thousands of children are needlessly suffering repeated infections, missing long stretches of school or ending up in hospital seriously ill.

Today, fewer than 27,000 patients have their tonsils removed on the NHS each year – in large part because it now classes the operation as a ‘low clinical priority intervention

Rebecca Davies decided to have her son Taron's tonsils removed after he had ten bouts of tonsilitis last year and was not eligible to have the procedure done on the NHS

Little wonder, then, that more and more parents are choosing to go private. Families who spoke to The Mail on Sunday said paying for the operation – which costs about £3,000 – was worth it to end their child’s suffering.

So when is the op right for your child – and is it fair that the NHS makes it so hard to get?

First, it helps to understand exactly what tonsillitis is.

The tonsils form part of the body’s first line of defence against germs, but they can themselves become infected and inflamed, causing a severe sore throat, pain when swallowing, fever and swollen glands.

Most cases are caused by viruses and clear up on their own within a week. But a significant minority are caused by bacteria, most often group A streptococcus, or strep A, and these are usually treated with antibiotics.

Until the 1980s, the operation was carried out almost on demand. But a US study led by the paediatrician Dr Jack Paradise at the Children’s Hospital of Pittsburgh, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1984, called into question whether so many children really needed it.

It followed children with frequent, severe throat infections, half of whom had their tonsils removed. To qualify, patients needed to have suffered seven or more documented bouts of tonsillitis in a single year, five or more a year for two years, or three or more a year for three years – the ‘3, 5, 7 rule’.

Those who had surgery did suffer fewer infections – an average of two in the following year, compared with three in those who did not – but the benefit was modest and faded over time.

The findings shaped NHS guidance, and the ‘3, 5, 7 rule’ became the official criteria for who was eligible – with a few exceptions, including recurrent quinsy, a serious complication in which abscesses form.

Experts have long argued that the rule is unscientific, in large part because Dr Paradise decided the criteria himself. It was not based on any prior research.

Most tonsilitis cases are caused by viruses and clear up on their own within a week. But a significant minority are caused by bacteria, most often group A streptococcus, or strep A

Then, in 2019, the NHS went a step further, putting tonsillectomies on a list of treatments to be rationed – alongside breast reductions and removing harmless skin lesions – in an effort to save £200million.

But experts say these criteria are arguably too strict.

‘I’m concerned the current guidelines make it harder than it could be for patients with severe tonsillitis to be offered this procedure,’ says Mr James O’Hara, a consultant ear, nose and throat surgeon and researcher at Newcastle University. ‘The NHS has to consider the cost-effectiveness of tonsillectomies to society, but the guidelines don’t take into account the potential impact of the illness on the lives of children and their parents.

‘For the child it’s a miserable illness, but there may be a financial cost for the family. When a child gets regular bouts of tonsillitis, their parents may end up having to take time off work to care for them, meaning they can lose out on pay. That can really add up.’

There is also evidence that many patients who do qualify are being wrongly refused. A University of Birmingham study published in the British Journal of General Practice in 2019, which examined the records of more than 1.6 million children, found that of nearly 16,000 who met the criteria, fewer than one in seven went on to have the operation.

And Newcastle University researchers have found some patients endure three times the recommended number of infections before they are even referred to a specialist.

‘Some areas will only count cases of tonsillitis that are recorded in medical records,’ says Mr O’Hara. ‘But many who regularly get tonsillitis don’t go to the doctor unless it’s really bad – meaning there’s no record.’

Between 1991 and 2011, the number of tonsillectomies in England fell by 44 per cent – but hospital admissions for tonsillitis rose by a staggering 310 per cent. In 2018, a study by Public Health England – now UK Health Security Agency – warned that since this reduction in surgeries, the number of children under 14 admitted to hospital with tonsillitis has soared.

So too, they added, have cases of invasive strep A, the most dangerous form of the infection.

It was supposed to be a routine procedure, but just days after having her tonsils removed, five-year-old Amber Milnes was dead.

Amber had the operation at the Royal Cornwall Hospital in Truro in April 2023.

The procedure was to treat Amber’s sleep apnoea – a condition where the back of the throat becomes obstructed during sleep, leading to a loss of oxygen. After recurrent tonsillitis, it is the most common reason a child would need a tonsillectomy.

Because she also had cyclical vomiting syndrome – a rare gut condition that caused her to retch every ten minutes for hours at a time – her parents expected her to stay in overnight. Instead, she was sent home that evening.

But by the early hours of the next morning she was vomiting, and was taken back to hospital that night after being sick around 20 times.

Then, at about 3am on April 9, she suffered a ‘massive bleed’, and doctors could not resuscitate her.

At her inquest, the pathologist concluded a large blood vessel at the site of the surgery had ruptured after becoming infected.

‘Amber was and always will be our magical little princess,’ said her parents, Lewis and Sereta, in a statement issued at the start of the inquest last year. ‘She filled our home with love and fun.’

Such deaths are extremely rare. Mr Kel Anyanwu, the surgeon who operated on Amber, told the inquest he had never seen one in 25 years at the hospital.

Of more than 318,000 children who had their tonsils out in NHS hospitals in England between 2008 and 2019, five died during their stay.

NHS figures suggest about six in 100 children have to return to hospital with bleeding within four weeks of surgery. About one in six of those children needs another operation to stop it.

The consequences can be tragic. During the winter of 2022, an unusually severe strep A outbreak claimed the lives of 61 children across the UK.

For most sufferers, tonsillitis is not life-threatening but it can be a distressing and debilitating condition. One of those affected is Taron Davies, seven, who suffered ten bouts of tonsillitis last year.

‘His tonsils would swell up so much that he would be in total agony,’ says his mother Rebecca, 34, a call centre worker. ‘He couldn’t speak, he couldn’t drink fluids. At times, he struggled to breathe. We were terrified he would stop breathing in the night. He would finish a course of antibiotics and the very next day his tonsils would start swelling up again.’

Although Taron met the official NHS criteria for a tonsillectomy, his local area had added requirements – something allowed under the 2019 rationing guidance.

‘We were told by our GP that Taron needed to have missed a significant number of school days to qualify,’ says Rebecca, who had her tonsils out at 20 after a bad case of quinsy. ‘But we’d tried to make sure he missed as little school as possible and some of his worst flare-ups had occurred on weekends. So we were told he didn’t qualify.’

Rebecca and her husband Jack decided to go private. The family had medical insurance, meaning it cost them only £100 – without insurance, it can cost between £2,500 and £4,000.

Taron had the surgery in August, which lasted about 30 minutes and he went home the same day. Since then, his mother says, he has not had any throat infections. ‘By now, he’d normally have had tonsillitis twice. The other day he was saying how nice it was to be able to breathe and eat normally.’

A new technique is increasingly used across the NHS, called coblation, where rather than cutting out the whole tonsil and surrounding tissue, as was done traditionally, surgeons use a low-temperature energy field to dissolve most of the tonsil while leaving a thin protective layer in place. Experts argue it means less pain, fewer bleeds and a faster return to eating and drinking normally.

‘There is a risk that the remaining tissue can get infected in future,’ says Mr Sri Mahalingam, a consultant ear, nose and throat surgeon at Nuffield Health Tunbridge Wells Hospital, who treated Taron. ‘But the risk is small.’

And there is a further problem. Many families simply cannot afford to go private – and research suggests they are the ones who need help most. A 2022 study of Scottish children found that rates of tonsillitis were highest in the most deprived areas.

‘I passionately believe that we need to conduct more research into the guidelines,’ says Mr O’Hara.

‘They are based on research that was carried out in the 1980s which lacked the input of patients, cost-effectiveness research, and consideration of the impact on a patient’s and their parents’ quality of life. Isn’t it time we looked at this again?’

#616. Hundreds of thousands march in France as protests take place across Europe – as it happened

French police have made 1,000 arrests and Italian officers have raided homes in Milan, with protests also taking place in Spain and Albania

French police arrested almost 1,000 people on Saturday during the protests held across the country, interior minister Laurent Nunez said.

He told reporters that the number “will rise” as more data from police becomes available.

Although marches over the cost of living “passed off well” in cities, officers found themselves later confronted with “an extremely elevated level of violence” from “ultra-left” groups, Nunez said.

French police arrested 1,000 people during protests about the cost of living and education, with that number expected to rise, according to the country’s interior minister Laurent Nunez

The government estimated that at least 400,000 people had marched across France. Trade unions estimated the number at double that.

Two serious injuries were sustained during the protests, Nunez said, including a 20-year-old man who had his fingers blown off.

A demonstration on the outskirts of Paris was largely peaceful but was marred by violence at the end, with police using a water cannon and teargas to quell the crowds.

More than 70,000 police were on the streets of French cities, with shops boarded up and many museums closed.

In Italy, nine were arrested and more than 370 people “briefly detained” by police.

Protests also took place in Belgium, Spain, Portugal and Albania over different issues.

A peaceful protest during the day in Paris descended into violent clashes with police by the time night fell. The sound of pop music blaring and chanted slogans was swapped for the sound of teargas being released and fireworks being released, according to reports. Eyewitnesses say the mood soured at the end of the march, where rows of police officers and vans awaited the crowd.

Protesters reportedly fired fireworks towards law enforcement officers, who responded with charges and baton strikes.

The AFP news agency quoted David, a protester who gave only his first name. He is said to have appeared shaken and had a gash on his face, which he said was caused by a police officer throwing a baton at him.

“The police started moving towards everyone, telling them to get down and back off. They were just taking people down, you know, beating protesters,” he said.

Mike, a 23-year-old student who also declined to give his surname, said: “Look around, they’re just teenagers. Is it normal for teenagers to be teargassed and beaten with batons?”

For Jessica, a 24-year-old student, said: “I just don’t understand why there’s so much violence. I feel like our right to protest is being trampled on.”

As night fell, police began clearing the streets and protesters started to disperse.

Italian police said nine people were arrested, and 371 briefly detained during protests in eight cities.

In a statement, the police said 110 of those either arrested or detained were minors.

My colleague Angelique Chrisafis has been reporting from the protest in Paris today, which has since dispersed. She writes about how a largely peaceful demonstration on the outskirts of the French capital was marred at the end by violence.

double quotation markThe mood in Paris on Saturday afternoon was peaceful and lighthearted, with brass bands playing and children and grandchildren present. Some people carried banners critical of the government’s policing, saying: “Oppression breeds rebellion” and “The right to protest”.

But at the end of the Paris demonstration, at Porte de Vincennes on the city’s eastern edge, different groups of masked men dressed in black emerged who had not appeared to have taken part in the peaceful march. Some groups of masked men threw glass bottles and stones at police, who responded with teargas, water cannon and stun grenades. A bin was set alight and fireworks were set off towards police.

A man reportedly had his fingers blown off during trouble in France, a minister has said.

France’s interior minister – equivalent to the home secretary in the UK – Laurent Nunez said two people had been “seriously injured” during what he called “an extremely elevated level of violence” at today’s protests.

A 20-year-old man in Toulouse, in southern France, is said to have had his fingers blown off, and the other serious injury occurred in Clermont-Ferrand in the centre of the country. He did not give details of either case.

In an update, Nunez said “ultra-left” groups had thrown projectiles and aimed fireworks at police to provoke clashes.

He struck a more positive tone than last week when violence erupted across French cities during protests about the level of investment into public services and the cost of living.

Nunez said that, while some shops and businesses had been vandalised and looted today, “the scale was far smaller” than a week earlier. He stressed that shopping centres had been well protected this time.

In Paris, where the main demonstration passed off largely peacefully but clashes broke out with police as the crowd dispersed, Nunez said “several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including about 500 individuals identified as rioters”.

Ensuing clashes in the French capital lasted for around two hours, he said.

The minister said that there were first-time clashes in the southern cities of Cannes and Montpellier between far-right activists who sought confrontations with “ultra-left militants” who he said claimed to be there to protect businesses.

The authorities will remain “on high alert” through the night and into Sunday, he said.

Demonstrations were held in the Italian cities of Rome, Turin and elsewhere, with some turning violent.

As we reported earlier, security was heightened in Rome, where authorities locked down luxury shopping streets and stepped up controls around the Circus Maximus and Piazza del Popolo.

A small number of protesters tried to force their way into the Colosseum, but were ushered out by guards.

Elsewhere in the city, several hundred students demonstrated peacefully to stress they were not rioters after unrest last week, particularly in Milan.

Riccardo Ponzio, national president of an Italian far-right student association, said: “I think the images from last week were truly something terrible, especially for the young people, for the students, for the vast majority of the younger generations who want to study … and do not accept being represented by those who use issues and needs to devastate entire cities.”

A separate anti-war march took place in central Rome. Organisers sought to distance themselves from potential unrest, urging participants to keep their faces uncovered and hands visible.

But it was these marchers who briefly clashed with police near the Piazza della Repubblica, even as organisers were trying to hold the crowd back using batons and teargas. In the end, the protesters pulled back when a water cannon was turned on. They retreated to a location about 500m away.

French police arrested almost 1,000 people on Saturday during the protests held across the country, interior minister Laurent Nunez said.

He told reporters that the number “will rise” as more data from police becomes available.

Although marches over the cost of living “passed off well” in cities, officers found themselves later confronted with “an extremely elevated level of violence” from “ultra-left” groups, Nunez said.

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the radical-left presidential candidate who marched in the Paris rally today, said in a social media post that the French police “ruined the day” by “shooting indiscriminately” at Paris protesters.

“In Paris, as a way to ruin the day and blow off some steam, the so-called ‘forces of law and order’ are firing tear gas and shooting indiscriminately into the crowd at the tail end of the march, all to secure footage for domestic television channels, which have spent the entire week broadcasting the very images that incited the killer in Trappes,” he wrote. “A non-stop display of shame.”

In addition to the earlier footage of police using tear gas against protesters in Lyon, we are now seeing tear gas being deployed in the cities of Paris, Marseille, Nantes, and Bordeaux.

Though the protests have been relatively contained so far, the use of tear gas has become an increasingly common tactic for police to disperse crowds at the end of organized rallies, even without an immediate threat. And taking past demonstrations into consideration, these situations often become more volatile as the sun begins setting and the organized gatherings are ending.

The Interior Ministry has put today’s nationwide turnout at 410,000 total protesters across France.

Clashes began to erupt late on Saturday, following a pattern of otherwise peaceful protests growing more tempestuous as the day draws to a close.

The Paris march began calmly, but near its endpoint at Porte de Vincennes, some protesters threw projectiles while police fired volleys of tear gas and used water cannons to disperse people.

Authorities had confined the capital’s march to the city’s southeastern edge, keeping protesters away from central neighborhoods hit by last weekend’s destruction.

Police in Paris say that about 110,000 people have marched across France’s capital today, but that the “situation remains calm” according to reporting from AFP. Authorities have now begun dispersing the crowds.

The 110,000 figure is roughly the same amount as the number of protesters in Paris last weekend. Considering the fears many people had that the protests could turn violent, as well as the rainy weather across the area, the number is an impressive showing.

The police also said more than 3,000 checks have been carried out and 65 people were arrested during the demonstrations in Paris.

Meanwhile in Albania, more than 2000 police have been deployed around Tirana on the 12th day of student-led protests amid reports of concerted efforts to stop demonstrators entering the capital.

Protests initially spurred by fury over a planned Trump family-backed resort in Albania have turned increasingly violent as students have joined what growing numbers are now calling a revolution to oust prime minister Edi Rama. Today, rally numbers swelled with demonstrators traveling to Tirana from cities across the Balkan state and as teachers, doctors and labour unions also weighed in.

But police also stand increasingly accused of heavy-handed tactics amid reports of civilians being plucked from the streets by masked officers and riot police increasingly resorting to using rubber bullets, batons, tear gas and water cannons to disperse crowds.

Speaking to the Guardian after spending several hours at Tirana’s National Trauma hospital earlier in the day, Kei Brisku, who heads the Abania Rehabilitation Centre for Trauma and Torture, said there were growing concerns about “the mass and random use” of rubber bullets.

“Nine protestors, five women and four men, were badly wounded by rubber bullets today and are now in hospital,” he said.

“The use of rubber bullets against violent protesters may be justified under applicable regulations ... however, their indiscriminate use against crowds is unacceptable, as it risks harming peaceful protesters and bystanders who pose no threat.”

In power for 13 years, Rama has resolutely refused to resign. While he has offered to discuss the “ legitimate concerns” of students, he has ruled out talking with hooligans who resort to violence.

Last week, the socialist leader told the Guardian the “violence in Tirana is very real,” as he dismissed accusations that his government was employing underhand tactics to fast-track the controversial resort championed by Jared Kushner, the US president’s son-in-law.

The NFL (American football league) closed its “NFL House” in Paris as the city braced for street protests with a heavy police presence and storefronts boarded up.

The league announced the closure to fans on Saturday morning through its “OnePass” app, according to the AP, citing “potential accessibility issues.”

Security concerns have overshadowed the NFL’s planned debut in Paris. The New Orleans Saints will play the Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday at Stade de France in the league’s first-ever regular-season game in France.

Major museums including the Louvre and Orsay Museum are also closed Saturday, though tourists were seen lined up to enter Notre Dame Cathedral.

Spanish authorities say about 25,000 demonstrators have marched through the country’s capital demanding protections to the state pension scheme.

Spain is voting in a snap parliamentary election in a few weeks and this has been a key topic of concern. Spain’s Socalist prime minister Pedro Sanchez, who called the snap election after struggling to get pension reforms through parliament, has accused conservative parties of holding back inflation-linked increases.

Protesters marched from the Atocha train station to the Gran Via shopping avenue in the Spanish capital.

Some expressed concern about portions of their state pensions being privatised in the future. About 6.8 million Spaniards receive a state pension and fiscally conservative, right-wing politicians have raised questions over how sustainable the current system is.

Spain has also seem major protests in recent months over increasingly unaffordable housing and renters’ rights.

Some are, namely in certain cities and low-income suburbs. Videos filmed by students and teachers have shown leaks, scurrying rats, holes in walls and ceilings, broken toilets and not enough chairs or tables, meaning teachers have to carry them from classroom to classroom. Some children said they had to learn in class while leaks were pouring into buckets, or move desks to avoid getting wet. Many school classrooms experienced temperatures over 35C (95F) in the heatwaves of last May and June.

Estimates in recent years have pointed to thousands of French schools at all levels, both primary and secondary, in need of repair. These include many 1960s school buildings. French regions are responsible for upkeep of high school buildings, but have asked for higher budgets from the government. A senate report has advised that billions need to be spent in the coming years to renovate and repair schools, as well as to address the impact of the climate crisis.

Tens of thousands of people have turned out to the heavily policed demonstrations across France and they have been, on the whole, quite contained so far.

Some sections of the crowd could be seen singing and dancing in Paris as they walked along the route, which was pushed to the city’s fringes at the last minute as police sought to move the march away from the fortified city centre.

In Lyon, police used teargas early on in the banned demonstration to disperse some of the crowd but people were still able to walk on.

In the last half hour there’s also a been of bit of rough activity in Marseille between police and a few dozen people. The French broadcaster BFMTV has shown live footage of masked attendees throwing bins, flares going off and spot fires in the street. There are cordons of riot police around.

Overall though, the heavy policing has appeared to be successful so far in staving off the type of looting, ransacking and violent activity we saw on the fringes of the marches last week. The government has added on 20% more officers, for a 70,000 strong force across the country.

Earlier today, the French interior minister had said protest numbers – at about 36,000 in the morning- were about half of what they were last Saturday.

At the Paris march, Nadège, a communications worker, said she was at Place de la République last Saturday when teargas hit. But that hadn’t deterred her.

double quotation markI’m out again peacefully today to support everyone who is brave enough to demonstrate. It does take courage. People are afraid now.

double quotation markWe have to keep our rights alive. We’ve seen what happens in the US when a bad president is in power. In France, it’s our legal right to protest in the street and I’m here to defend that.

The French president had hosted student representatives for a highly anticipated meeting yesterday afternoon.

Going in, the student leaders had already expressed cynicism over whether the French president would adequately address their concerns.

Pupils in Paris began protests over the quality of their education four weeks ago – and their spirit has since inspired demonstrations elsewhere, across the nation and also into other countries, such as Italy and Greece.

French high schoolers say they’re fed up with the deteriorating state of their school buildings, overworked and underpaid teachers, and packed classrooms.

They’re demanding school renovations and upgrades, better study conditions and the scrapping of the Parcoursup univeristy admissions platform which was introduced in 2018 and has long been criticised for lack of transparency.

Macron held a two-and-a-half hours-long meeting with 20 students.

Nathanael Combary, president of campaign group High School Renewal, said the president had been “attentive” and they would continue talks with Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Monday on proposed changes like reform of Parcoursup.

But he and other student leaders called on their peers to continue protesting this weekend.

The radical-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the La France Insoumise party, is also marching in the Parisian procession.

Speaking to the press earlier he said the protests would continue every week until Emmanuel Macron and his government addressed the public’s demands.

He said Macron “is going to understand that this is going to repeat itself every week” and urged the president, “there is still time for him to concede” to the students’ wishes.

Macron met with student leaders on Friday for the first time since the demonstrations began a month ago. More on that meeting next.
