#617. ‘Cuts mean jobs’: Skydance staff brace for shake-up after $110bn megamerger

Battle far from over after Paramount and Warner Bros deal creates new global entertainment powerhouse

“It feels like the calm before the storm,” says an executive at Skydance, the newly minted media empire formed from the megamerger of Paramount and Warner Bros Discovery (WBD). “David has got what he wanted, but now there is a price to pay.”

Earlier this month, David Ellison, Skydance’s chief executive, sealed the $110bn (£82bn) deal, creating a global powerhouse spanning two Hollywood studios each more than a century old, the TV networks HBO, MTV and Discovery, and news outlets CBS and CNN.

Having seen off a rival bid from Netflix and faced significant political and industry opposition, in a process Ellison told employees was at times “downright ugly”, the battle is far from over for Hollywood’s newest magnate.

With an aggressive target of reducing an eyewatering debt load of more than $80bn in just three years, it is what is going to be cut, sold and restructured that will be uppermost in the minds of Skydance’s more than 53,000 employees.

Ellison, 43, who studied film and acted in the 2006 film Flyboys before moving into producing, is targeting $6bn in savings within three years. Executives and financial backers are steering away from the need for swingeing job losses, but a memo from management earlier this month warned that there would be “difficult decisions that affect our workforce”.

“It is business as usual but, to be honest, everyone is worried about what happens next,” says another Skydance executive. “Cuts inevitably mean jobs.”

There are also concerns about the political direction of the new entity, given Ellison’s closeness to Donald Trump – a longtime friend of his father, Larry, who co-founded the software company Oracle. David Ellison has pushed back at such framing, stating: “We do not want to politicise the company.”

Nevertheless, fears in the news division have been stoked by events at Paramount before the merger. It came under fire for cancelling the long-running Late Show with Stephen Colbert after its host said it had paid a “big fat bribe” for settling a $16m lawsuit with Trump.

Days later, US regulators agreed the $8.4bn merger of Paramount with Ellison’s Skydance Media, with Trump ally Kenneth Weinstein’s appointment as ombudsman at CBS News to root out “complaints of bias” as one of the conditions to get regulatory approval.

Christiane Amanpour, CNN’s international anchor, criticised the “ideological realignment of CBS” and warned that changes and cuts could lead to the potential “destruction” of flagship news show 60 Minutes. This week, she announced she was leaving CNN after 43 years, although her exit is not thought to be tied to the new ownership.

CNN staff were relieved at Skydance’s decision shortly after closing the deal to keep Mark Thompson, the former New York Times boss and BBC director general, as chair and chief executive.

Many had feared that the network, which alongside MS Now and Politico had faced a now-lifted White House media ban in apparent retaliation for critical coverage of Trump, might face a sweeping overhaul that could have seen the divisive Bari Weiss, the editor in chief of CBS News, installed at the top.

While Thompson has said that Skydance supports CNN’s independence, fresh concerns over rightwing influence emerged this week when it was reported that Elon Musk, a Trump ally and supporter of far-right causes through his X platform, has invested $1bn for a stake in the media conglomerate.

“The preservation of editorial independence is a growing concern among media consumers,” said Mike Proulx, an analyst at Forrester. “Private wealth is getting a greater foothold on public information channels.”

In terms of creative television output, star performers such as HBO will be left to keep churning out the all-important hits the business needs.

Ellison immediately extended the soon-to-expire contract of Casey Bloys, promoting the HBO boss to also oversee streaming services Paramount+ and HBO Max, to ensure the golden goose keeps making must-watch dramas such as The White Lotus, Game of Thrones, The Pitt, Succession and The Sopranos.

However, there are longer-term questions over some of the group’s cable and TV channels – such as MTV, Nickelodeon, the UK’s Channel 5 and Network 10 in Australia – which are in decline but still account for 70% of profits, according to CreditSights.

“In a world where the majority of consumers can access content through a smart TV, it should be a natural consideration to sell physical broadcast assets,” said Brian Wieser, chief executive of consultancy Madison and Wall.

“At a Skydance level they have made the choice to go all in on streaming. But the problem you have is maybe you don’t get offered enough to sell it, and, given the cashflow we know they make, they might be better served to hold on.”

Newly filed accounts for Channel 5 show the broadcaster paid a £215m dividend to Paramount last year. In the UK, the culture secretary only cleared the takeover after Ellison made commitments including pledging to keep Channel 5 operating as a free-to-air, public service broadcaster until at least the end of 2034. However, according to sources, these agreements do not preclude any potential sale of Channel 5 in the future.

Last month, Paramount moved its £300m TV advertising sales business from Sky’s sales team to Channel 4. That came after WBD extended its deal for Sky to handle its £90m-£100m ad sales business from January, covering TNT Sports, Discovery, Animal Planet and streaming service HBO Max. However, multiple media sources believe now the Skydance deal is done the business will eventually also move to Channel 4.

The megamerger also paves the way for BT to exit its joint venture with WBD – TNT Sports – which would finally end the telecoms company’s costly foray into pay-TV sport after almost 15 years.

Last year, Paramount outbid WBD for the rights to Champions League football, the flagship rights owned by TNT Sports. That blow prompted BT to write off the entire value of its stake in the joint venture.

However, with Ellison intending to merge Paramount+ with HBO Max, the rights will effectively be retained, and viewers will not have to sign up to yet another streaming or pay-TV service to watch all top-flight football.

Skydance says it will spend an estimated $30bn a year on content across all divisions, and as part of the takeover Ellison promised to release at least 30 major films a year until 2031.

This promises to be a boon for the UK production industry, especially for WBD’s studio at Leavesden, which is home to all of its DC superhero franchises and the forthcoming Harry Potter TV series destined for HBO Max this Christmas.

However, Warner is enduring one of its worst box office showings for years, the most recent flop being Tom Cruise’s Digger, prompting Ellison to put Paramount’s leadership in charge of both studios.

Analysts point out that Ellison is unlikely to maintain that level of moviemaking beyond the five-year pledge, as it goes against the grain of a Hollywood trend towards fewer films and lessons from past takeovers.

Since Disney’s acquisition of Rupert Murdoch’s entertainment assets in 2019, which included the then 20th Century Fox and Fox Searchlight studios, the number of film releases has broadly halved.

“After the 2031 deal ends there will be fewer films, obviously,” says Tom Harrington, a media analyst at Enders. “It has never happened before when there has been a takeover that more have ended up being made.”

#619. The candid meeting that 'changed' Spurs - are they finally on way back?

Spurs pick up rare Stamford Bridge win with victory over Chelsea

Whisper it quietly, but could Spurs finally be on their way back?

Tottenham's 2-0 win at Chelsea on Saturday moved them up to the heady heights of 12th in the Premier League - their highest league position since 2 January.

And, after back-to-back 17th-placed finishes, there are growing signs Roberto de Zerbi's side are showing there is real light at the end of a pretty dark tunnel.

Saturday's impressive win at Stamford Bridge was just the second time they have won two league games in a row in 42 attempts - inspired by starring roles from James Maddison and Mathys Tel.

It was also the first time they have enjoyed as much as 68% possession in a match since April 2025.

The win was deserved too, although Chelsea certainly gave them a helping hand with goalkeeper Mike Penders punching the opener into his own net and Cole Palmer sent off for two yellow cards.

Spurs had taken seven attempts to get their first league win of the season against Coventry on Monday and on Saturday they looked transformed from the side that did not even score a goal until September 1.

It left De Zerbi glowing with positivity, despite another injury setback for Maddison, as he highlighted a team meeting earlier this month that sparked their revival in fortunes.

"Seven points after Manchester. Before Manchester we spoke a lot, we had a big meeting," he said. "We removed the masks and spoke honestly and clearly in front of ourselves. From that moment, I think something started to change within us.

"I think we have put something different into Tottenham in the last period. Not a different attitude, but different relationships with the players, different relationships within the group.

"We have changed the spirit of the group and improved the performances of the players, especially some of the more fragile players, maybe the younger players. We have suffered enough."

Former Chelsea goalkeeper Rob Green added on BBC Radio 5 Live: "A dream afternoon for Tottenham. They looked controlled, looked at ease, they looked like they were comfortable on the ball.

"Results like this galvanise a side. When you look at the players coming back, yes Maddison got injured and he'll be a question mark over the next few weeks, but players coming back, momentum coming back - you feel, and say it quietly, Tottenham might just be coming back."

Italian De Zerbi was appointed Spurs boss at the end of March 2026 with the club in crisis.

He arrived as the club's third manager of the campaign and, with seven games remaining, Tottenham were just one point clear of the drop zone.

After securing safety, albeit after a few scares, the club spent more than Â£300m on summer signings for the first time in their history as they backed De Zerbi to restore them to former glories.

And, after a slow start to the campaign and still lacking firepower in attack, the long-suffering Tottenham fans will be left feeling more positive than they have done for a long time.

"Tottenham have made a big statement in a really convincing performance," former Arsenal defender Martin Keown told BBC Sport.

"I thought Maddison was magnificent in midfield. He's like the Artful Dodger, isn't he? That midfield is full of mischief, but he's brave against the ball.

"I thought Tel was magnificent out on the left-hand side, [Mohammed] Kudus on the right was also really effective, and everybody really managed to handle the ball really well on the night.

"Spurs had almost 70% possession, which is remarkable for a team which was just a few places from the bottom of the table. I think what's changed for Spurs is the key personnel."

De Zerbi ran on to the pitch to celebrate with the travelling supporters at the final whistle, while his coaches and substitutes raced towards the players in the corner of the ground.

He has previously spoken of how he inherited players that cried after matches and lost all confidence - and believed his unprecedented control over the summer transfers was vindication for Spurs from last season.

It was fitting that Tel, who has attracted criticism from his own supporters since arriving from Bayern Munich for Â£30m in June 2025, provided the decisive moment to seal just a second league success in 36 years at Chelsea - a stunning low finish after a driving run.

The French forward, 21, told Sky Sports: "It is very special because we have come to Chelsea so many times and not got a win. We showed great mentality today and we need to enjoy this win.

"We created a lot of chances today. We walk out together, the goal is something special for me, I'm happy about it and let's keep pushing now."

Summer signing Matheus Fernandes added: "We are here to change the club's mentality, we want to beat the top teams, and make this victory for the fans."

'You have to fight' - De Zerbi delighted after Tottenham beat Chelsea

Tottenham spent more than Â£300m on signings in the summer

In the summer, Spurs twice broke their transfer record with three of their first signings, as they added centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke from Brighton, Fernandes from West Ham and Sandro Tonali from Newcastle.

And all three impressed De Zerbi against Chelsea as he added: "Jan Paul van Hecke played very well, Matheus Fernandes played very well, Sandro Tonali played very well.

"I think it was Tonali's best game since joining Tottenham. Omar Marmoush played a good game. It was a tough game for him, but he fought in the right way.

"Mathys Tel played very well too. I think we won the game with our two wingers, Mohammed Kudus and Mathys Tel. They made the difference."

It was notable Fernandes, 22, was criticised by his manager last month.

The return of Maddison, who missed almost all of last season with a serious knee injury, was key in Monday's 3-1 home victory over Coventry City - and he again looked impressive before being withdrawn in the second half with a suspected groin injury.

"I don't think it is a very important problem," said De Zerbi. "I hope it is not a big problem. He is a special player for us. We need him."

Maddison is part of a returning group of players, including Kudus and Dejan Kulusevski, who are making comebacks from lengthy absences.

Spurs are now unbeaten in three games, with back-to-back victories following the 1-1 draw at Manchester United in which they were arguably the better side.

As well as the team meeting before the Old Trafford encounter, Spurs enjoyed a warm-weather training camp in Marbella, where heavyweight boxer Anthony Joshua paid them a visit.

It feels as though some semblance of the old Spurs is returning, although they remain unconvincing in attack with just eight goals in as many games.

Manchester City loanee Marmoush misfired again and his replacement Dominic Solanke was underwhelming in previous matches, while Richarlison has been frozen out in the reserves after being left out of their Premier League squad.

But after this notable derby victory at Chelsea - earning a clean sheet there too for the first time since 1986 - it felt like the first part of De Zerbi's rebuild is well under way.

#620. Andy Burnham: Time for honest discussion about freedom of movement between UK and EU

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Prime minister says it is time for ‘evidence-based debate’ about what a new relationship with the EU would look like

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Andy Burnham has said he wants an “honest discussion” about Britain readopting freedom of movement with the European Union.

The prime minister has said he is ready for a “very factual, quite evidence-based debate” about a new relationship with Brussels.

He said that ending free movement has come with reduced access to European data on migration, telling The Sunday Times: “Consider what we’ve lost, which was the ability to be part of Eurodac and all the data collaboration around migration. You’ve got to see it in the round, rather than just looking at freedom of movement on its own”.

Eurodac is the EU’s biometric database, which assists border control and supports management of asylum claims. The UK’s border security commander Major General Duncan Capps told MPs this week that “we would very much like to be part of that [Eurodac], however we can make that work”.

Mr Burnham wants to consider various options for a new relationship with the EU, potentially including a return to full EU membership or joining the single market – which would require free movement.

The Independent revealed in September that Mr Burnham was going to edge Labour closer to rejoining the EU, with ministers saying that it was now a question of “how it is expressed in the manifesto, rather than if”.

One senior minister told The Independent that “the mood has completely changed on this subject.”

Mr Burnham has said it was “possible” that Labour’s next election manifesto could include an in-out referendum on EU membership. And the EU’s former chief Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier said that Britain would be welcomed back - but with strings attached.

Speaking to The Sunday Times, Mr Burnham said: “Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now].

“Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”

The prime minister has previously committed to the red lines in Labour’s 2024 election manifesto – which ruled out the return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union – suggesting any fundamental change in the relationship would have to wait until after a general election.

The issue of migration was one of the dominant factors during the 2016 Brexit referendum campaign.

But he suggested the type of migration experienced during the years of EU membership was different from the challenges faced now.

“It was generally younger people, not always, but spending a few years, then going back,” he said.

“And obviously the ease of that worked for British people as well.”

Mr Burnham will meet the European Union’s chiefs at a summit on November 20 in Brussels.

He has said he will take the opportunity around the summit to lay out to the British public different options for the future relationship with the bloc.

But Mr Burnham said he could not imagine recommending the UK joins the Schengen borderless area or ditches the pound to adopt the euro.

“I can’t see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen,” he said.

Nigel Farage said the prime minister’s comments were a betrayal of voters who backed Brexit, including in Mr Burnham’s Makerfield constituency.

The Reform UK leader said: “This is a total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch.

“He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty.”

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said: “Andy Burnham knows full well that a return to EU free movement would mean handing back control of our borders and allowing uncontrolled migration from across Europe.

“The British people voted to end free movement, and there can be no return to it.”

#622. "Superintelligenz" statt KI: Trumps neue Sprachregelung

Donald Trump hat die US-Behörden angeordnet, statt "Künstliche Intelligenz" künftig den Begriff "Superintelligenz" zu nutzen. Warum der US-Präsident KI für unpassend hält und was Tech-Experten dazu sagen.

Was ist nur los mit Donald Trump und seinem Bedürfnis, alles Mögliche neu zu benennen? Erst wurde der Golf von Mexiko zum Golf von Amerika - zumindest in offiziellen Dokumenten der USA, wenn auch nicht global. Dann kam der Ontariosee, nun nach Willen des US-Präsidenten der Amerikasee. Und nun soll auch die neue Technologie, die unser Zeitalter prägen wird, die künstliche Intelligenz oder KI, einen neuen Namen erhalten.

Anfang September behauptete der US-Präsident auf seiner Plattform Truth Social, der Begriff "künstliche Intelligenz" sei "ungenau" und "unzutreffend". Bessere Alternativen wären "überlegene", "extreme" oder "höchste" Intelligenz.

In einer über drei Tage in den sozialen Medien durchgeführten Umfrage gaben Trump-Fans mit 65 Prozent dem Begriff "Superintelligenz" (SI) den Vorzug über "Überlegene Intelligenz" (35 Prozent). Daraufhin verkündete Trump vergangene Woche vor der Vollversammlung der Vereinten Nationen, dass von nun an in Dokumenten der US-Bundesregierung diese neue Bezeichnung verwendet werde.

Bislang hat die Tech-Branche die Bezeichnung jedoch noch nicht übernommen und Akademiker weisen darauf hin, dass Superintelligenz ein Begriff für die Zukunft sei, wenn die Technologie den Menschen in allen Bereichen überlegen ist. Aktuelle KI-Modelle seien davon noch Jahre entfernt, betonen sie.

"KI ist in den meisten Fällen keine Superintelligenz sondern lediglich eine andere Intelligenz", sagt Pedro Domingos, emeritierter Professor für Informatik und Ingenieurwissenschaften an der University of Washington, zur DW. "KI macht andere Dinge als die Menschen, sie als Superintelligenz zu bezeichnen ist also irreführend."

Computerwissenschaftler und Mathematiker prägten den Begriff "künstliche Intelligenz" 1956 während eines Sommer-Workshops am Dartmouth College in New Hampshire, USA. "Künstlich" hieß dabei einfach "von Menschen gemacht", im Unterschied zur natürlichen menschlichen Intelligenz.

Nicht alle Experten waren mit dieser Bezeichnung einverstanden. In ihrem Buch "Denkmaschinen: Die Geschichte der künstlichen Intelligenz" zitiert Pamela McCorduck den KI-Pionier Arthur Samuel, der der Meinung war, der Begriff lasse einen an "etwas Unechtes" denken.

Doch in den vergangenen 70 Jahren hat sich der Begriff durchgesetzt. Ihn zu ändern wird die vielen Ängste im Zusammenhang mit KI - dass Jobs verloren gehen, der Mensch überflüssig wird oder wir die Kontrolle über die Maschinen verlieren - nicht mindern, sagen Kritiker.

"Die Namensänderung fördert solche Ängste: 'Oh, es handelt sich um Superintelligenz und die wird uns Menschen überflüssig machen, sich gegen uns wenden, unsere Jobs wegnehmen", warnt Domingos. "Wenn du die Gegenbewegung gegen KI maximieren willst, dann nenne sie Überlegene Intelligenz."

Die Ängste der Bevölkerung nehmen rasch zu. In einer Anfang des Monats von Public First für Politico durchgeführten Studie sprach sich etwa die Hälfte der Befragten in sechs Ländern - den USA, Kanada, Frankreich, Spanien, Deutschland und Großbritannien - dafür aus, weitere Entwicklungen im Bereich KI zu pausieren, um das Risiko zu verringern, dass die neue Technologie die Menschheit auslöschen könnte.

Einer weiteren, von SSRS für CNN durchgeführten Studie zufolge sind fast neun von zehn US-Amerikanern eher besorgt als begeistert darüber, dass die KI die menschliche Intelligenz übertreffen könnte.

Diese Bedenken haben auch den US-Kongress erreicht. Gemeinsam mit anderen hat der parteiunabhängige Senator von Vermont, Bernie Sanders, einen Gesetzesentwurf für ein "dauerhaftes Verbot der Entwicklung künstlicher Superintelligenz", die vom Menschen nicht kontrolliert werden kann, eingebracht.

Der Gesetzesentwurf fordert außerdem eine Aussetzung der Entwicklung fortschrittlicher KI-Technologien, bis entsprechende Tests und Kontrollmechanismen auf Bundesebene eingerichtet sind.

Den großen KI-Entwicklern in den USA, die ihre Modelle gerne ins Zentrum der Aufmerksamkeit rücken wollen, könnte die von Trump geforderte neue Bezeichnung natürlich gelegen kommen. Ihre Systeme sind den Menschen bereits in vielen spezialisierten Aufgaben überlegen und waren China bis vor kurzem weit voraus.

Doch sowohl Anthropic, das Unternehmen hinter dem Modell Claude, als auch OpenAI, das ChatGPT entwickelt hat, haben Pläne für einen Börsengang verschoben. Einige Marktbeobachter machen dafür die jüngsten Vorfälle verantwortlich, bei denen KI-Modelle sich in Computersysteme gehackt oder Aufgaben ausgeführt hatten, die sie nicht ausführen sollten.

Während chinesische Modelle den Qualitätsrückstand bei deutlich geringerer Rechenleistung weitgehend aufholen, könnte den US-Entwicklern eine Umbenennung, die den Eindruck bestärkt, dass sie weiterhin führend im Rennen um KI sind, durchaus gelegen kommen. Laut Zahlen von Goldman Sachs sollen die Ausgaben für KI bald die Marke von einer Billion US-Dollar (880 Milliarden Euro) übersteigen.

"Es ist ganz im Interesse der US-Entwickler, von Super-, Hyper-, überlegener oder sonstiger Intelligenz zu sprechen, weil es ihre Fähigkeiten hervorhebt. Es ist schlicht Marketing", sagt Domingos, Autor des 2015 veröffentlichten Buchs "The Master Algorithm".

Die aktuellen KI-Modelle werden immer besser und führen viele Aufgaben bereits eigenständig aus. In den Entwicklungslaboren wird jedoch viel über den nächsten Schritt, KI-Systeme, die sich selbst verbessern, diskutiert. Dies wird als rekursive Selbstverbesserung oder RSI bezeichnet.

Elon Musk hat bereits vorhergesagt, dass die Lernprozesse der KI bis Ende des Jahres oder bis 2027 automatisiert werden könnten, ohne die Notwendigkeit menschlicher Eingaben. Bei OpenAI geht man davon aus, dass es bis dahin ein Jahr länger dauern könnte. Doch selbst dann werden die KI-Systeme nicht vollständig rekursiv sein.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Anfang September argumentierte Jürgen Schmidhuber, ein deutscher Informatiker, der in der Schweiz arbeitet, in einem Blog-Eintrag: "Für eine vollständige RSI ist nicht nur sich selbst verbessernde (KI-)Software, sondern auch sich selbst verbessernde Hardware erforderlich."

Mit anderen Worten, um Superintelligenz oder RSI zu erreichen, müssten die Tech-Unternehmen Chips und humanoide Roboter produzieren und ganze Fabriken bauen, die keinen menschlichen Input benötigen.

Auch wenn die KI die Chipentwicklung beschleunigt, kann sie den Fertigungsprozess noch nicht alleine ausführen. Bis Maschinen sich ohne jede menschliche Beteiligung selbst verbessern können, vergehen vermutlich noch Jahrzehnte.

Doch neben den Wissenschaftlern, die am maschinellen Lernen arbeiten, wird auch die Politik eine große Rolle dabei spielen, ob sich die Bezeichnung "Superintelligenz" durchsetzt. Auch wenn Trump behauptete, dem chinesischen Präsidenten Xi Jinping habe der Begriff gefallen, gibt es noch keine Anzeichen dafür, dass China sich von "KI" verabschiedet.

Auf einem Tech-Gipfel mit führenden Vertretern der Branche unterzeichnete Trump am Dienstag eine Durchführungsverordnung, die US-Behörden und -Agenturen anweist, den Begriff Superintelligenz zu verwenden. Doch auch wenn einige der führenden Köpfe von Big Tech den Begriff übernommen haben, halten Experten es für unwahrscheinlich, dass er sich durchsetzen wird.

"Angesichts der politischen Ausrichtung der meisten Menschen im Bereich KI ist es wahrscheinlicher, dass sie genau im Gegenteil sagen, 'Zur Hölle mit dir. Jetzt sprechen wir erst rechtvon künstlicher Intelligenz", meint Domingos.

Adaptiert aus dem Englischen von Phoenix Hanzo.

#623. INSOLITE. "On était dans le viseur" : Ce célèbre bar bien connu des fêtards ouvre un restaurant de finger food

Article rédigé par Emmanuel Droillard

l'essentiel Burgers, tenders et street food américaine... Le Rooster, bar de nuit bien connu des fêtards d'Albi, ouvre un nouveau restaurant en face du marché couvert. Son nom : le Hall Mess 333. Pour son gérant, Tristan Dupuy, il s'agit de répondre aux fringales de ses clients... mais aussi de mieux encadrer la consommation d’alcool. Voici tout ce qu'il faut savoir sur cette nouvelle adresse.

"Beaucoup de clients me demandent si on fait à manger", raconte Tristan Dupuy, le gérant du Rooster, le bar de nuit en face du marché couvert. Voilà un petit moment que celui qui est aussi le capitaine des Tigers y pensait. Et l'occasion s'est présentée. Il a pu reprendre le local de l'ancien Italien qui jouxte son établissement. Dans quelques jours, il y ouvrira un restaurant : le Hall Mess 333. Un lieu où "les 'soldats' du Rooster pourront se restaurer". La référence ? "Beaucoup de clients me disent souvent, 'hier c'était la guerre au Rooster'", plaisante-t-il.

Le restaurant servira de la street food américaine, de la finger food "avec des produits de qualité". Des burgers, des tenders... Un thème apprécié par les jeunes, principaux clients du bar (entre 20 et 30 ans). Pour faire tourner la boutique, le gérant embauchera deux salariés de plus, soit six personnes au total (lui compris).

Le restaurant sera ouvert sur les jours et ouvertures du Rooster. Et peut-être le dimanche matin pour proposer des brunchs. Il disposera d'une salle en haut et en bas et d'une terrasse. Pour Tristan Dupuy, c'est un beau challenge. Il a deux salariés de plus et s'attaque à un "domaine inconnu" pour lui : la restauration. Il a donc embauché en conséquence.

Outre nourrir ses clients, Tristan Dupuy pense que cette ouverture va l'aider à mieux contrôler la consommation d'alcool de ses clients. L'établissement est dans le viseur des autorités. Il a déjà écopé d'une fermeture administrative, il y a quelques mois. "C'est un point important pour moi", avoue-t-il.

En proposant une restauration à côté, il estime pouvoir faire venir les gens plus tôt et ainsi avoir un œil sur leur consommation d'alcool. "En plus, on saura d'où ils viennent", commente-t-il.

Aujourd'hui, c'est un sujet primordial pour lui. Ainsi, il refuse des clients désormais. "Je refuse pas mal de gens, je suis obligé. Je protège mon établissement", insiste-t-il.

Voilà sept ans que le Rooster a ouvert ses portes dans ce petit local de 50 m² en face du marché couvert. Depuis deux ans, Tristan Dupuy, qui en était responsable, est devenu le seul gérant. Rapidement, l'établissement a gagné sa clientèle et s'est taillé une petite notoriété sur la ville. "On a créé quelque chose, une identité sur Albi", se réjouit-il.

Le Rooster est le rendez-vous des sportifs. Du XIII, bien sûr, dont Tristan Dupuy est une figure, mais pas que... L'établissement sponsorise beaucoup d'autres sports, collectifs comme individuels. "C'est une fierté pour moi et cela fait vivre le Rooster", souligne le patron.

Enfin, le bar de nuit est connu pour ses soirées avec des DJ locaux. "C'est important de leur donner de la visibilité. Ils ont besoin de se produire. Je les aide. Ils sont la pièce maîtresse de la soirée", conclut-il.

Vous souhaitez suivre ce fil de discussion ?

Le boss Tristan Dupuy est une belle personne qui véhicule de belles valeurs, il est un travailleur entrepreneur infatigable qui mérite le respect. Bravo jeune homme et bonne chance pour ce nouveau projet

#624. Albania: Students demand political change and resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama

Empty lecture halls, burning buildings and demands for change: Albanian students are spearheading a protest movement that has become the biggest challenge to Prime Minister Edi Rama in years.

The luxury high-rises transforming Tirana's skyline are meant to project the image of a modern European capital. But at the foot of one of these buildings, Samanta, a 22-year-old master's student in economics, is in tears.

She removes the mask she had been wearing to protect herself from tear gas.

"How could I ever afford an apartment in one of these towers on a salary of €540 [$608]?" she shouts, as she stands facing a line of police officers. "I share the rent with people I don't even know because my family has emigrated. We're exhausted."

University lecture halls in Tirana stand empty as students boycott classes and take to the streets, demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has been in power since 2013.

Albanians have been protesting since late May as part of a broader anti-government movement known as the "Flamingo Revolution." The protests began in response to a multimillion-euro tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, in the protected coastal area of Zvernec.

The movement has, however, since grown into a broader challenge to Rama's government.

Over the past three days, the student demonstrations have erupted into violent clashes. Bins, businesses, buildings and banks have been set ablaze, with some completely burning out. Tear gas has filled the air.

A total of 152 people have been arrested and 324 are under investigation over the three days of protests. Injuries have been reported among both protesters and police officers, with the police saying 71 officers have been injured in the clashes.

The students are angry about conditions at universities, the cost of higher education and poor employment prospects after graduation. But above all, they want the government to step down. They say they are not willing to negotiate any of their other demands with the prime minister.

"You didn't listen to us for four months while we protested peacefully. Now you'll listen as the city burns," said Samanta.

During the first two days of the student protests, the prime minister remained silent.

Then, at 8:03 a.m. local time on Thursday, Rama appeared in a video message recorded inside the fire-damaged College of Europe building, just meters from his office on Tirana's main street, the Boulevard of the Martyrs of the Nation.

"These are the hands of an opposition that, hiding behind masked people, wants to drag Albania back to a place it will never return to," he declared.

Later that day, Rama addressed the protesters' central demand — his resignation. In comments to Reuters, he ruled out stepping down, saying governments are changed in elections.

The following day, he also accused "foreign hands" of seeking to prevent Albania from joining the European Union.

The unrest comes at a critical moment for Albania's bid to join the EU. Brussels has called for calm and restraint, urging all sides to avoid further escalation and engage in dialogue.

Sali Berisha, the 82-year-old leader of the opposition Democratic Party and a former prime minister, rejected Rama's accusations that the opposition was behind the violence.

"We have no idea whether it's Greece, Iran, Serbia or someone else," he told a press conference, mocking Rama's claims of foreign interference. "The Democratic Party fully supports this protest and will stand by it until the end. Resign and leave immediately!"

For Rigels Xhemollari of the Albanian civil society organization Qendresa Qytetare (Civic Resistance), the student revolt is the culmination of months of peaceful protests.

"The main reason is the prime minister's failure to respond during four months of protests and his mockery of the demonstrators. Other reasons include the economic situation, corruption cases and successive scandals," Xhemollari told DW, referring to a number of corruption investigations involving senior government officials.

But the anger is not directed at Rama's administration alone. Protesters have also voiced their frustration with Albania's political opposition.

"We want the political class of the past 35 years to go. We want a new Albania with new leaders," Skerdi Topalli, a 20-year-old journalism student, told DW.

For political analyst Mark Marku, dean of the Faculty of History and Philology at the University of Tirana, the protests mark a turning point.

"This is the reaction of a generation. In a society that was not responding, they woke people up and made us think about change," he told DW.

But Marku warns that even Rama's resignation and fresh elections would not necessarily bring new political leadership.

"Challenging the government is not an end in itself. A protest must produce a result," he said. "There must be a platform, a political alternative. You cannot vote for a protest."

Xhemollari, meanwhile, sees Rama's resignation as the only way to end the revolt.

"The protest has just one political demand, and it requires a political solution: the prime minister's resignation," he told DW.

Xhemollari says that Albania's president should bring political parties together to form a caretaker government led by a non-partisan prime minister, paving the way for local and parliamentary elections in May 2027.

#625. Suspect arrested over fire at Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ retreat in Bavaria

About 200 firefighters deployed to tackle blaze at former Nazi mountain retreat in remote part of southern Germany

Police have arrested a 33-year-old German citizen after a fire ripped through Adolf Hitler’s former mountain retreat in Bavaria, leaving the historic Nazi meeting place – known as the Eagle’s Nest – largely destroyed.

About 200 firefighters were deployed on Friday night to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote, purpose-built Kehlsteinhaus residence, a protected building on the peak of Obersalzberg in southern Germany.

Flames rose high into the air as firefighters approached the scene to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said, adding that nobody was injured in the fire.

Lisa Maier, a police spokesperson, said firefighters struggled to tackle the blaze due to its location at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000ft).

The building, which was one of the few undamaged monuments of the Hitler era, was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”, she said.

Built by the Nazis and formally inaugurated by Hitler on his birthday in 1939, the Eagle’s Nest has been preserved as a monument to “the insanity of the regime”, according to its website.

The building is only accessible via a road cut into the mountain through previously impassable terrain. Nazis would enter a tunnel and take a 124-metre brass lift buried in the mountain to get inside the building.

Authorities were alerted to the fire when a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm at about 9.15pm, police said. When firefighters arrived on the scene at about 9.50pm, the entire building was engulfed in flames.

Fire departments from six municipalities sent emergency personnel to tackle the blaze and the Bavarian Red Cross, the local mountain rescue service and the police also attended.

No reason for the fire was given, but German media reported that investigators suspected it was the result of arson. Firefighters found no one inside the building.

Efforts to fight the fire were hampered by a strong wind and rain, which turned into the year’s first snow, and firefighters had to pull out overnight after several hours.

The blaze was reportedly still burning at 7am on Saturday but appeared to be out later in the morning, although smoke continued to rise from the building.

A police spokesperson told the German tabloid Bild: “It is damaged to a large extent. The house is unlikely to be saved.” Officers blocked access to the road leading to the retreat, according to an Agence France-Presse photographer.

Maier said police were still investigating and would hold a news conference later on Saturday.

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

The 33-year-old suspect arrested by the police was a German citizen who had ties to the area but did not live there. Prosecutors said he showed signs of mental illness and after being questioned he was being sent to a psychiatric facility.

The possibility of a political motive for the blaze would be investigated, but police said there was nothing to indicate anyone else was involved.

The Eagle’s Nest was constructed between 1937 and 1938 and forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews as well as Roma, LGBTQ people and communists in the Holocaust.

It became legendary in the postwar period and was often depicted as an essential meeting place in US war films, although in reality Hitler rarely visited the complex.

Since 1952 the building has housed an exhibition by the Institute for Contemporary History recounting its Nazi history, and a restaurant.

Officials indicated that the building, which is owned by Bavaria’s state government, would be restored after discussions with local officials, historians and conservators.

“We’re not going to leave a ruin there,” Joachim Herrmann, Bavaria’s interior minister, told reporters, adding that it was important to continue to do “the work of remembrance”.

Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

#626. My mother donated her body to science. I really wasn’t prepared for what came next

The process included a gala featuring medical students doing aerial yoga and singing Taylor Swift to donors’ families. In some ways, it was absolutely perfect

When my mother, Erin O’Connell, was diagnosed with a rare and aggressive cancer in late 2022, one of her first thoughts was: “What will I do if I can’t work?”

At the time, she was 62 years old and working as a physical therapist in Portland, Oregon, where she had recently moved to live closer to me and my family. Reluctantly, she filed for short-term disability from her job and paused her training to become a volunteer search and rescue EMT.

My mom was 40 when she started physical therapy school. I was already a teenager. Despite her newfound stress, I remember how deeply it affected me to watch her fall in love with her work. The year she took anatomy lab she told my sister and me – and anyone who would listen – that dissecting a real human body was the coolest thing she had ever gotten to do, and when she died, she wanted to donate her body to science, too.

I spent so much of my childhood wanting nothing more than my mother’s hard-earned approval, and here she was, utterly devoted to a dead body. On some level, I was jealous of that cadaver.

Now here I was, 25 years later, with my mom’s illness progressing, printing out the paperwork from the nearest med school: “Enrollment Form To Bequeath a Body On Behalf of an Individual”. And all I could think was how jealous I would be of the students who would dissect my mother – who would get to do what I never could, crack her open and peek inside.

This paperwork, though, was its own form of clarity. My mom was going to die, too young and against her will, but we had a plan – an easy, free, meaningful one at that.

Of course, the reality ended up being more complicated and more absurd than I imagined.

After her death, my mom’s body was transported to Oregon Health & Science University (OHSU), just across the river from where we had both lived in Portland.

I worried that, in my grief, I might drive to campus to find out where she was. Would I be tempted to wander the halls, looking for her? Better not to dwell on it, I decided. Instead, I imagined she had been shipped elsewhere, used for something vaguely embarrassing like rectal science or dentistry.

Every year, roughly 25,000 Americans sign up to donate their bodies to science after death. But demand far outstrips supply. According to Tamara Ostervoss, director of OHSU’s body donation program, “it remains an unpopular choice,” partly because so few people even know it’s an option. In Oregon, she told me, only about 1% of people choose to donate their bodies.

For my mom, the registration process was simple: a two-page consent form, signed in front of two witnesses. My mom agreed that her family would not profit from the donation or any discoveries that resulted from it, and that we would have no say in how her body was used. She chose to have her remains cremated and mailed back to us. Eighteen months later, they arrived in a red, white and blue US Postal Service box marked “HUMAN REMAINS”, with an illustration of an urn on the side.

By the time I spoke to Ostervoss, the remains were safely in my closet – and I had a darkly funny story about my awkward visit to the post office to prove it.

Still, talking to the woman who had overseen my mom’s donation was emotionally fraught. As Ostervoss likes to say, your life dictates how you go on to teach others. Thanks to the progression of her cancer, my mom was missing so many internal organs by the end that I joked she would have given some poor anatomy student a pretty limited education.

It’s a credit to Ostervoss’s professional, respectful demeanor that she didn’t laugh so much as smile warmly, with pity in her eyes.

I didn’t tell her that, when my mom was still alive, I had asked her how she would feel if she ended up sold to one of those Bodies exhibits from China. Would my kids recognize her without her skin on?

She laughed, then shrugged. “What do I care? I won’t be there.”

You can decide what happens to your body after you die, if you’re willing to plan ahead. But that doesn’t necessarily mean that, once you’re no longer there to insist, your family will follow through with your plans.

If your loved ones are firmly opposed to body donation, they can simply call a funeral home instead. Which is why, if you’re considering donating your body to science, it’s a conversation worth having while you’re still alive.

Most families, though, fall somewhere in the squeamish-but-accepting middle. “We’ve had families where they might not choose it for themselves, but they really want to honor and support their loved ones’ wishes,” Ostervoss said. “So they’re more along the lines of, “I don’t want to hear anything about it, I don’t want to know about it. I just want to support my mom.”

For me, the mild unease of never knowing exactly what happened to my mom’s corpse at the university was peanuts compared with the prospect of being upsold a coffin by a funeral director while I waded through grief. According to the National Funeral Directors Association, the average cost of burial in our home state of Oregon is $7,895 and the average cost of cremation is $5,812 – numbers that don’t even include a funeral or memorial service.

With body donation, you can always do a memorial later, but in the meantime there are no grief-stricken decisions about embalming or viewings. No deciding what goes on the gravestone, no grave. What does happen is a brief phone screening (in our case, by a hospice nurse), followed by a brief, in-person physical assessment. Then, voilà, off my mom went to fulfill her destiny as, in the language of the body program, someone’s first patient.

The reality is that about 25% of registered donors don’t meet the eligibility requirements at the time of death, per Ostervoss’ estimate. “It’s like medical school,” she said, “Not everyone gets in.”

A common disqualifier is high or low body weight, and privately my sister and I feared my mom had lost too much to be accepted. When she was, I found myself literally jumping up in the air to cheer. “She passed her final test!” I wrote to her sibling group chat, triumphantly. “PTL!” her sister wrote back. Praise the Lord!

Was it odd to feel jubilant on the same day I watched my mother take her final breath? Absolutely, but it was also a gift. It really did feel like her version of a med school acceptance, I told Ostervoss.

Those 150 bodies who do “get in” are able to go on to teach approximately 5,000 learners across the state of Oregon, encompassing not just the first-year medical students you might think of, but surgical residents and practicing doctors, dentists and other healthcare workers.

For students, the benefits of learning about human anatomy and practicing procedures on the real thing, with no risk of hurting them, are intuitive and obvious – the difference between a flight simulator and piloting an airplane. Think of all the variation in vasculature and body size. In reality, no surgeon would see the same internal organs twice. It’s the kind of thing that can’t be replicated, not even with advanced 3D models with haptic feedback.

The emotional side of the student experience is another story. Facing your cadaver for the first time as a new med student has always been a rite of passage, but as western life expectancy increases and our end-of-life rituals become more and more sanitized, anatomy lab is more and more often students’ first encounter with a dead person.

Historically, med school programs have dealt with this by cultivating what the writer Mary Roach calls “a sort of sink or swim mentality about dealing with death”, a kind of future doctor hazing ritual that encouraged future providers to desensitize themselves.

Roach talked to the director of the medical anatomy program at Vanderbilt University, Art Dalley, who says that, “There was a time not all that long ago when students were taught to be insensitive, as a coping mechanism.” In the past, she writes: “Humor – at the cadaver’s expense – was tolerated, condoned, even.”

Not so in our current era. Instead, I received an invitation to a gala in the mail.

At OHSU, the anatomy class culminates in what Ostervoss calls, “the body ceremony”, a 25-year tradition where students plan a memorial to honor the donors and families who have made their education possible.

The service was created to honor the donors, but it’s also important emotionally for the students who are encouraged to have conversations with the families at the reception afterward.

After a year of almost willful dissociation on my part, it was a bizarre experience to be welcomed in. The invite explained that the service would include a slideshow of the 100 or so donors who had given their bodies that year. Students would show their gratitude through performances and reflections they had programmed themselves.

It sounded bizarre but earnest, like a talent show for death. I was thrilled.

Once we were in the auditorium, my eyes darted over to the section of nervous future doctors in new blazers and kitten heels. There was a kind of aura of promise about them, and I felt almost maternally proud. It was clear that families and students had a wild interest in each other and my heart raced as I scanned the rows, looking, as I imagine they did, for some glint of recognition.

I leaned over to whisper to my sister, a note of hope in my voice. “Do you think they’ll recognize us?”

“But maybe our height?” (My mother, like us, was around 5ft tall with shoes on.)

Lauren just gave me a look and I went back to studying the program.

In accordance with HIPAA laws, no one would tell us who dissected whom. It was clear what a bizarre human exchange we had been party to, despite never having met. It had to be acknowledged, ritualized. Otherwise, it made no sense.

Not that a collective death talent show made a whole lot of sense either. As the students took the stage to share their talents – someone played Taylor Swift’s Bigger Than The Whole Sky, a member of the school of dentistry’s class of 2028 sang Sweet Creature by Harry Styles – I wanted to feel something like closure, but all I could muster was affectionate bemusement.

Who were these children, I wondered, and what did they know about death?

When two svelte near-adults took the stage in spandex (their leggings a respectful shade of black) and did what I can only assume was aerial yoga accompanied by Debussy, I had to avoid eye contact with my sister to avoid laughing. Still, as they balanced on each other’s shoulders and knees in midair, I had the urge to text my mom, to tell her how weird it was. I wished I believed she could see it. I know she would have thought it was cool.

When a chaplain got to the podium. “We know that your loved one’s participation in this program has probably complicated your grief, and prolonged it.” She talked about how when someone dies, there is a human need for closure, and we families probably hadn’t quite gotten it yet. They wanted to acknowledge the sacrifice we had made.

Truthfully, I hadn’t thought of it as a sacrifice at the time, more like a “get out of jail free” card, but I was beginning to understand. The chaplain’s words reminded me of the recurring dreams I had had after the two polite, somber men had taken my mom’s body away in a sprinter van. In real life, my sister and I had watched her take her last breath. When it happened it was so obvious, on an almost existential level, that to check her pulse would have been absurd. We didn’t need a nurse to come out. We declared her dead ourselves.

In sleep, though, my subconscious had its say. In recurring dreams, my mom would show up, back from the morgue and on her doorstep again, a little worse for the wear. She would push past us to get inside, clearly miffed we had sent her away prematurely.

After enough of these dreams, I came to understand why we bury our dead. Sure, no one wants the finality of loss but maybe the brain has a hard time moving on without it. It wasn’t until the chaplain alluded to this that that I realized that the lack of closure was exactly what I wanted. I didn’t want to move on. The ambiguity, the mystery even, meant the story of my mother wasn’t over yet.

Near the end of the ceremony, families were invited up to speak. When it was my turn, I gripped the podium, shaky-voiced but not crying. I remember knowing for certain what my mom would want me to say.

I told the students about my mom’s own experience in anatomy lab, all those years ago. The way our dining room had been overtaken by her schoolwork – the table strewn with flash cards and textbooks, colored-pencil anatomical drawings papering the walls. Those years we would find candy corn and York peppermint patty wrappers in the couch cushions – Mom’s study snack of choice.

She was more scatterbrained and short-tempered than ever, but I loved watching her find something she loved, something that was only hers. She learned a kind of devotion, then, an awe that would stay with her even in the darkest days of her illness.

I told them that they would have this, too.

A few weeks ago, after getting up the nerve to ask Ostervoss, I signed a HIPAA form and a media release to find out how my mom’s body came to be of use after she died. Five days later, a media relations specialist from the university forwarded me the answer in the body of an email. It read:

During her time with us, Erin played a crucial role in teaching spine anatomy, associated surgical techniques, and stereotactic and functional neurosurgery skills at OHSU. Through these educational experiences, neurosurgery and neurology trainees gained greater foundational knowledge that will inform their patient care throughout their careers.

After supporting these learners, she went on to teach in several orthopedic residency training courses.

In total, 121 learners directly benefited from your mother’s gift. Her legacy will live on through countless patients cared for by the healthcare professionals she helped educate.

Reading it, I felt the thrill of new information, of something happening in the world of my mother.

Then came the pang of loss, knowing that the one person who would truly appreciate this information was necessarily not available to receive it.

She would think it was so cool. She would have loved to know all of it.

#629. Osborne lists Tory Brexiteers who ‘stopped him cutting welfare’ in warning to Badenoch

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The former chancellor said the biggest opposition he faced to bringing down the welfare bill came from his own Conservative Party

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Former Tory chancellor George Osborne has lashed out at Brexiteers in his own party for blocking his attempts to cut the welfare bill, just days before John Healey is to unveil his first Budget.

Talking with Ed Balls, Labour’s former shadow chancellor, on their Political Currency podcast, Mr Osborne offered Kemi Badenoch his backing for her aim of cutting welfare if she wins power back for the Conservatives.

But he warned that her main opposition would not come from the left and Labour but from rightwing Tories in her own party as he recounted his own experience as chancellor between 2010 and 2016.

The former chancellor then went on to list a number of leading Tory Brexiteers including Boris Johnson, Sir Iain Duncan Smith, Lord Nigel Lawson and Rishi Sunak for getting in his way for trying to cut benefits and then massively increasing welfare spending.

While he did not specifically mention Brexit, all those listed were on the opposite side to him in the EU referendum 2016 when he led the Remain campaign.

In conversation with his former Labour rival Mr Balls, he said: “The problem I had were not with the left, not with my political opponents where I was happy to have the fight which is an echo of the current fight around the welfare party and Kemi Badenoch’s messaging on that. It was the right.

“Who opposed the benefits cap, which was the cap on the total number of benefits one family could receive? Mayor of London Boris Johnson was the biggest opponent.

Who was the biggest opponent when I tried to curb the sickness benefits bill which is now the big talking point? Who resigned from the cabinet over it? Iain Duncan Smith, former Tory leader.

“Who was the person who tried to stop me from cutting the generosity of tax credits? Nigel Lawson, the great Margaret Thatcher chancellor.”

He went on: “It was the Tories who were against cutting welfare.”

He said that his experience should serve as a warning to Ms Badenoch who has made her pitch on increasing defence spending, cutting debt and lowering taxes predicated on slashing the welfare bill by £36bn a year.

Her measures include restoring the two-child benefit limit to save £3.1bn, cutting housing benefit by about 4.5bn, ending benefits for non-UK nationals to save £9.5bn, overhauling sickness and disability benefits to save up to £13bn, introducing a “subsistence allowance” for some long-term unemployed Universal Credit claimants who have not paid sufficient national insurance contributions to save £0.5bn and ending VAT relief on Motability vehicles to save another £1bn.

But Mr Osborne warned: “I think one of the challenges for Kemi Badenoch, and I very much think she is on the right vein here when she is talking about welfare bills, is the welfare bill exploded under the Tory governments of Boris Johnson and then Rishi Sunak.

“They will say it is partly to do with covid, for sure that had a big impact but let’s be clear the big rise of young people getting on to benefits happened under Conservative governments. By the way, the right wing press was not supportive of my welfare cuts at times.

“That’s the challenge. You have got to try to assemble the coalition on your own side before you can win the argument with the other side.

“That’s why welfare benefit reform is so difficult. Were there to be a Conservative government and while I think the list of things Kemi Badenoch wishes to do is fairly sensible, the first opposition she would run into would be the Conservative Party and the conservative press.”

But the Tories have said anyone who stands for the party at the next election have signed up to support Ms Badenoch’s plans.

Sir Iain Duncan Smith hit back at Mr Osborne’s claims pointing out that he had delivered the equivalent of £28bn of welfare savings as work and pensions secretary.

He said: “I resigned because of George Osborne’s top-down cut to pip would not work.

“Of course always worth reflecting that it was while I was work and pensions Secretary that we set in train the cuts to welfare that amounted to £28bn in today’s money. More than had ever been done before.

“I don’t agree that the Conservative Party will fail to do it under Kemi. They will be elected on a pledge to do it.”

A Conservative spokesman said: “Under Kemi Badenoch, we have built a new Conservative Party, with new policies and new people.

“All Conservative MPs will be expected to back our plans to cut £36 billion from the welfare bill by reforming sickness and disability benefits, ending access to benefits for non-EU nationals, reintroducing the two-child benefit cap, and much more.

“Whilst Andy Burnham says national security cannot come at the expense of social security, the Conservatives are the only party with a serious plan to cut welfare and get people working again.”

#631. Antonelli stands on brink of history in Austin

Kimi Antonelli is aiming to become the first Italian F1 world champion since Alberto Ascari in 1953

Kimi Antonelli stands on the brink of history at the United States Grand Prix, where he can become Formula 1's youngest world champion on Sunday, but far from feeling the pressure he says he is enjoying himself more than usual.

It certainly looked like it on Saturday at the Circuit of the Americas as he took a surprise pole position by 0.179 seconds from Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

Antonelli will become world champion on Sunday if he wins the race while his Mercedes team-mate George Russell is lower than eighth and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton below fourth.

Hamilton and Russell start the race fifth and sixth.

Antonelli had not been on pole since the Belgian Grand Prix in July after Mercedes' early season dominance came under challenge from first McLaren and then Red Bull. And his delight was clear as he whooped over the team radio on his slowing down lap.

Antonelli takes US pole on weekend he can win title

He came into the weekend insisting he was going to try to apply the "same mindset as I had all year - one race at a time".

But on Saturday he acknowledged that this one was a new kind of weekend.

"It does feel a little bit different," he said. "But the goal stays the same. I just need to keep doing my job. And, actually, I feel like I can enjoy more driving, everything.

"But, of course, we're going to do the race tomorrow. We're going to try and win. And then we'll see what happens. Obviously, I'm in a very good position."

Antonelli is typically accompanied by his father, Marco, at grands prix, but he said this weekend he had brought other people with him as well to help keep him in the right frame of mind.

"I have a great group of people around me," he said. "I have a lot of friends here as well, so we enjoy the evenings together.

"We play cards in the evening, so we're just doing the fun stuff. And that's what helps, to just relax a little bit and just connect with the mind, and then once you go on track you are back full focus."

The maths suggest the most likely scenario is that Antonelli will not win the title on Sunday - it would, as he put it on Thursday, require "something catastrophic to happen to the others".

If this is a bit of an overstatement - Russell and Hamilton would need only to crash together on the first lap, for example - the fundamental truth is real.

Antonelli was embraced by his father, Marco, after securing his seventh pole of the campaign

He has such a huge advantage - he is 102 points clear of Russell and 111 ahead of Hamilton - that the championship is an inevitability at some point, as Verstappen pointed out when he was asked if he had any advice for his young friend before the race.

"He doesn't need that," the four-time world champion said. "He knows what he's doing. He just needs to try and win the race. If it doesn't happen here, it will happen next weekend (in Mexico City). If it doesn't happen next weekend, it will happen the weekend after (in Sao Paulo).

"It's just been an incredible season. So, you have to also just try and enjoy, of course, this kind of ride over the last months that you've been in. And at one point it's official, and then you can celebrate."

"Incredible" is an over-used word, but an entirely appropriate one in the circumstances.

When it happens, Antonelli will beat the record for youngest champion by more than three years - he will be 20 years and 61 days old on Sunday and Sebastian Vettel, the current record holder, was 23 years and 133 days old when he won his first title in 2010.

Antonelli has taken this season by storm, with eight victories in the 17 races so far, including a run of five in a row after Russell won the first grand prix of the year in Australia.

In doing so, he has dramatically turned the tables after a shaky maiden season in 2025 in which flashes of promise interspersed a generally disappointing year in the context of him being hailed before his debut as a potential generational talent.

This year, he has looked every bit that, but that does not mean a victory on Sunday is a foregone conclusion.

Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Live from 19:30; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app

His pole was a surprise because the people most likely to achieve it before qualifying had appeared to be one of the Ferrari drivers or Verstappen.

But Ferrari faded, as they so often do, Charles Leclerc complaining about his tyres losing grip as the sun and temperature dropped, Hamilton saying: "The car felt really good. The lap was solid, so they were just quicker."

Verstappen, meanwhile, went into the final session with "high hopes" after setting a competitive time on used tyres in the second session, only to find his grip had evaporated in the final session.

The race, though, is a different matter. Verstappen's race pace was strong on Friday and he said: "Yes, we have been happier in the long runs. And I hope that it will be the same tomorrow."

Leclerc said he believed he could battle for the win if he could make a good start but Hamilton was not so sure.

He said: "You have to be realistic. We're fourth and fifth. It's very hard to overtake here. Even if you're P2 on the grid, it's hard to beat someone (on pole) over a race distance. I raced here since 2012. It took a lot to get past Vettel back then. But maybe with strategy, we can progress."

There's really only one story on Sunday, though. Antonelli will be champion sooner or later. Which will it be?

Article rédigé par Auxence Cames

l'essentiel Touché par plusieurs tirs, Pengo Bossio Wangi a succombé à la suite de la tragique attaque qui a fait cinq autres blessés ce vendredi 23 octobre à Trappes puis La Verrière, dans les Yvelines. L'homme de 26 ans, friand de sports de combat et très apprécié, laisse derrière lui une communauté sous le choc.

Il a eu le malheur de se retrouver "au mauvais endroit" et "au mauvais moment". Ce vendredi 23 octobre, un homme a été abattu par balles en plein square Louis-Pergaud, à Trappes, victime d'une fusillade à caractère raciste selon les premiers éléments de l'enquête. Cinq autres blessés, dont une jeune fille de 12 ans, sont également à déplorer. L'identité du défunt, Pengo Bossio Wangi, a finalement été révélée un peu plus tard dans la journée.

À lire aussi : REPLAY. Fusillade à Trappes : Emmanuel Macron dénonce un "attentat" commis "sur la base d'une idéologie raciste"

Âgé de 26 ans, Bossio Wangi était originaire de Poissy, en banlieue ouest de Paris, et souhaitait devenir un combattant professionnel de MMA. Pour s'y faire, il s’entraînait plusieurs fois par semaine à l’Atch Academy, un complexe reconnu d’Aubervilliers. Concourant dans des catégories de poids intermédiaires, entre mi-moyens (-77 kg) et moyens (-84 kg), "PBW" était une figure locale qui faisait l'unanimité, à en croire ceux qui l'ont côtoyé.

Vendredi soir, l’Atch Academy a tenu à rendre un vibrant hommage à son licencié, en saluant son engagement sans faille. "Pengo faisait partie des nôtres. Sur les tapis comme en dehors, il était de ceux qui donnent l’exemple : présent, respectueux, toujours prêt à pousser les autres vers le haut. Son sourire, son énergie et sa générosité resteront gravés dans nos murs et dans nos cœurs", peut-on lire sur Instagram. "Aujourd’hui, les mots manquent. Rien ne justifie qu’une vie soit arrachée ainsi."

À lire aussi : Fusillade à Trappes : connu de la police, appartement piégé... Qui est Kevin T., le suspect de cette attaque terroriste ?

Face à ce drame, de nombreuses personnalités ont publiquement réagi, à commencer par l'athlète français Salahdine Parnasse. "Repose en paix... Toutes mes pensées à sa famille et ses proches, on ne t’oubliera pas", écrit sur X celui qui s'entraînait dans la même salle que le défunt.

#633. Who was Eva Mamlok? Berlin square renamed after Jewish anti-fascist resistance fighter

She started taking action against Hitler as a teenager and never stopped until her death in a concentration camp. Berlin's Blücherplatz is now being renamed after her.

In the history of German resistance to Nazism, some names have become symbols: Sophie Scholl, Claus von Stauffenberg, Dietrich Bonhoeffer and Georg Elser. Yet many others have remained largely forgotten.

Among them is Eva Mamlok, a young Jewish woman from Berlin whose acts of defiance began in her teenage years and continued until her murder in a Nazi concentration camp.

Now more people will get to know her story as Berlin renames Blücherplatz, a square in the district of Kreuzberg, Eva-Mamlok-Platz on October 16.

"Eva Mamlok was a very remarkable person. As a young Jewish woman from Berlin, her spirit of resistance was particularly striking," said cultural researcher Alexandra Weltz-Rombach, who has worked extensively with the historians' network "Gruppe Eva Mamlok."

Mamlok was born on May 6, 1918, into a Jewish family in Berlin. They ran a wholesale wine business, and the family belonged to the vibrant Jewish middle class that formed an important part of Berlin's social and economic life during the Weimar Republic.

But Eva came of age just as Germany was descending into dictatorship. When Hitler became chancellor in 1933, she was only 14 years old. She was also a member of the Socialist Workers' Youth (SAJ). Following the suppression of the left-wing political youth organization later that year, she became active in the underground resistance.

According to testimony from Inge Berner (1922-2012), the sole survivor of Mamlok's later resistance group, Eva climbed onto the roof of a department store on Blücherplatz as a teenager and painted the slogan "Down with Hitler."

"She was caught doing that, though she wasn't arrested at that particular moment — that didn't happen until a year later," noted Weltz-Rombach.

Mamlok first appeared in official records in November 1934, after she was arrested for taking part in commemorations for socialist leaders Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht at Berlin's Friedrichsfelde Cemetery.

Authorities determined that the 16-year-old held "hostile views toward the state" and placed her in "protective custody until further notice" — a euphemism the regime used to justify imprisonment without trial. She was sent to the women's concentration camp at Moringen in Lower Saxony, where she remained until May 1935.

After her release, she continued her anti-Nazi activities despite the increasing danger, facing persecution both as a political dissident and as a Jew.

In these underground circles, she met Pieter Siemsen (1914–2004), and they remained a couple until he emigrated to Argentina in 1937. The only known surviving photograph of Eva comes from his personal archive.

She had a daughter, Tana, in 1939. The father's identity is unknown, however. The child was placed in a Jewish orphanage in Berlin and deported in 1942 to the Auschwitz-Birkenau extermination camp, where she was murdered.

Meanwhile, because she was Jewish, Mamlok was forced to perform compulsory labor at the Berlin firm F. Butzke Schrauben-Industrie in 1940. There she met other women who shared her opposition to Nazism.

Together they formed what later became known as the "Eva Mamlok Group," an informal resistance network of Jewish and non-Jewish women. They distributed anti-Nazi leaflets and wrote slogans critical of Hitler.

They also shared banned books. "They were books that are today part of Germany's educational canon," from Thomas Mann to Lion Feuchtwanger, said Weltz-Rombach. That the Berlin Central and Regional Library (ZLB), Germany's largest public library, stands on the new Eva-Mamlok-Platz is a fitting symbol of this act of resistance and the importance of books, she added.

Mamlok and others in her group were arrested for distributing this forbidden literature. On January 13, 1942, she was deported from Berlin to the Riga Ghetto in occupied Latvia.

According to Inge Berner's testimony, Mamlok remained active in the resistance there too. For example, she arranged for a contact still in Berlin to send her a cake with a miniature camera hidden inside it to document persecution in the ghetto.

In October 1944, she was sent to the Stutthof Nazi concentration camp, where she died in December of that year.

Blücherplatz was named after the Prussian field marshal Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher, whose most renowned achievement was leading his army against Napoleon at the Battle of Leipzig in 1813 and the Battle of Waterloo in 1815.

Several places, including streets and parks, have been named after him in Germany.

"There is no shortage of Blücher memorial sites," said Weltz-Rombach. "And perhaps it's also time to put an end to this old Franco-German enmity — which is, of course, inherent in the name Blücher, given its Prussian tradition — and to establish, in its place, a different form of remembrance."

The square also happens to be the site of the Carnival of Cultures, a multicultural street festival and parade held every year to celebrate Berlin's global diversity.

Having first heard about Mamlok when a Stolperstein commemorating her was laid in 2011, Weltz-Rombach has been researching her biography for the past few years. The Berlin-based filmmaker, producer and curator has also been sharing the resistance fighter's story through various projects, including an exhibition in 2024 and a podcast series with young Berliners.

Since Mamlok was only a teenager herself when she became politically active, the workshop participants can easily relate to her fate.

These teenagers learn about Mamlok's experiences at the actual locations where she was active, helping them imagine what it would be like to be arrested and imprisoned for six months without trial for doing things that normally wouldn't be considered crimes — such as simply expressing an opinion publicly or laying flowers at a commemorative event, explained Weltz-Rombach.

"Above all, she is, of course, a role model — an example of how one would like to act oneself, and how courageous one would like to be."

"[Women's] resistance was often of a more everyday nature, rather than planting bombs," said Weltz-Rombach. Their stories offer examples of "forms of resistance that have only recently received more attention." Other examples include a 2024 exhibition and the launch of a database dedicated to female resistance fighters.

Even though many of the eyewitnesses are now dead, Weltz-Rombach believes there are still many more of these stories that deserve to be brought into the spotlight: "There are definitely many names we do not know, that are waiting to be further researched."
