#634. Bundestrainer Jürgen Klopp reagiert verständnislos auf Rassismus gegen das DFB-Team

Rassistische Kommentare begleiten die DFB-Elf seit Tagen. Rund um das Spiel gegen Serbien antwortet jeder auf seine Weise: Klopp mit klaren Worten, sein Team mit starkem Auftritt und die Fans mit viel Schwarz-Rot-Gold.

Immer wieder hallten Sprechchöre wie "Schwarz-Rot-Gold" oder "Deutschland, Deutschland" durch das Stadion in München. Die Fans schwenkten stolz ihre Fahnen, sangen und feierten ihre Nationalmannschaft. Der 2:0 (1:0)-Sieg gegen Serbien wirkte wie ein Befreiungsschlag - auf mehreren Ebenen.

Zum einen war es der erste Sieg für den neuen Bundestrainer Jürgen Klopp, dem an diesem Abend "alles" an seiner Mannschaft gefallen hatte. "Die Anfangsphase, der Mittelteil, das Ende. Es war ein perfekter Abend. Ich bin so happy und stolz auf das, was wir gezeigt haben", so der 59-Jährige.

Die Nationalmannschaft zeigte das beste Spiel unter dem neuen Bundestrainer und auch von den Rängen wurde das Team lauter und emotionaler unterstützt als bei den vergangenen Partien.

Nach der Niederlage gegen Griechenland am vergangenen Sonntag hatte es erstmals seit Klopps Verpflichtung leichte Kritik gegeben - dazu Pfiffe nach dem Spiel. Zudem häuften sich in den Sozialen Netzwerken rassistische Kommentare über die DFB-Elf.

Schon bei Veröffentlichung der Mannschaftsaufstellung vor der Partie wurde das DFB-Team als "nicht weiß genug" oder "nicht deutsch genug" für eine deutsche Nationalmannschaft bezeichnet und aufs Übelste beschimpft.

"Es gibt keinen Grund, sich über diese Menschen Gedanken zu machen. Meine Gedanken kriegen sie nicht", hatte Klopp in der Pressekonferenz vor dem Spiel gegen Serbien auf Nachfrage der Deutschen Welle (DW) erklärt. Er habe schon im normalen Leben für Dummheit wenig Zeit und in sozialen Medien auch nicht.

"Die große Crux in unserem Leben ist, dass jeder seine Meinung sagen darf", so der Bundestrainer. Solche Kommentare seien "Wahnsinn".

Auch auf politischer Ebene ist die Nationalmannschaft immer wieder Thema, vor allem einige Mitglieder der Partei "Alternative für Deutschland" (AfD) schießen regelmäßig gegen die DFB-Elf, die bereits seit Jahren Projektionsfläche für die Frage ist, wer als deutsch gelten soll.

Politiker Björn Höcke schrieb beispielsweise bei X mit Blick auf die Hautfarbe und Namen der Spieler, die während der Heim-EM 2024 auf dem Platz gestanden hatten: "Heute kann ich mich nicht mehr mit unserer Nationalmannschaft identifizieren."

Zur Mannschaftsaufstellung gegen Griechenland kommentierte der AfD-Bundestagsabgeordnete Kay Gottschalk auf X den Fotovergleich der Weltmeisterelf von 1990 mit der aktuellen Startelf, den eine rechtsextreme Influencerin dort gepostet hatte.

Er schrieb über kulturell gewachsene "Charaktereigenschaften, bestimmte Tugenden und Teamgeist". Was diese Tugenden mit der Hautfarbe der Spieler zu tun haben, erklärte er allerdings nicht.

Sein AfD-Fraktionskollege Christopher Drößler, ein Polizeibeamter der Bundespolizei, warnte davor, eine "multiethnische Gesellschaft mit der Harmonie einer Fußballmannschaft gleichzusetzen - und fordert 'Remigration im gesetzlich maximal möglichen Umfang.'"

Der österreichische Rechtsextremist Martin Sellner behauptete auf X, dass man ohne die kleine deutsche Flagge keine Ahnung hätte, welche Nationalmannschaft dort eigentlich auf dem Platz stehe.

"Diese Rassismus-Debatte ist Quatsch. Jeder gibt sein Herzblut für die Nationalmannschaft und da ist es egal, ob er schwarz ist, weiß oder welche Hautfarbe auch immer er hat", sagte DFB-Fan Jannik der DW. Jeder sei Deutscher, jeder gebe alles für Deutschland. Und auch die deutsche Fahne gehöre für ihn dazu.

"Man sollte stolz sein, die deutsche Flagge zu zeigen. Das hat nichts mit Rassismus zu tun. Es darf genauso einer, der gerade erst hierhergekommen ist, die Flagge zeigen, wie die anderen auch." Die Flagge gehöre zur deutschen Nationalmannschaft dazu.

Deutschland-Fan Pablo ergänzte: "Es ist Wahnsinn, dass man 2026 immer noch dagegen kämpfen muss. Bunter geht es kaum in Deutschland und das soll sich auch in der Nationalmannschaft widerspiegeln." Viele der angereisten Fans stehen voll und ganz hinter der Elf von Bundestrainer Klopp.

Der 59-Jährige hatte vor einigen Wochen eine Pressekonferenz für eine Grundsatzrede gegen rechts und für "positiven Patriotismus" genutzt und gesagt: "Ich würde mir oder uns gerne die Fahne zurückholen. Ich möchte, dass wir sie immer so schwingen, dass niemand denkt, was mit dir nicht in Ordnung ist. Sondern dass man einfach nur das Gefühl hat, du bist happy und verstehst, dass du Glück hattest, dass du in diesem wundervollen Land geboren, aufgewachsen und zugezogen bist."

Er wolle "Nationalstolz nicht den falschen Leuten" überlassen. "Ich kann stolz darauf sein, deutsch zu sein und trotzdem offen und vielfältig und nett, freundlich."

Klopp hat mit seinen Aussagen viele Fans in Deutschland beeindruckt. "Ich habe Gänsehaut bekommen als er das gesagt hat. Mit Blick auf die aktuelle Entwicklung in der Welt, finde ich es wichtig, dass eine Persönlichkeit wie Klopp sich so positioniert", erklärte Pablo.

Leistungen wie die seines Teams gegen Serbien begeistern die Menschen in Deutschland - und fördern den von ihm geforderten "positiven Patriotismus". Und sie lassen die rassistischen Stimmen vielleicht bisschen leiser werden - so zumindest ist die Hoffnung des Bundestrainers, der mit Blick auf sein Team noch einmal betonte:

"Die Gruppe könnte nicht großartiger sein. Die Welt dürfte sich ein Beispiel an einer Sport-Umkleidekabine nehmen. Da wird jeder aufgrund der genau richtigen Tatsachen respektiert und nicht aufgrund der falschen Meinung diskreditiert", so Klopp. In keiner Mannschaft, in keinem Sportverein sei das ein Thema.

#635. Nine killed and 40 injured after gunmen open fire at church funeral in Jordan

Footage broadcast on state TV shows three attackers approaching Greek Orthodox church and firing shots

Nine people have been killed after gunmen opened fire at a funeral at a church in Jordan in a rare attack ⁠on the country’s Christian minority.

Authorities described the attack on Friday as a terrorist act by extremists.

Maj gen Abdallah al-Maaytah, the head of Jordan’s ⁠Public Security Directorate, said most of those injured in the shooting at St George’s Greek Orthodox church in Hamoud, in Karak governorate, were receiving treatment, and that the ⁠hunt for the attackers was continuing. Jordan’s health minister said 40 people were injured.

The interior minister, Mazin Al Farrayeh, said the attack had been carried out by “extremists”, but it was too early to tell whether they had any links to known groups ⁠inside or outside Jordan.

Such attacks are rare in Jordan, which is relatively stable, though authorities in the US say in recent years they have repeatedly ​foiled attempted attacks by Islamist militants.

There was no immediate claim of responsibility.

A ‌video, aired on Jordan’s state-owned Al-Mamlaka television station ‌that appeared to be from a security camera on the church, showed three people firing at it from a pavement and hiding behind trees and a ‌low wall. It then showed the attackers running towards the church’s entrance. Reuters was able to verify the video from the entry path and wall surrounding the church, as well as other details.

In a post on X, Jordan’s prime minister, Jafar Hassan, said: “This is a result of a terrorist ideology and blind extremism and we will not allow society to go down this path.”

A priest described how he and ‌others ordered people to ‌get to the ground at the church. “A sense of panic took hold among those present,” Theodoros Soueiss said. “The gunfire was indiscriminate, and you never knew where a bullet might land.”

Khaled Burqan, who was at the funeral, told Al-Mamlaka that dozens of people were present and the gunmen opened fire on them for several minutes.

Ihab Ammareen, another witness, told the station he saw bloodied people collapse ‌on the floor after the attack. “People were crying, wailing, screaming – it’s hard to describe,” he said.

Jordan’s King Abdullah, a leading US partner in the fight against militant Islamist groups, visited Karak hours after the attack and said the perpetrators would ​be punished “with an iron fist”.

“The terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation. Those who delude themselves into thinking they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity,” he said in a statement.

Reuters footage from the church after the attack showed blood smeared on the floor near its entrance, where security forces were deployed.

Security has been ⁠stepped up at malls, ⁠foreign embassies ​and other locations across Jordan, the US embassy in Amman said on Saturday.

In a post on X, the UN secretary general, António Guterres, condemned the violence and said attacks against civilians and places of ⁠worship were unacceptable.

People who gathered at a Karak government hospital to support the injured expressed shock. “What happened today has ​left people unable to speak or raise our voices. ​But our only reproach to the state is that ​it must investigate these dark ideas – where they come from and how they enter the minds of our children,” said Hani Al-Mbaydeen, who was outside the hospital.

Christians make up ‌a minority of Jordan’s population. ​The country is home to several ​biblical sites that attract Christian pilgrims from around the world. The US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, described it on X as a “depraved and brutal attack on a house of worship”. Jordan was among the US allies in the region to be hit by Iranian attacks this year after the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February.

#637. Outback kaleidoscope: Australia’s fabled desert lake bursts to life in rare sight

A prodigiously wet monsoon season has brought damaging floods to parts of Australia, but transformed Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre in a way not seen in decades

The Australian desert is green. Not just green – depending on where you look from above, it could also be a marbled reddy-pink and blue or yellow-brown with flecks of purple. But green is the most striking colour because the desert is not supposed to look like this.

It won’t last. But for now, in late September, the deep outback – a celebrated part of the Australian continent that few people get to see – is blanketed in plant life. There is sandhill wattle, saltbush and lignum, and grasses and desert flowers. The vegetation is thickest along hundreds of twisting rivers and creeks that cut across the landscape.

These rivers and creeks carry water from a prodigiously wet monsoon season that brought flooding rains to western Queensland. Rainfall nearly 50% above the long-term average caused havoc, killing livestock and cutting outback tracks, some of which remain underwater. But it also filled up three major river systems – the Georgina, the Diamantina and Cooper Creek.

They run to one place: Kati Thanda-Lake Eyre. Local rainfall, which persisted between March and August, added to the flow. The result is that the centre of the continent is being transformed in a way that hasn’t happened since 1974.

We are flying north in a six-seater light aircraft from William Creek, a tiny outpost that operates as something like an independent kingdom in the middle of Anna Creek station, the world’s largest cattle property. At nearly 24,000 sq km, Anna Creek is bigger than Wales.

William Creek is much, much smaller. Lying on the traditional lands of the Arabana people, and owned by charter flight operator and unofficial mayor Trevor Wright, it has about a dozen buildings, huddled together in a vain attempt to shelter from the elements, about halfway along the famed Oodnadatta Track.

Kati Thanda is about 60km north-east of the town. They are separated by the Tirari Desert, which now looks more like scrubby parts of the coastal east than arid backcountry.

After a few minutes the lake appears on the horizon like an ocean. Soon, mirror-like water is all we can see as the horizon disappears.

It’s Australia’s largest lake by surface area. Stretching 144km in length and 77km in width, it covers about 9,500 sq km – almost as much as suburban Melbourne. It includes the country’s lowest point, about 15 metres below sea level.

Kati Thanda is endorheic, meaning the water it collects has nowhere to drain. Most of the water from the region’s river systems enters via the Warburton Creek. Once in the lake it becomes the Warburton Groove, a north-south geological channel that paints a dark band as it spreads across the lake for up to 90km.

It empties by evaporation, sometimes at an astonishing rate, losing up to 1cm of depth a day. Given the infrequency of the sort of heavy rains experienced this year, it is empty most of the time. When it is, it turns into a vast salt plain.

Its crust is estimated to be made up of 400m tonnes of salt. The salt flats not underwater, mainly in the north, shimmer with vibrant white. They are stable enough when completely dry for British driver Donald Campbell to have chosen it as the place to set a land speed record of 648 km/h in 1964.

When we visit, the salinity of the lake is roughly equivalent to an ocean. Soon, as evaporation kicks in, it will be as much as seven times saltier than the Coral Sea. That has already happened in small pockets that filled last year in the Madigan Gulf, in the lake’s south-eastern corner. From above, the water appears as an extraordinary burst of pink.

The strawberry sheen is caused by bacteria and algae that relish the salt. The high salt content has other side-effects. In a remarkable act of survival, zooplankton and phytoplankton eggs lie dormant in the salt while the lake is dry and hatch after the next influx, creating a basin thick with life – what some describe as “invertebrate soup”. It kicks off the return of a food chain that results in the return of fish: spangled perch, bony bream and species of hardyhead.

The invertebrates and fish, in turn, bring birds.

Initially we see only a smattering of birds here and there. A few silver gulls hang on the breeze about 700km from the nearest sea. Later, we catch a darting pod of pelicans flying low over the lake’s surface.

As we sweep over Halligan Bay near the lake’s western shore, it becomes clear where they are headed – to join thousands of other pelicans standing in the shallows and nesting on exposed sand within the lake. A scientific aerial survey of birdlife two weeks later, in early October, finds a smaller flock – about 800 adults and mostly nearly fledged young. Prof Richard Kingsford, the director of the Centre for Ecosystem Science at the University of New South Wales, who has been studying birdlife across the continent for more than 40 years, says they also saw a few hundred dead pelican chicks.

As H5N1 bird flu spreads, there has been concern it may have reached the arid centre. But Kingsford says they saw no pelicans showing the abnormal behaviour associated with sickness. It is more likely the deaths were a result of a more regular event: some breeding pelicans may not have been able to get enough food for their chicks as the lake became more saline.

This theory was supported by signs of pelicans flying to flourishing rivers to the west, in search of fish. “There is nothing there to indicate it isn’t a natural event,” Kingsford says.

Elsewhere on the lake there are terns: gull-billed, whiskered and the large Caspian. Banded stilts are scattered about. But not as many as you might expect. “This is indicative of an ecosystem which is salty and not productive for high diversity and numbers of waterbirds,” Kingsford says.

As we head north, the lake gives way to the Munga-Thirri-Simpson Desert and its 200km-long lines of parallel sand dunes, currently a patchwork of green tones. Millennia ago this was home to megafauna such as the SUV-sized, wombat-like Diprotodon. Today, it includes the Kalamurina Wildlife Sanctuary, a protected area larger than Tasmania that takes in gibber plains, floodplains and ephemeral lakes.

We cross the Goyder Lagoon, an important bird area that is part of the Diamantina river system. Periodically, we pass over mound springs – unusually vibrantly coloured areas that are a sign of water being released from the world’s deepest underground freshwater reservoir, the Great Artesian Basin.

The Diamantina was the greatest contributor to the flooding, and Kati Thanda filling, last year. It had a devastating impact, including killing about 130,000 cattle. It flooded again this year, but not as much. As we approach the south-eastern Queensland outpost of Birdsville, its flow is a distinctive yellow, and the spillover continues to affect daily life, swallowing the show grounds and cutting off the Birdsville Track – an unsealed, 500km lifeline to other communities – all this year.

From there, it is time to return. With the plane’s back side door removed to allow better camera access, we trace part of the 1,300km Cooper Creek back towards the lake. There are waterbirds here in larger numbers than in Kati Thanda itself – according to Kingsford there are more than 10,000, including grey teal and pink-eared ducks.

The creek and its tributaries provide a final burst of colour: a turquoise-blue that is in sharp contrast to the swirling, vibrant red of the iron oxide smothering the rocks and sand of the Sturt Stony Desert.

It’s an arresting scene, but it’s also ephemeral. In the hot months ahead, the water here and in the lake will likely retreat as a super El Niño bites and daytime temperatures rise to 45C. More of the dust, salt and red earth beneath will be revealed. But for now, in this century at least, it is a one-of-a kind show.

#638. Who actually controls Ukraine's access to Starlink?

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky says unexplained limits on Starlink and Starshield services continue to affect Ukrainian forces, while US officials and Elon Musk offer conflicting accounts of who controls the restrictions.

Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed.

The networks use 10,000 satellites to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and on the battlefield. Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.

The BBC's Washington correspondent Daniel Bush looks at what officials have said about the technology.

#639. Nearly 1 million chickens killed at egg farm as nation’s largest bird flu outbreak grows

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Losing nearly a million hens could cut egg supplies and drive prices higher

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Nearly 1 million chickens were killed at an Illinois farm after a bird flu outbreak became the nation’s largest active outbreak this week.

The outbreak affected 934,600 birds at a commercial table egg layer facility in Clinton County, Illinois, the United States Department of Agriculture confirmed. It reportedly occurred at Rose Acre Farms, located outside Germantown, village officials told KSDK.

Rose Acre Farms is the second-largest egg producer in the U.S., according to the company's website. With no treatment available for highly pathogenic avian influenza, better known as bird flu, authorities must kill infected and exposed birds to contain the virus.

Losing nearly a million hens could disrupt egg production and put further pressure on prices as supplies tighten.

The scale of the Illinois outbreak far exceeds other active cases nationwide. Minnesota had the next-highest number of birds affected, with 168,880 statewide, according to the USDA.

The outbreak is part of a nationwide bird flu epidemic first detected in the U.S. in February 2022. Since then, more than 210 million birds have died or been killed as a result of the outbreak, according to the report.

Bird flu detections typically increase during the fall and spring, when migrating wild birds can spread the virus to domestic poultry. The virus can spread through contact with infected birds, contaminated surfaces and materials, making farms vulnerable when the disease reaches their flocks.

Replacing nearly a million hens takes time, meaning fewer eggs could reach grocery stores and prices could rise. That’s what happened in 2024, when bird flu killed tens of millions of egg-laying hens, shrinking supplies and sending prices soaring.

By January that year, a dozen cage-free eggs averaged $5.26 in advertised retail prices, according to the USDA. As of last month, the national averages were sitting around $3.80 to $3.88, according to the agency.

The Trump administration even sued California and Michigan over cage-free egg laws, arguing the state requirements drive up prices and that egg production should be governed by federal standards. The lawsuits were dismissed, with judges finding the administration had not established it had legal grounds to bring the challenges.

The USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service said it continues to work with state animal health officials to monitor commercial poultry operations, backyard flocks and wild birds for signs of infection.

"We also continue to encourage all bird owners to practice strong biosecurity—that means reducing opportunities for wildlife to spread the virus to their birds and preventing the spread of the virus from one premises to another,” the agency said on its website.

The Independent has contacted the USDA and Rose Acre Farms for comment.

#640. Pupils as young as five suspended from school over sexual misconduct

Published: 22:02 GMT, 24 October 2026 | Updated: 03:51 GMT, 25 October 2026

Children barely out of nursery are among record numbers being kicked out of class for sexual misconduct, with schools in England handing out almost 40 suspensions every school day.

Pupils were suspended 7,278 times for sexual misconduct in the 2024/25 school year – the highest total since the current recording method began in 2020, Department for Education figures show.

Shockingly, 20 children aged five or under were suspended for sexual misconduct, including 19 in reception year.

Five children in the infant years were expelled outright (with no conditional return) and primary schools alone handed out 759 of the suspensions.

Suspensions in the category cover sexual assaults, abuse, harassment and lewd behaviour, whether aimed at classmates or staff.

The sexual misconduct tally is up 12 per cent from 6,479 in the previous year – and the rise comes despite the total number of suspensions for all other reasons falling.

Ofsted has found sexual harassment normalised among schoolchildren, and teaching leaders warn that misogynist online influencers such as Andrew Tate are shaping how boys treat girls in class.

Department for Education figures have shown children barely out of nursery are among record numbers being kicked out of class for sexual misconduct (stock image)

The Netflix drama Adolescence was backed by ministers for screening in secondary schools because it laid bare how online misogyny can poison teenage boys.

Pupils aged 13 and 14 were the most frequent offenders, with 1,564 suspensions between them.

The worst cases saw 143 pupils permanently excluded from school last year. Schools can log up to three reasons for each suspension.

Christopher McGovern, chairman of the Campaign for Real Education, said: 'These shocking figures represent only the tip of the iceberg of misogyny in schools. Most cases go unreported.

'Schools are no longer safe places for girls and for female teachers. The Government needs to greatly expand the option of single-sex schooling rather than allowing it to largely disappear.'

Soma Sara, chief executive of the Everyone's Invited charity, said: 'We hope that schools are now more conscious of the reality of sexual harassment and abuse among children and young people, and are better equipped to identify it and intervene when it happens.

'For too long, the harm children were experiencing was not always being recognised or understood by the adults around them.'

A government spokesman said: 'As part of our strategy to halve violence against women and girls, we have pledged to make sure all young people are taught about healthy relationships and consent from an early age.

'We have also forced tech companies to tackle harmful content and protect young people online through the Online Safety Act.'

#641. Man Utd not an unmanageable club - Carrick

Michael Carrick appeared to apologise to travelling supporters following his side's midweek defeat at Como

Manchester United head coach Michael Carrick has dismissed a theory the Old Trafford club are unmanageable.

Carrick is clinging on to his job after a desperate run of seven games without a win before Sunday's Premier League home game against Bournemouth (14:00 GMT).

The pressure on him has been heightened by controversial comments from senior players Lisandro Martinez and Bruno Fernandes attacking the club's recruitment and his tactics.

If Carrick were to lose his job, it would be the third change of manager in as many seasons and mean eight long-term bosses, including Ralf Rangnick, have lost their jobs after failing to get close to the heights of Sir Alex Ferguson, who retired in 2013.

Given the pressure on the club is heightened by the number of prominent ex-players who have their own media outlets, and the proliferation of fan channels that attract large numbers of viewers, there is an argument it makes United an impossible club to manage.

Carrick had a one-word answer to that notion: "No."

However, Carrick does take issue with some of the claims made about his team by former professionals and casual observers.

He is vexed at the sense his team do not run enough, and do not press the opposition when they are out of possession.

Carrick has accepted the general performance of his team in a 4-1 Champions League defeat at Como on Wednesday was "unacceptable".

However, he does not see how claims his team do not press stand up to much scrutiny.

"You've got to be careful with just saying 'not running'," he said.

"We've won a lot of games over a period of time and this pressing thing; pressing is one small part of football.

"There are all sorts of different ways that are classed as a press. What actually is it? What are you doing it for? Is it to your strength? Is it covering up other spaces?

"It's just thrown about as a bit of a word at the minute. You don't necessarily need to press to win games of football. Sometimes you do, sometimes you don't.

"It's not necessarily just running stats that define football games either.

"We've just got to get back to doing a lot of the things that we were doing last season and for certain parts of this season."

Although Carrick was appointed ahead of his former boss and team-mate Ole Gunnar Solskjaer as Ruben Amorim's replacement in January, the pair remain close.

Solskjaer drove up to United's base in Trondheim before the pre-season victory over Rosenborg in July to spend time with Carrick and his backroom team.

They have been in touch this week, with Carrick also confirming he had spoken to Ferguson, who is a regular at matches as he approaches his 85th birthday.

Ferguson signed Carrick from Tottenham in 2006 and also managed the midfielder's Manchester United team in his testimonial game at Old Trafford in 2017.

"I speak to both of them quite regularly," he said. "There's nothing particular in that. I'm close to both of them. It's nothing different this week."

Carrick is convinced he can turn the situation around but knows he needs his underperforming squad to deliver against Bournemouth.

"I definitely trust them, 100%," he said.

"We'll be a different team on Sunday. We have to be a different team on Sunday."

#642. EU promotes sovereign, trusted AI as it struggles to catch US and China

At an international AI summit in Dublin, EU leaders promoted trusted and independent artificial intelligence. Critics question whether the bloc can close the gap with the US and China while maintaining strict regulation.

If supremacy in artificial intelligence was an Olympic discipline, there would only be two serious contenders for gold on current trajectories: the US and China. The European Union, as has been the case in many areas of cutting-edge technology in recent times, is barely in the AI conversation.

Former European Central Bank President Mario Draghi, whose 2024 report highlighted the EU's desperate need to be more innovative to become more competitive, said recently that AI is "perhaps the most promising" route the EU has to raise growth today. However, he decried the fact that the European Union controls little of the value chain.

"Being cut off from AI, once the economy runs on it, would be more like being cut off from the US financial system," he wrote in an opinion piece for the Financial Times. "The effects would be catastrophic."

Draghi's spirit was on full display in Dublin on Wednesday at an international AI summit the Irish government convened as part of its six-month stint hosting the rotating EU presidency.

The summit's motto, "Harnessing AI to Revolutionize Europe's Competitiveness," might as well have been dreamed up by the Italian former prime minister.

Harnessing AI has become a lot more complicated. A slew of controversies around AI agents going rogue, from the Hugging Face attack in June when 1,200 agents hacked an online platform, to an Anthropic-designed agent sending a fake tip to US police over an unsolved murder, have caused alarm.

Many from within the tech industry, including Microsoft founder Bill Gates and the leading AI frontier labs themselves, have called for a development pausein order for safety measures to catch up.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet positivity was largely the name of the game at the summit, with tech and AI industry leaders joining Irish and EU politicians to declare AI's transformative economic and societal potential — while also emphasizing the need for strong regulation and safety standards.

Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin made it clear that Ireland was all in on AI. He echoed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's recent assertion that the technology represented a "tipping point." He also repeatedly highlighted what he sees as the bloc's commitment to safety.

"We are determined to capture the dividend by mitigating the risks," Martin told the event. "In Europe, we have charted our path ... balancing innovation and opportunity with a trustworthy, human-centered approach to AI."

Meanwhile, Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, security and democracy, revealed at the event that the EU had begun its first enforcement actions under its new AI Act, requesting information around security and safety from advanced AI model providers.

However, other topics that concern AI's many critics, from those fearing the massive environmental impact of data centers to others warning about possible AI-related job losses, were largely absent from the discussions.

Outside the venue, a group of protesters led by People Before Profit, a left-wing Irish political party, criticized the summit for not focusing on these issues.

"There is a deliberate blurring of the line here with the type of AI that is being promoted," Alexandra Day, one of the protest organizers, told DW.

"It is really being pushed on workers with very little consent. There's no right for workers to opt out of using AI now that it's coming into the workplace."

A sense of urgency was palpable from the speakers inside the summit. Executives from some of the world's biggest AI and tech firms talked up Europe's potential. Yet the EU evidently has plenty of ground to catch up on in terms of AI development.

Despite ramping up its data center capacity, it still lags far behind the US and China. It hosts 5% of the world's AI computing capacity compared to around 75% for the US.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The EU is conspicuously absent from lists of the leading AI frontier labs, with only French company Mistral coming close to rivaling the top labs. Its production of leading-edge chips is also nowhere near that of the top US or Taiwanese producers.

As part of its plan to make ground on the US and China, the Irish government, in its role as EU presidency host, presented a policy document at the event.

The so-called "Dublin Declaration" outlines political commitments to strengthen Europe's AI capabilities, including infrastructure investment and financial backing for European AI companies.

In keeping with Draghi's calls for Europe to develop its own AI sovereignty, particularly in supply chains and infrastructure, the declaration suggests that European firms reliant on non-EU cloud and computing services may face additional compliance pressures.

However, not everyone is convinced by the EU's capacity to either ramp up AI capacity or develop effective regulation.

Eddie Wilson, CEO of European airline Ryanair, said he doubted Brussels could regulate AI well without stifling innovation.

"The last thing you want is people regulating this industry who don't know anything about it," he told DW. "That's generally what happens in Brussels."

Ryanair recently made a major deal with Google to use its cloud data system and its AI platform Gemini Enterprise. It's precisely the kind of collaboration with US AI supply chains that the EU says it wants companies to move away from.

"I worry for Europe because these tech companies need to move at speed," said Wilson. He believes the environment in the US is more amenable to innovation.

"If they're not going to do it here, they're going to do it elsewhere. They're going to do it in China and they're going to do it in the US."

#643. Manifestation du 24 octobre à Toulouse : pas de mariages au Capitole, stations de métro fermées, marché du Cristal seulement jusqu'à midi, le point sur les perturbations dans le centre-ville

Article rédigé par Emmanuelle Rey

Journaliste Santé, sciences, spatial, vie locale

l'essentiel La manifestation de ce samedi 24 octobre, "Acte II" contre la vie chère démarrera à 14 heures à Toulouse, du haut des allées Jean-Jaurès. Un important dispositif de sécurité est mis en place une semaine après les violences et les pillages. Plusieurs perturbations impactent la vie du centre-ville. Voici ce qu'il faut savoir et comment vous déplacer.

Une nouvelle manifestation "contre la vie chère" et au soutien des revendications lycéennes et étudiantes aura lieu ce samedi 24 octobre à Toulouse. Une semaine après les violences et les pillages, un dispositif de sécurité important a été mis en place au centre-ville et le défilé s'élancera à 14 heures pour un parcours inédit, plus à l'écart que d'habitude. Les manifestants sont autorisés à défiler du haut des allées Jean-Jaurès vers le boulevard Bonrepos à suivre le canal du Midi jusqu'à la rue Sébastopol puis place Héraclès, pont des Catalans, allées Charles-de-Fitte jusqu'à Patte-d'Oie.

À lire aussi : REPLAY. Manifestations du 24 octobre : entre 410 000 et 800 000 manifestants en France, des heurts dans plusieurs villes

Le parcours de la manifestation de ce samedi 24 octobre à Toulouse.

De nombreuses perturbations sont annoncées dans les transports et les déplacements s'annoncent compliqués. Dès 10 h 30, des stations de métro seront fermées : Capitole (ligne A), Jeanne-d'Arc (ligne B) ainsi que le nœud de correspondance Jean-Jaurès (lignes A et B). Tisséo précise que d’autres fermetures inopinées pourraient intervenir au fil des heures selon l'évolution de la situation. Par ailleurs, l'Espace Voyageurs et l'agence commerciale de Jean-Jaurès restent portes closes toute la journée.

Ce samedi matin, le secteur de la gare était sous surveillance. DDM-FREDERIC CHARMEUX Dès 10 heures ce matin, au centre-ville de Toulouse, de nombreux camions de police étaient en place. DDM

À lire aussi : Manifestation du 24 octobre à Toulouse : gendarmes dans le centre-ville, RAID, militaires de Sentinelle, véhicules Centaures... des moyens exceptionnels déployés pour la sécurité

À noter que la station Marengo SNCF reste ouverte pour permettre aux manifestants de se rendre au point de départ, situé près de la statue Pierre-Paul Riquet, à l'angle du haut des allées Jean-Jaurès et du boulevard Bonrepos.

Au niveau du tramway, le trafic de la ligne T1 est quant à lui tronçonné en deux temps : jusqu'à 14 heures, les rames circulent uniquement entre les stations Arènes et MEETT (circulation interrompue entre Palais-de-Justice et Arènes). À partir de 14 heures, l'interruption se prolonge de Palais-de-Justice à Purpan, il ne sera possible de circuler qu'entre les portions Purpan et MEETT.

La circulation des bus sera plus impactée que d'habitude au regard du trajet de la manifestation. Dès 12 heures, une vingtaine de lignes sont déviées de leur itinéraire habituel : la Navette Aéroport, les lignes Linéo (L1, L2, L3, L4, L5, L8, L9, L14) ainsi que les bus 13, 15, 18, 23, 27, 29, 34, 39, 44, 63, 67 et 70. La Navette Centre-Ville ainsi que les lignes 45 et 66 sont totalement suspendues. Un retour à la normale est envisagé en fin d’après-midi, en fonction de la progression du cortège.

Seul le téléphérique urbain Téléo fonctionne normalement et échappe aux perturbations.

À lire aussi : TÉMOIGNAGE. "Rien que ce matin, dix bombes lacrymos ont été achetées" : des commerçants de Toulouse s'équipent en armes de défense, un vendeur de surplus confirme la hausse des ventes

Le marché Cristal, sur les boulevards, fermera ce samedi matin à midi. Par ailleurs, le musée des Abattoirs et la chapelle La Grave, qui se trouvent à proximité du parcours de la manifestation à Saint-Cyprien, sont fermés aujourd'hui. Enfin, la mairie a délocalisé les mariages qui n'ont pas lieu ce samedi au Capitole mais dans une salle municipale hors centre-ville. Certains magasins, comme le Décathlon de Toulouse centre-ville ont annoncé leur fermeture. La place du Capitole reste particulièrement sécurisée mais l'accès aux commerces et restaurants reste possible.

Les réformes dites sociétales, non financées ont affaiblies notre pays. Les gouvernants dits responsables ont fait preuve de démagogie et de couardise. Ils trompent depuis 40 ans les Française et la jeunesse. La casse ne résout rien, mais c'est la réponse du mouton au berger. Ils vont être virés mais devraient être poursuivis pour leur gestion ou plus exactement pour leur non gestion. Leur seule motivation : le poste et ses avantages.

Contre la vie chère certains ont trouvé la solution.

La vie chère est avant tout un choix de redistribution économique. Ces gens veulent le beurre et l'argent du beurre : on veut des produits pas chers, mais on veut un SMIC élevé, les 35h, des cotisations sociales élevées... Si on retranche des dépenses de consommation toutes les aides qui augmentent ce pouvoir d'achat (prime rentrée scolaire, cantine gratuite ou quasi, aides à l'achat de X ou Y, subventions rénovations, remboursement des soins etc...) alors les prix seraient bien plus bas. LFI veut faire croire que quelques uns s'en mettent plein les poches à coups de statistiques et concepts économiques bidonnés. La vérité c'est que des millions de personnes vivent bien en France sans travailler, tout le monde se goinfre d'aides, moi compris. Enfin il est encore remarquable de voir que le privé ne manifeste pas. Et pourtant leur pouvoir d'achat est très largement inférieur à celui du public puisque chaque mois nous devons épargner faute de sécurité de l'emploi. Épargne de précaution de plus en plus taxée, et bientôt même confisquée pour permettre la rente de ceux qui manifestent et qui sont les vrais privilègiés de la République.

#644. PTBS in der Ukraine: Wie der Krieg die Psyche belastet

Fast ein Drittel der ukrainischen Bevölkerung erfüllt die Kriterien für eine Posttraumatische Belastungsstörung. Ein zentraler Auslöser sind Russlands Angriffskrieg und seine Folgen – auch jenseits der Front.

Mehr als vier Jahre dauert Russlands umfassender Angriffskrieg gegen die Ukraine bereits an. Er wird nicht nur an der Front geführt. Immer wieder zerstören Raketen auch Wohnhäuser und zivile Infrastruktur, wie etwa Anlagen zur Stromversorgung.

Tote, Verwundete, Zerstörung, Flucht – all das hinterlässt auch Spuren, die erst auf den zweiten Blick sichtbar werden: In der ukrainischen Zivilbevölkerung erfüllt fast jede und jeder Dritte (31,2 Prozent) die Kriterien für eine Posttraumatische Belastungsstörung (PTBS) oder sogar für eine sogenannte komplexe PTBS, eine noch schwerere Form.

Zu diesem Ergebnis kommt eine repräsentative Umfrage, die das internationale Forschungsnetzwerk "Kooperation und Konflikt im östlichen Europa" (KonKoop) durchgeführt hat. Die Forschenden aus den Bereichen psychische Gesundheit und Sozialwissenschaften befragten mehr als 2500 Ukrainerinnen und Ukrainer, die in den Regionen leben, die weiterhin oder wieder unter Kontrolle der Regierung in Kyjiw sind. Die Studie wurde vom deutschen Forschungsministerium (BMFTR) gefördert und in der Fachzeitschrift European Journal of Psychotraumatology veröffentlicht.

Von einer Posttraumatischen Belastungsstörung (PTBS) spricht man, wenn Menschen ein Trauma erleben – also eine potenzielle oder reale Bedrohung der körperlichen Unversehrtheit oder des Lebens bei sich oder anderen – und sich dieses Erlebnis in der Psyche festsetzt. Betroffene durchleben das traumatisierende Ereignis in sogenannten Flashbacks immer wieder, leiden unter Angstzuständen, Reizbarkeit und Schlafstörungen. In der Regel treten die Symptome erst einige Zeit nach dem Erlebten auf.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Weltweit finden sich bei weniger als zehn Prozent der Allgemeinbevölkerung die Kriterien einer solchen Belastungsstörung, so schätzen Fachleute. In der ukrainischen Bevölkerung ist der Wert laut der neuen Studie also gut dreimal so hoch.

Die Studie beruht auf selbst berichteten Symptomen. Das Ergebnis könnte also davon beeinflusst sein, wie die Teilnehmenden die Fragen interpretierten, so die Forschenden.

"Besonders auffällig an den Ergebnissen ist das enorme Ausmaß der Traumatisierung", so Studienleiterin Deirdre MacManus, Dozentin für Forensische Psychiatrie am King's College London (KCL) in einer Pressemitteilung.

Mehr als 90 Prozent der Befragten gaben an, dass sie mindestens ein traumatisches Erlebnis im Erwachsenenalter hatten. Nicht alle, aber doch viele dieser Erlebnisse hatten mit dem Krieg zu tun. Die Hälfte gab an, einen Angehörigen im Fronteinsatz zu haben. Mehr als 70 Prozent haben Beschuss in ihren Wohngebieten erlebt und 65 Prozent generelle Zerstörungen durch den Krieg.

"Es gibt in der Ukraine keine Familie mehr, die nicht unter dem Krieg gelitten hat, in der jemand entweder gestorben oder im besetzten Gebiet zurückgeblieben ist", berichtet Ruslana Lutsyk-Andrushko der DW. Sie arbeitet als psychosoziale Beraterin für die Hilfsorganisation Ärzte ohne Grenzen in der ukrainischen Stadt Winnyzja.

"Wir können die Ursache nicht allein der Invasion zuschreiben, da es andere Traumata gegeben haben mag, die zur Entwicklung einer PTBS beigetragen haben", sagt die Hauptautorin der Studie, Emma Facer-Irwin. Die Wissenschaftlerin am KCL ist auch als klinische Psychologin bei der britischen Gesundheitsbehörde mit den Schwerpunkten Trauma und PTBS tätig.

Je mehr traumatische Ereignisse eine Person im Laufe ihres Lebens erlebe, desto höher sei die Wahrscheinlichkeit, dass sie eine Posttraumatische Belastungsstörung entwickelt, erklärt Facer-Irwin im DW-Gespräch. Aber: "Wenn man bedenkt, dass es sich hier um die Zivilbevölkerung handelt, nicht um Militärangehörige oder ausschließlich um Vertriebene oder Flüchtlinge, dann können wir schon vermuten, dass der Krieg ein wesentlicher Faktor für die Entwicklung und Verbreitung von PTBS ist."

Viele Menschen in der Ukraine seien täglich der Bedrohung durch Beschuss, Vertreibung, Trauer und Ungewissheit ausgesetzt, betont Studienleiterin MacManus. "Trotz dieser Umstände gelingt es vielen weiterhin, unter außerordentlich schwierigen Bedingungen zu funktionieren und sich anzupassen."

So berichteten zwar viele Menschen von traumatischen Erlebnissen, aber nicht alle von ihnen entwickelten anhaltende Belastungsstörungen, so Facer-Irwin. "Das sagt uns, dass zwei Drittel der Bevölkerung traumatische Ereignisse anders verarbeiten."

Möglicherweise spiele dabei auch das starke ukrainische Nationalbewusstsein eine Rolle, meint die Psychologin: "Dieses Gefühl einer starken kollektiven Kultur, in der man gemeinsam gegen die Invasion vorgeht." Die Forschung zeige, dass das Gefühl, sozial aufgefangen und verbunden zu sein, vor Posttraumatischen Belastungsstörungen schützen kann.

"Deshalb geht es auch darum, unterstützende Umgebungen zu schaffen. Viele Menschen leben in Situationen, denen sie aufgrund des andauernden Krieges nicht einfach entfliehen können. Wir brauchen also PTBS-Traumatherapien, aber auch soziale Hilfsangebote, die einer größeren Bevölkerungsgruppe angeboten werden können."

Einen solchen Ansatz verfolgt das Rehabilitationszentrum von Ärzte ohne Grenzen im ukrainischen Winnyzja. "Wenn Menschen zu uns kommen, sind Stabilisierung und Ressourcenaufbau der erste Schritt", erklärt Ruslana Lutsyk-Andrushko. Erst wenn sich die Menschen besser fühlten, könnten die traumatischen Erinnerungen bearbeitet werden. In einer dritten Phase folge dann die Reintegration der gewonnenen Erfahrungen.

"Dieser Plan zielt darauf ab, Selbsthilfe zu vermitteln, also was man in einer Stresssituation tun kann. Nach dem Aufenthalt im Zentrum verfügen die Betroffenen dann über eine Art Erste-Hilfe-Set, das sie für sich selbst, ihre Kinder, ihre Freunde und in schwierigen Situationen nutzen können."

Derzeit verstärkt Russland seine Angriffe auf die Ukraine, und das belaste die psychische Gesundheit vieler Ukrainerinnen und Ukrainer, berichtet Lutsyk-Andrushko. "Wenn ein Mensch unter Stress lebt und keine Hoffnung auf Besserung sieht, dann ist das natürlich zermürbend. Die Menschen brauchen Zuversicht, Vertrauen in eine bessere Zukunft."

Und so sei ihre Studie vor allem eine Momentaufnahme, sagt Psychologin Facer-Irwin. Die gesamten Auswirkungen des Krieges auf die psychische Gesundheit ließen sich noch gar nicht abschätzen. "Die langfristigen Folgen werden vermutlich erst deutlich, wenn die Menschen die Möglichkeit hatten, sich in Sicherheit zu bringen und sich vollständig vom Krieg zu erholen."

#647. Britain must be ready for war in 1,000 days, Wes Streeting warns

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Wes Streeting has warned that Britain’s adversaries will be ready to attack UK by 2030

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Defence secretary Wes Streeting has said that Britain must be ready for war in 1,000 days as the government tells Britons to stock up with tinned food and bottles of water.

Writing in The Telegraph, Mr Streeting warns Britain’s adversaries could be ready to attack the UK in 2030.

He wrote: “Our adversaries’ willingness to harm us is not new. What has changed is there capacity. By 2030 their force strength and war economy could put them in a position to attack.

“That gives us a little over 1,000 days to complete our mission: to be ready with our allies to fight and win.”

Referencing the potential of Russian aggression, he added: ‘To prevent the worst, we have to prepare for it”.

His comments come amid a government campaign to ready Britons for a potential break-down in essential services.

Every Briton is being urged to stock up to nine litres of bottle water and three days’ worth of food to ensure that they can survive a weather, cyber or other critical emergency.

Mr Streeting has said the Britain should be ready for “state-sponsored terrorism” from Russia.

Explaining the ‘Be Ready’ campaign, he said: “In the face of those threats, which are not hypothetical but real, and not somewhere else but increasingly here, we have to step up and take seriously our national resilience as well as our national defence.

“It’s really important that we ask households and businesses are they prepared?”.

People have also been told to keep a supply of blankets, cash, a first-aid kit, a torch with batteries, and a wind-up FM radio.

Prime minister Andy Burnham has also advised people to stock up on food and water in case of emergencies. He told the BBC: “It’s not about panicking...It’s about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation”.

Earlier this month, MI5 director general Sir Ken McCallum called for a “whole-of-society effort” to face threats to national infrastructure, warning that hacks could disable banking services, drones could disrupt flights, and cyber attacks on hospitals could have an adverse impact on health treatment.

Asked whether Britain would be able to get back to a less fractious time, Sir Ken said: “Our planning assumption is not that this is a temporary blip and we will all be back to normal by next Christmas.

“We are planning on the basis that, in effect, the period of comparative geopolitical stability following the end of the Cold War has sadly ended and we are back in a more contested era now. We are planning on the basis that these risks will endure.”

#648. The Stone Roses showed me the power of being an introvert

At boarding school in the early 90s, quietness was seen as weakness. But then I saw the band’s guitarist John Squire making a vast noise while hiding behind a fringe – and learned the strength of understatement

In September 1991, I had just been thrown into the meat-grinder of a Midlands boarding school. In this bear pit, there were predators and there was prey. You were either the swaggering rugby alpha, whipping a wet towel at pale bodies in the eight-boy dormitory; or the homesick ghost, keeping your guard up, endlessly braced for your toilet cubicle to be kicked open or your washbag chucked off the fire escape.

My mind had always been loud, racing with opinions, stories, jokes. But by the time I adequately considered a thought, the conversation had raced on without me. Suddenly, under 24/7 social scrutiny in a world where bullhorn confidence is king, I felt dismissed.

Up to that point, music hadn’t helped. Every rock star I had ever seen – Elton John, Freddie Mercury, Mick Jagger – was a showboating peacock, all hips, handclaps and absurd glasses, seeming to whisper in my ear: “This isn’t for you, bookworm.” But that September, I stumbled across the Stone Roses’ self-titled 1989 debut album. I must have seen John Squire’s genius before I heard it, on his paint-splashed, lemon-drizzled sleeve art.

Hearing his cascading, iridescent guitar solos, I assumed Squire must be an extrovert axe hero: foot on the monitor, diamante codpiece, the works. But there he was on the CD inlay: pipecleaner-skinny, dressed in Manchester streetwear and inscrutable beneath a bird’s-nest fringe (until the mid-90s, I genuinely wasn’t sure if Squire had eyes), slinging a Gretsch Country Gentleman guitar but not treating it like a penis extension.

Years before YouTube, it wasn’t easy to find out more. But when I dug up back issues of NME, I went from fan to disciple. A sometime model-maker who once worked on The Wind in the Willows – but also a child of 70s punk – Squire was enigmatic and otherworldly, softly spoken yet intense as a laser-cutter. Asked by one interviewer what the Roses were all about, his answer was the perfect collision of sky-scraping ambition and bone-dry Britishness: “Love and hate. War and peace. Morecambe and Wise …”

In those formative weeks, for the first time, I realised that “quiet” could also mean charismatic, insolent, snarky, simmering with latent attitude and temperamentally suited for a life in the arts. Through Squire, I discovered painting (Jackson Pollock’s “drip and splash” influence was all over his sleeves and guitars), modern history (the Paris riots of May 68 referenced on Bye Bye Badman), fashion and even religion (you only had to read his lyric to 1994’s Love Spreads, a take on the Passion, with Jesus imagined as a Black woman, to sense the iconoclast claws below the still waters).

Hearing the Roses at school, meanwhile, was my ticket into a secret society of indie kids that I hadn’t known existed, all swapping albums, making mixtapes, easy in each other’s company, building each other’s confidence. I picked up the guitar that same year, too, went on to write about it for the music press – and now play so loud in my own band that I can drown out a thousand braying show-offs.

Squire doesn’t do many interviews, and when I drove to his Cheshire farmhouse for Guitarist Magazine, I was worried he wouldn’t actually speak. But perhaps he recognised a kindred spirit. Over an hour’s encounter in his studio, the musician who had meant so much to me proved thoughtful, witty and profound, signed the schoolboy-era guitar I’d flecked Pollock-style with paint, and even gave me a parting hug.

Get our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every Friday

John Squire didn’t change me; he stopped me fighting myself. Under his influence, I stopped trying to turn up the volume, accepted being an introvert and held him in mind whenever anyone equated quietness with dullness. Fast-forward 35 years – to a time when influencers squeal and preen, flogging every last grain of themselves to the attention economy – and the Roses guitarist seems a few degrees cooler for existing on his own terms, leaving something to the imagination, and treating Jonathan Ross with chilly disdain. Perhaps we could all stand to be a little more Squire?

#649. Israeli soldiers raze neighbourhood in Hebron, driving families from homes

PM Benjamin Netanyahu vows ‘to destroy this place’ in retaliation for militant attack on army checkpoint

Israeli troops have levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron, driving out hundreds of families in collective punishment for a militant attack on an army checkpoint outside the West Bank city, local Palestinian authorities said.

The Hebron municipality estimated that 35 hectares (86 acres) had been destroyed or marked for destruction and about 1,500 people had been evicted from their homes by Saturday afternoon in the district of Ein Deir Baha. The whole city of 250,000 people was sealed off by checkpoints on every point of entry.

Videos sent by a Hebron resident showed a substantial area of devastation with every house over several blocks flattened in an urban area. One video showed soldiers marking Palestinian houses with a sprayed black cross, another showed a bulldozer tearing down a stone wall on a hillside and another showed a large residential building festooned with Israeli flags.

People said the building was the home of a prominent Hebron family that had been commandeered as a temporary military headquarters.

The large-scale demolitions follow an attack on Friday on an Israeli military checkpoint outside Hebron by two gunmen. After a 20-minute gunfight, two Israeli soldiers were killed, three injured and the two gunmen were also killed.

Israeli elections will take place in four days and the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the extreme-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, travelled to the site of the attack to promise an immediate and ferocious response.

Netanyahu said Israel would “act to destroy this place”. Smotrich who is standing for election in a smaller coalition party, had himself filmed wearing body armour in front of a Palestinian building being demolished. He said he had ordered “the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site”.

Smotrich also called for “a comprehensive military campaign … exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon”. Ein Deir Baha, the focus of the demolitions, was alleged to be the home district of the two gunmen.

A spokesperson for the Hebron municipality said that about 300 families had been evicted. Some had taken refuge in the homes of friends and relatives, while the municipality said it had opened community halls and children’s play areas to shelter others.

A Palestinian news agency, Wafa, reported Israeli plans to displace a further 2,500 people. “We are being collectively punished for something we neither did nor supported,” a Hebron civil rights activist, Issa Amro, said. “Our suffering is being turned into political material for Israel’s elections, while innocent families pay the price.”

Amro said his sister’s family was one of the hundreds driven out of their homes.

“We are talking about hundreds of families who left their homes because of this, and they are not at all connected to what happened yesterday [Friday],” Amro said in a telephone interview. “It’s a very big area and we don’t know what’s going on, whether it is only election propaganda or if it’s a serious plan from decisions on what to do after the election.”

The Israeli army was approached for comment on the operations and on videos showing extensive devastation.

#650. 'A massive storage of images' - Arteta has technical area receipts

Arsenal go level at the top after victory over Everton

Wandering Premier League managers beware, Mikel Arteta has the receipts.

The Arsenal boss has developed a reputation for straying outside the technical area in recent years but, he claims, he is far from the worst offender.

After receiving his second yellow card of the season for the offence during the Gunners' victory over Everton on Saturday, Arteta revealed he has a dossier of evidence that proves other Premier League managers are getting off lightly.

"I do have to be careful. They should put sensors there," he said.

"There are managers who have the record in the league, 36 times in 10 minutes [they] leave the touchline - no yellows.

"I am clipping all of that so I have now a massive storage of images, so if somebody comes to me I can say, 'I am not in the record yet'. Somebody else has the record so let's see.

"Then it's 36 yellow cards in 10 minutes for the managers. I don't know what we are going to do - let's see."

What is Arteta planning to do with this treasure trove of touchline images? Who is the mystery manager holding that surely unbreakable record?

For now we can only speculate, although a BBC Sport study in April 2025 found that of current top-flight bosses, Aston Villa's Unai Emery spent the most time outside his technical area. Could he be the culprit?

Until all is revealed, though, Premier League bosses must watch their step - Arteta is watching.

#651. How Band of Brothers kick-started the legendary careers of a brigade of British A-listers including Stephen Graham, Tom Hardy and Damian Lewis

Published: 00:21 GMT, 25 October 2026 | Updated: 03:36 GMT, 25 October 2026

Casting an ensemble of mainly unknown Britons to tell the story of an elite American parachute regiment during the Second World War certainly raised an eyebrow or two when Band Of Brothers began 25 years ago.

Many of the actors had been chosen to take advantage of UK tax breaks - but they not only mastered the US accents, but used the show as a launchpad for stellar careers.

The ten-part HBO series, still available on Sky and Amazon Prime, first aired in the UK on October 5, 2001.

Chronicling the wartime experiences of so-called Easy Company, the real-life 2nd Battalion of the 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment of the US Army's 101st Airborne Division, it won acclaim and countless awards.

Filmed mainly at Hatfield Aerodrome, the £90million production - at the time the most expensive TV series ever - was the creation of Steven Spielberg and Tom Hanks, adopting the gritty realism that had made their film Saving Private Ryan a hit three years earlier.

While the cast included US stars like David Schwimmer - already famous from Friends - it was the British and Irish contingent who shone, as our guide shows...

Stephen Graham played Sergeant Myron 'Mike' Ranney who is demoted for standing up to sadistic commanding officer Captain Herbert Sobel, played by Friends actor David Schwimmer.

He had starred the previous year in Guy Ritchie's gangster flick Snatch, and his career was soon to take off with a role as a violent racist skinhead in the cult film This Is England.

Now 53, he has gone on to star in TV's Line of Duty, Peaky Blinders and Time - while notably co-writing and starring in Adolescence, which told of a 14-year-old arrested for murder and sparked a national debate about toxic masculinity online. The director of that acclaimed drama? Philip Barantini - who played Private Wayne 'Skinny' Sisk in Band Of Brothers.

Stephen Graham as Myron Mike Ranney in Band of Brothers. Band of Brothers is a highly acclaimed ten part American war drama miniseries released in 200

Yet to make his breakthrough in the zombie comedy Shaun Of The Dead, Simon Pegg had a blink-and-you-miss-it role as 1st Sergeant Bill Evans, Sobel's right-hand man - quite a change of direction for a proudly geeky comedian best known at the time for Channel 4's slacker sitcom Spaced.

His subsequent films included Run Fatboy Run, directed by Schwimmer. However, Pegg said he didn't have much to do with the Friends star on the Band Of Brothers set, as Schwimmer was both too famous and intent on staying in character as an anti-social sort 'who kept himself separate from the rest of us grunts'.

Pegg, 56, is now a stalwart of Hollywood blockbusters as Benji in the Mission: Impossible franchise and Scotty in Star Trek.

Should British actors play American war heroes, or should roles stay true to nationality?

Simon Pegg as First Sergeant William S Evans in Band of Brothers

He's Hollywood's go-to hardman now, but Band Of Brothers was Tom Hardy's first screen role... if you don't count him winning the Find Me A Supermodel contest

on Channel 4's Big Breakfast three years earlier.

His first scene was a memorable one as his character, Private John A Janovec, was caught by his captain in flagrante with a German woman. Despite his relatively small role - he called it 'two episodes and 12 lines', he has spoken of how he worked hard to do justice to a real person.

Also in 2001 he made his movie debut in Black Hawk Down, starting a CV that, at 49, now includes Mad Max, The Dark Knight Rises, Venom, The Revenant and MobLand.

Tom Hardy as Private John A. Janovec in Band Of Brothers

Long before becoming a chat show host, US comic Jimmy Fallon had a cameo role as 2nd Lieutenant George C.

Rice, who drives a Jeep carrying supplies and ammunition to Easy Company. Fallon later admitted he did not know how to drive a manual car at the time, so crew members had to push while he pretended to steer.

Then, as a cast member on Saturday Night Live, he became a talk show host in 2009, interviewing the likes of Taylor Swift, above.

Jimmy Fallon as Lt. George C. Rice in Band of Brothers 2001

Singer-songwriter Taylor Swift during an interview with host Jimmy Fallon on The Tonight Show With Jimmy Fallon

No one was more surprised than Damian Lewis when he got cast in the lead role of Major Dick Winters. At the time, he was 'just another pale Englishman doing lots of auditions' - with the Band of Brothers casting agents apparently seeing 'every actor in London under 30 who still has both his legs'.

Yet Lewis proved impressive enough to be flown to LA, where he auditioned for Hanks, which went so well he hit the town to celebrate... only to be called to a meeting with Spielberg the next morning after 'three hours' sleep, three cold showers and five coffees'.

So began a stellar career that has encompassed Homeland, Billions and playing Henry VIII in Wolf Hall.

But personally he experienced tragedy when his wife, Peaky Blinders star Helen McCrory, died from cancer in 2021, aged 52.

Damian Lewis starred as Major Richard 'Dick' Winters in the acclaimed HBO miniseries

Damian Lewis was cast by Steven Spielberg after being noticed for his stage work with the Royal Shakespeare Company

For many, he will forever be Fleabag's 'Hot Priest', even though he may next year become the first person to be nominated twice for Best Actor at the Oscars in a century.

In Band of Brothers, Andrew Scott played Private John 'Cowboy' Hall for one episode, but later said he 'didn't love playing a soldier' because of his dislike of weapons.

Nonetheless, the Irish actor went on to star in Sam Mendes's epic 1917, while returning to the D-Day landings at the centre of Band Of Brothers for this year's film Pressure, playing a meteorologist whose work is crucial to the success of Operation Overlord. It is one of the two films for which the 50-year-old has been tipped for an Oscar, with a rule change allowing him to compete against himself. The other is the forthcoming Elsinore, about Shakespearean actor Ian Charleson, who died of Aids.

Andrew Scott as Private First Class John D Hall in Band of Brothers

Scott features in the BBC show, Fleabag, as the Hot Priest. Phoebe Waller-Bridge is pictured on the left

Producers today would kill to have James McAvoy in their cast - but on Band Of Brothers, his character Private James W Miller died in his first episode.

Now a star of the X-Men franchise, the 47-year-old this month said Band of Brothers was not a happy shoot, as a co-star he declined to name 'decided to bully me, on my first day as a professional actor out of acting school. So he got his buddies to just stand and point at me and laugh at me for three minutes.'

If living well is the best revenge, McAvoy can claim victory with hits such as Atonement, Split and His Dark Materials under his belt. But he did miss out on one blockbuster role. Fresh from Band Of Brothers, he auditioned for Pirates Of The Caribbean but lost to Orlando Bloom.

James McAvoy as Private James W Miller in Band of Brothers 2001

He plays Lord Asriel Belacqua, a powerful explorer and scientist who investigates the mysterious substance known as Dust in 'His Dark Materials'

Band Of Brothers marked the screen debut of Michael Fassbender - who, after acting school did night shifts in a warehouse and frittered his days away playing video games.

However, his role as machine-gunner Burton 'Pat' Christenson in seven episodes of the war drama, did not prove to be the breakout he had hoped... and he spent most of the next two years in LA unemployed, before returning, dejected, to the UK.

But he persisted, and his big break came playing IRA hunger-striker Bobby Sands in the 2008 film Hunger.

Roles in the likes of 300, Inglourious Basterds and the X-Men series - playing Magneto alongside James McAvoy - followed. Married to actress Alicia Vikander, he took a hiatus from acting from 2020 to 2023 to indulge his love of motor racing, and now stars in The Agency on TV.

Michael Fassbender as Technical Sergeant Burton P. (Pat) Christenson in Band of Brothers

#652. Formula One in Rwanda: Sportswashing claims vs. hopes for African legacy

Formula One will return to Africa for the first time since 1993. There is concern Rwanda are using it as another sportswashing opportunity, but there is also hope the event's legacy can impact wider African society.

Rwanda's sports portfolio has grown after confirming it will host Formula One races from the early 2030s. The track is to be built in Bugesera near Kigali International Airport, which Qatar Airways, an F1 sponsor, owns 60% of.

"To be an African and to see it happening in real time, for me in my lifetime because Kyalami [the track in South Africa where F1 was last hosted in Africa] was before I was born, I'm more than happy to have it on the continent," South African presenter and content creator Nqobile Khwezi told Sky Sports.

"To be able to give that taste back to the rest of the world and the audience of Formula One would be an absolute delight."

F1 have also highlighted the benefits for the host nation.

"Through this race we have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to our more than 100 million fans across Africa and firmly believe that sport can be a positive force for good," an F1 spokesperson told The Athletic.

DW contacted Rwanda's Ministry of Sports for comment, but did not receive a promised reply.

For the country's President, Paul Kagame, another move into sport is hardly a surprise given his ventures into European football and the NBA in recent years. Rwanda even sponsored Bayern Munich, but fan and media backlash over the deal caused the Bundesliga club to drop the commercial element with the country's tourist arm, Visit Rwanda, last year.

With many critics accusing Kagame and Rwanda of sportswashing, the arrival of F1, a sport valued at approximately $34 billion (€30 billion), according to sports business website Sportico, brings fresh questions.

"This deal may have positive economic and social impacts across Africa, but we should be realistic about circumstances on the ground in Rwanda," Lewis Mudge, Central Africa director at Human Rights Watch, told DW.

"Human Rights Watch wrote to Formula One in February 2025 to ask how it is addressing the human rights impacts of its activities, including regarding Rwanda and other countries’ bid to host a F1 Grand Prix. We did not receive a response," said Mudge, adding that F1 should only approve racing in the country after addressing the human rights impacts of hosting a race there.

"Rwanda, like other countries, has also used high-profile sports deals and races in the past to distract from its abysmal human rights record. Rwanda is currently the power behind the abusive M23 rebel group in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo and its military forces have been implicated in unlawful displacement and deaths of civilians in violation of international humanitarian law."

For Mohamed Keita, returning the sport to Africa is overdue, but the choice of country is telling.

"The fact that F1 excluded the world's second largest continent from its race series for three decades is indefensible in its own right and is actually a stain on a sport which claims to be global," Keita, Senior Policy Officer, Africa, at the Human Rights Foundation told DW.

"The choice of Rwanda, however, is deeply controversial," Keita continued. "Rwanda is a brutal dictatorship. Its regime is under partial US sanctions for its military occupations of territories of eastern DRC. Rwanda is arming and financing a militia involved in rapes, massacres, forced recruitment and violent plunder of natural resources."

Formula One has history on the continent. In 1958, there was a race in Morocco and more recently, in South Africa, where the last F1 race in Africa took place at the Kyalami racetrack in Johannesburg in 1993. Many previous races in the country were overshadowed by the policy of apartheid.

Despite Rwanda securing the deal first, South Africa believes it will host before them. When Rwanda announced their hosting, South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa sent his congratulations in a social media post, adding: "This contract is a recognition of the capabilities of the Rwandan nation and of our continent more broadly."

South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie also congratulated Rwanda, but pivotally added that South Africa "will get F1, even before 2030."

There is no denying that hosting a race in South Africa would cost significantly less time and money, given the existing infrastructure.

In either country, comes a legacy opportunity. Sports such as Formula One, where the majority of decision-makers, drivers, team principles and engineers are white men, are a living example of the unlevel playing field. The hope of racing in Africa is that it will go some way to changing that.

"I think that's the kind of aspirational drive of hosting a Formula 1 race. It's leveraging STEM [science, technology, engineering, and mathematics] education, technology, aspiring young girls or women, leveling the playing fields, if it's for all those other reasons and we can make it work then I say yes to Formula 1 in Africa," Dr. Kamilla Swart-Arries, an expert in South Africa's events industry and the legacy of sports events, told DW in 2024.

"I hope F1 will consider further investment in developing African talent in motorsport," said Keita. "There's a lot of good that F1 can do if it genuinely wants to grow the sport in Africa, but Rwanda does not make sense at this moment unless you're doing it purely for the benefit of one dictator and the beauty of the hilly terrain."

"The proposition here is to take the world's most expensive sport to Rwanda, which is one of the world's poorest countries. Rwanda is consistently listed among the UN's list of the 25 least developed countries in the world," said Keita.

The return of the fastest show in sports is a huge moment for both Rwanda and Africa. It raises questions about President Kagame's use of sport, but it also offers an opportunity to shape the event's legacy. Unlike the race Rwanda wants to host, this is not about being the fastest but about making the most of the chance.

#653. "Ma carrière professionnelle est ruinée, je suis marqué au fer rouge" : devant le tribunal, l'embarras d'un fonctionnaire de la préfecture ayant falsifié un document en copiant la signature de son supérieur

l'essentiel Un ancien fonctionnaire de la préfecture du Tarn a vu sa carrière voler en éclats après avoir falsifié un document administratif en copiant la signature de son supérieur, afin d'obtenir l'utilisation de son compte CPF pour financer une formation. Il est revenu sur les motivations d'un tel acte, devant le tribunal judiciaire d'Agen, vendredi 23 octobre.

Avec un prévenu dont le parcours est davantage semblable à celui des magistrats chargés de le juger, qu'à celui des individus qui défilent régulièrement à cette barre, le tribunal judiciaire d'Agen était saisi d'un dossier bien "particulier" ce vendredi 23 octobre. Spécialement venu de la Guadeloupe - où il est désormais installé - pour répondre à sa convocation devant la justice, un ancien fonctionnaire de la préfecture du Tarn a tenté d'éclairer la présidente quand celle-ci s'est étonnée de l'irrationalité de la faute commise, au regard de l'expérience professionnelle "brillante" dont cet homme âgé de 45 ans peut se prévaloir.

"C'est la conséquence de l'impact de personnes nocives, sur quelqu'un de normal." Le quadragénaire s'est livré sur la dégradation de ses relations professionnelles, qui l'aurait poussé à falsifier un document administratif en y apposant la signature de son supérieur hiérarchique, à son insu. À l'époque gestionnaire en défense et sécurité civile au sein de la préfecture, à Albi, le fonctionnaire doté d'une habilitation secret défense aspirait à rejoindre un master 2 à l'université de Toulouse pour étendre ses compétences. C'est en complétant le formulaire de demande de mobilisation de son compte personnel de formation (CPF) qu'il a démérité - 750 euros, sur les 8 000 à débourser, lui étaient alloués par l'État pour s'insérer dans cette formation.

Voyant la date limite d'inscription approcher, il reconnaît avoir profité du renouvellement de l'habilitation secret défense de son directeur pour copier sa signature avant de la joindre à l'avis favorable lui permettant de débloquer les fonds de son CPF. Et ce de manière quelque peu maladroite, en effectuant une capture d'écran. Sur le formulaire falsifié, la signature "pixelisée" et "de couleur grise" de l'adjoint à la sous-préfète fait tache au côté de celle du mis en cause, "noire et bien lisible." Sa "N+2" n'a pas été dupée au moment d'en consulter les modalités.

À lire aussi : "C'est du jamais-vu à Albi..." Prison avec sursis, lourde amende et interdiction d'exercer : un avocat condamné en même temps que son client pour complicité de banqueroute

Une sanction disciplinaire et un signalement au procureur de la République ont fait suite à ce manquement sur décision du préfet du Tarn, avant que le dossier ne soit dépaysé au parquet d'Agen. "La procédure, l'authenticité des actes, ce n'est pourtant pas quelque chose qui fait débat pour vous", a légitimement soulevé la juge, le prévenu ayant occupé un poste de greffier à l'instruction pendant des années, avant de prendre ses fonctions en préfecture.

"Il faut se rendre compte que, pour cette demande, il fallait remonter jusqu'à mon N+3, essaie-t-il. L'avis favorable, je l'avais déjà obtenu. C'était plus une question logistique, je ne voulais pas attendre encore des semaines, me prendre de nouvelles réflexions. J'étais sous terre. Je ne pensais qu'à une chose : ne plus remettre un pied dans cette préfecture." La légitimité de l'infraction reprochée a été au cœur de la réflexion de l'avocat de la défense, dès lors "qu'un avis favorable existait déjà. Constitue un faux toute altération frauduleuse de la vérité, a cité le conseil. Nous sommes au degré zéro de cette atteinte."

Si l'ancien greffier a depuis réintégré le ministère de la Justice, il est aujourd'hui en disponibilité et paie les lourdes conséquences de son acte. "Ma carrière professionnelle est ruinée. Toutes mes candidatures restent sans réponse, je suis marqué au fer rouge. Je suis suivi par un psychologue, avant tout pour comprendre comment j'en suis arrivé là." À son endroit, la représentante du ministère public a requis 2 000 euros d'amende avec sursis. Le délibéré est attendu le 4 décembre prochain.
