#670. Man City's leaky defence highlights Donnarumma & Guehi struggles

Nicolas Jackson scores twice as Aston Villa end Manchester City's winning start to the season

Manchester City's 100% winning start to the Premier League season came to an abrupt end against Aston Villa - leaving Enzo Maresca with glaring defensive issues to resolve.

Nicolas Jackson's double in a 2-1 home win for Villa means City have now managed only one clean sheet in their past six games and the form of goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma and defender Marc Guehi is of concern.

Since the start of last season, only eight players have made more errors leading to Premier League goals than Donnarumma and Guehi with three each.

City's most recent shutout came in their impressive victory at Liverpool two weeks ago but, around that game, City have conceded against teams ranging from Champions League holders Paris St-Germain to top-flight strugglers Sunderland.

Maresca was forced to try different combinations at the back against Villa, but as the legendary Sir Alex Ferguson once said, "attack wins you games, defence wins you titles".

Though still early days in the campaign and guaranteed to be in the top two come the end of the weekend, City need to shore up their backline if they are to stay there.

By contrast, title rivals Arsenal moved level on points at the top of the table later in the day with a comfortable 2-0 win at home to Everton.

The Gunners have conceded just five goals in eight matches, with Saturday's goals coming from centre-backs Ezri Konsa and Gabriel.

That's back-to-back Premier League clean sheets for Mikel Arteta's men, with the luxury of centre-back William Saliba still to come back into the side.

Only Manchester United - 1.16 in 1996-97 and 1.18 in 1999-00 - have won the Premier League title with a goals against rate worse than Man City's current 1.13 per game. Arsenal's goals against rate is currently 0.625 per game.

Asked if the two goals the conceded were avoidable, Maresca told TNT Sports: "Absolutely, both.

"Sometimes you have to be a bit more lucky because we only conceded those two chances, but we created a lot of chances.

"We played most of the game in their box but you have to be clinical and avoid mistakes like the two goals we conceded."

Jackson stars with two goals - player ratings for Aston Villa v Man City

Jackson double for Villa ends Man City's 100% start

City 'deserved more' from 2-1 defeat at Aston Villa - Maresca

City were undone by goals in each half from the brilliant Jackson at a raucous Villa Park to end their streak of seven straight wins at the start of this campaign.

Maresca's team started the season by conceding eight goals in their first nine games but that has seen a dramatic downturn, with nine goals hitting the back of their net in the past four matches.

The signing of Donnarumma last summer was heralded as the acquisition of one of the best goalkeepers in the world to replace Ederson.

The Brazilian changed the face of English football with his footwork, spraying short and long passes across the pitch, and there are few keepers who can come close to matching that.

But Italy captain Donnarumma struggles with the ball at his feet and often puts his team-mates in trouble with passes out from the back.

On Saturday, City captain Ruben Dias gesticulated to his team-mate to send the ball up the pitch after the Portuguese failed to control a difficult pass.

Maresca decided to sell James Trafford to Leeds for Â£45m in the summer, and the England international has been impressive at Elland Road.

Trafford has made more passes than Donnarumma this season, has a slightly better rate at preventing goals and has come out to sweep the ball 11 times compared with Donnarumma's one.

Though Donnarumma could do little about Jackson's thumping finish for the opening goal, he should have done better for the second as a low shot seemed to squirm under him.

Former City defender Steph Houghton said on BBC Radio 5 Live: "I think Villa really utilised keeping the ball and being a real threat to Manchester City. Donnarumma, especially with the second goal, could probably have done a little bit better.

"But I don't want to take anything away from Villa. I think they performed really, really well and the gameplan was spot on, just to nullify City as much as possible."

Centre-back Guehi's Â£20m arrival from Crystal Palace in January was considered a bargain.

But it was his loose pass at Everton late last season which cost City dearly in the title race, drawing that game and losing the impetus to eventual champions Arsenal.

This season has been a struggle for the England defender, culpable for both goals scored by Ipswich last weekend and being picked off by John McGinn deep in his own half for Villa's first goal.

Later in the half, he hauled down Jackson on the edge of the box before being shown a yellow card, and was put out of his misery by being taken off at half-time.

City sources had said they were targeting signing a right-back in the summer before pivoting elsewhere, saying Abdukodir Khusanov can provide back-up should Matheus Nunes not be available.

Khusanov started out wide but struggled before being moved inside in place of Guehi, while Rico Lewis was brought to fill the gap, with Maresca acknowledging afterwards he needs to "find that balance" in defence.

Villa supporters provided constant reminders to the travelling fans of their side being "cheats", and the vitriol faced following the guilty verdict of the financial charges may be beginning to weigh on the players' minds.

Asked by BBC Sport if Guehi's form is a worry, Maresca said: "No, I'm not worried about Marc at all.

"I know he is playing every minute since the season started with us and the national team, so it's not easy but the change was also because he was on a yellow card.

"The way we want to be aggressive sometimes, to have one yellow card can be dangerous but I am not worried at all."

Maresca, though, should be concerned by coming up against Fabian Hurzeler's free-scoring Brighton twice next week - in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday, and Premier League on Saturday.

The Italian needs to fix the defensive leaks before they become something more serious.

#672. Katie Zacharia stays 'ruthlessly loyal' to Trump despite president saying she 'freaked out' in front of press corps

Published: 16:46 GMT, 24 October 2026 | Updated: 03:25 GMT, 25 October 2026

Former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia says she remains 'ruthlessly loyal' to Donald Trump even after the president told a crowd she had 'freaked out' in her brief time working for him.

Zacharia, 41, lasted just five days on the job before a series of gaffes and nervous performances led Trump to fire her last week.

Despite Trump revisiting her tumultuous tenure at a Florida rally on Friday by branding her a 'poor young woman,' Zacharia had nothing but good things to say about the president after the rally.

'No wonder that poor young woman - she was a perfect, beautiful woman - when she walked into that press room and they started screaming at her, she freaked out,' Trump said.

Still, Zacharia told Newsweek: 'It was an honor to work for President Trump, and no one has been more relentlessly attacked by the media than him.'

She vowed that 'the best is yet to come,' and said her week in the Trump administration included working 'around the clock' ahead of the midterm elections.

'As Rudyard Kipling wrote, "If you can talk with crowds and keep your virtue, or walk with Kings—nor lose the common touch." After a week with him on the midterm blitz, I saw that in action,' Zacharia said.

'Working around the clock with world leaders - bringing hostages home and brokering peace - while speaking to crowds of Americans to win the midterms and deliver for the people.

'No one has carried the water for the Republican Party and America First like he has for over a decade, all without losing the common touch.'

Former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia says she remains 'ruthlessly loyal' to Donald Trump even after the president mocked her for 'freaking out' in her brief time working for him

Zacharia, 41, lasted just five days on the job before a series of gaffes and nervous performances led Trump to fire her last week

Zacharia's praise of Trump comes after she was brutally ousted after less than a week, making her the shortest-serving press secretary in White House history.

Trump initially defended Zacharia after her tough start, accusing the media of treating her unfairly and saying questions over her background were irrelevant.

The president went on to say he asked Zacharia, 'Is this for you?' and said he would have reconsidered if he was in her position, telling her: 'You don't need this.'

After Zacharia left the post, her predecessor Karoline Leavitt shared a scathingly blunt assessment of her performance, saying the role 'obviously wasn't for her.'

'Look, the White House press secretary is a tough job,' Leavitt told Fox News.

'I know that because I did it, obviously, for almost two years, and many people say it’s one of the hardest jobs in politics. It takes a lot of preparation, and sometimes you don’t know how someone will perform until they go out there.'

Leavitt also implied that Zacharia was not prepared enough to take on the high-profile job, recalling that she 'prepared like heck' when she started.

'I poured myself into my preparation. I read, I studied, I talked to every Cabinet member, I talked to the president. I just absorbed as much information as this noggin up here could,' she said.

Should loyalty to a leader outweigh public criticism and professional performance in politics?

Zacharia said she stands by the president because 'no one has been more relentlessly attacked by the media than him'

Zacharia became the shortest-serving press secretary in White House history

Zacharia also faced questions over her legal credentials after it was brought to light that she had failed the California bar exam in 2011.

She then moved to Beijing with her husband and worked at a Chinese law firm.

Despite never passing the bar exam, Zacharia frequently appeared on news channels as a legal analyst, offering commentary on legal and political issues while identifying herself as a lawyer.

Zacharia's rocky debut was followed by an uncomfortable appearance on Sean Hannity's Fox News show on October 15, just hours before she was pushed out of the job the following day.

Hannity delivered a notably tough grilling, confronting her over her widely criticized briefing, pressing her on why she had repeatedly described herself as a lawyer despite failing the California bar exam.

He challenged her explanation for the short briefing, asking: 'Why only three questions in 14 minutes?' before warning her that the White House briefing room would 'never be a friendly room to you.'

Zacharia defended herself by blaming the whirlwind hiring process and lack of preparation time, but the combative interview added to the scrutiny surrounding her brief tenure.

#673. TFC : face à Troyes, le moment idéal pour une performance totale ?

l'essentiel Plus d'un mois après son dernier match au Stadium et sa première victoire à domicile, le TFC espère enchaîner ce dimanche face à Troyes. Après un succès probant au Mans et face à un adversaire qui reste sur cinq défaites de rang, le moment semble idéal pour enfin faire fructifier les belles promesses du début de saison.

La confusion de Jens Berthel Askou, ce vendredi en fin de conférence de presse, est peut-être plus révélatrice qu'il n'y paraît : "Nous avons fait des progrès dans le jeu ces dernières semaines, et j'espère que dimanche sera le jour pour célébrer notre première victoire à domicile", a glissé l'entraîneur de Toulouse, avant de se reprendre. "J'avais oublié Le Havre !" Oui, le TFC a déjà gagné au Stadium cette saison, lors de son dernier match devant son public, le 19 septembre (3-2). Cela semble déjà une éternité ; il y a eu, depuis, quatre matchs des Bleus de Zidane et deux déplacements pour les Violets, à Monaco (2-2) puis au Mans (3-0), mais ce n'est pas le temps qui fait perdre la mémoire au Danois. "Je l'ai sans doute oublié parce que ce n'était pas un bon match, pas selon nos standards" a-t-il ajouté. Il était à moitié sérieux, mais l'anecdote raconte assez bien l'exigence de ce nouveau TFC qui veut s'en sortir par le haut, par le jeu, et ne veut pas gagner n'importe comment.

À lire aussi : Le Mans-TFC : "C’est merveilleux de le voir venir nous aider..." Pour Aron Donnum, des larmes et de la sueur mélangées au bonheur à l'occasion de son retour

Décalé à dimanche en raison de la mobilisation des forces de l’ordre lors des manifestations de la veille, le match face à Troyes semble tomber au moment idéal pour signer un acte II avec l’art et la manière, qui viendrait enfin récompenser la flopée de bonnes minutes produites depuis le début de saison, notamment face à Lyon et à Lille. Le TFC, qui n'a plus perdu depuis quatre matchs, sort d'une victoire probante au Mans, semble avoir de plus en plus de certitudes collectives permettant à ses individualités de se révéler, à l'image d'un Casper Tengstedt qui ne s'arrête plus, à la fois de bien jouer et de marquer, avec cinq buts sur les quatre dernières rencontres de Ligue 1. En face, Troyes, avant-dernier, reste sur cinq défaites de rang.

À lire aussi : Le Mans-TFC : "Notre meilleure performance..." La satisfaction de Jens Berthel Askou après la première victoire de Toulouse à l'extérieur

Une victoire permettrait à Toulouse de potentiellement basculer dans la première moitié de tableau, mais est surtout attendue pour enfin consacrer sa domination sur un adversaire, comme cela avait été le cas face à l'OL et au Losc. "Oui, il y a une progression, et j’espère que cela va continuer. Je sais aussi que chaque match est différent, et exige des choses différentes. Nous avons bien géré les différentes phases du match face au Mans, ce qui était très important pour garder le contrôle durant toute la partie. C’est très important que chaque semaine nous continuions à progresser, que notre jeu s’améliore" a insisté Jens Berthel Askou, qui est aussi en recherche de constance pour une équipe qui a marqué onze de ses douze buts en deuxième période.

À lire aussi : "Grandir au Canada m’a fait voir les choses différemment de certains Croates" : comment Niko Sigur, joueur de Toulouse, s'est construit entre ses deux pays

"Notre style de jeu est très agressif. Nous travaillons beaucoup sur nos actions offensives. Un bloc bas est difficile à percer, mais pour l’adversaire, ça peut être difficile de maintenir le même niveau d’exigence face à nous, quand on est constamment en train de basculer le jeu, de piéger l’adversaire avec de faux changements, de jouer des une-deux… Au bout d’un moment, ils s’épuisent un peu" a expliqué Niko Sigur avant de retrouver un public qui espère une performance totale.

#674. Ruins of Limoges city hall a symbol of France divided by national protests

A town in mourning: One week after protests left historic French town hall in ruins

"It is a historical tragedy for France, not just Limoges".

Just six months into his mayoral term, it is hard to imagine Guillaume GuÃ©rin having a more momentous week.

We talk next to what became the defining image of last week's nationwide protests: the still impressive, yet fragile exterior of his town's 19th-Century town hall, charred from a fire.

The sight of its wooden clock tower collapsing into the flames drew widespread shock and anger, and GuÃ©rin, who was in tears when he first saw the scale of the damage this week, believes the reaction is "legitimate and completely understandable".

Watch: Moment historic French town hall spire collapses in flames amid protests

Limoges city hall was set on fire last weekend with its wooden clock tower collapsing on Saturday

What is apparent from the array of flowers and sombre onlookers gathered at the hall's entrance, is that this is a town mourning the loss, or at the least the harm inflicted on its most iconic and, frankly, most beautiful building.

GuÃ©rin blames the damage on the French hard left, "supported by rioters". Two men have been arrested, a 66-year-old, as well as another suspect who is 34. Prosecutors say they have links to "radical-left networks".

Limoges' conservative mayor claims he has received a message of support from US Vice President JD Vance, but not Emmanual Macron, his own, outgoing president.

"What happened here will have an influence on the upcoming presidential election. This country is not doing well at all," he says.

Two men have been arrested in connection with the fire. Prosecutors say they have links to "radical-left networks"

For weeks, hundreds of thousands of people, mostly young, have engaged in protests that have only increased in size and scope. What started off as a demonstration over the poor state of high schools has expanded to a general frustration, even anger, over how challenging and expensive life has become.

In the backdrop is a daunting fiscal deficit, one of the biggest in Europe, and political candidates from across the spectrum claiming to have the answers ahead of presidential elections in six months' time.

In the middle is a centrist government, which is short on solutions, a majority in the National Assembly and time. Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu visited Limoges on Friday evening.

Officials have banned demonstrations in various cities and promised to boost police numbers over the weekend to avoid a repeat of the rioting. That includes in Limoges, where overnight curfews have been announced, along with a limit on gatherings to 10 people in the centre.

Proud as the French are of their politics being rooted in street demonstrations, many in Limoges felt the town hall's destruction went far beyond the parameters of reasonable protest. But not everyone.

Whether the destruction of Limoges town hall changes the course and tone of an increasingly polarised political debate depends on who you ask.

Jade, a 19-year-old medical student, says she has to get by on â¬300 per month and is frustrated by French politics

"Of course it was really sad, it's a symbol of the republic, but what is more important: a town hall or people living in poverty?" asks Alexander, 24.

It is student night at the Lord John pub, and Alexander is one of several wearing a faluche, a colourful, traditional French student beret. Many chatting under the mist from their vapes took part in the demonstrations last weekend.

I ask Alexander whether the widespread looting and fires seen last weekend, with â¬500,000 (Â£420,000) of reported damage in Limoges, helped his argument?

"For some people it's a catastrophe and some things are not acceptable," he admits.

Jade, a 19-year-old, medical student, has a similar opinion: "I think burning the town hall is sad, but it's not the saddest part of the protests."

She complains of having to live on â¬300 per month.

"I feel we are not respected as young adults."

Their views on the town hall's fate are not replicated in Limoges' imposing market halls, where neat, narrow timbers sitting upon studded steel girders have been painted a duck-egg blue, using the same engineering approach as the Eiffel Tower.

This has been a "week of chaos" that 63-year-old Jean Roger Faucher would like to forget.

In a region renowned for producing beef, his family has run his fishmonger stall here for more than a century.

"It left us stunned," he says. "I got married in the town hall, so it had an unimaginable effect on us."

Jean Roger Faucher got married in Limoges town hall. He says he cannot accept protests when they put people's lives at risk

Asked whether he had sympathy for the protesters, Faucher said it was more complicated than that.

"On one side you have people with grievances you can understand, but from the moment there is vandalism and the lives of local residents are put at risk, then we can't accept it," he adds.

Among those tending to their iced displays of fresh produce or quietly sipping a steaming coffee, there is a desire for the temperature of the demonstrations to decrease.

"Of course, life is expensive!' says Pascale Vuylsteke, 59. "Life isn't all a calm river, it's complicated, but we grit our teeth and we work," she tells me leaning over shelves of butchered pork.

Pascale says she works 100 hours a week and struggles to understand why so many others have taken to the streets so easily.

Limoges has found itself at the heart of social action before. In the 19th Century, around the time the town hall was built, the development of its industries, notably in porcelain, led to it becoming a major centre for the French labour movement.

In 2026, the town sits centre-stage once more in a political rupture, although there is a broad hope that the loss of a prominent piece of its history will steer the demonstrations away from destruction and back to debate.

With France's political polarisation set to continue and further protests planned, it is a scenario far from assured.

#675. AI-assisted dying? Doris Dörrie's new film addresses prospect of care robots

While the world debates the dangers of artificial intelligence, filmmaker Doris Dörrie explores how humanoid robots could change the way we deal with aging, caregiving and how people choose to die.

Hamburg in the near future: Instead of human drivers, robots deliver parcels. In cafes, robots roll between the tables, serving diners. On the streets, one encounters humanoid robots walking dogs — or the other way around, people taking their robot dogs for a walk.

This is the setting of Doris Dörrie's new film, "Frau Winkler verlässt das Haus" ("Mrs. Winkler Leaves the House"). At the core of the plot is an elderly woman who can no longer live on her own after a fall. With her only daughter unable to provide permanent care, the solution seems simple enough: a care robot with a built-in EOL program, or "End of Life" mode. This robot not only assists with everyday life but can also provide assisted dying under certain conditions, namely when the person explicitly wishes to end their life and meets the relevant medical criteria.

Dörrie's film tackles several major social issues with remarkable lightness. These include the challenges facing aging societies such as Germany, Japan and China, the question of dying on one's own terms and a mother-daughter relationship that raises questions of guilt and responsibility. Even though the story is set in Germany, such issues resonate globally.

"I write about what personally moves and interests me," Dörrie told DW.

One of the best-known contemporary German film directors, Dörrie achieved her breakthrough in 1985 with the comedy "Men…" She gained further international recognition with films such as 2008's "Cherry Blossoms" and "Greetings from Fukushima" (2016).

Assisted suicide is one of the most complex ethical questions of our time. Laws vary around the world. Though some countries permit active euthanasia under certain conditions, others prohibit and criminalize all forms of assisted dying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In her film, Dörrie asks what happens when artificial intelligence begins calculating the cost of caring for an elderly person and weighing whether that cost is still "worth" bearing for society.

The underlying idea isn't new, Dörrie said, pointing to the Japanese legend of Narayama, which is also mentioned in the film. According to the legend, the eldest children were responsible for taking their ageing parents to a mountain and leaving them there to die because there was not enough food for everyone. "And that's also the debate we are currently facing to a certain extent: Can we really afford to let older people live longer and longer?"

In Dörrie's film, elderly people are allowed to make their own decisions once they reach a certain state of health — but they can't change their minds afterwards. Yet what does it really mean to make a decision freely? "It's a tricky situation," says Dörrie, because the question is to what extent one is also pressured into making this decision, "not only because it makes more economic sense, but also because one is no longer a burden on one's loved ones — in this case, one's daughter..."

The film often raises these questions indirectly and with plenty of dark humor. At one point, a care adviser presents the EOL feature to Mrs. Winkler as an attractive and, above all, straightforward additional option, making it sound as though there would be nothing more for her to worry about.

Dörrie is not interested in demonizing AI in her film — quite the opposite. In the film, the care robot, which Mrs. Winkler names Pavlovich, helps the elderly woman rediscover some of her zest for life and get out of the house.

"When you travel through Germany, you see small houses everywhere, and statistics show that an elderly person lives alone in every other house," Dörrie said. "If AI can help in these circumstances, why not use it?" She said she sought to explore this ambiguity in her film. Dividing things into black and white would neither be interesting nor, in her view, accurate.

Dörrie and her crew were surprised during filming by how quickly people can develop emotional bonds with robots. She attributes this to the human brain. "We regard anything that moves and speaks as a living being. We can't help it," she explains. And that is precisely what we need to pay attention to when interacting with AI, Dörrie says. "How often are we truly aware that we are talking to a machine rather than a living being? These are things we still have to learn."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As AI develops, it seems that the boundaries between humans and machines are becoming increasingly blurred. That is precisely why we need to talk about it, Doris Dörrie says. In her view, things become problematic "when we can no longer distance ourselves from technology and stop forming our own thoughts."

Human beings need to ask who we are and what truly defines us, Dörrie said. "I believe there is a major difference between robots and us, and that is the ability to play. A robot might be able to initiate a game, she explains, "but play itself is something profoundly human because it has no particular meaning or purpose."

Alongside these philosophical questions about what it means to be human, Dörrie makes a clear call for AI regulation. "At some point, we had to discuss nuclear weapons internationally, too. We've talked about all kinds of issues in the past, and we haven't just talked about them — we've also managed to find solutions," she points out.

"And I believe we need to move very quickly on this, too," Dörrie said.

This article was originally written in German.

#676. Israel launches collective punishment campaign in Hebron after two soldiers killed

Benjamin Netanyahu and ministers promise demolitions and forced displacement after deadly gunfight

Israel has launched a campaign of collective punishment against Palestinians in Hebron after gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers and injured three near a checkpoint outside the city.

Benjamin Netanyahu announced a siege on Hebron and neighbouring Halhul and said residents of the gunmen’s home neighbourhoods would all be forced out. He promised mass demolitions of homes.

The first destruction began within hours of the attack, as ministers who had been on the campaign trail ahead of elections on Tuesday rushed to the site of the shooting.

The far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, posted a video of himself in front of a bulldozer as it tore down a Palestinian home near the site of the firefight.

The destruction of a home built without permits aimed to “create deterrence and exact a price”, Smotrich said. There was no claim of a connection between the building’s owners and the attackers.

Soon after the destruction began, Israel’s high court issued a temporary order to stop the demolitions. A human rights lawyer, Mohammed Dahleh, filed an urgent petition on behalf of two factory owners nearby, arguing that the demolition violated international law on collective punishment and Israeli administrative law.

“What we saw today was an attempt to copy the illegal practices used in Gaza, in the heart of the West Bank,” Dahleh said. “They want to wipe out entire areas exactly as they did in Gaza and the refugee camps in the West Bank.”

Michael Sfard, a leading Israeli lawyer, said Smotrich’s video was a “direct admission” that the demolitions were a collective punishment. He noted that deterrence had been used as an excuse for collective punishment since antiquity.

The defence minister, Israel Katz, promised further mass demolitions and forced displacement. He drew an explicit comparison with Gaza and said Hebron would be targeted in the same way as Jenin refugee camp, where nearly 20,000 people have been forced from their homes. Hebron is the largest Palestinian city in the occupied West Bank, with about 250,000 residents.

Katz said: “The Jenin refugee camp model arrives in Hebron. Every clan neighbourhood in Hebron from which the terrorists emerged today will be evacuated of its residents. Just like in Gaza, just like in Lebanon.”

Netanyahu announced that plans had been drawn up for the largest military operation in the West Bank since 1967, when Israeli forces occupied the Palestinian territory and forcibly displaced about 300,000 Palestinians.

No date had been set “but it is on the way”, he said in a statement that also pledged mass forced displacement and demolitions in Hebron and the expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

The attack was launched by two men armed with an assault rifle and a handgun, according to the Israeli military. The men, who were driving a car with Israeli number plates, opened fire after they were stopped by soldiers at a temporary checkpoint outside Hebron. They were killed after a 20-minute gunfight.

An AFP photographer who was on the way to another assignment and witnessed the gun battle saw two Palestinian men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle exchanging fire with Israeli forces.

Prominent Israelis, including a candidate for the far-right Amcha Yisrael party, shared conspiracy theories groundlessly accusing the AFP photographer of links to the gunmen after he documented the Hebron attack.

The Foreign Press Association (FPA) said it was deeply alarmed by claims the photographer had been tipped off, describing them as “dangerous and defamatory”. “He is a longtime professional who was on his way to another assignment and courageously documented what he saw in keeping with his professional duties,” the FPA said in a statement.

The incident came a week after settlers severely injured the photographer Heidi Levine as she documented attacks on Palestinians attempting to harvest olives in the occupied West Bank. Israel has also denied entry to several European journalists and an academic.

Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion, ethnic cleansing and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.

Attacks have intensified further since the start of the annual olive harvest in late September. Israeli settler militants have used violence to stop Palestinians bringing in a crop that is economically and culturally vital to their communities.

Israel holds elections on Tuesday. The current far-right coalition, which backs settlers politically and financially, is seeking to shore up voter support in the face of polls that show it is likely to loose its majority.

Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right national security minister, also travelled to Hebron on Friday and demanded the dismantling of the Palestinian Authority and restrictions on Palestinians’ freedom of movement, which is already heavily curtailed by Israeli controls, checkpoints and roadblocks.

#677. Roma-Künstler Norbert Olah: Zwischen Orban und Aliens

Norbert Olah ist Künstler - und Rom. Lange mied er seine Herkunft als künstlerisches Thema, aus Angst, darauf reduziert zu werden. Dann begann er, genau damit zu arbeiten. Über die Kunst, sich nicht festlegen zu lassen.

Auf der bemalten Leinwand spielt ein Mann gegen einen Roboter Schach. Sein Gesicht aus Ölfarbe glänzt noch feucht. Norbert Olah hat bis in die frühen Morgenstunden in der Bura-Galerie gearbeitet, die er den Sommer über als Atelier nutzt. Nachts, wenn Ungarns Hauptstadt Budapest langsam zur Ruhe findet, kann er sich am besten konzentrieren.

Im hinteren Teil der Galerie hat Olah den Fliesenboden mit Folie und Pappe abgeklebt. Über den Raum verteilt stehen Pinselbecher und Farbtuben, Bleistift-Skizzen und immer wieder Bilder mit der blau-grünen Roma-Fahne.

Norbert Olah ist Künstler - und Rom. Lange klammerte er diesen Teil seiner Identität aus seiner Kunst aus. Nicht, weil seine Herkunft für ihn unwichtig gewesen wäre, sondern aus Angst vor dem Etikett, das damit hätte einhergehen können: das Etikett des "Roma-Künstlers". "Es gibt so viele Vorurteile über Roma-Kultur und Roma-Kunst", sagt Olah. "Die Kunstszene sieht sie als naiv an, als unprofessionell, unbedarft und kitschig."

Doch je älter Olah wurde, desto schwerer ließ sich die eigene Geschichte künstlerisch ausblenden. Erst recht nicht in einem Land, in dem Roma-Sein nicht nur eine Frage der Herkunft, sondern auch der politischen Realität ist.

Als Viktor Orbans Fidesz-Partei 2010 zum ersten Mal mit absoluter Mehrheit die Parlamentswahl gewinnt, hat Olah gerade die Schule abgeschlossen und beginnt sein Studium der Malerei an der Ungarischen Universität der Bildenden Künste in Budapest. In einer Zeit im Leben, in der die Welt eigentlich größer wird, hat er das Gefühl, dass sich immer mehr Grenzen auftun.

Als Künstler und als Rom bekommt Olah die Folgen der politischen Neuausrichtung Ungarns unmittelbar zu spüren: Die Kulturszene wird politisch vereinnahmt und auf Linie gebracht, die Roma werden rhetorisch zur Zielscheibe. Auch durch Orban selbst. Er fällt immer wieder mit rassistischen Bemerkungen über Roma auf.

Für die etwa 700.000 Roma in Ungarn bedeutete die Orban-Herrschaft 16 Jahre zwischen offiziellen Integrationsversprechen und anhaltender Ausgrenzung. Orbans Regierung führte zwar ein staatliches Beschäftigungsprogramm ein, in dem vor allem Roma arbeiten - statt ihnen dabei zu helfen, auf dem Arbeitsmarkt Fuß zu fassen, hält es viele Roma jedoch nur in prekären, schlecht bezahlten Aushilfsjobs fest. Für tatsächliche Veränderungen tat die Regierung wenig. Roma sind in Ungarn bis heute überproportional häufig von Armut und sozialer Ausgrenzung betroffen.

Irgendwann kann und möchte Norbert Olah nicht länger zusehen.

Bei der Off-Biennale in Budapest, der größten unabhängigen Veranstaltung für zeitgenössische Kunst in Ungarn, mauert Olah 2021 gemeinsam mit seinem Vater eine Wand aus Backsteinen, direkt vor dem Eingang des sogenannten Roma-Parlaments, ein Roma-Kulturzentrum mit Kunstsammlung, Archiv, Bibliothek und Veranstaltungen. Das ließ die Orban-Regierung 2016 räumen, angeblich aufgrund von baulichen Sicherheitsbedenken - verbunden mit dem Versprechen, dort ein nationales Roma-Kulturzentrum zu errichten. Das Gebäude steht bis heute leer.

"Die Ängste des Roma-Künstlers" nennt Olah sein Werk, in die Backsteine hat der Künstler Wörter wie "Integration", "Assimilation" und "Segregation" gemeißelt. Einige Wochen später schlägt Olah bei einer Performance mit einem Vorschlaghammer so lange auf sein Kunstwerk ein, bis es in sich zusammenbricht.

In einem Begleittext zu dem Kunstwerk schreibt Olah zum ersten Mal öffentlich über die Ängste, Vorurteile und Erwartungen, denen er als Künstler mit Roma-Wurzeln begegnet. Es ist ein Text voller Fragen. Sollte sich die Kunst eines Roma-Künstlers um Roma-bezogene Themen drehen? Was hat Herkunft mit Ästhetik zu tun? Würde man einen Künstler mit Roma-Wurzeln nur anfragen, wenn ein Roma-Künstler gesucht - oder auch, wenn ein ungarischer Künstler gebraucht werde?

"Natürlich suchen wir alle immer nach Antworten. Aber manchmal ist es interessanter, die Frage selbst zu betrachten", sagt Olah und zupft ein Stück Kreppklebeband vom Boden. "Wenn sie sich unangenehm anfühlt, ist sie eine gute Frage."

So erschafft Olah ein neues Etikett für Roma-Künstler - abseits aller äußeren Zuschreibungen. Die 2021 von Roma-Aktivisten ins Leben gerufene Bura-Galerie im 8. Budapester Bezirk wird unter seiner künstlerischen Leitung zu einem Ort dafür, zu einer Plattform für zeitgenössische Roma-Kunst. "Wir bitten nicht um Akzeptanz in der Kunstszene. Wir öffnen die Tür und bitten andere herein", sagt Olah.

Identität und Ausgrenzung, Macht und Machtmissbrauch - diese Themen werden für Olah zentral für sein künstlerisches Schaffen. An Inspiration wird es ihm während der Orban-Jahre nicht fehlen.

Obwohl Fidesz kaum Politik für die Roma machte, konnte die Partei von Viktor Orban bei Wahlen lange auf die Stimme der Minderheit zählen - etwa, weil Lokalpolitiker über die kommunalen Beschäftigungsprogramme die Möglichkeit hatten, Druck auf sozial schwächere Wähler auszuüben. Außerdem wurden immer wieder Fälle von Stimmenkauf dokumentiert. Tatsächlich war Fidesz sich so sicher, dass ein Großteil der Roma weiterhin für sie stimmen würde, dass sie den immer noch weit verbreiteten Antiziganismus in der Gesellschaft offen schürte.

So sprach sich kurz vor der Wahl im April 2026 der damals noch amtierende Fidesz-Verkehrsminister Janos Lazar öffentlich gegen Arbeitsmigration aus mit dem Hinweis, dass es noch "interne Reserven" wie die Roma gebe, die die "vollgeschissenen Toiletten" in den Intercitys reinigen könnten. Auch diese Szene hat Olah künstlerisch aufgegriffen, in einem fingierten Wahlplakat, auf dem ein Mann in Sturmhaube auf einer goldenen Toilette sitzt und eine Klobürste schwenkt, darunter der Schriftzug "Gypsy Criminals for President".

"Gypsy Criminals", das ist der Name des Künstlerkollektivs, das Olah 2024 zusammen mit einem Freund und dessen Zwergpinscher gegründet hat. Der einschlägige Begriff stammt eigentlich aus der ungarischen Kriminalstatistik und wird seit den 2000er Jahren von rechten Politikern verwendet, um Roma pauschal kriminelles Verhalten zu unterstellen. Der Name des Kollektivs ist ironisch gebrochen, wie vieles in Olahs Arbeiten.

Analysen der Roma for Democracy Stiftung zeigen, dass bei der Parlamentswahl im April 2026 viele Roma nicht mehr für Orbans Fidesz stimmten. Der neue Premier Peter Magyar schlug schon im Wahlkampf einen anderen Ton an gegenüber Roma an: Er traf sich mit Vertretern der Minderheit, im Wahlprogramm gab es einen eigenen Abschnitt zur Roma-Chancengleichheit. Vier der neuen Abgeordneten der Tisza-Partei im Parlament sind Roma, einer von ihnen wurde zum stellvertretenden Parlamentspräsidenten gewählt.

Seit der Wahl herrscht so etwas wie vorsichtiger Optimismus, dass sich nun tatsächlich etwas an der prekären Situation vieler Roma im Land ändern könnte. Gleichzeitig hat sich in den vier Monaten seit der Wahl außer dem Tonfall gegenüber der Minderheit noch nichts Grundlegendes geändert. "Ich sehe aktuell vor allem viele symbolische Gesten", sagt Olah.

Während einige seiner Freunde aus der eher liberalen Kunstszene langsam ungeduldig würden, weil sie sich eine deutlich liberalere Politik von Magyar wünschen, bleibt Olah Realist: "Er ist ein konservativer Politiker. Wir haben ihn gewählt, damit er das Orban-System abschafft. Mehr hat er nicht versprochen." Die Wahl im April böte aber die Chance für einen politischen Neuanfang. "Ich denke, wir werden langfristig wieder in einer normalen Gesellschaft leben, die von einer normalen Regierung geführt wird, die manches gut machen wird und anderes nicht so gut. Als Künstler wird es meine Aufgabe sein, das zu kritisieren", sagt er.

Auch in seinen Werken beschäftigt sich Olah mit der Zukunft. Die ersten Bilder für sein nächstes Projekt hängen bereits im Atelier. Es geht um Roma-Futurismus: ein Roma-Paar beim Mars-Spaziergang, die blau-grüne Roma-Fahne auf dem Mond, ein schwereloser Astronaut mit einer traditionellen Cegled-Kanne, wie sie Roma-Musiker verwenden, außerdem ist eine zwei Meter große Raumstation in Form des Roma-Speichenrads geplant.

Die Raumfahrt ist für Olah auch eine Metapher für sozialen Aufstieg - für den Wunsch von Menschen und Gemeinschaften, die Grenzen zu überwinden, die ihnen Herkunft, Armut oder das Leben als Minderheit setzen. Was wäre, fragt er, wenn man eine Gesellschaft noch einmal von vorn denken könnte? Würden Aliens Roma vorurteilsfrei begegnen? Was bleibt von einer Identität, wenn sich alles an ihr wandelt?

Olah zerrupft das Klebeband zwischen den Fingern. Wieder so viele Fragen ohne Antwort. Aber genau das macht sie ja so interessant.

#679. ‘Outrageously good’: the best (and worst) supermarket ready-made custard, tasted and rated

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Which supermarket pots are ambrosial heaven and which are a gummy disaster?

It was only when I sat down to taste 10 custards that I realised this was a dangerous test to judge on my own. I tried a range of ready-made offerings, from cans to cartons to tubs of fresh custard from the supermarket chiller section, some of which I found hard not to drink by the pint.

I analysed each custard for aroma, texture and taste, and awarded extra points for minimal processing and the use of free-range eggs; I deducted points for the inclusion of palm oil, modified maize starches and colourings, all of which are often used to replace the colour, fat and thickening ability of eggs. It was, however, the long-life cartons that most provoked nostalgic memories of bananas and custard as a child.

My main take-home is that cans and cartons are great for when you need a quick dessert, but if you want the real thing – a proper crème anglaise made with hot, vanilla-infused cream and milk, egg yolks and sugar – go for the fresh stuff and check the label for additives.

An outrageously good, medium-thick, pale cream-coloured custard made with West Country milk and cream. Seductively sweet (11.9% total sugar), and thickened with tapioca starch and free-range eggs.

A medium-thick, pale cream-coloured custard made with Jersey and Guernsey cows’ milk and British cream. Super-sweet (12.1%), and thickened with tapioca starch, cornflour and free-range eggs.

Very thick, pale yellow and velvety-smooth, but a touch gloopy and lacking in substance. Egg-free, with buttermilk and vanilla extract, thickened with “sustainable” palm oil and modified starches. Contains colours (plain caramel and carotene) and pretty sweet (11.1%), too.

A thick, pale custard with an even speckling of vanilla. Made with British dairy, beautifully sweet (10.3%) and thickened with maize starch, tapioca starch and carob gum stabiliser, which makes it a touch slimy. Contains eggs, but no welfare data specified.

A very thick, pale cream-coloured custard speckled generously with vanilla seeds. Made with British milk and not too sweet (8.4%), it’s thickened with tapioca starch, cornflour and indoor-reared eggs.

Get the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.

Very thick and yellow, this is smooth, light, yet luxurious and creamy, and dotted with vanilla. Pretty sweet (10.8%), thickened with free-range eggs and tapioca starch, and contains flavouring.

An addictive, very creamy, pale custard. Quite sweet (11%), but a clean dairy and egg flavour and a thin, saucy consistency thickened with tapioca starch, cornflour and free-range eggs. Minimally processed ingredients.

Thick, bright yellow and super-smooth, this is egg-free, so not actually custard as such, but rather an OK imitation. Perfectly sweet (9.6%), thickened with modified maize starch, buttermilk and whey powders, and contains palm oil and flavouring. Insanely cheap, though.

Thin and canary-yellow, and its sweet aroma smells of raw cornflour; it tastes of it, too, as well as being relatively sweet (10.4%). Another egg-free custard, this one is made with modified maize starch, palm oil and flavourings.

Smooth, thin, pale yellow and on the sweet side (11%), this egg-free custard is instead made with reconstituted skimmed milk and buttermilk, hence its slightly powdery texture. Contains palm oil and colouring (carotene).

#680. Suspect fired more than 800 rounds as cops arrived at his Texas home leaving one deputy dead

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Deputy Ahmed 'Adam' Sherifi is survived by a wife and a newborn child

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

I would like to be emailed about offers, events and updates from The Independent. Read our Privacy notice

A suspect fired more than 800 rounds of ammunition at Texas police when they arrived at his home leaving one officer dead.

The suspect, who was later found dead from a gunshot wound, also injured another cop in the confrontation.

On Tuesday, a Van Zandt County Sheriff’s deputy and members of the Canton police went to the home of 42-year-old Mi Van Nguyen to serve two felony arrest warrants, according to NBC 5.

Around 10:20 p.m., Nguyen opened fire from inside the home using a semiautomatic rifle, unleashing more than 800 rounds at authorities, according to the report. Sheriff’s Deputy Ahmed 'Adam' Sherifi was killed and Canton police officer Chris Watson was injured.

“Think about that. 800 rounds shot at the men and women whose only purpose was to carry out their duties to protect this community,” Sheriff Kevin Bridger said at a Friday press conference, according to NBC 5. “This was not simply an attack on law enforcement. It was an attack on the peace and security that every family in Van Zandt County, in all counties, deserve."

Nguyen was later found dead inside the home from a gunshot wound, NBC 5 reported. The Texas Rangers are now investigating the incident.

He was wanted on two felony charges for aggravated assault with a deadly weapon and aggravated assault on a peace officer, authorities said. No additional motive for firing at police Tuesday was released during the Friday press conference.

Bridger described the attack on cops as “pure evil.”

“Where one man chose violence, Adam chose a life of service,” Bridger said. “Where one man brought fear and destruction, Adam took an oath and gave his life. Providing the safety for our community.”

Sherifi is survived by a wife and a newborn and both were near the sheriff during the press conference.

“Adam represents everything that makes our community strong. He represents duty, bravery and service,” Bridger said. “Adam was a young officer with his whole life ahead of him. He was a husband. He was a father, and he was a son. A friend to all of us and a beloved member of our law enforcement family.”

Funeral services for Sherifi are expected to be held next week.

During the shooting, fellow deputy Brandon Fonteneau provided lifesaving care to Watson, Bridger stated. He fired at the suspect to protect the wounded officers and allow for other personnel to take Watson to safety. Watson continues to recover in the hospital.

“In the middle of the extraordinary, dangerous situation. Brandon did what he had been trained to do, and that saved lives and protect the community,” Bridger said. “His courage and quick decision helped save lives. And I want Brandon to know how proud I am of him, how grateful to this office and this community for what he did.”

#682. Are California voters about to impose 'world's first' tax on billionaires?

Few places on the planet have as many ultra-wealthy residents as California, a US state known for glamour, coastal mega-mansions, and being home to the rich and famous.

Now voters are about to decide whether the mega-rich among them - including media mogul Oprah Winfrey, Meta head Mark Zuckerberg, Skims cofounder and reality television star Kim Kardashian, and filmmaker George Lucas - should hand over billions of dollars to pay for improvements to healthcare.

Proposition 40 is aimed at levying a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of all of California's billionaires.

There are a little more than 200 such individuals in the state - but that hasn't stopped the measure from dividing leaders and causing some of its ultra-wealthy residents to flee. One billionaire businessman says he's brought jobs to California, but the proposition made him feel "a little bit like I wasn't wanted".

But the vote is also offering regular residents a voice on an issue that has roiled politics for decades.

"I believe this is the first billionaire tax - meaning a wealth tax that is targeting a very extreme percentile of the wealth distribution," says Francesco Trebbi, a public policy professor at the University of California, Berkeley. He noted the measure's historic nature and how it could help even out California's wealth gap.

The state has the largest economy in the country and boasts the fourth largest global economy, bigger than India and the UK. And it is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the world. But it also has the largest share of homeless people in the nation and one of the highest wealth gaps.

Those who back the measure have argued it helps ensure that the ultra-wealthy are contributing their fair share and will help backfill gaps in the state's budget. The move aims to raise $100bn (Â£75bn) to make up for federal funding cuts to the state's health-care system.

Suzanne Jimenez, chief of staff for Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, which helped lead the charge for the initiative, says the measure is a "short-term solution" for massive federal funding cuts coming to California as a result of US President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill.

"If we do nothing, we're going to see a collapse of our healthcare system, while we figure out a longer-term solution to fund our healthcare," she tells the BBC.

While the ballot measure has many supporters - including some billionaires like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang - it has faced fierce opposition from a variety of figures, from billionaires to the state's liberal governor.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin has given more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax, the Los Angeles Times reports, external.

California Governor Gavin Newsom, whose tenure is coming to an end, is perhaps the most notable political leader opposing it. He has voiced concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue.

A September poll, external from the Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times found the proposition has not clearly won over a majority of voters, with 45% of likely voters in favour of the tax, 42% opposed and 13% undecided.

The statewide ballot measure would need to be approved by a majority of residents.

California is not the first place to toy with the idea of taxing the rich. Also on the West Coast, voters in US state of Washington are considering whether to accept or reject a "millionaires tax" - a 9.9% tax on income over $1m a year.

While wealth taxes were once a fairly common form of taxation in Europe, they have rapidly fallen out of favour and now only exist in three European countries â Spain, Norway and Switzerland, says Dr Kristian Niemietz, head of political economy at the Institute of Economic Affairs.

Niemietz believes wealth taxes are "more trouble than they are worth" because they cause administrative issues, suppress investment, lead to capital flight and, in the end, do not raise much revenue.

In the case of Norway, a local news organisation found that an increase in the wealth tax led to more super wealthy people leaving the country in 2022, external than in the preceding 13 years combined. A study on Switzerland, external found that a 0.1 percentage point increase in a wealth tax reduced taxable wealth by 3.5%.

IN DEPTH: The real reasons there are so few young US politicians

EXPLORE: How the US midterms will be won and lost

VERIFY: How the US economy is really doing under Trump

NEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inbox

The California measure, if approved, would apply retroactively to those with a net worth of at least $1bn who resided in California as of 1 January 2026. At least six of the state's 200 plus billionaires have reportedly left California ahead of that deadline to avoid the tax.

They include Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin, venture capitalist Peter Thiel, former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick and Hankey Group founder Don Hankey.

Hankey, a Los Angeles billionaire who has lived in California all his life, told Forbes he left for the state of Nevada as a result of the proposed wealth tax.

"I think we've created a lot of jobs in California. We have a few thousand people working for us and we have a profit sharing plan. And I have to leave the state," he said, adding that the measure made him feel like he wasn't "wanted" in the state.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin has reportedly given more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax

Meta chief executive Mark Zuckerberg told the company's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California over the proposed tax.

To prevent him from leaving the state - where the company is headquartered - Meta agreed to a new stock deal that gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn, even more shares in the company to make up for the billions he would lose if the measure passes in November. Estimates say he could owe as much as $12.5bn.

DoorDash cofounder Andy Fang, who has an estimated net worth of $1.6bn, has called the measure "stupid" and wrote on X that "proposals like this make it irresponsible for me not to plan leaving the state".

Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax

Meanwhile, businessman Tom Steyer, who ran an unsuccessful bid for California governor earlier this year, is one of the few billionaires who has said, external he would vote in favour of the tax. Steyer said that although he believed the way the measure was written was "problematic", it was necessary to protect vulnerable Californians.

Huang, too, has expressed support of paying the levy.

"I don't mind paying taxes. The more you make, the more taxes you pay. I'm okay with that," the Nvidia chief said in an interview with the BBC's US partner CBS. "I am the ultimate American Dream."

Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, a vocal champion against income inequality, has campaigned in support of Prop 40.

While at a Los Angeles rally, Sanders said billionaires "believe, like the monarchs of the 19th Century, that they have a God-given right to rule".

"They have all the wealth, they got all the power, and who the hell do you think you are challenging them? Well, I think on November 3 they're going to learn a very powerful lesson."

US Senator Bernie Sanders speaks at the "Ballots Over Billionaires" rally on 5 October in Los Angeles.

Income inequality in the US is at some of its highest levels, external in over three decades, with the top 1% of households owning nearly 32% of all US wealth in the third quarter of 2025. It is also near historic highs in California.

Economic inequality is a concern among most Californians, with 72% believing that the gap between the rich and poor is widening and a similar share holding that state government should do more to reduce the gap, according to a statewide survey, external from the Public Policy Institute of California.

Trebbi says it is an "anti-elite, anti-system sentiment" driving the policy.

"This is really not about Prop 40," he says, but rather about trying to "re-balance the scale a little bit".

Correction 24 October: An earlier version of this article contained a graphic which incorrectly said median income in California was $288,000. This has been corrected to median household net worth.

#683. REPLAY. Guerre en Ukraine : un drone d'origine inconnue retrouvé en Lettonie après s'être écrasé sur le territoire

l'essentiel Retrouvez dans ce replay les informations du samedi 24 octobre concernant la guerre en Ukraine.

L'armée lettone annonce avoir retrouvé ce samedi un drone écrasé dans la paroisse de Liepna, dans la région d'Aluksne. L'engin "a vraisemblablement pénétré l'espace aérien letton le 18 octobre". Une enquête a été ouverte pour déterminer les circonstances de l'incident. Aucun blessé ni dégât matériel n'a été signalé, précise l'armée sur X.

Informācija papildināta 24. oktobra plkst. 19.50Informējam, ka Zemessardzes 2. Vidzemes brigādes 54. kaujas atbalsta bataljona Sprādzienbīstamu priekšmetu iznīcināšanas rotas karavīri ir pabeiguši atrastā drona atlūzu izņemšanu no incidenta vietas, tādējādi noslēdzot darbu… https://t.co/X7gGTkA5k3

La Russie a menacé samedi 24 octobre de riposter à l'expulsion d'un de ses diplomates par la Moldavie. Cette décision fait suite à l'incursion présumée d'un drone russe dans l'espace aérien moldave, qui se serait écrasé près d'habitations et d'une installation énergétique, selon la présidente Maia Sandu.

La porte-parole de la diplomatie russe, Maria Zakharova, a dénoncé un "prétexte sans fondement", affirmant que l'origine russe de l'appareil n'avait "pas été prouvée". Elle a assuré que ces "actions hostiles" ne resteraient pas sans une "réponse ferme et adéquate" de Moscou.

La Maison-Blanche a annoncé ce 24 octobre une trêve dans la ville ukrainienne d'Oleskhy, occupée par la Russie depuis les premiers jours de la guerre. Cette trêve aurait été obtenue par Melania Trump elle-même, selon la présidence des États-Unis. Le cessez-le-feu entrera en vigueur le 29 octobre prochain afin d'approvisionner la localité en médicaments et en denrées alimentaires. 👉 Notre article ici

Au moins trois personnes ont été tuées et une autre grièvement blessée samedi dans une frappe ukrainienne dans la partie contrôlée par la Russie de la région de Kharkiv, dans le nord-est de l'Ukraine, ont annoncé les autorités russes."Trois civils ont trouvé la mort et une femme a été grièvement blessée à la suite d'une frappe d'un drone ukrainien sur une voiture dans le village de Pisky, dans la région de Kharkiv", a indiqué sur Telegram le gouverneur local installé par Moscou, Vitali Gantchev.

L'Ukraine a indiqué samedi avoir de nouveau une "connexion stable" au système Starlink de SpaceX, crucial pour son armée, après plusieurs jours de bridage de sa vitesse sur fond de tensions avec Washington. "Les systèmes de surveillance du ministère de la Défense enregistrent une reprise de la vitesse de Starlink/Starshield. Nous enregistrons une vitesse supérieure à 400 km/h, la connexion est stable", a indiqué le ministre ukrainien de la Défense Ievguén Khmara dans un communiqué.

Le ministère de la Défense russe a assuré avoir intercepté plus de 600 drones ukrainiens la nuit dernière, d'après Le Monde .

Steve Witkoff, émissaire de Donald Trump, a suscité une vive polémique mercredi 21 octobre à Saint-Pétersbourg en qualifiant Vladimir Poutine d'"humaniste". Ses propos, tenus lors d'une rencontre avec le président russe, ont été vivement critiqués, notamment par des responsables ukrainiens et des sénateurs américains. 👉 Notre article ici

L'armée ukrainienne a indiqué qu'elle observerait également à partir de mardi une trêve à Olechky, une ville sous occupation russe dans la région de Kherson, afin d'y assurer la tenue d'une opération humanitaire."Afin de mener une opération humanitaire dans la ville d’Olechky, située dans la région de Kherson et temporairement occupée, l'Ukraine instaure un cessez-le-feu dans une zone délimitée, à compter du 27 octobre à 3 heures, heure de Kiev", a indiqué vendredi l'état-major ukrainien dans un communiqué.

Bienvenue dans ce direct consacré à la guerre en Ukraine.

L'Ukraine mène une guerre existentielle, ce qui renforce sa détermination. Parmi les précédents où le plus faible l'a emporté : le Japon en 1905, la Pologne en 1920, la Finlande en 1940, l'Afghanistan dans les années 1980. Poutine affirme que ses forces progressent sur tout le front, mais elles n'ont réalisé pratiquement aucun gain net en 2026, au prix de plus de 40 000 victimes par mois. La culture du mensonge dans l'armée russe (« beaux rapports », cartes de gains fantômes) trompe peut-être Poutine lui-même, et l'Ukraine en tire parti pour piéger des troupes russes. La Russie compte 3,6 fois plus d'habitants, mais ses forces en Ukraine ne dépassent pas les effectifs ukrainiens. Elle a subi plus de 1,5 million de morts et de blessés graves. Le recrutement volontaire s'essouffle (29 250 contrats par mois en 2026, contre 32 500 en 2025), et depuis décembre 2025 les pertes dépassent les engagements. Poutine hésite à ordonner une nouvelle mobilisation forcée par crainte de troubles sociaux, d'autant que les frappes ukrainiennes sur l'énergie provoquent des pénuries de carburant. Les bombardements stratégiques ne suffiront probablement pas. La Russie a pris un avantage temporaire dans le ciel (drones à réaction, pénurie de missiles Patriot), mais l'Ukraine s'adapte, et aucune campagne de ce type n'a jamais forcé un pays à capituler.

Des agitations médiatiques quotidiennement . Cela n'empêche nullement les bombardements Russes sur l'Ukraine. Les sanctions économiques ? La Russie les contourne. Elle a trouvé d?autres partenaires que les Européens. ( Chine, Inde, Afrique du Sud , Corée du Nord, Iran et même les pays du golfe. Des pays de l'UE continuent sous le manteau à commercer avec la Russie, Les magouilles existent dans tous les pays, après 2017 peut être qu il y en un qui va goûter du cachot comme Sarko. Et pour lui Versailles et ses fastes , ce sera terminé. .

Les dirigeants d'une entreprise énergétique américaine ont démissionné alors que la famille Trump est prise en flagrant délit d'accélérer secrètement le transfert de 25 milliards de dollars d'un géant énergétique russe sanctionné, en échange de l'autorisation donnée aux Russes d'obtenir un projet de gaz naturel en Alaska. Selon des enquêtes menées par The New York Times et Financial Times, la Novatek russe aurait dissimulé son implication financière dans le projet américain par le biais d'un intermédiaire lié aux Émirats arabes unis. Gentry Beach, un allié de longue date de Trump et proche ami de Donald Trump Jr., a signé un accord avec Novatek pour développer le gaz naturel en Alaska. Reuters a documenté cet arrangement en février. Pendant ce temps, Vladimir Poutine a discuté de cette coopération sur le projet énergétique en Alaska avec les représentants de Trump, Steve Witkoff et Jared Kushner, lors de négociations impliquant la Russie et l'Ukraine.

La controverse s'est approfondie lorsque le PDG de Polar Train LNG, Joel Riddle, a exprimé des inquiétudes concernant un financement russe dissimulé et de possibles violations de sanctions. Il a quitté l'entreprise en septembre, suivi par d'autres hauts dirigeants. Financial Times a également décrit des discussions sur un éventuel arrangement dans lequel Novatek fournirait une technologie pour le projet en Alaska en échange d'un allègement des sanctions bénéficiant à son développement Arctic LNG 2 en Sibérie. Selon The New York Times, Riddle et deux autres dirigeants partants ont averti l'administration Trump au sujet du financement russe et ont exhorté les responsables à enquêter. La Maison Blanche affirme que le projet n'a été mentionné que brièvement et qu'aucune discussion détaillée n'a eu lieu. Il n'existe aucune preuve établie que Kushner ou Witkoff étaient au courant du financement prétendument dissimulé. Polar Train LNG nie toute faute. La question centrale est de savoir comment une entreprise énergétique russe sanctionnée s'est impliquée dans un important projet énergétique américain alors que Poutine discutait de coopération économique potentielle avec les représentants deTrump et qu'un associé de longue date de la famille Trump poursuivait un accord séparé avec la même entreprise russe. Sources: deux articles du New York Times et du Financial Times
